articles.article_title: Normet’s new centre in Finland to drive underground mining technology
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: The centre is focused on fostering advancements in autonomy, robotics, software development and other technologies.
articles.content:
Normet has opened a new technology centre in Pirkkala, Finland, to expedite the future of underground mining.
The facility is intended to bolster research, development and testing capabilities for technologies aimed at improving safety, productivity and sustainability in underground mining operations.
The new centre is focused on fostering advancements in autonomy, robotics, software development and other digital technologies.
As mining operations extend to deeper levels and face more challenging conditions, these technologies become crucial in enabling remote and autonomous functionalities that can minimise human exposure to hazardous environments.
Normet conducts more than 95% of its business outside Finland and has a presence in roughly 50 locations across 30 countries.
Normet president and CEO Ed Santamaria said: "Today is an important milestone for Normet. This investment expands our technology development and testing capabilities and reinforces our commitment to staying at the forefront of innovation in underground mining.
"Customer demand for advanced mining technologies continues to grow, and this centre will help us accelerate the development of solutions that improve safety, productivity and sustainability underground."
The company manufactures mining equipment in Chile, Finland and India. Demand for its products is supported by global trends such as the green transition, urbanisation and increased investment in critical minerals.
The facility will also serve as a venue for customer demonstrations, highlighting autonomous functions, tele-remote operation and battery electric equipment.
Pirkkala was chosen for its location within a prominent ecosystem known for electrified mobile work machines and mining technology.
Santamaria further added: "We have already hired more than 50 people in Finland this year to support our growth, particularly in manufacturing, and we expect this new centre to create additional high-value technology roles in the future."
In April 2025, Normet secured a contract to provide an ancillary underground equipment fleet for South32's Hermosa project, located in a mining district in the Patagonia Mountains of southern Arizona, US.
"Normet's new centre in Finland to drive underground mining technology" was originally created and published by Mining Technology, a GlobalData owned brand.

articles.content: Arn Net reports that ConnectWise is focusing on rebuilding trust and investing in new technologies following a cyberattack believed to be carried out by a nation-state actor. CEO Manny Rivelo emphasized the importance of transparency in the aftermath of the breach, which affected a small number of customers using its ScreenConnect solution.ConnectWise experienced a security incident in the past year, suspected to be linked to a sophisticated nation-state actor targeting its ScreenConnect solution. While the breach impacted a limited customer base, its effects were felt globally by partners. CEO Manny Rivelo stated that transparency and clear communication were paramount in addressing the situation, acknowledging that no system is entirely immune to zero-day attacks.The company has since focused on mitigating vulnerabilities within its environment to prevent similar incidents from having a significant impact. This includes enhancing security through governance, systems, and controls, and adjusting product functionalities to improve safety, even if it means adding extra steps for users. ConnectWise is also investing in technology stack consolidation, agentic functionality, and establishing local data centers and hiring new employees in the Australia and New Zealand region to support its partners.Source: Arn Net

articles.summary: UNMC medical illustrator combines art and technology to improve patient care
articles.content:
Technology is taking off, but medical care starts with art
UNMC medical illustrator combines art and technology to improve patient care
Bill Glass, a medical illustrator at UNMC, uses his artistic skills and technology to enhance medical education and make procedures safer.
Article:
Doctors and researchers at the University of Nebraska Medical Center (UNMC) are using technology and art to advance medical care.
Bill Glass, a medical illustrator at UNMC, creates detailed illustrations and animations of human anatomy to focus attention on critical information. "We know what to leave in and what to take out to focus your eye on the important information," Glass said.
Glass has been an artist for decades, specializing in drawing human anatomy. "This would probably take me 3 to 4 hours, this is a skull," he said, describing his process.
Ten years ago, Glass joined UNMC, recognizing the potential of technology and innovative teaching methods to transform medical care. "A faculty can request a project, and we have a committee that meets and prioritizes which projects we will pursue," he said.
Glass creates animations tailored for professors to use in class and simulations of surgeries to ensure doctors are aligned in their approach. "I can adjust what colors I assign to the different levels of gray so I can visualize different pieces of the anatomy," he said.
His work makes learning easier and medical procedures safer. "Those are some of the most rewarding parts of our job, to see the direct impact," Glass said.
Despite the rapid advancements in technology, Glass emphasized that it all starts with art.

articles.article_title: TCU Lab to Test, Research Wearable Technology Across Industries
articles.heading: TCU Lab to Test, Research Wearable Technology Across Industries
articles.summary: Texas Christian University's Department of Fashion Merchandising launched the Athlete Equipment and Materials Design Lab, a new research and testing space focused on the products people depend on in extreme and demanding environments.
articles.content:
TCU Lab to Test, Research Wearable Technology Across Industries
The clothes we wear do more than complete a look. They help control body temperature, manage sweat, protect the skin and support how people move, work and perform every day.
This fall, Texas Christian University’s Department of Fashion Merchandising launched the Athlete Equipment and Materials Design Lab, a new research and testing space focused on the products people depend on in extreme and demanding environments. Reaching far beyond the College of Fine Arts, the facility will support projects connected to athlete performance, rehabilitation, wearable health technologies, protective equipment and NASA-inspired soft goods research. Future work may also include recovery products, wound care materials, adaptive equipment and smart integrated gear for military personnel, first responders and industrial workers.
“We didn't build an academic research lab,” said Charles Freeman, professor and chair of fashion merchandising and director of research and creative scholarship in the College of Fine Arts. “We built an industry lab. We want students to walk into their first job and recognize the equipment because they've already used it here.”
The work has broad interdisciplinary applications. From athletes training in Texas heat to first responders in protective uniforms, military personnel in extreme conditions and astronauts preparing for space environments, the lab will help answer a practical question: how can the materials closest to the body help people perform better and stay safer?
“People often think of fashion as what they see in stores,” Freeman said. “But clothing does much more than that. It creates the environment around the body. How a garment handles heat sweat, movement and protection affects comfort, recovery, performance and safety.”
Beyond the Runway
Designed as part of TCU's continued investment in research and innovation, the lab
brings industry-level testing capabilities to campus and gives students, faculty and
partners a place to study how apparel, equipment and wearable materials perform in
real conditions.
Inside the lab, researchers will test how materials manage sweat, heat, movement, friction, pressure and exposure to water. The goal is to better understand how the products people wear can support the body in everyday life and in high-stress/high-demand environments. The university recently announced a new certificate and research partnership focusing on textiles and soft-goods engineering.
“How we interact with our clothing throughout the day — whether we're sitting on the couch watching TV, saving lives or traveling to space — matters because clothing helps protect the human body,” Freeman said. “That's really the science of what we do, and it broadens people's perspective of what fashion truly is.”
Built for Collaboration
The lab was designed as a shared space for researchers, students and industry partners
working on problems that connect the body, materials, movement and performance. It reflects
TCU’s continued investment in interdisciplinary research and gives faculty across
campus a new way to test the products and materials used in sports, health, work and
extreme environments.
The facility is already supporting projects with the Roach Institute for Athlete Engineering, which was made possible by a $10 million gift from the Roach Foundation of Fort Worth.
“At the Roach Institute, we’re interested in the entire ecosystem that influences human performance, and what someone is wearing is a major part of that,” said Jim Weinstein, director of the Roach Institute. “This lab gives us the ability to connect what we measure in the human body, movement, heat strain, fatigue and performance, with what is happening in the materials and equipment closest to it. That opens up an entirely new level of research for athletes, first responders, military personnel and others performing in demanding environments.”
Reuben Burch, vice provost for research, said that building a good research enterprise is like establishing departments in an organization. The new lab complements the work at the Roach Institute.
“We brought a new capability to Texas that wasn’t here before, and now it’s at TCU. So, we can expand beyond human performance and into the equipment and materials that all athlete personas will wear. This is the kind of research, invention and creation that people can continue to expect from TCU.”
The new lab is also working with TCU’s engineering, physics and kinesiology programs.
“I’ve been pleasantly surprised at the level of collaboration I've experienced since coming to TCU, said Graci Finco, assistant professor of kinesiology in the Harris College of Nursing & Health Sciences. “Our Limb Loss & Difference Lab has already begun several collaborations with both Charles and the Roach Institute to improve care and performance for people with limb loss and limb difference. I’m excited for what we are building together at TCU with other academic and industry partners.”
Research that Starts with Students
Faculty also anticipate the lab will play a central role in TCU’s new Ph.D. program in advanced soft goods and textile systems launching in 2027 by giving doctoral students access to applied research, product testing and industry-facing projects. It will also expand opportunities for undergraduate research, giving students the chance to work alongside faculty with real-world applications. Students will use the same tools found in industry while contributing to work connected to athlete performance, health, safety, product development and wearable technology.
For Freeman, the investment represents more than a new facility. It reflects the growing role of the College of Fine Arts in TCU’s research mission and the value of giving students access to applied research early in their academic careers.
“Investments like this demonstrate TCU’s commitment to becoming a leading R1 institution,” Freeman said. “Most importantly, they give our students the opportunity to ask big questions, solve real problems and take their ideas all the way to the finish line.”

articles.title: What Happens When the Fire Department's Technology Person Leaves?

articles.article_title: What Happens When the Fire Department's Technology Person Leaves?
articles.heading: What Happens When the Fire Department's Technology Person Leaves?
articles.summary: Highlighting the risks of relying on a single technology expert, Jason Moore advocates for fire departments to plan, build redundancy, and create formalized processes to maintain...
articles.content:
What Happens When the Fire Department's Technology Person Leaves?
Key Takeaways
- Fire departments often depend on individual technology experts, risking knowledge loss and platform access when personnel leave or change roles.
- A well-built system resembles a strong rope with solid anchors, formalized processes, and multiple layers of support like training and feedback loops.
- Implementing documentation, training, and redundancy strategies helps safeguard critical systems and ensures operational continuity.
Looking back over my career, I remember building elaborate spreadsheets, access databases, automated workflow forms, and countless other technology solutions to address a fire department problem. Unfortunately, I also watched nearly every one of those initiatives or systems degrade and revert back to the original state after I left because these were personal proficiencies, not departmental proficiencies.
This is an all-too-common story, and it does not always happen when the department techie leaves. Sometimes it is due to a promotion, change in work, burnout, or even just a change in tech that they do not want to learn. To be fair, departments often do this for multiple aspects of operations, especially in smaller or volunteer fire organizations. There is the radio tinkerer, the computer-aided dispatch guru, the drone pilot, the records management system genius, and/or the social media savant. As technology gains greater acceptance, leaders need to consider if technology should continue to be an alternate duty for a firefighter, a paid position in the department, or something outsourced.
The tech expert accident
Rarely does a department plan to hire people with alternate proficiencies. It is often a happy accident when we discover someone who can weld, do mechanic work, or in this case has technical proficiency. I look back fondly at the times when I would hear my battalion chief yell from his office, “Jaasson!” Everyone in the station knew what it meant, he was having some sort of computer issue and needed help.
I never set out to be the tech expert, I was never paid extra for having skills beyond my core duties, and like most firefighters who are put in a position to help someone, we just do it. Looking back, if I had spent more time teaching and developing others, rather than just being the happy accident, things may have not regressed as much after I left. This unofficial promotion came with no title, no pay, and eventually led to me gaining administrative credentials to nearly every tech system our department had access to. The point is, having an expert is great but having only one expert is dangerous and does not qualify as a plan.
Other duties as assigned
I have rarely read a job description that did not have, "other duties as assigned” as the catch all for the things you will be asked to do that are outside of the core functions. This is becoming more of a liability as regulations, standards, and employee burn-out are hitting our career field hard. You must ask yourself as a fire service leader, is it fair to have a firefighter do everything that others are doing plus try to be system administrators, trainers, troubleshooters, vendor liaisons, data analyst, and help desk attendants? Is it good practice to have single points of failure as these systems go from needed infrastructure to critical components of a modern operation? Does your technical proficiency as a department actually exist or is it one change away from evaporating?
Systems survive when people leave
I am not advocating to abandon internal talent, in fact it is the combination of our diverse pasts, histories, capabilities, and passions that make the fire service so useful and resilient. What I am saying is that this is an aspect of the department that warrants deliberate, strategic, and thoughtful integration into the way business is conducted. Individual knowledge whether tech related or some other fire service discipline, like the person who knows every knot and rope system configuration, must be captured and turned into organizational knowledge. As a general framework:
- Document it – from purchasing through implementation, and into sustained maintenance and use. Document all aspects of the configurations, workflows, processes, passwords, renewal dates, and contracts.
- Two is one, one is none – like other areas of the fire service, at least two people should have an in depth understanding of critical and fundamental systems.
- Make it official – legitimize the specialty as a department function making it an organizational responsibility.
- Train on it – we are often good at end-user training but add administrator level training and ensure you have staff that take the training. Even if they will never be the primary, it makes it much easier to pick up the pieces if you have an awareness level proficiency.
- Reality check it – use the “hit by a bus” scenario or if that is too morbid, “won the lottery” scenario. Essentially, if this person were no longer here, could the fire department continue to operate every system and process? If the answer is no, then you do not have a personnel problem, you have a system problem.
With this framework, organizations can build identify weaknesses, establish redundancy, weather departures, and avoid costly and sometimes critical regressions.
A well-built system
Using the framework will help you down the path towards building a good system that will support any department initiative, but what does a well-built system look like?
Imagine a well-built rope system and let us overlay that with this example. All rope systems have a bomb-proof anchor… a point that is solid, strong enough to support the load, and in many ways cannot fail. This is the organization, the aspect that generally outlasts any individual member of the department. You then need a way to connect the object (individual knowledge) you are trying to move to the anchor (organization). This rope is the formalized strands of policy, procedure, people, workflows, and processes that get the object to the anchor.
As things become more complicated you can add pulleys and devices to the rope system to make it more robust, redundant, and safer. These are the force maximizers such as training, education, experience, and hands-on practice that ensure the object never falls away from the anchor.
A system works together, has immediate feedback loops if things are going wrong, and can be adjusted to fit the emerging issues. A system can outlive the people who built it and in some cases be a foundation in which other systems are built.
Conclusion
To absorb individual knowledge into the collective, it takes energy, effort, and a willingness to make sure that knowledge never leaves. This goes well beyond tech knowledge as retirees leave the fire service every day, taking with them decades of knowledge and experience that is often lost forever. Creating systems to capture, disseminate, and progress that knowledge is how departments progress with minimal regression. It takes leaders who are deliberate about creating department proficiency from individual proficiency and a willingness to stop treating a core function as a side project or alternate duty.
About the Author
Jason Moore
Jason Moore is a 23-year veteran of the fire service who began his career with the U.S. Air Force as a fire protection specialist. Moore is involved with the International Association of Fire Chiefs’ Technology Council and is a founding member/associate director of the Indiana University Crisis Technologies Innovation Lab. He delivered presentations on implementing technology, using technology for community risk reduction and best practices to justify funding for innovative programs. Moore was the keynote speaker at FireFusion 2024 and is a member of the Firehouse Editorial Advisory Board.

You must ask yourself as a fire service leader, is it fair to have a firefighter do everything that others are doing plus try to be system administrators, trainers, troubleshooters, vendor liaisons, data analyst, and help desk attendants? Is it good practice to have single points of failure as these systems go from needed infrastructure to critical components of a modern operation? Does your technical proficiency as a department actually exist or is it one change away from evaporating?

Systems survive when people leave

I am not advocating to abandon internal talent, in fact it is the combination of our diverse pasts, histories, capabilities, and passions that make the fire service so useful and resilient. What I am saying is that this is an aspect of the department that warrants deliberate, strategic, and thoughtful integration into the way business is conducted. Individual knowledge whether tech related or some other fire service discipline, like the person who knows every knot and rope system configuration, must be captured and turned into organizational knowledge. As a general framework:

  • Document it – from purchasing through implementation, and into sustained maintenance and use. Document all aspects of the configurations, workflows, processes, passwords, renewal dates, and contracts.
  • Two is one, one is none – like other areas of the fire service, at least two people should have an in depth understanding of critical and fundamental systems.
  • Make it official – legitimize the specialty as a department function making it an organizational responsibility.
  • Train on it – we are often good at end-user training but add administrator level training and ensure you have staff that take the training. Even if they will never be the primary, it makes it much easier to pick up the pieces if you have an awareness level proficiency.
  • Reality check it – use the “hit by a bus” scenario or if that is too morbid, “won the lottery” scenario. Essentially, if this person were no longer here, could the fire department continue to operate every system and process? If the answer is no, then you do not have a personnel problem, you have a system problem.

With this framework, organizations can build identify weaknesses, establish redundancy, weather departures, and avoid costly and sometimes critical regressions.

A well-built system

Using the framework will help you down the path towards building a good system that will support any department initiative, but what does a well-built system look like?

Imagine a well-built rope system and let us overlay that with this example. All rope systems have a bomb-proof anchor… a point that is solid, strong enough to support the load, and in many ways cannot fail. This is the organization, the aspect that generally outlasts any individual member of the department. You then need a way to connect the object (individual knowledge) you are trying to move to the anchor (organization). This rope is the formalized strands of policy, procedure, people, workflows, and processes that get the object to the anchor.

As things become more complicated you can add pulleys and devices to the rope system to make it more robust, redundant, and safer. These are the force maximizers such as training, education, experience, and hands-on practice that ensure the object never falls away from the anchor.

A system works together, has immediate feedback loops if things are going wrong, and can be adjusted to fit the emerging issues. A system can outlive the people who built it and in some cases be a foundation in which other systems are built.

Conclusion

To absorb individual knowledge into the collective, it takes energy, effort, and a willingness to make sure that knowledge never leaves. This goes well beyond tech knowledge as retirees leave the fire service every day, taking with them decades of knowledge and experience that is often lost forever. Creating systems to capture, disseminate, and progress that knowledge is how departments progress with minimal regression. It takes leaders who are deliberate about creating department proficiency from individual proficiency and a willingness to stop treating a core function as a side project or alternate duty.

Moore is involved with the International Association of Fire Chiefs’ Technology Council and is a founding member/associate director of the Indiana University Crisis Technologies Innovation Lab. articles.summary: Parents of young children at school or in childcare are able to check-in throughout the day thanks to technology that makes being away a little easier.
articles.content:
Missing your kids? Now there’s technology to help with that
BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - Parents of young children at school or in childcare are able to check in throughout the day thanks to technology that makes being away a little easier.
“You can send a picture or an update if the child was struggling at drop-off for some reason, like they’re crying,” said Caryl Jaques, the owner of Little Ones University.
A day at work might mean several hours away from a child for a parent, but some childcare centers like Little Ones University use technology to give parents a window into their kids’ day without stepping foot into the classroom.
“Three minutes later, you can send a picture to show the parent things weren’t as bad as we thought they were going to be,” Jaques added.
For parents like Caitlin Flood, this information offers reassurance. “When I first brought my son here, he was 3 months old, and I was like, oh my goodness, someone else is going to be watching my kid, but I got to see literally everything,” Flood said.
The constant connection can also have a downside. Jaques said some parents expect updates right away.
“The only drawback can sometimes be a frustration for families if they monitor closely. Obviously the children come first, so we’re going to focus on children in the classroom and get to our technology when we can,” Jaques said.
This tension is part of a larger question in childcare: How much technology is helpful and how much is too much?
“There are a lot of parents that would like to be stay-at-home moms or dads because who doesn’t want to be with their children full time? And there’s also a little bit of fear when they’re trusting us with their most precious little beings and want to be able to say and see everything that goes on,” Jaques said.
In Jericho, Catherine Bowes’ daughter Riley starts sixth grade without a phone and appreciates the availability of technology in school to stay updated throughout the day.
“We’re really lucky, she goes to Camels Hump and it’s a great school with a lot of communication between the school and parents,” Bowes said.
The goal of childcare centers like Little Ones University is to keep parents informed without creating the expectation that every moment needs to be documented.

London, UK, Sept. 04, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) --

Koinvex has announced the development of an AI-powered technology platform focused on making complex information easier to understand, organize and interact with through artificial intelligence.

The company is developing a technology environment that combines artificial intelligence with an interactive AI Companion, creating a more connected experience for users seeking information, context and technology-assisted decision support.

As artificial intelligence continues to become more integrated into digital services, businesses are exploring ways to make advanced technology more accessible and useful in everyday workflows. Koinvex is positioning its platform within this broader development, with a focus on creating an interactive technology experience rather than simply providing traditional software tools.

Koinvex Develops AI-Powered Technology Platform

The Koinvex platform is being developed around the idea that technology should help users process information more efficiently.

Modern digital environments can involve large amounts of information presented across multiple interfaces and systems. Finding relevant information, understanding changing circumstances and organizing different data points can require considerable time and attention.

Koinvex is addressing this challenge through an AI-assisted approach designed to bring information and interaction into a more connected environment.

The company's technology incorporates an AI Companion intended to provide users with an interactive way to engage with available information. Instead of relying exclusively on conventional menus and interfaces, users can interact with technology through a more conversational experience.

According to the company, the objective is to make information easier to access while helping users better understand the context surrounding the information they are reviewing.

AI Companion Designed for a More Interactive Experience

A central element of the Koinvex technology is its AI Companion.

Traditional software applications often require users to navigate through different sections, tools and information sources to find what they need. Koinvex is exploring a different approach by incorporating an AI-driven interface that can help users interact with information more naturally.

The AI Companion is intended to support users by helping organize information and provide additional context when required.

Rather than positioning artificial intelligence as a replacement for human decision-making, Koinvex is developing the technology as a supporting layer that can help users interact with digital information more efficiently.

This approach reflects the company's broader focus on combining automation with human oversight.

Focus on Accessibility and Information

Koinvex's development comes as AI technology continues to expand across multiple industries.

Businesses are increasingly using artificial intelligence for information management, data analysis, workflow automation, customer interaction and other technology-driven processes. As these applications become more common, the ability to interact with AI in a straightforward manner is becoming an increasingly important consideration.

Koinvex is focusing on this accessibility through its AI-powered technology and interactive platform design.

The company aims to create an environment where users can engage with information without having to rely exclusively on complex navigation or multiple disconnected tools.

The platform is designed around several key technology concepts, including:

- AI-assisted information processing

AI-assisted information processing

- Interactive AI Companion technology

Interactive AI Companion technology

- More accessible digital information

More accessible digital information

- Connected user experiences

Connected user experiences

- Technology-assisted decision support

Technology-assisted decision support

- Human-focused interaction with artificial intelligence

Human-focused interaction with artificial intelligence

Supporting Human Decision-Making

Koinvex emphasizes that artificial intelligence is intended to serve as a support technology rather than replace human judgment.

The company believes AI can provide value by helping users organize information, identify relevant context and interact with complex digital environments more efficiently.

This approach allows users to remain at the center of the decision-making process while using technology as an additional resource.

As AI systems continue to develop, Koinvex expects interactive technologies to become increasingly capable of helping users manage information and complete digital tasks.

Building Toward the Future of AI Technology

Koinvex's latest development reflects the company's broader interest in the future of artificial intelligence and interactive digital platforms.

The company is working toward a technology model in which AI is integrated directly into the user experience rather than operating as an isolated feature.

By combining AI technology with an interactive AI Companion, Koinvex aims to create a more connected environment where users can access and interact with information through a simplified digital experience.

The company expects continued developments in artificial intelligence to create new opportunities for businesses and technology providers seeking to improve the way people interact with digital platforms.

Koinvex's current development represents part of that broader technological evolution, with the company focusing on accessibility, interaction and practical applications of AI.

More information about Koinvex and its technology is available at Koinvex.com .

Koinvex is a technology platform focused on developing AI-powered solutions designed to improve information accessibility, digital interaction and technology-assisted decision support. Through its AI Companion and AI-driven technology, Koinvex is working to create a more connected and interactive user experience.

articles.article_title: 2027 elections technology: IEBC ordered to review tender rules
articles.heading: 2027 elections technology: IEBC ordered to review tender rules
articles.summary: Procurement board directs IEBC to clarify evaluation criteria and technical requirements.
articles.content:
2027 elections technology: IEBC ordered to review tender rules
Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has been ordered to review its tender for the procurement of technology to be used in the 2027 General Election after the Public Procurement Administrative Review Board (PPARB) found deficiencies in the document’s evaluation criteria and technical requirements.
The board said the tender, as drafted, did not sufficiently explain how compliance with technical parameters would operate alongside the weighted scoring system, creating uncertainty that could allow evaluators to award different scores to materially similar proposals.
“The tender document ought to clearly state whether compliance with every individual parameter is mandatory or whether alternative means of demonstrating compliance are permissible,” the board said.
Where a specification contains several requirements, the board said, the tender document should also make clear whether all the requirements must be met or whether compliance with a specified number or combination would be sufficient for a tender to be considered responsive.
The board further directed IEBC to seek advice and technical support from the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority (PPRA) before proceeding with the procurement.
The review should ensure that the requirements are stated with sufficient certainty, the evidence needed to demonstrate compliance is clearly identified, and the evaluation criteria and allocation of scores are objectively ascertainable.
The board directed IEBC to make the necessary corrections, clarifications and amendments to the tender document and subsequently publish a new version, giving prospective bidders the period prescribed by law, but not less than seven days, to consider the amendments and submit their tenders.
The decision followed a challenge by Galadirel Investment Limited, which had sought to halt the procurement, alleging that the tender was discriminatory and contained requirements tailored to favour Miru Systems, a South Korean election technology company.
The tender covers the Integrated Elections Management System (IEMS) and related hardware that will support the Kenya Integrated Elections Management System (KIEMS) kits used for biometric voter identification and transmission of election results.
It is one of two major international procurements floated by IEBC in preparation for the 2027 General Election. The other covers the printing of ballot papers, tactile ballot folders for visually impaired voters, the Register of Voters and statutory election forms.
Galadirel challenged the tender arguing that the tender document contained restrictive requirements that could lock out potential competitors.
The company challenged, among other things, the requirement that bidders demonstrate at least five years’ experience in supplying election technology, devices, hardware and accessories.
Bidders are also required to demonstrate that they have undertaken at least one election technology contract worth at least $50 million between 2021 and 2025 and supplied at least 50,000 devices to a single client during the same period.
The firm argued that the requirements appeared to mirror the experience and achievements of Miru Systems.
“It is the applicant’s case that the specifications mirror the achievements Miru Systems has attained in previous tenders,” the firm submitted.
The board, however, rejected the claim that the mere fact that the requirements were specific to the procurement amounted to unlawful tailoring.
It said a procuring entity is entitled to prescribe the level of experience, technical capacity and professional competence reasonably necessary for the successful performance of a particular contract.
The board said the procurement involves specialised information technology, biometric systems, infrastructure, integration, implementation and ongoing support, the board noted.
“In such circumstances, it cannot be said merely because the respondents have prescribed specific experience and qualification requirements, that they were precluded from requiring a tenderer to demonstrate previous experience of a comparable nature and scale,” the board said.
The applicant, it added, had not identified a specific requirement that only Miru Systems could satisfy, nor demonstrated that the combination of experience, qualification and technical requirements had deliberately been formulated around Miru Systems’ corporate profile.
However, the board found problems with the methodology for awarding technical scores.
It said the issue was not simply that criteria were assigned scores within ranges, but that the tender document did not sufficiently disclose the methodology or objective benchmarks evaluators would use to determine the particular score awarded within those ranges.
For example, the board said, one tenderer could demonstrate relevant experience in the Kenyan administrative system but lack working-level fluency in a local language, while another could demonstrate language proficiency but have limited knowledge of the Kenyan administrative system. A third tenderer, the board said, could demonstrate both.
The tender document did not explain how these different attributes would translate into particular scores or provide objective benchmarks for distinguishing between, for example, two, seven or 10 points.
“The tender document must disclose sufficient parameters to enable tenderers to understand how a particular level of compliance, quality, experience or competence will translate into the score awarded,” the board said.
The board said uncertainty was material because the technical evaluation carries 100 points and bidders must attain a minimum technical score to proceed.
A bidder’s success or failure could therefore turn on points awarded under criteria for which the tender document had not provided a sufficiently definite scoring methodology.
The board also found deficiencies in the way some mandatory requirements were framed and said the tender document should clearly identify the precise documents or standards that prospective bidders were required to provide to demonstrate compliance.
On technology ownership and manufacturer authorisation, the board said IEBC was entitled to require evidence of ownership or manufacturer authorisation.
The problem, it said, was the failure to clearly establish the relationship between ownership and dealership and the evidence required to demonstrate compliance.
“Where a qualification is intended to operate as a mandatory requirement, the tender document ought to make clear both the requirement itself and the objective evidence upon which a tenderer will be found compliant or non-compliant,” the board said.
The same concern applied to qualifications prescribed for key personnel.
The board said it was not questioning IEBC’s discretion to require a master’s or bachelor’s degree for a project manager. Rather, the issue was whether the tender document gave bidders sufficient information on the evidence they were required to submit and provided evaluators with a uniform basis for determining compliance.
The board cited Section 70(6)(a) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, which requires evaluation criteria to be disclosed and, to the extent possible, to be objective and quantifiable.
“Having specifically drawn them to the attention of the parties and afforded them an opportunity to be heard thereon, we consider it appropriate to direct that the respondents address and clarify the identified deficiencies before proceeding further with the procurement,” the board said.

2027 elections technology: IEBC ordered to review tender rules

Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) Chairperson Erastus Edung Ethekon speaks during a High-Level National Election Security Roundtable Consultative Forum organised by the IEBC at Serena Hotel in Nairobi on August 2, 2026.

Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has been ordered to review its tender for the procurement of technology to be used in the 2027 General Election after the Public Procurement Administrative Review Board (PPARB) found deficiencies in the document’s evaluation criteria and technical requirements.

The board said the tender, as drafted, did not sufficiently explain how compliance with technical parameters would operate alongside the weighted scoring system, creating uncertainty that could allow evaluators to award different scores to materially similar proposals.

“The tender document ought to clearly state whether compliance with every individual parameter is mandatory or whether alternative means of demonstrating compliance are permissible,” the board said.

Where a specification contains several requirements, the board said, the tender document should also make clear whether all the requirements must be met or whether compliance with a specified number or combination would be sufficient for a tender to be considered responsive.

The board further directed IEBC to seek advice and technical support from the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority (PPRA) before proceeding with the procurement.

The review should ensure that the requirements are stated with sufficient certainty, the evidence needed to demonstrate compliance is clearly identified, and the evaluation criteria and allocation of scores are objectively ascertainable.

The board directed IEBC to make the necessary corrections, clarifications and amendments to the tender document and subsequently publish a new version, giving prospective bidders the period prescribed by law, but not less than seven days, to consider the amendments and submit their tenders.

The decision followed a challenge by Galadirel Investment Limited, which had sought to halt the procurement, alleging that the tender was discriminatory and contained requirements tailored to favour Miru Systems, a South Korean election technology company.

The tender covers the Integrated Elections Management System (IEMS) and related hardware that will support the Kenya Integrated Elections Management System (KIEMS) kits used for biometric voter identification and transmission of election results.

It is one of two major international procurements floated by IEBC in preparation for the 2027 General Election. The other covers the printing of ballot papers, tactile ballot folders for visually impaired voters, the Register of Voters and statutory election forms.

Galadirel challenged the tender arguing that the tender document contained restrictive requirements that could lock out potential competitors.

The company challenged, among other things, the requirement that bidders demonstrate at least five years’ experience in supplying election technology, devices, hardware and accessories.

Bidders are also required to demonstrate that they have undertaken at least one election technology contract worth at least $50 million between 2021 and 2025 and supplied at least 50,000 devices to a single client during the same period.

The firm argued that the requirements appeared to mirror the experience and achievements of Miru Systems.

“It is the applicant’s case that the specifications mirror the achievements Miru Systems has attained in previous tenders,” the firm submitted.

The board, however, rejected the claim that the mere fact that the requirements were specific to the procurement amounted to unlawful tailoring.

It said a procuring entity is entitled to prescribe the level of experience, technical capacity and professional competence reasonably necessary for the successful performance of a particular contract.

The board said the procurement involves specialised information technology, biometric systems, infrastructure, integration, implementation and ongoing support, the board noted.

“In such circumstances, it cannot be said merely because the respondents have prescribed specific experience and qualification requirements, that they were precluded from requiring a tenderer to demonstrate previous experience of a comparable nature and scale,” the board said.

The applicant, it added, had not identified a specific requirement that only Miru Systems could satisfy, nor demonstrated that the combination of experience, qualification and technical requirements had deliberately been formulated around Miru Systems’ corporate profile.

However, the board found problems with the methodology for awarding technical scores.

It said the issue was not simply that criteria were assigned scores within ranges, but that the tender document did not sufficiently disclose the methodology or objective benchmarks evaluators would use to determine the particular score awarded within those ranges.

For example, the board said, one tenderer could demonstrate relevant experience in the Kenyan administrative system but lack working-level fluency in a local language, while another could demonstrate language proficiency but have limited knowledge of the Kenyan administrative system. A third tenderer, the board said, could demonstrate both.

The tender document did not explain how these different attributes would translate into particular scores or provide objective benchmarks for distinguishing between, for example, two, seven or 10 points.

“The tender document must disclose sufficient parameters to enable tenderers to understand how a particular level of compliance, quality, experience or competence will translate into the score awarded,” the board said.

The board said uncertainty was material because the technical evaluation carries 100 points and bidders must attain a minimum technical score to proceed.

A bidder’s success or failure could therefore turn on points awarded under criteria for which the tender document had not provided a sufficiently definite scoring methodology.

The board also found deficiencies in the way some mandatory requirements were framed and said the tender document should clearly identify the precise documents or standards that prospective bidders were required to provide to demonstrate compliance.

On technology ownership and manufacturer authorisation, the board said IEBC was entitled to require evidence of ownership or manufacturer authorisation.

The problem, it said, was the failure to clearly establish the relationship between ownership and dealership and the evidence required to demonstrate compliance.

“Where a qualification is intended to operate as a mandatory requirement, the tender document ought to make clear both the requirement itself and the objective evidence upon which a tenderer will be found compliant or non-compliant,” the board said.

The same concern applied to qualifications prescribed for key personnel.

The board said it was not questioning IEBC’s discretion to require a master’s or bachelor’s degree for a project manager. Rather, the issue was whether the tender document gave bidders sufficient information on the evidence they were required to submit and provided evaluators with a uniform basis for determining compliance.

The board cited Section 70(6)(a) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, which requires evaluation criteria to be disclosed and, to the extent possible, to be objective and quantifiable.

“Having specifically drawn them to the attention of the parties and afforded them an opportunity to be heard thereon, we consider it appropriate to direct that the respondents address and clarify the identified deficiencies before proceeding further with the procurement,” the board said.

articles.heading: Global benchmarks trade mixed following rally on Wall Street led by technology issues
articles.summary: Global shares are trading mixed as market sentiment for some regional benchmarks got a boost from the tech-led rally on Wall Street. Shares fell in France early Friday, while rising
articles.content:
TOKYO (AP) — Global shares were trading mixed Friday, as market sentiment for some regional benchmarks got a boost from the tech-led rally on Wall Street.
France's CAC 40 slipped 0.1% to 8,275.17 in early trading, while the German DAX was little changed, inching down less than 0.1% to 25,982.69. Britain's FTSE 100 gained less than 0.1% to 10,834.34.
U.S. shares were set to be little changed with Dow futures down nearly 0.1% at 53,697.00, while S&P 500 futures inched up less than 0.1% to 7,757.00.
In Asia, Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 rose 1.3% to finish at 65,020.94. South Korea's Kospi gained 1.6% to 6,687.21. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.2% to 9,005.90. Hong Kong's Hang Seng jumped 1.7% to 25,650.87, while the Shanghai Composite lost 0.3% to 3,930.12.
In energy trading, benchmark U.S. crude edged down 55 cents to $90.75 a barrel. Brent crude fell 30 cents to $95.22 a barrel.
The six-month U.S. war with Iran, which has intensified lately, is the main cause behind the recent surge in energy prices.
Many nations depend on access to the Strait of Hormuz to import oil from the Middle East.
Iran fired at Kuwait on Thursday in retaliation for U.S. bombardments earlier in the week.
On interest rates, some investors are taking the recent remarks by Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller as a sign that perhaps the Fed isn’t as likely to raise its short-term interest rates at its next policy meeting in two weeks as previously expected.
Waller said that, if new data next week shows inflation is cooling, he “would be inclined” to keep the Fed’s benchmark interest rate unchanged. Should the data show hotter inflation, he would consider a rate hike.
Market players are also closely watching what Japan's central bank might do on interest rates when its policy board meets later this month. Some analysts expect the Bank of Japan to raise its benchmark rate, and the question is by how much. Some reports say Japan is facing pressures to raise the interest rate so that the yen will move higher.
In currency trading, the U.S. dollar edged up to 156.41 Japanese yen from 155.84 yen. The euro cost $1.1624, down from $1.1631.
AP Business Writer Alex Veiga contributed to this report.
Yuri Kageyama is on Threads: https://www.threads.com/@yurikageyama

articles.heading: China’s AI ‘little giant’ Yunxi Technology files for Hong Kong IPO: sources
articles.summary: The confidential filing could see the hi-tech provider listed in Hong Kong by year-end.
articles.content:
China’s AI ‘little giant’ Yunxi Technology files for Hong Kong IPO: sources
The confidential filing could see the hi-tech provider listed in Hong Kong by year-end
Yunxi Technology, officially one of China’s “little giants”, has submitted a confidential initial public offering application to Hong Kong’s stock exchange, according to people familiar with the matter.
The Guangzhou-based start-up was valued at 10 billion yuan (US$1.27 billion) in its latest private funding round and was working with Bocom International on the deal, aiming to raise “several hundred million [US] dollars”, said the people, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue.
While the listing is targeted to take place by the end of this year, the timing and size remain subject to change, the people said. High-profile backers include Chinese billionaire Jack Ma’s Yunfeng Capital and investment firm HSG Capital.
Yunxi did not immediately respond to South China Morning Post’s request for comment.
Founded in 2016, Yunxi provides end-to-end digital growth products and tools to help major clients across the consumer goods, retail, real estate and automotive sectors integrate artificial intelligence into their operations.

articles.article_title: Datamaran Appoints Bert Sinnema as Chief Technology Officer
articles.heading: Datamaran Appoints Bert Sinnema as Chief Technology Officer
articles.summary: /PRNewswire/ -- Datamaran, the AI-powered risk and governance software provider, today announced the appointment of Bert Sinnema as Chief Technology Officer....
articles.content:
LONDON, NEW YORK and LEEUWARDEN, Netherlands, Sept. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Datamaran, the AI-powered risk and governance software provider, today announced the appointment of Bert Sinnema as Chief Technology Officer. Based out of the company's Leeuwarden office in the Netherlands, Sinnema will lead Datamaran's global engineering and product teams, including the engineering hub in Valencia, Spain, driving the technology and product vision behind the platform that helps organizations understand and manage evolving risks and opportunities.
As CTO, Sinnema will own Datamaran's product vision, strategy, and technology roadmap, from setting direction to architecture, delivery, and the teams building it. He steps into the role at a pivotal moment for the company, as Datamaran deepens its use of AI across the platform to give customers faster, more decision-ready insights into risk, regulation, and stakeholder expectations. His mandate: lead the engineering and product organization, accelerate the pace of AI-driven product development, and ensure the platform keeps pace with the increasingly complex and fast-moving risk landscape.
A track record scaling product engineering teams
Sinnema brings more than 12 years of product engineering leadership experience spanning startups, scale-ups, and category-leading platforms, with deep expertise at the intersection of engineering, cybersecurity, and AI. He joins Datamaran from Eye Security, Europe's fastest-growing cybersecurity company, where he served as VP of Engineering and built the product and engineering organization from the ground up, scaling the multi-hub international team 3x and helping the company reach a €60M Series C round.
Before Eye Security, Sinnema spent over three years at HackerOne, the world's leading ethical hacking and bug bounty platform, rising to Director of Engineering. Earlier in his career, Sinnema founded and served as CTO of SmartLockr, a secure communications and privacy platform he bootstrapped, scaled across three countries, and took through Microsoft's Ventures Accelerator in Berlin.
Building for Datamaran's next chapter
"Bert has spent his career building engineering organizations from the ground up and scaling them through some of the most demanding environments, including as a founder himself. He knows firsthand what it takes to turn conviction into something real, and to keep adapting as the market evolves," said Marjella Lecourt-Alma, CEO and co-founder of Datamaran. "As Datamaran evolves from ESG issue management into an AI-powered governance platform, Bert's founder mindset and experience building teams, technology, and culture make him exactly the right leader to shape what comes next for our teams, customers, and partners."
"I like to operate at the intersection of product engineering leadership and AI, where the hardest problems live, and the highest-leverage decisions get made," said Sinnema. "Datamaran is applying AI to help organizations navigate a genuinely complex risk landscape, and I'm excited to bring my experience building and scaling engineering and product organizations to that mission. This is the most interesting time to be building in tech, and I'm looking forward to being in the middle of it with the team."
Contact: Helen Skeen, Director of Communications and Insights: [email protected].
SOURCE Datamaran Limited

September 4th, 2026 by Rob Powell · Leave a Comment

This Industry Viewpoint was authored by Biju Anidil, Regional VP Sales, EMEA & APAC, Evergent

Every monetisation vendor, mine included, will tell you to modernise your BSS. You have heard it a hundred times, which is why most of you have not acted. The advice is not wrong. It is incomplete, and the missing part is the reason operators stay stuck.

For a decade the industry has chased the same reinvention: telco to techco, the operator remade as a technology company. Done properly that means a software and cloud operating model, AI and data in the core, agile delivery, and revenue from platforms, network APIs and new value pools rather than connectivity alone. It is a change in how the business runs, not a catalogue of services bolted on top. Technology companies reinvest between a tenth and a quarter of revenue into R&D; most telcos reinvest under three percent. That gap is the real distance between ambition and reality.

Here is where it goes wrong. Most operators have bought the technology of a techco, the modernised stacks and multi-year programmes, without adopting its commercial operating model. They still price, measure and move like a telco. That is the techco trap: you have modernised the technology without moving the number that actually matters, which is how fast you turn a commercial opportunity into revenue. Whether that is a streaming bundle or an enterprise network-API product, it still reaches market far too slowly.

The uncomfortable version is simpler. Most operators do not have a technology problem. They have a measurement problem. A real techco scores itself on customer value and speed. Trapped operators still score systems delivered and milestones hit, and almost nothing on speed to revenue. So that is what gets sacrificed.

Why you are actually stuck

Most programmes begin with the right objective and then collide with time. Large IT transformations run two to four years, and by the time they land the market has moved on. But the deeper reason the obvious fix stays undone is not ignorance, it is risk. Your monetisation logic is welded into a stack that is often twenty years old, so ripping it out carries migration risk that can end careers, and it keeps getting deferred. Admitting a multi-year programme optimised the wrong metric is politically expensive in any large operator. These are real obstacles, not excuses, and any vendor who says the fix is simple has never sat in your chair.

Revenue velocity, and what it costs you

A sharper measure is revenue velocity: how quickly you move from identifying an opportunity to earning money from it, counted in weeks from signed partner to first invoiced revenue.

The cost of getting this wrong is not abstract. Take an operator with twenty million subscribers launching a bundled offer that adds five euros a month and reaches one customer in twenty. That is a million subscribers at five euros: five million euros a month, fifteen million a quarter. Launch a quarter late and that fifteen million is not deferred, it is gone: you never recover the lost quarter, and a faster rival may take the window outright. Then multiply by every offer you launch in a year.

This is why the sharper operators have stopped chasing full-stack replacement and modernise only the layer that manages revenue: pricing, bundling, entitlements and billing. After rebuilding its BSS for exactly this, Astro, Malaysia’s leading pay-TV operator, halved its time to market for new offers and cut operational costs by two-thirds, replacing a twenty-year-old platform in nine months, not the multi-year cycle these projects usually run. Commercial agility depends far more on modernising that layer than on replacing everything beneath it.

Agentic AI cannot outrun bad foundations

AI now dominates the conversation, and its potential is real, but its role is misunderstood. Agentic AI is an orchestration layer, not a transformation strategy. It connects information across systems, speeds decisions and automates manual work, and it is only as good as the data beneath it. Point it at fragmented data and inconsistent rules and you simply automate the mess faster. AI can accelerate revenue velocity, but only on a monetisation foundation that is already clean.

Are you in the trap?

Three questions tell you. Does launching a new bundle require a project, or a configuration change? Have your last three launches each taken more than a quarter? Do your AI pilots keep stalling on data quality and entitlement gaps? Two yeses out of three and you are in the techco trap, whatever your roadmap says.

The techco ambition is right, and unchanged. What has to change is the definition of success: not milestones delivered, but revenue captured, and how fast. The operators that win will be the ones that shorten the distance between a commercial decision and the revenue it produces. Everyone else will keep buying transformation and wondering why it never quite arrives.

Every monetisation vendor, mine included, will tell you to modernise your BSS. You have heard it a hundred times, which is why most of you have not acted. The advice is not wrong. It is incomplete, and the missing part is the reason operators stay stuck.

For a decade the industry has chased the same reinvention: telco to techco, the operator remade as a technology company. Done properly that means a software and cloud operating model, AI and data in the core, agile delivery, and revenue from platforms, network APIs and new value pools rather than connectivity alone. It is a change in how the business runs, not a catalogue of services bolted on top. Technology companies reinvest between a tenth and a quarter of revenue into R&D; most telcos reinvest under three percent. That gap is the real distance between ambition and reality.

Here is where it goes wrong. Most operators have bought the technology of a techco, the modernised stacks and multi-year programmes, without adopting its commercial operating model. They still price, measure and move like a telco. That is the techco trap: you have modernised the technology without moving the number that actually matters, which is how fast you turn a commercial opportunity into revenue. Whether that is a streaming bundle or an enterprise network-API product, it still reaches market far too slowly.

The uncomfortable version is simpler. Most operators do not have a technology problem. They have a measurement problem. A real techco scores itself on customer value and speed. Trapped operators still score systems delivered and milestones hit, and almost nothing on speed to revenue. So that is what gets sacrificed.

Why you are actually stuck

Most programmes begin with the right objective and then collide with time. Large IT transformations run two to four years, and by the time they land the market has moved on. But the deeper reason the obvious fix stays undone is not ignorance, it is risk. Your monetisation logic is welded into a stack that is often twenty years old, so ripping it out carries migration risk that can end careers, and it keeps getting deferred. Admitting a multi-year programme optimised the wrong metric is politically expensive in any large operator. These are real obstacles, not excuses, and any vendor who says the fix is simple has never sat in your chair.

Revenue velocity, and what it costs you

A sharper measure is revenue velocity: how quickly you move from identifying an opportunity to earning money from it, counted in weeks from signed partner to first invoiced revenue.

The cost of getting this wrong is not abstract. Take an operator with twenty million subscribers launching a bundled offer that adds five euros a month and reaches one customer in twenty. That is a million subscribers at five euros: five million euros a month, fifteen million a quarter. Launch a quarter late and that fifteen million is not deferred, it is gone: you never recover the lost quarter, and a faster rival may take the window outright. Then multiply by every offer you launch in a year.

This is why the sharper operators have stopped chasing full-stack replacement and modernise only the layer that manages revenue: pricing, bundling, entitlements and billing. After rebuilding its BSS for exactly this, Astro, Malaysia’s leading pay-TV operator, halved its time to market for new offers and cut operational costs by two-thirds, replacing a twenty-year-old platform in nine months, not the multi-year cycle these projects usually run. Commercial agility depends far more on modernising that layer than on replacing everything beneath it.

Agentic AI cannot outrun bad foundations

AI now dominates the conversation, and its potential is real, but its role is misunderstood. Agentic AI is an orchestration layer, not a transformation strategy. It connects information across systems, speeds decisions and automates manual work, and it is only as good as the data beneath it. Point it at fragmented data and inconsistent rules and you simply automate the mess faster. AI can accelerate revenue velocity, but only on a monetisation foundation that is already clean.

Are you in the trap?

Three questions tell you. Does launching a new bundle require a project, or a configuration change? Have your last three launches each taken more than a quarter? Do your AI pilots keep stalling on data quality and entitlement gaps? Two yeses out of three and you are in the techco trap, whatever your roadmap says.

The techco ambition is right, and unchanged. What has to change is the definition of success: not milestones delivered, but revenue captured, and how fast. The operators that win will be the ones that shorten the distance between a commercial decision and the revenue it produces. Everyone else will keep buying transformation and wondering why it never quite arrives.

articles.content:
Gasgoo Munich- Ningbo Sunrise ELC Technology Co., Ltd. (Ningbo Sunrise) announced it has signed a strategic framework agreement with Leadrive Technology (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. The two companies plan to collaborate on electric vehicle power control, robotics, and solid-state transformers.

Image Source: Company Announcement

Under the agreement, Ningbo Sunrise intends to subscribe to a portion of Leadrive Technology's future initial public offering. The companies will also establish a priority cooperation mechanism for core electric drive components. Additionally, they plan to jointly develop structural parts for robotic joints and components for solid-state transformers, while coordinating their efforts to explore the European market.

Operationally, the two companies share clear synergies. Ningbo Sunrise specializes in precision components, with automotive electronics as a key segment, and has recently expanded into emerging fields such as robotics and AI servers. Leadrive Technology, meanwhile, has long focused on NEV power control, with products covering control units, power modules, and power bricks. It is gradually extending its power electronics technology into scenarios like robotics and data center power supplies.

The significance of this partnership lies in the potential for the relationship to evolve from supply chain integration to capital and technical collaboration. However, the current agreement remains a framework. With businesses like robotics and solid-state transformers still in the industrial expansion stage, it is uncertain whether they will yield designated projects, mass production orders, or actual revenue.

Ningbo Sunrise also explicitly stated that this agreement will not have a material impact on the company's operating performance for the current year. Overall, the collaboration leans more toward medium-to-long-term strategic positioning, offering limited immediate boost to financial results.

articles.heading: Capitolis Appoints Manickam as Chief Technology Officer
articles.summary: Capitolis, a financial technology company, appointed Murugan Manickam as chief technology officer (CTO). Reporting to Okan Pekin, president of Capitolis,
articles.content:
Capitolis, a financial technology company, appointed Murugan Manickam as chief technology officer (CTO). Reporting to Okan Pekin, president of Capitolis, Manickam will be responsible for leading Capitolis’ global engineering organization and its data and AI strategy, driving innovation and execution to support the company’s continued growth. Amos Arev, head of engineering and general manager, Israel, will remain with Capitolis.
Manickam brings 28 years of technology leadership largely focused in financial services, with deep expertise across global markets and specializing in fixed income, currencies and commodities (FICC), trade management, post-trade platforms, regulatory technology and AI-driven development.
Manickam joins Capitolis from Bank of America, where he most recently served as managing director and global head of FICC Macro Trade Management & Emerging Markets Technology. During his 17-year tenure, he led large-scale transformation initiatives across FX, fixed income, credit, rates and emerging markets, modernized trading infrastructure, consolidated legacy platforms and advanced Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) adoption and AI-driven development and automation. Earlier in his career, he held technology leadership roles at Merrill Lynch and General Reinsurance.
“Murugan is an accomplished technology leader with deep capital markets expertise and a proven track record of driving transformation at scale,” Okan Pekin, president of Capitolis, said. “His experience and vision will be invaluable as we continue to innovate and expand our platform. We also want to thank Amos for the pivotal role he has played over the past seven years in building the engineering organization and technology strategy that underpin our business today. His vision, leadership and dedication have made a significant impact on Capitolis.”
Murugan Manickam, CTO of Capitolis, added, “Capitolis is tackling complex challenges in financial markets with a combination of innovation, scale and industry expertise. It has been relentlessly optimizing capital solutions for major financial institutions. I’m excited to join the team and help advance the company’s technology platform to deliver innovative and AI-driven solutions that create even greater value for our clients and the broader financial ecosystem.”

articles.content:
LAKE FOREST, Calif.—STAAR Surgical Company (NASDAQ: STAA), the global leader in phakic IOLs with the EVO family of Implantable Collamer Lenses (EVO ICL) for vision correction, has announced the appointment of Ben Park, Ph.D., as the new chief technology officer (CTO). Park joins STAAR from Align Technology, Inc., a global medical device company, where he served as head of emerging technology since 2018. Park will join STAAR's executive committee and report to Warren Foust, president and CEO, according to the announcement.
"Evolving STAAR from a single-product focus into a multi-product platform is central to our strategy—and requires the right leader," said Foust. "Ben Park is that leader. We have been delivering on revenue growth and profitability, and now it's time to match that momentum with equal urgency on innovation. With our R&D and advanced research teams preparing for first-in-human studies of our next-generation products, the moment to accelerate is now. Ben's track record of success in building and commercializing breakthrough medical device platforms makes him the ideal person to advance our innovation roadmap and unlock the full potential of our proprietary Collamer technology."
While at Align Technology, Park built and led a global multidisciplinary team—spanning biomedical engineering, hardware, embedded systems, and software across the U.S. and Asia-Pacific markets to define next generation product platforms and address unmet clinical needs, from concept through to market launch.
"STAAR has built something genuinely rare, a clinically proven product portfolio with over 30 years of real-world results, a proprietary material that no one else has, and a market opportunity that is only growing as myopia becomes one of the defining health challenges of our time," said Park. "What drew me here is the ambition to go further: to take everything STAAR has learned and apply it across myopia and beyond. I see a real opportunity to build a multi-product platform by bringing a fresh perspective to how we identify and solve unmet clinical needs. This team is ready to execute, and I'm energized to help accelerate what we can deliver together—for surgeons, for patients, and for the future of refractive surgery.”
Prior to Align Technology, Park served as CTO of Fingertips Lab, Inc., where he led the development and commercial launch of a health technology product designed for the visually impaired in markets across more than 10 countries. Prior to Fingertips Lab, he served as chief technologist at Volcano Corporation, where he led the development of a novel intracardiac imaging platform. He also co-founded Fluid Medical, Inc., where he invented a new intravascular ultrasound imaging platform utilizing shape memory alloy materials and forged strategic development partnerships with Boston Scientific and Olympus Corporation.
According to the company, Park is set to join other STAAR executives and leaders at the upcoming 44th Congress of the ESCRS in London from September 11–15, 2026, the company noted.
Last month, STAAR delivered net sales totaling $93.5 million for the second quarter of 2026, up 111 percent from $44.3 million in the prior-year quarter. China accounted for more than half of quarterly revenue at $52.3 million and was the principal growth driver, the company reported.

articles.content:
- GOOG +1.59%

- EOSE -3.05%

- EOS-USD +0.99%

- EOS +0.74%

MN8 Energy, Eos Energy Enterprises, Inc. (NASDAQ: EOSE ), and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOGL )'s Google announced a collaboration on September 2 to deliver new, clean, around-the-clock energy resources to the PJM grid in support of growing demand in the region. For Eos, this deal marks an important validation point for its long-duration battery technology.

In response, Stifel analyst Stephen Gengaro reiterated a Buy rating on the stock with a $9.00 price target. The analyst views the Eos-Google collaboration positively despite the initial project being small.

Google Adds Credibility to EOS

EOS will provide a 10MW/ 100 MWh Z3 battery to provide long-duration energy storage as part of an integrated solution supporting data centers. AI data centers are creating demand for power sources that go beyond the shorter-duration energy storage resources and deliver dependable capacity across more hours of the day.

EOS's system is a step in this direction, offering 10 hours of storage and enabling solar power to remain available for substantially longer periods. According to Nathan Kroeker, Chief Commercial Officer at Eos, the company's work with Google is focused on deploying long-duration storage and solving real grid reliability challenges.

EOS operating backdrop also serves positively. For the second quarter, EOS generated a revenue of $68.8million, up 351% year-over-year, while backlog reached a record $807 million. The company also highlighted a commercial opportunity pipeline of $24.6 billion, as of June 30, 2026.

These numbers, together with the new collaboration with Google, point to growing interest in Eos's technology, which may in the future lead to scaling revenues and growing orders for EOS.

Small and Years Away

While Gengaro views this Google deal positively, the analyst also pointed out that the initial project is small and scheduled to start operating in 2030. The solar component of the project is likely to start in 2028, lithium-ion storage will follow in 2029, while the long-duration storage component of the project isn't expected to begin operations until 2030.

Besides this, the company itself remains far from profitability. For the second quarter, gross loss for EOS stood at $48.8 million, compared to $31.0 million in the prior-year period. Gross margin was negative 71%, even though it did improve 132 percentage points year over year and 7 percentage points sequentially.

The headline revenue growth coming from Q2 also has a concentration risk. Almost $55 million, or roughly 80% of Q2 revenue, came from a pre-existing project. The project was contributed to Frontier Power USA upon closing, while the project and FPUSA represented 49% of backlog volume at quarter end.

Management also reported tightening full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $300 million to $350 million, from the prior range of $300 million to $400 million.

Hedge Funds are Building Positions

Recent filings from Insider Monkey's database shows hedge fund interest building for both EOS and Alphabet. For the second quarter, 45 hedge funds held positions in EOS, up from 33 in the prior quarter. Meanwhile, 275 hedge funds held positions in Alphabet, up from 265 in the prior quarter.

Hudson Bay Capital Management held an estimated 13.68 million shares in EOS at the end of Q2, while Electron Capital Partners also increased its position by 25% to 6.68 million shares.

Overall, the EOS-Google-MN8 collaboration serves as a positive for all three companies, particularly Eos. For EOS, the deal can be seen as a potential technology-validation point rather than an event that can radically transform its financial outlook. Provided all goes well, Google could become evidence that EOS's long-duration storage holds strategic importance in the data-center power market.

While we acknowledge the potential of EOS and GOOGL as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk.
