articles.title: Micron Technology Stock Has Stumbled, but Here's Why I'm Not Buying the Dip
articles.description: Micron Technology Stock Has Stumbled, but Here's Why I'm Not Buying the Dip The Motley Fool
articles.description_html: Micron Technology Stock Has Stumbled, but Here's Why I'm Not Buying the Dip  The Motley Fool
articles.article_title: Micron Technology Stock Has Stumbled, but Here's Why I'm Not Buying the Dip | The Motley Fool
articles.heading: Micron Technology Stock Has Stumbled, but Here's Why I'm Not Buying the Dip
articles.summary: The artificial intelligence infrastructure spending boom has run into some turbulence.
articles.content:
Micron Technology (MU +4.00%) stock closed at $958.73 on Monday, Aug. 31, which was 21% below its June all-time high. But just to keep things in perspective, the stock is still sitting on an eye-popping one-year gain of 680%.
Micron supplies some of the world's best high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for data centers, a critical component in the artificial intelligence (AI) hardware stack. Demand is currently through the roof and supply remains tight, giving the company an unprecedented ability to dictate prices.
However, the supply-demand imbalance could resolve during the next year or two, potentially hurting Micron's financial performance. Therefore, although its stock is trading at a very attractive valuation, it isn't a straightforward buy right now. Here's why I'm steering clear despite the recent dip.
Why Micron stock is pulling back
According to Nvidia, the five largest hyperscale companies (which includes the likes of Microsoft and Amazon), will spend nearly $800 billion combined on AI data center infrastructure during 2026, with a substantial chunk of that money going toward chips and components. Nvidia says that spending figure could top $1.3 trillion in 2027.
Those companies have to earn a return on all of that spending; otherwise, it won't make economic sense. Some of them will make money by renting computing capacity to other businesses for a fee, whereas others will charge for the use of their AI models and software applications. But making money isn't easy with hardware costs surging; a recent report by Bloomberg suggests Nvidia has informed customers of a 15% price increase, partly because of rising HBM prices.
To recoup some of the climbing costs, companies like Microsoft and Anthropic recently implemented passive price increases for the use of their AI models and software, which has forced some organizations to rethink their spending. Uber Technologies, Walmart, AT&T, and Amazon are just some of the companies that have implemented AI usage caps on their employees to prevent budget blowouts.
According to a recent survey by UBS Group, about 60% of businesses are now routing tasks to cheaper, more efficient AI models to help reduce usage costs. These models typically consume less computing power, which might be bad news for semiconductor demand.
To make matters worse, lawmakers in more than a dozen U.S. states have introduced legislation to temporarily ban the construction of new data centers while they weigh the social, economic, and environmental impacts. This will be a problem for many planned infrastructure projects, and the effects could flow through to Micron and other chip makers in the form of lower sales.
Micron's revenue continues to skyrocket
The aforementioned AI headwinds haven't shown up in Micron's financial results. The company generated a record $41.4 billion in total revenue during its fiscal 2026 third quarter (ended May 28), a staggering 346% increase from the year-ago period. All four segments of its business produced triple-digit percentage growth, thanks to AI-related memory demand for data centers, computers, smartphones, and even cars.
The supply-demand imbalance in the memory market is giving Micron an unprecedented ability to dictate prices, which is a big reason for its rapid revenue growth. That is also boosting the company's profit margins, which is why its third-quarter earnings soared by an eye-popping 1,368% to $24.67 per share.
Management's forecast points to another set of blockbuster results in the fourth quarter, which just ended on Aug. 31. The company is expected to have $50 billion in sales and earnings of $30.73 per share. The final numbers will be revealed at the end of September.
Why I'm not buying Micron stock on the dip
Micron stock looks like an absolute bargain right now. Based on the company's trailing 12-month earnings of $44.23 per share, its stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 21, making it cheaper than both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 indexes, which have P/E ratios of 24.5 and 34.3, respectively.
Plus, if Micron's earnings rise to $155.03 per share in fiscal 2027 like Wall Street expects (according to Yahoo! Finance), then its stock has an even more attractive forward P/E ratio of just 6.
NASDAQ: MU
Key Data Points
Why would a company growing at Micron's pace be trading at a discount to the broader market? Simply put, I think Wall Street knows the company's earnings will eventually crash back down to Earth. If a slowdown in demand doesn't cause it, then an increase in supply might, because every memory company is racing to build more manufacturing capacity right now. During the next few years, higher supply levels will erode Micron's ability to dictate prices, so the company probably won't be able to maintain its current level of earnings.
As a result, if we look a few years into the future, Micron stock might be more expensive than it currently appears. That's why I don't plan to buy the recent dip.

articles.summary: As agentic AI moves from pilots to enterprise-wide deployment, orchestration, data, governance, and clear business objectives are becoming critical for scaling, says chief operating officer at NiCE Arun Chandra.
articles.content:
Sponsored
Scaling agentic AI pilots across the enterprise
As agentic AI moves from pilots to enterprise-wide deployment, orchestration, data, governance, and clear business objectives are becoming critical for scaling, says chief operating officer at NiCE Arun Chandra.
In partnership withNiCE
As agentic AI moves from experimentation toward enterprise deployment, the challenge is figuring out how agents can work together, connect to the systems and data they need, and operate safely across the workflows that run a business. Although agentic AI has been adopted by some 80% of Fortune 500 companies, progress toward meaningful scale remains uneven, with many organizations still working through isolated pilots.
For Arun Chandra, chief operating officer at NiCE, the first step is moving beyond experimentation for its own sake. “Everybody's trying to figure out what can we do with this technology?” he says. But scaling requires a clearer connection to business strategy: Organizations need to define whether they are trying to increase revenue, reduce costs, or pursue another strategic or financial objective. From there, they need to rethink the workflows where agents will operate instead of just layering AI onto existing processes. “The last thing you want to do is to apply AI on an outdated or an inefficient workflow,” Chandra says.
That shift requires organizations to treat agentic AI as a cohesive system. Agents need access to the data, knowledge, and context required to make effective decisions, as well as connections to back-end systems if they are expected to take action. Fragmented information can undermine those capabilities: “The efficacy of these AI agents is purely a function of the context, the knowledge, and the data they can ingest and use,” Chandra says.
The organizational implications are equally noteworthy. Scaling agents can create a new form of fragmentation if teams build isolated systems that don’t connect with one another, while governance, privacy, security, and change management become more important as agents take on more consequential work. Chandra argues that AI agents should ultimately be held to the same standards as human workers, with organizations thinking of their workforce as a combination of humans and AI agents.
Looking ahead, that connected approach could enable agents to work proactively and even communicate with other agents to resolve customer needs. For organizations making the transition from pilots to scale, the priority is not to “boil the ocean,” Chandra says, but to instead build a connected strategy around high-value use cases, workflows, workforce changes, and measurable outcomes.

articles.article_title: Micron Technology Stock Has Stumbled, but Here's Why I'm Not Buying the Dip
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
authors: Anthony Di Pizio, The Motley Fool
articles.summary: The artificial intelligence infrastructure spending boom has run into some turbulence.
articles.content:
- MU -0.75%

- NVDA +2.14%

Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) stock closed at $958.73 on Monday, Aug. 31, which was 21% below its June all-time high. But just to keep things in perspective, the stock is still sitting on an eye-popping one-year gain of 680%.

Micron supplies some of the world's best high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for data centers, a critical component in the artificial intelligence (AI) hardware stack. Demand is currently through the roof and supply remains tight, giving the company an unprecedented ability to dictate prices.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

However, the supply-demand imbalance could resolve during the next year or two, potentially hurting Micron's financial performance. Therefore, although its stock is trading at a very attractive valuation, it isn't a straightforward buy right now. Here's why I'm steering clear despite the recent dip.

Why Micron stock is pulling back

According to Nvidia , the five largest hyperscale companies (which includes the likes of Microsoft and Amazon ), will spend nearly $800 billion combined on AI data center infrastructure during 2026, with a substantial chunk of that money going toward chips and components. Nvidia says that spending figure could top $1.3 trillion in 2027.

Those companies have to earn a return on all of that spending; otherwise, it won't make economic sense. Some of them will make money by renting computing capacity to other businesses for a fee, whereas others will charge for the use of their AI models and software applications. But making money isn't easy with hardware costs surging; a recent report by Bloomberg suggests Nvidia has informed customers of a 15% price increase, partly because of rising HBM prices.

To recoup some of the climbing costs, companies like Microsoft and Anthropic recently implemented passive price increases for the use of their AI models and software, which has forced some organizations to rethink their spending. Uber Technologies , Walmart , AT&T , and Amazon are just some of the companies that have implemented AI usage caps on their employees to prevent budget blowouts.

According to a recent survey by UBS Group , about 60% of businesses are now routing tasks to cheaper, more efficient AI models to help reduce usage costs. These models typically consume less computing power, which might be bad news for semiconductor demand.

To make matters worse, lawmakers in more than a dozen U.S. states have introduced legislation to temporarily ban the construction of new data centers while they weigh the social, economic, and environmental impacts. This will be a problem for many planned infrastructure projects, and the effects could flow through to Micron and other chip makers in the form of lower sales.

Micron's revenue continues to skyrocket

The aforementioned AI headwinds haven't shown up in Micron's financial results. The company generated a record $41.4 billion in total revenue during its fiscal 2026 third quarter (ended May 28), a staggering 346% increase from the year-ago period. All four segments of its business produced triple-digit percentage growth, thanks to AI-related memory demand for data centers, computers, smartphones, and even cars.

The supply-demand imbalance in the memory market is giving Micron an unprecedented ability to dictate prices, which is a big reason for its rapid revenue growth. That is also boosting the company's profit margins, which is why its third-quarter earnings soared by an eye-popping 1,368% to $24.67 per share.

Management's forecast points to another set of blockbuster results in the fourth quarter, which just ended on Aug. 31. The company is expected to have $50 billion in sales and earnings of $30.73 per share. The final numbers will be revealed at the end of September.

Why I'm not buying Micron stock on the dip

Micron stock looks like an absolute bargain right now. Based on the company's trailing 12-month earnings of $44.23 per share, its stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 21, making it cheaper than both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 indexes, which have P/E ratios of 24.5 and 34.3, respectively.

Plus, if Micron's earnings rise to $155.03 per share in fiscal 2027 like Wall Street expects (according to Yahoo! Finance), then its stock has an even more attractive forward P/E ratio of just 6.

Why would a company growing at Micron's pace be trading at a discount to the broader market? Simply put, I think Wall Street knows the company's earnings will eventually crash back down to Earth. If a slowdown in demand doesn't cause it, then an increase in supply might, because every memory company is racing to build more manufacturing capacity right now. During the next few years, higher supply levels will erode Micron's ability to dictate prices, so the company probably won't be able to maintain its current level of earnings.

As a result, if we look a few years into the future, Micron stock might be more expensive than it currently appears. That's why I don't plan to buy the recent dip.

Should you buy stock in Micron Technology right now?

Consider when Netflix made this list on December 17, 2004... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $435,803 !* Or when Nvidia made this list on April 15, 2005... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $1,334,577 !*

articles.title: Bring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reserves
articles.description: Bring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reserves The Guardian
articles.description_html: Bring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reserves  The Guardian
articles.article_title: Bring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reserves
articles.heading: Bring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reserves
articles.summary: As graduates of an online training course gather from across the continent, the consensus is overwhelming: computers and saving animals go together
articles.content:
On a bitingly cold night in Lapalala Wilderness nature reserve in South Africa’s Limpopo province, Duncan Kanyakera watches as instructor Jacques Viljoen deploys a thermal drone in search of a lone cheetah. Once the drone has disappeared into the inky sky, Kanyakera, from Tsavo in Kenya, and 20 other conservation professionals from across Africa turn their attention to the open-air screen in anticipation.
Many of the students – from 11 African countries as far flung as Benin, Liberia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar – witnessing the demonstration have earned their places at Lapalala after performing well on an online training programme for protected area technicians (PAT) run by the Connected Conservation Foundation (CCF). Also on the course, are five members of Peace Parks staff in training.
“Data and technology are critical to modern conservation,” says CCF’s Sophie Maxwell. “Cameras and collars and software like EarthRanger have transformed the fight against poaching … But then an elephant knocks over a pole and you are back to square one.”
Since 2015, the CCF has installed state-of-the-art tech systems in parks across Africa with remarkable success, helping to protect nearly 10m hectares (25m acres). “Parks with tech solutions are safer and more biodiverse and they have better relationships with communities,” says Maxwell.
Over the years, the CCF has “identified a critical gap”, says Carien Soldatos who oversees the PAT training programme: “Tech is fantastic, but it all depends on having trained technicians on the ground. Without people who know how to use, repair and maintain them, the fanciest gizmos in the world aren’t much use.” While there are such people in some parks, they are sorely lacking in many parts of Africa.
After searching everywhere for a tech course aimed at conservation professionals, the CCF decided to create its own. Their 10-module course, which launched in July 2025, was a global first. In the first year, 680 people from all over the world finished at least one module. Those who completed all 10 modules were invited to interviews, with the top 16 chosen to attend the practical component at Lapalala.
In less than 10 minutes, the heat sensor technology in the drone launched by Viljoen locates the cheetah resting with her cubs. Once he has locked its location, the operator sends a pin to the park’s on-duty field rangers, who rush to the scene. “I was stunned,” says Kanyakera. “There was no moon and the cheetah was miles away from us. But we could see exactly what was happening as the rangers got out of their vehicle and checked up on her.”
Kanyakera, who works for the Taita Taveta Wildlife Conservancies Association (TTWCA) to support a network of 35 conservancies and ranches in Kenya’s vast Tsavo landscape, recognised immediately how handy a drone would be back home. Human-wildlife conflict is a challenge in Tsavo: “If an elephant gets into a corn field, it causes havoc,” he says. “And then you have the problem of humans retaliating.”
The aim, says Kanyakera, is to keep humans and animals apart via designated wildlife corridors. But this gets tricky in the dry season when animals and humans alike are drawn towards water. Currently, if Kanyakera gets reports of an elephant near a village, he has to first work out where the elephant is and which direction it is moving in, before deploying rangers to intervene. This can take hours.
“With a drone, we could find the elephant in minutes,” he says. “The noise of the drone alone would probably be enough to scare the animal off. And if that doesn’t work, I can deploy rangers much more accurately.”
While a night-vision drone is the most exciting item on Kanyakera’s Christmas list, the course has also shown him how simple changes could drastically improve the tech “stack” back in Tsavo. This has a lot to do with the course design, explains Maxwell: “Each day, they build a new element of the stack,” she says, “before breaking it down at the end of each day and building it again the next morning to add another layer. It’s all about building muscle memory.”
And it seems to be working. “As soon as I get home, I’ll reconfigure our camera traps to make the most of AI,” says Kanyakera who also has his sights set on re-equipping the ops room in Tsavo. “In the past, we would just Google and make a decision. Now I know so much more, I can target what I really want. The learnings from this course can make a big difference to the people and animals of Tsavo.”
The course – which featured guest lectures and practicals from nine experts on topics including connectivity, communication, power systems, monitoring sensors, hardware integration and GIS visualisation tools – is having an impact far beyond Tsavo.
Effort Zivengwa, who works at the Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority head office in Harare, is part of a tech team responsible for 11 national parks. “We were content with what we were doing,” he says. “But, after completing this course, I think we have to do more. We are already using EarthRanger and we do have sensors, but they are not integrated.
“We have park headquarters and lodges that don’t have internet access,” he adds. “Using point-to-point internet can fix that problem easily.” The learning module on solar power further shifted his understanding of what is possible. “We have a lot of remote stations,” he says. “But the sun shines everywhere.”
Mabel Nokhuthula Piki, who teaches wildlife monitoring skills at the Chinhoyi University of Technology in central Zimbabwe, has also found the course empowering. “My students didn’t comprehend that tech was important. They couldn’t get the link between saving animals and computers. But now I am going to change their minds,” she says. “It is impossible to understand the value of tech until you have seen it.”
The CCF is planning to run a second practical course with another batch of students in the first quarter of 2027. What is more, says Soldatos, “we will be supporting five participants from the first course with internships and/or hardware donations”. The lucky five have not yet been chosen, but Kanyakera, Zivengwa and Piki are all in the running.

Effort Zivengwa, who works at the Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority head office in Harare, is part of a tech team responsible for 11 national parks. “We were content with what we were doing,” he says. “But, after completing this course, I think we have to do more. We are already using EarthRanger and we do have sensors, but they are not integrated.

“We have park headquarters and lodges that don’t have internet access,” he adds. “Using point-to-point internet can fix that problem easily.” The learning module on solar power further shifted his understanding of what is possible. “We have a lot of remote stations,” he says. “But the sun shines everywhere.”

Mabel Nokhuthula Piki, who teaches wildlife monitoring skills at the Chinhoyi University of Technology in central Zimbabwe, has also found the course empowering. “My students didn’t comprehend that tech was important. They couldn’t get the link between saving animals and computers. But now I am going to change their minds,” she says. “It is impossible to understand the value of tech until you have seen it.”

The CCF is planning to run a second practical course with another batch of students in the first quarter of 2027. What is more, says Soldatos, “we will be supporting five participants from the first course with internships and/or hardware donations”. The lucky five have not yet been chosen, but Kanyakera, Zivengwa and Piki are all in the running.

articles.title: I went looking for surveillance cameras in my neighbourhood: I found so many more than I thought
articles.description: I went looking for surveillance cameras in my neighbourhood: I found so many more than I thought BBC

articles.article_title: I went looking for surveillance cameras in my neighbourhood: I found so many more than I thought
articles.heading: I went looking for surveillance cameras in my neighbourhood: I found so many more than I thought
articles.summary: In the trade-off between privacy and security, it helps to know the extent of your local surveillance infrastructure. There are now easy ways to find out.
articles.content:
I went looking for surveillance cameras in my neighbourhood: I found so many more than I thought
In the trade-off between privacy and security, it helps to know the extent of your local surveillance infrastructure. There are now easy ways to find out.
I didn't tell anyone I was meeting Michelle Dahl, executive director of the Surveillance Technology Oversight Project, a watchdog group. But by the time I greet her in Brooklyn, New York, the system knows we're together.
"It's kind of invisible if you're not looking for it," says Dahl, pointing up to a lamppost, where two tiny cameras labelled New York City Police Department hide in black plastic domes.
They're part of the NYPD's massive AI surveillance platform: the Domain Awareness System (DAS). "Every police officer in the city can access it on their phones and pull up a profile of basically anyone walking around," she says.
The platform connects more than 80,000 cameras with drones, social media data, even systems that follow cars when you drive to another state. Dahl says it can unveil who I've seen and everywhere I've been in the last week. My whole life: tracked.
Every day, across the US, your life is also being recorded by a growing system of mass surveillance that reaches far deeper than many of us may realise. Controversy around an American surveillance company called Flock Safety exploded in recent months, but it's only one player in a giant industry.
Flock and other advocates say we need to strike a compromise between privacy and safety.
Is it worth the trade-off? To decide for yourself, it's worth understanding how comprehensive the surveillance really is. So I went looking for cameras in my own neighbourhood. You can too, and you don't even need to leave the couch to find them.
'The more you start looking, the more you'll see'
Some of those concerned about surveillance seem to think Flock is the whole issue. New York City demonstrates why that's not true. The company doesn't operate here, but we're still being watched.
Dahl is taking me on a surveillance tour to the BBC's Manhattan office, pointing out cameras and other devices along the way. I've covered privacy for 10 years, but even I was stunned by the infrastructure following our every move.
After just a few steps, we stop and look around. I count 16 different cameras.
"I would assume these are owned by businesses, buildings and renters," she says. These are additional to cameras run by the city," she says. "But the NYPD likely has easy access. They often just ask the owner if there's an investigation, and people hand over the footage."
Some camera vendors, like Amazon's Ring, even have automated systems to make it easier for police to request and receive footage directly from users.
Cameras in public are now so ubiquitous I barely notice them anymore. But with Dahl's help, my eyes refocus: small pill-shaped cameras hanging in front of stores, ageing grey devices on the corners of buildings, advanced dual-camera systems run by the city that pan, tilt and zoom to laser in on people of interest.
I try to count as we walk, but there are so many it's impossible to keep track and hold up a conversation. "The more you start looking, the more you'll see," Dahl says.
Why the Flocklash?
These systems can capture and store your every move, and Flock has become the posterchild for surveillance. In recent months, there's been nation-wide, bipartisan backlash against the company.
On reason is Flock's staggering power. The company says it operates more than 100,000 cameras spread across 6,000 American communities. It's best known for tools that track drivers, scanning cars 20 billion times a month, according to Flock. But it also makes facial recognition tools to track your body.
Such technology allows law enforcement to look far beyond its jurisdiction. A Texas sheriff reportedly accessed more than 83,000 Flock cameras across the US to hunt for a woman in an abortion case, including in states where abortion is legal.
Flock says their tools keep people safe and that every day it helps solve crimes that would otherwise go unsolved. Yet in at least 46 cases, law enforcement officers have reportedlyused Flock's systems for unauthorised purposes, including to stalk partners, exes and strangers. (After months of bad press, Flock implemented safeguards to root out abuse. A Flock spokesperson says the misuse is a "betrayal of the tool's purpose and completely unacceptable" and that officers who abuse the system should be held accountable.)
The backlash includes waves of people destroying and even urinating on Flock cameras. Over 50 cities have cut ties with Flock this year alone.
But again, Flock doesn't operate everywhere, and it isn't the only company in the businesses. Some cities that cancelled Flock contracts just quietly hired other surveillance firms instead.
"Communities continue to choose Flock at a rate far outpacing those that leave," a Flock spokesperson says. "We're adding new customers at roughly 10 times the rate of churn."
Safer, or just more surveilled?
Behind the growing world of surveillance infrastructure is a wider argument about how to police.
"Every day, Flock helps solve crimes that would otherwise go unsolved – from finding missing children to solving murders, violent crime, and recovering stolen vehicles," a company spokesperson says.
They also note Flock is "actively asking for clearer state and local regulation", so it isn't the sole decider on law enforcement's use of the tools.
The NYPD makes similar points. A spokesperson says their surveillance systems keep the city safe, and the department publishes transparency reports on its tools. "We are committed to using technology with care and precision, and ensuring our use is consistent with the law," the spokesperson says.
However, experts question the data and methodology Flock – and others –use to their promote crime-solving approach.
How to watch the cameras that watch you
There are tools to help you get a feel for where these cameras are in your own neighbourhood.
One is the Atlas of Surveillance from the EFF. It lets you search by city, state, law enforcement agency or surveillance technology company. It's incomplete but includes an interactive map based on data sourced by students and researchers.
Another option is DeFlock. The idea is similar: a crowdsourced map that highlights the locations of tens of thousands of cameras made by Flock and other companies.
Anyone can edit DeFlock, so it may be less reliable. But the map identified four AI surveillance cameras in walking distance from my front door.
"The idea that surveillance makes us safer keeps being used as an excuse," says Rindala Alajaji, associate director of state affairs at the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), a digital rights group. In fact, she says, this technology makes the world more dangerous.
"Surveillance has been used to criminalise people for being bystanders, with stories of innocent people being pulled over and having guns drawn on them because a licence plate reader read a letter wrong," Alajaji says.
This isn't just a US issue, either. Facial recognition systems are expanding in the UK, which police credit with thousands of arrests, while critics describe an alarming and "significant expansion of the surveillance state". Across the globe, cameras are spreading.
Dahl and I walk nearly a mile and get on the subway. Cameras stare us down as we swipe at every stage, and document us when we exit. As we emerge onto the street in Midtown Manhattan, we're greeted by – you guessed it – more cameras.
More like this:
"I would encourage people to take a minute to pay attention to where you're being watched and tracked and learn where the data is going," says Dahl. "The more that people are aware, the more you can join in efforts to exert legislative pressure."
For example, one reason some communities have cancelled Flock contracts was people pressuring leaders at city council meetings – including by dressing like Darth Vader.
Dahl and I have been together over an hour, and barely a moment has passed that we weren't being surveilled. I say goodbye and walk to the BBC's office.
I step into the building and hit a button for the elevator. The doors open with a ding, and there, staring me in the face, is a gleaming black camera. Like everywhere else, it seems, someone is watching.
--

articles.title: Science, technology, engineering, math oh, my: science organization round-up
articles.description: Science, technology, engineering, math oh, my: science organization round-up The Daily Cardinal
articles.description_html: Science, technology, engineering, math oh, my: science organization round-up  The Daily Cardinal
articles.source: Science, technology, engineering, math oh, my: science organization round-up - The Daily Cardinal
articles.article_title: Science, technology, engineering, math oh, my: science organization round-up
articles.heading: Science, technology, engineering, math oh, my: science organization round-up
articles.summary: As students return to campus this fall, student organizations across campus are offering opportunities to find community and explore STEM interests outside of the classroom.
articles.content:
Science at the University of Wisconsin-Madison doesn’t end when class is out of session. Here at UW-Madison, undergraduate students can explore their interests in science, technology, engineering and the environment through registered student organizations that offer everything from professional development days and volunteering to field trips and hands-on projects.
For new students, these organizations can also provide a community of peers navigating similar coursework, interests and career goals.
Life sciences and health
For Badgers interested in biology, medicine, public health and other health-related fields, student organizations can provide opportunities to explore potential careers while connecting with peers on similar trajectories.
Sam Qastin, a junior at UW-Madison majoring in biology with a certificate in global health on the pre-dental track, serves as president of Mu Epsilon Delta (MED), a pre-health organization.
“Through MED, I’ve had access to incredible opportunities across Madison, including volunteering at Ronald McDonald House Charities, hosting blood drives, touring hospitals and learning directly from practicing healthcare professionals and alumni,” Qastin told The Daily Cardinal.
Qastin said MED’s combination of leadership opportunities and community has helped prepare him for a career in health care.
“The greatest benefit has been the mix of hands-on leadership and a community of like-minded peers. By encouraging every member to step into leadership roles, MED builds lasting communication skills and confidence, which has strongly solidified my own preparation for dental school,” Qastin said.
Students interested in other health and life science careers can find organizations tailored to specific fields. The Bucky Pre-Health Volunteering Association combines pre-health interests with community service, while the Pre-Genetic Counseling Organization introduces students to the field of genetic counseling with workshops and meetings. The Pre-Veterinary Association offers a similar community for students pursuing careers in veterinary medicine.
STEM Greek Life and professional development
Moira Ahern, a junior majoring in biology, told the Cardinal she joined Alpha Chi Sigma, a professional chemistry fraternity, during her freshman year.
“The frat also introduced me to many new people who I now consider my closest friends. One of my favorite parts has been being able to build a community of people who share the same STEM related interests, are taking the same classes, and are pursuing similar careers,” Ahern said.
The community has also provided academic support as students navigate difficult STEM coursework.
“I’ve known people in or who have taken the majority of my more difficult classes, which has been a great support system while studying for and choosing my classes,” Ahern said.
Kappa Eta Kappa offers a professional and social community for students in electrical engineering, computer engineering and computer science. Triangle Fraternity similarly offers a social and professional community for engineers, architects and scientists, with an emphasis on academics and career preparation.
Climate, environment and wildlife
Environment and wildlife organizations give students chances to engage with issues ranging from conservation and climate change to local ecosystems and biodiversity.
For Haily Hintz, a senior majoring in zoology with certificates in environmental studies and classics, three years in the Undergraduate Zoological Society (UZS) have provided opportunities to explore her interests and connect with like-minded peers.
“I have participated in a variety of activities including volunteering, group trips, social nights, grad student panels and faculty presentations,” Hintz said.
Last spring, UZS visited the Shedd Aquarium as a group, following a trip to the Brookfield Zoo the year before, Hintz said.
The Audubon Society offers another option for students interested in wildlife and conservation, with activities such as bird hikes and helping monitor tree swallow nest boxes. The organization aims to connect UW-Madison students and community members through dialogue, observation and study of birds and bird conservation.
Students interested in atmospheric and oceanic sciences can join the American Meteorological Society Student Chapter, which connects students with working professionals through educational and recreational opportunities.
Other environment and climate clubs offer opportunities to engage with environmental issues through conservation, sustainability, advocacy and professional development.
Engineering
More than 60 engineering-related clubs offer students ways to apply classroom concepts in hands-on projects, competitions, professional development and service. Options range from discipline-based to service, competition and identity-based organizations.
One hands-on option is the Wisconsin Space Program (WiSP), a student team working to be the first student team to fly a liquid rocket to the edge of space. WiSP members design, analyze, manufacture, test and launch high powered rocketry systems. Students can also compete in large intercollegiate rocketry competitions.
Identity-based clubs, such as the Society of Hispanic Professional Engineers or Women in Electrical & Computer Engineering, focus on professional development, leadership and opportunities for students in typically underrepresented identity groups in the field.
The Wisconsin Engineering Student Council maintains directories of these organizations for students looking to explore additional options.
Getting involved
Students do not need previous experience to get involved with many of these registered student organizations. For those still figuring out their interests, following organizations on social media, attending a meeting or visiting the Student Organization Fair can be a low-commitment way to explore options.
The fair will take place Wednesday, Sept. 9 and Thursday, Sept. 10 from 5 to 8 p.m. at the Kohl Center.

articles.title: With education technology, engagement is not the same as learning
articles.description: With education technology, engagement is not the same as learning American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.description_html: With education technology, engagement is not the same as learning  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.article_title: With education technology, engagement is not the same as learning
articles.heading: With education technology, engagement is not the same as learning
articles.summary: An APA report warns that educational technology and generative AI may boost student engagement and performance without fostering real learning, urging schools and families to prioritize evidence-based tools that build lasting knowledge and skills.
articles.content:
Washington — A new report from the American Psychological Association warns that student engagement with educational technology is not the same as learning—and that generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools pose particular risks by improving students’ immediate performance without building their underlying knowledge or skills.
The APA Expert Report on Children’s and Adolescents’ Learning with Educational Technology argues that students’ ability to apply new knowledge outside of an app or screen is a much stronger indication of learning than how much time a child spends on a screen, and that parents and educators working with children and young people ages 5 to 18 should be wary of marketing claims that run ahead of scientific evidence.
The report stresses that even if a student is paying close attention to an app, such as by clicking frequently, responding to animations, or interacting with rewards, that engagement does not necessarily mean that the student is learning.
“Educational technology has the potential to profoundly advance students’ learning and abilities, but parents, teachers, and school districts need tools that are safe, supported by evidence, and can genuinely help students learn,” said APA CEO Arthur C. Evans Jr., PhD. “These recommendations, based in psychological research, can help determine whether EdTech tools actually produce the learning outcomes they promise.”
Compiled by a multidisciplinary panel of cognitive and educational psychologists, learning scientists, and EdTech experts, the report synthesizes evidence across a wide range of technologies, including educational apps, games, intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI tools, and digital learning platforms. It offers 10 evidence-based recommendations to help families, educators, policymakers, and developers ensure that technology promotes meaningful learning.
Drawing on research from psychological science, the report recommends that schools, families, and developers prioritize tools that build durable knowledge and skills that students can carry into other contexts, instead of evaluating apps based on flashy features. Additional recommendations include making adult involvement a significant part of EdTech implementation and investing in research that can keep pace with rapid technological change.
Educators should exercise particular caution when introducing generative AI tools into learning environments, said Nicole Barnes, PhD, APA’s executive lead psychologist for education.
“AI can help a student produce a better essay, but the improved final product does not necessarily mean the student has become a better writer,” Barnes said. “Just as we need to separate engagement from learning, we will increasingly need to separate performance from learning.”
Rather than trying to prevent children and adolescents from using AI tools altogether, the report recommends teaching students to actively evaluate AI-generated responses. Students should learn to question chatbots’ assumptions and identify gaps in chatbots’ reasoning, compare responses against other sources and consider how answers might change under different circumstances. In this sense, students should approach AI less as an answer machine and more as something they are continuously testing, challenging, and learning from.
The report stresses that primary responsibility for ensuring that EdTech products are supported by evidence lies with the companies that develop them and the institutions that choose to adopt them. Developers should be prepared to demonstrate that their products improve learning, while schools and districts should expect credible, independent evidence before investing in educational technology.
APA also offers simple advice to parents: look and ask.

articles.content_html:
Washington — A new report from the American Psychological Association warns that student engagement with educational technology is not the same as learning—and that generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools pose particular risks by improving students’ immediate performance without building their underlying knowledge or skills.

The APA Expert Report on Children’s and Adolescents’ Learning with Educational Technology argues that students’ ability to apply new knowledge outside of an app or screen is a much stronger indication of learning than how much time a child spends on a screen, and that parents and educators working with children and young people ages 5 to 18 should be wary of marketing claims that run ahead of scientific evidence.

The report stresses that even if a student is paying close attention to an app, such as by clicking frequently, responding to animations, or interacting with rewards, that engagement does not necessarily mean that the student is learning.

“Educational technology has the potential to profoundly advance students’ learning and abilities, but parents, teachers, and school districts need tools that are safe, supported by evidence, and can genuinely help students learn,” said APA CEO Arthur C. Evans Jr., PhD. “These recommendations, based in psychological research, can help determine whether EdTech tools actually produce the learning outcomes they promise.”

Compiled by a multidisciplinary panel of cognitive and educational psychologists, learning scientists, and EdTech experts, the report synthesizes evidence across a wide range of technologies, including educational apps, games, intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI tools, and digital learning platforms. It offers 10 evidence-based recommendations to help families, educators, policymakers, and developers ensure that technology promotes meaningful learning.

Drawing on research from psychological science, the report recommends that schools, families, and developers prioritize tools that build durable knowledge and skills that students can carry into other contexts, instead of evaluating apps based on flashy features. Additional recommendations include making adult involvement a significant part of EdTech implementation and investing in research that can keep pace with rapid technological change.

Educators should exercise particular caution when introducing generative AI tools into learning environments, said Nicole Barnes, PhD, APA’s executive lead psychologist for education.

“AI can help a student produce a better essay, but the improved final product does not necessarily mean the student has become a better writer,” Barnes said. “Just as we need to separate engagement from learning, we will increasingly need to separate performance from learning.”

Rather than trying to prevent children and adolescents from using AI tools altogether, the report recommends teaching students to actively evaluate AI-generated responses. Students should learn to question chatbots’ assumptions and identify gaps in chatbots’ reasoning, compare responses against other sources and consider how answers might change under different circumstances. In this sense, students should approach AI less as an answer machine and more as something they are continuously testing, challenging, and learning from.

The report stresses that primary responsibility for ensuring that EdTech products are supported by evidence lies with the companies that develop them and the institutions that choose to adopt them. Developers should be prepared to demonstrate that their products improve learning, while schools and districts should expect credible, independent evidence before investing in educational technology.

APA also offers simple advice to parents: look and ask.

  • Spend a minute watching the app and pay attention to what is happening on the screen—if much of the experience involves dressing a character, selecting accessories, collecting rewards, or responding to flashing images, it is reasonable to question the app’s educational value.
  • Ask a teacher, principal, early childhood leader, or school board whether there is credible, independent evidence showing that the app leads to learning.

articles.summary: How GM engineers integrate new technology, customer feedback, and plenty of testing into a cohesive experience.
articles.content:
Cadillac ESCALADE IQ shows the power of customer-informed technology


2026-09-02











The Cadillac ESCALADE IQ is a technology leader. It’s a vehicle that shows how GM puts customers first, by first understanding how customers use their vehicles, then engineering technology around those needs.
In GM’s own studies, the all-electric ESCALADE IQ delivered a significantly more appealing customer experience than competitors in the segment. Cameras, climate and comfort, and personalization drove positive impressions of the ESCALADE IQ.
Turn-signal side cameras can help build confidence around blind spots, while additional camera views support drivers making tight maneuvers1. Instead of digging around menus and submenus in the infotainment interface, a dedicated HVAC screen makes climate adjustments feel readily available. Profile-based personalization helps a shared vehicle feel tailored to each driver.
“When you’re engineering a product as iconic as an Escalade, the pressure’s high to wow a discerning customer group,” said Mandi Damman, executive chief engineer for the Escalade IQ. “Every piece of tech, from the pillar-to-pillar screen to each camera, has to be beautifully integrated.”
Customer research helps GM determine which technologies earn a place in the vehicle and how they should work together. “We do have insights on the tech, experiences, and messages that resonate most with customer segments and brands,” said Julia Hedrick of Global Customer Research.
That insight is visible in developing features such as the Rear Camera Mirror, power-closing doors and Super Cruise2. Each can help address a tangible need — visibility, ease and reduced stress on longer drives — rather than adding technology for its own sake. Premium audio enriches a daily experience, while connected cameras support confidence and connection inside the cabin.
Behind every effortless interaction is extensive engineering, testing, and iteration. For Escalade IQ, customer feedback continues shaping the experience and informing the next generation of GM vehicles, including more integrated, updatable software-defined technologies.
1Limited to low speeds. Always pay attention to your surroundings. Read the vehicle Owner’s Manual for important feature limitations and information.
2Always pay attention while driving and when using Super Cruise. Always use Super Cruise in accordance with local laws. Do not use a hand-held device. Requires active Super Cruise plan or trial. Terms apply. Visit Chevrolet.com for compatible roads and full details.

National IT Industry Promotion Agency (NIPA)

K-AI Semiconductor Pavilion Brings Korea’s Next-Generation AI Semiconductor Technologies to IFA 2026
| National IT Industry Promotion Agency (NIPA) / Key word(s): Miscellaneous K-AI Semiconductor Pavilion Brings Korea’s Next-Generation AI Semiconductor Technologies to IFA 2026 03.09.2026 / 09:05 CET/CEST The issuer is solely responsible for the content of this announcement. 12 Korean companies and organizations to showcase AI computing, NPU, on-device and edge AI technologies, while K-AI Connect connects global buyers, investors and industry partners BERLIN, Sept. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Korea’s AI semiconductor ecosystem will take center stage at IFA 2026, as 12 Korean companies and organizations showcase advanced technologies and real-world applications at the K-AI Semiconductor Pavilion from September 4 to 8 at Messe Berlin. Organized by the National IT Industry Promotion Agency (NIPA), the pavilion aims to promote the global competitiveness of Korea’s AI semiconductor industry and help Korean technology companies expand into international markets. NIPA is a Korean public agency dedicated to strengthening the competitiveness of the country’s AI and ICT industries and driving digital innovation. Its key initiatives include strengthening national AI computing infrastructure, accelerating AI transformation across industries, and supporting Korean AI and ICT companies in expanding into global markets. In the AI semiconductor sector, NIPA supports technology development and commercialization, helping promising technologies move into real-world industries and services. Located at Hall 5.2b, Stand 400, the K-AI Semiconductor Pavilion brings together 12 Korean companies and organizations. It shows how Korea’s AI semiconductor technologies move beyond chips to become practical AI solutions across industries and everyday life. Visitors can explore technologies ranging from high-performance AI computing infrastructure and Neural Processing Units (NPUs) to on-device and edge AI solutions. The pavilion will present real-world applications in smart cities, safety, mobility and robotics, demonstrating how Korean AI semiconductor technologies can be integrated into products, services and industrial environments. Organized by the National IT Industry Promotion Agency (NIPA), the pavilion aims to promote the global competitiveness of Korea’s AI semiconductor industry and help Korean technology companies expand into international markets.

NIPA is a Korean public agency dedicated to strengthening the competitiveness of the country’s AI and ICT industries and driving digital innovation. Its key initiatives include strengthening national AI computing infrastructure, accelerating AI transformation across industries, and supporting Korean AI and ICT companies in expanding into global markets. In the AI semiconductor sector, NIPA supports technology development and commercialization, helping promising technologies move into real-world industries and services.

Located at Hall 5.2b, Stand 400, the K-AI Semiconductor Pavilion brings together 12 Korean companies and organizations. It shows how Korea’s AI semiconductor technologies move beyond chips to become practical AI solutions across industries and everyday life.

Visitors can explore technologies ranging from high-performance AI computing infrastructure and Neural Processing Units (NPUs) to on-device and edge AI solutions. The pavilion will present real-world applications in smart cities, safety, mobility and robotics, demonstrating how Korean AI semiconductor technologies can be integrated into products, services and industrial environments.

Through exhibits and demonstrations, global buyers, investors and technology partners can discover Korean AI semiconductor capabilities and explore potential business and technology partnerships.

articles.title: CONSUMABLES TECHNOLOGY OUTLOOK—The Invisible Side of Automation: Ink Management
articles.description: CONSUMABLES TECHNOLOGY OUTLOOK—The Invisible Side of Automation: Ink Management WhatTheyThink
articles.description_html: CONSUMABLES TECHNOLOGY OUTLOOK—The Invisible Side of Automation: Ink Management  WhatTheyThink
articles.article_title: CONSUMABLES TECHNOLOGY OUTLOOK—The Invisible Side of Automation: Ink Management
articles.heading: CONSUMABLES TECHNOLOGY OUTLOOK—The Invisible Side of Automation: Ink Management
articles.summary: CONSUMABLES TECHNOLOGY OUTLOOK—The Invisible Side of Automation: Ink Management
articles.content:
Much of this Technology Outlook issue has focused on automation, and a lot has been written here and elsewhere about software automation, production automation, the ubiquitous AI, and even robotics. And yet, offset shops still often have a press operators manually adding ink to the fountain. So one aspect of production automation that often gets overlooked is automated ink management.
“It’s a gap in automation,” said David Doucette, Director of Sales for Sentinel Ink Management Systems. “We’ve had this product for decades and it’s probably more relevant now than it was when it came out, because it’s always been about automating and improving operational efficiency.”
The product is the Sentinel Ink Management System, a computer-controlled, fully automated ink dispensing solution that monitors ink levels across an entire ink fountain and automatically adds the correct amount of ink precisely when and where it’s required. “It’s only adding ink into the fountain where it’s low,” said Doucette. “It’s not just arbitrary, or dumping ink across the whole fountain. It reads the fountain and only adds it where it needs it.”
The Sentinel System constantly monitors the ink fountain and automatically adds ink only when and where it is needed.
The system lets print businesses optimize their labor, especially given the latest press trends. “Most of the presses we’re seeing now are eight colors—we see very few that are less than eight colors,” said Doucette, “and they’re running faster than they’ve ever run, which means they’re consuming ink faster than they ever have. So when you put together all these colors and the fast speeds, you’d need one guy basically just filling ink if you’re doing it by hand.” By automating this process, it allows the press operator(s) to focus on the quality of the current job and queuing up the next one. “It's a huge boon for the guys running the press.”
And one Sentinel customer has a 14-color Heidelberg—as far as I know, the largest press in the Western Hemisphere. It would be very difficult to monitor and refill all that ink manually.
The advantages to this system are not just in terms of not needing a press operator to manually monitor ink and refill the fountain, but also better color consistency. “Even with the automation to maintain color that the press has, it’s chasing it because you can’t get away from the fact that if you have a lot of ink one moment and 20 minutes later you’re almost out of ink, it doesn’t print the same,” said Doucette.
Another advantage of automated ink management is reduced costs—not just labor, but because there is far less ink waste. And of course less waste also translates to better sustainability.
The Sentinel system uses large ink canisters that then feed the fountain, but what happens when the canisters themselves run low? When ink in the canister reaches a certain level, an audible alarm goes off and lights flash—alerts that are pretty hard to miss—and replacing the canister is a 10-second swap.
Swapping out an ink canister takes only 10 seconds.
The Sentinel Ink Management System is compatible with any offset press from any manufacturer, and accepts automated cartridges from all ink vendors and suppliers in both 8-lb. and 2kg sizes. It also handles PMS colors—an ink type that in particular benefits from effective ink management. “When you run a PMS color, it’s going to be the most expensive ink you buy,” said Doucette, “so you don’t want to waste it.” And excess ink will keep better and longer in a canister than if it’s put back in a can.
The Sentinel system can even be retrofitted to older presses—even very old presses. “I got a call a from a guy who said, ‘My press is really old,’” said Doucette. “I said, ‘How old is really old?’ and he said, ‘It’s 62.’ ‘Yeah, we can set that up, no problem.’ We do a lot of retrofits.”
There are three varieties of the Sentinel System:
- Sentinel iPro monitors and dispenses ink, keeping it at a consistent level.
- Sentinel Ranger connects to a bulk ink system for uninterrupted flow.
- Sentinel RemoteLinc is an adapter that replaces an 8-lb. cartridge and draws ink directly from bulk supply drums via a hydraulic hose to deliver consistent feed pressure.
The Sentinel RemoteLinc adapter draws ink directly from bulk supply drums.
As we saw in the previous article, a big trend in ink today is a move to energy-curable ink, especially UV-curable ink. “One of the things that we see with UV inks is their viscosity—they’re very thick and don’t want to flow down into the nip in the fountain,” said Doucette. So the Sentinel system always includes agitators called plows that keep the viscous ink from just sitting in the fountain and get it flowing.
Another major trend in print businesses today is data collection, and Sentinel includes an ink reporting system that shows every station on the press, how much ink is left in each canister, and how much ink has been consumed on the job so far. At the end of the job, the system can print out a report that specifies exactly how much ink was used on each color for that job. This data can then be uploaded to the costing and estimating department to confirm that what was estimated vis-à-vis ink was what was actually used. This can then increase the accuracy of estimates on future jobs, such as reprints.
“I find that the press manufacturers particularly like that because they’re telling me that most of their customers are very data-driven right now,” said Doucette. “They’re looking for all of those data points to be part of their costing model.”
If you’re going to be at the upcoming PRINTING United, Sentinel will be demonstrating their system.
Even if you opt for another kind of ink management system, it’s an important yet often undiscussed aspect of the automation conversations the industry has been having more and more often—and will in all likelihood continue to have.

articles.summary: Some Texas lawmakers have suggested plans to move toward new regulations aimed at reducing how much water data centers use as the industry rapidly expands acros
articles.content:
Technology could cut water usage by data centers. Will it be required by Texas law?
AUSTIN, Texas — Some Texas lawmakers have suggested plans to move toward new regulations aimed at reducing how much water data centers use as the industry rapidly expands across the state.
The boom in data centers has brought growing concern about the power and water needed to keep the facilities running, and lawmakers say some sites use far more water than others.
State Sen. Charles Perry, R-Lubbock, said during a Senate hearing on Tuesday that he wants to curb the use of evaporative cooling systems, which rely on a constant input of water that evaporates during the cooling process.
“There’s no reason you should waste water on an evaporative cooling system. I hope that’s loud and clear. That won’t be allowed coming out of next session,” Perry said.
Evaporative cooling is one approach used in some data centers, where water is brought in to cool equipment and then evaporates out.
Another design uses a closed loop, in which coolant circulates through the servers. But researchers say its water footprint depends on how the system releases heat: dry or air cooling can sharply reduce direct water use, while an evaporative cooling tower still consumes water.
RELATED| Austin City Council unanimously moves forward with new data center regulations
Margaret Cook, vice president of water and community resilience at the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC), noted that closed-loop technology could significantly reduce water usage by data centers, depending on the technology used to cool the internal water.
"Whatever that technology is will dictate the water consumption. So if you have something that's an air cooler or a dry cooler, then it's not going to have significant water consumption, but if you use a water chiller or a cooling tower, as I mentioned before, then that will have significant use, and the amount of water that's used can really vary a whole lot," Cook said.
Cook said certain closed-loop systems can use more electricity than water-based cooling, potentially shifting some of the water footprint to power generation.
“To be able to switch to air or dry cooling, that will increase the amount of power that is needed for operating that facility,” Cook said.
Instead of mandating certain technologies in data centers, Cook supports setting water-efficiency standards, arguing that a technology mandate could become outdated and that regulators should evaluate a facility’s full water-and-energy footprint.
There are also less direct water inputs for data centers, including the plants needed to power them.
Risto Paldanius, vice president of Wärtsilä Energy, described the closed-loop technology his company uses to provide power to data centers around the world during an interview on Wednesday.
“We use a thousand times less water than, for example, the turbine technologies,” he said of the company's engine power plants.
Paldanius said the data center industry is still relatively new at its current scale.
“Right now, we’re providing large power plants, hundreds of megawatts, to data center utilization, which is of course great, that these power plants of ours don’t use water,” he said.
Companies have also been making commitments to lawmakers this week about their water usage.
“Since 2019, every single data center that QTS has built has been a closed-loop system that consumes essentially zero water for cooling once we’re operational,” Ryan Kuithe, senior vice president of facility operations at QTS Data Centers, told lawmakers Tuesday.
Lawmakers plan to take up the issue when they return to the Capitol in January.

articles.title: G20 nations reach consensus on global technology policy
articles.description: G20 nations reach consensus on global technology policy Anadolu Ajansı
articles.description_html: G20 nations reach consensus on global technology policy  Anadolu Ajansı
articles.article_title: G20 nations reach consensus on global technology policy
articles.heading: G20 nations reach consensus on global technology policy
articles.summary: Ministers adopt Carolina Principles to secure AI intellectual property, strengthen industrial supply chains | Anadolu
articles.content:
G20 ministers concluded a two-day Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on Wednesday, reaching a consensus on the governance and deployment of emerging technologies.

“Achieving consensus in the G20 is no small feat, but the topic of innovation as a driver of growth brought us together for a historic moment of unity,” said US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He asserted that the agreement provides entrepreneurs with the confidence to invest while ensuring that intellectual property frameworks foster and protect innovation.

The consensus statement, known as the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, outlines shared objectives in six critical pillars. They include pro-innovation policy frameworks, technology for opportunity and prosperity, and skilled technical workforce development. The principles specifically urge member nations to invest in foundational research and strengthen commercialization pathways.

The framework also prioritizes intellectual property policies for Artificial Intelligence (AI) alongside the creation of standards for AI systems and industrial innovation through investment in supply chains.

The meeting also launched the AI Prosperity Objectives and the AI Prosperity Compact to further “technical workforce development across G20 nations and expand opportunities for private sector partnership.”

Michael Kratsios, director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), which advises the US executive branch on tech issues, noted the vision relies on flexible policy frameworks to drive global growth.

The summit, hosted by the US Commerce Department and OSTP, featured high-level fireside chats with prominent tech leaders including Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, Jensen Huang of NVIDIA, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Mark Zuckerberg of Meta.

The meeting included representatives from 20 nations and unions, including Türkiye, China, the European Union, Russia and the UK.

articles.title: Descreened: Helping young people find balance with technology
articles.description: Descreened: Helping young people find balance with technology North Texas e-News
articles.description_html: Descreened: Helping young people find balance with technology  North Texas e-News
articles.article_title: Descreened: Helping young people find balance with technology
articles.heading: Descreened: Helping young people find balance with technology
articles.summary: Technology has become an important part of everyday life for young people. Students use laptops for school, phones to communicate with friends and family, and screens for entertainment. While technology can be useful, spending too much time on screens can make it harder for young people to focus on other important parts of life. A group of North Texas students recognized this issue and created Descreened, a student-led nonprofit that encourages healthier and more intentional relationships with technology.
articles.content:
Technology has become an important part of everyday life for young people. Students use laptops for school, phones to communicate with friends and family, and screens for entertainment. While technology can be useful, spending too much time on screens can make it harder for young people to focus on other important parts of life. A group of North Texas students recognized this issue and created Descreened, a student-led nonprofit that encourages healthier and more intentional relationships with technology.
Descreened does not believe that technology itself is bad. Instead, the organization focuses on finding a healthy balance between digital and offline activities. Its leaders encourage young people to continue using technology for education, communication, and creativity while also making time for hobbies, physical activity, friendships, and other experiences that do not involve screens. This approach is different from simply telling teenagers to stop using their phones because it gives them meaningful alternatives.
One of Descreened's major projects is its screen-free activity kit initiative. The organization has donated approximately 40 kits through Health Services of North Texas. These kits give children activities they can enjoy without a phone, tablet, or television. The idea is that reducing screen time is easier when children have interesting activities to replace it. These activities can encourage creativity, problem-solving, movement, and interaction with other people.
Descreened has also worked to understand how students themselves experience technology. The organization has surveyed more than 1,000 students about their technology habits. Through its programs and initiatives, Descreened reports that approximately 250 students have reduced their screen time, with participants reporting an average decrease of about one hour and 49 minutes. These results show how students can take an active role in addressing an issue that directly affects their generation.
Another important part of Descreened's mission is encouraging young people to spend time in community spaces, sometimes called "third places." Libraries, parks, recreation centers, and other public spaces give young people opportunities to socialize and build relationships outside of home and school. Descreened believes these spaces are especially valuable as more communication and entertainment move online. Activities such as playing sports, creating art, playing board games, spending time outdoors, or simply having a conversation can help young people reconnect with the world around them.
Ultimately, Descreened is trying to create a different conversation about technology. The organization does not ask young people to give up smartphones or return to a world without technology. Instead, its student leaders encourage their peers to be more thoughtful about when they use technology and when they should put it down.
As Descreened continues to grow, it plans to expand its screen-free programs, create more educational resources, strengthen community partnerships, and reach more children and families. Its goal is not simply to reduce screen-time numbers, but to help young people make more room for meaningful experiences that cannot happen through a screen.

articles.title: LA Unified School District examines future of AI in education
articles.description: LA Unified School District examines future of AI in education CBS News
articles.description_html: LA Unified School District examines future of AI in education  CBS News
articles.article_title: LA Unified School District examines future of AI in education
articles.heading: LA Unified School District examines future of AI in education
articles.summary: While LAUSD has restricted student access to generative AI platforms this school year, staff is examining how to teach students to use the technology without becoming reliant on it.
articles.content:
LA Unified School District examines future of AI in education
The Los Angeles Unified School District is examining how to integrate generative AI platforms into its educational programs.
While the district allowed students 13 and older to use AI tools under certain conditions last year, the school board restricted access to the platforms this year as its Generative AI Committee crafts a curriculum for the technology.
"They make mistakes when you ask them a question and so not to take their responses face value," aid Dominic Kagiwa, director of Educational Technology and Innovation.
LAUSD said the goal of the curriculum is to teach students how to use AI without becoming reliant on it.
"Not only professional learning, but also a curriculum across grade levels that does not necessarily require students to use an AI platform but still understand, without using the technology, what AI is and what it is not," Kagiwa said.
AI experts said the answer isn't necessarily to ban the technology but to teach students how to use it responsibly.
"Tech has sort of come in and said, we have a platform that can let you do all these things, please buy it, and your kids will learn," said Steven Aguilar, an associate professor of education at USC. "That often isn't true. But that doesn't mean that we need to exclude our kids from actually using AI."
For now, LAUSD students looking to get some help from AI are out of luck.
"I feel there are positives and negatives to it," high school senior Sophie Barnett said. "I definitely think it will have a good impact on certain people who actually want to learn in school."

articles.title: South Plains producers turn to new technology to sustain ranching legacy
articles.description: South Plains producers turn to new technology to sustain ranching legacy fox34.com
articles.description_html: South Plains producers turn to new technology to sustain ranching legacy  fox34.com
articles.article_title: South Plains producers turn to new technology to sustain ranching legacy
articles.heading: South Plains producers turn to new technology to sustain ranching legacy
articles.summary: The Ranching and Technology Summit features new innovations farmers and ranchers are using.
articles.content:
South Plains producers turn to new technology to sustain ranching legacy
Farmers and ranchers gathered at the National Ranching Heritage Center for the Ranching Technology Summit
LUBBOCK, Texas (KCBD) - Farmers and ranchers met at the National Ranching Heritage Center for the Ranching Technology Summit on Wednesday.
Jim Bret Campbell, executive director of the Heritage Center, said the industry needs new innovation.
“We focus here at the Ranching Heritage Center on the heritage of ranching. And we tell that story...over the past 200 years. But there have always been innovations in ranching. And we’re really blessed right now to be in an era where there is so much innovation and so many tools and resources available to really help make ranching successful,” Campbell said.
Campbell said these technologies range from healthier soil to smarter rotational grazing to new cattle management. He said it starts in the ground.
“So, we’re really focusing on several main buckets of technologies. One that really all starts with soil health and how do we improve our soil health across our rangelands, really across the semi-arid areas of the Great Plains, and what we actually focus on here on the South Plains,” Campbell said.
Focus on water conservation
In West Texas, every drop of water counts.
“We’ll also be looking at water and how do we capture the precious inches of rainfall that we do get here on the South Plains and really maximize that,” Campbell said.
Farming and ranching is passed through generations. Rancher Tye Chesser said that’s why new tools matter.
“What my granddad did in the ’50s and what my dad has done and what we are working to do differently now is making it to where hopefully my kids will have an opportunity, if they want to, to go back to the ranch and be a part of it,” Chesser said.

articles.title: Jim Cramer says investors aren't ditching tech — they just want cheaper stocks
articles.description: Jim Cramer says investors aren't ditching tech — they just want cheaper stocks CNBC
articles.description_html: Jim Cramer says investors aren't ditching tech — they just want cheaper stocks  CNBC
articles.article_title: Jim Cramer says investors aren't ditching tech — they just want cheaper stocks
articles.heading: Jim Cramer says investors aren't ditching tech — they just want cheaper stocks
articles.summary: CNBC's Jim Cramer said investors aren’t abandoning AI or technology stocks — they’re rotating out of high-multiple names and into cheaper stocks.
articles.content:
CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday investors aren't abandoning artificial intelligence or technology stocks altogether — they're ditching expensive stocks.
"There's no revulsion to the data center or AI stocks or even momentum plays, it's just that when bond yields go up, money managers dump their expensive stocks and swap into cheaper ones," the "Mad Money" host said.
Some of the market's highest-flying technology stocks have come under pressure in recent weeks, fueling concerns that enthusiasm for AI is fading. Cramer said that's not the case and investors have simply become less willing to pay premium valuations for stocks that need near-perfect results to keep climbing.
A common way to compare valuations is the forward price-to-earnings multiple, which divides a company's share price by its expected earnings per share over the next 12 months. The higher the multiple, the more investors are paying for each dollar of expected earnings.
"The buyers aren't fleeing from the data center or tech in general, they're just fearful of high multiple tech stocks, ... because they have to be perfect," he said.
Cramer pointed to MongoDB, which trades at roughly 52 times expected earnings over the next 12 months. Shares of the database software company dropped around 13% Wednesday despite reporting better-than-expected earnings and upbeat guidance.
Dell, on the other hand, trades at roughly 16 times forward earnings and rallied 16% after reporting strong results Tuesday. For Cramer, the contrasting reactions show that investors remain willing to buy technology and AI stocks when valuations and fundamentals are attractive.
"As it happens, many of the data center plays have high multiples, but the ones that don't, like Dell, are doing fine," Cramer said.
Nvidia offered another example, he said. Despite being at the center of the AI boom, the chipmaker trades at roughly 17 times expected earnings over the next 12 months — significantly cheaper than many slower-growing technology companies.
Cramer said Nvidia's relatively low multiple reflects skepticism that its extraordinary earnings growth can continue as investors question the durability of data center spending. He said those concerns are misplaced, pointing to Dell's results as evidence that customers are beginning to generate meaningful returns from their AI investments.
"What the heck is Nvidia doing with such a low price to earnings multiple despite the phenomenal growth?" Cramer said.
For Cramer, the recent sell-off isn't evidence that the AI trade is broken. Investors still want AI and technology stocks, he said, but they're becoming much more selective about the price they're willing to pay.
"We hear that investors are fleeing the artificial intelligence trade. Or that they don't want to own technology anymore. Or the data center's become a nightmare. Or, worst of all, the momentum trade is broken," he said. "These are all wrong. ... They're getting the symptoms right — these groups truly are going down — but missing the real cause."
