articles.title: Westside issues new limits on technology as parent group pushes for school screentime legislation
articles.description: Westside issues new limits on technology as parent group pushes for school screentime legislation WOWT
articles.description_html: Westside issues new limits on technology as parent group pushes for school screentime legislation  WOWT
articles.article_title: Westside issues new limits on technology as parent group pushes for school screentime legislation
articles.heading: Westside issues new limits on technology as parent group pushes for school screentime legislation
articles.summary: A group of parents advocating for less screen time in classrooms is gaining momentum and now wants to change Nebraska law.
articles.content:
Westside issues new limits on technology as parent group pushes for school screentime legislation
OMAHA, Neb. (WOWT) - A group of parents advocating for less screen time in classrooms is gaining momentum and now wants to change Nebraska law.
The group, called Pencils Before Pixels, has been working with Westside Community Schools leaders since July. The district started the school year with new rules for student iPad use.
New Westside rules
In an email sent to parents, Westside said it will no longer allow students to use iPads during recess. The district is also taking away the option during free time.
Westside will restrict YouTube access to third through 12th grade students, and only with teacher instruction and for educational purposes. The district is also banning YouTube Shorts for all students at every grade level.
Parents say district more aware of concerns
Paul Vonderfecht is a co-founder of Pencils Before Pixels and a Westside Community Schools parent. He said parents feel the district has become more cognizant of their concerns.
“We feel like if there is that transparency, then just that in itself will affect behavior so that there is truly educational, intentional usage,” Vonderfecht said.
Vonderfecht said parents have noticed through communication with principals and teachers that the district is more aware that parents are concerned about technology usage, and that the district wants iPad use to be more educational and intentional. He said there are still specific learning programs the group wants to limit.
Group expands to other districts
Vonderfecht said parents of Omaha Public Schools, Millard and Gretna students are now joining Pencils Before Pixels. He said the group is also looking for a maximum daily screen time limit for all grades, not just for classroom use but also when iPads are sent home for homework.
“We’re also trying to get just a maximum screen time daily limit, which is not just for the classroom, but also when it’s sent home to be used for homework. So, same stuff that Iowa enacted, we’re trying to get the same legislation in Nebraska,” Vonderfecht said.
Parents to meet with state senators
Vonderfecht and other parents from multiple districts plan to travel to the Capitol next week to meet with state senators on the Education Committee. The group is seeking legislation that would place stricter regulations on schools so they are more transparent with parents about their children’s technology usage.
Other districts’ policies
Omaha Public Schools shares some information about the iPads students take home, but not how often they are used or what they are used for. The district’s superintendent said at the start of this school year that OPS is working on guidelines so elementary students use iPads less.
No technology policy was found in the handbooks or codes of conduct for Millard or Gretna. Those districts were contacted for comment but did not respond.

articles.article_title: New TDOT technology aims to keep truck drivers off I-40 shoulders, ramps
articles.heading: New TDOT technology aims to keep truck drivers off I-40 shoulders, ramps
articles.summary: TDOT is testing new technologies to track open truck parking spaces at the Interstate 40 Welcome Center in Smith County.
articles.content:
New TDOT technology aims to keep truck drivers off I-40 shoulders, ramps
TDOT said the technologies will be evaluated over the coming months.
What This Story Is About
- TDOT is testing new technologies to track open truck parking spaces at the Interstate 40 Welcome Center in Smith County.
Why It Matters
- A national truck parking shortage leads to drivers parking dangerously on shoulders and ramps.
What Happens Next
- TDOT said the technologies will be evaluated over the coming months to determine the recommended technologies and standards for future statewide scaling across all truck parking facilities.
SMITH COUNTY, Tenn. (WSMV) - The Tennessee Department of Transportation is testing new technology that tracks open truck parking spaces at the Interstate 40 Welcome Center in Smith County.
The pilot project, which was a coordinated effort with TDOT and Stantec, was designed to help commercial truck drivers find safe, reliable parking when moving essential freight across the Southeast.
Truck drivers can use QR codes on signs in the area and are encouraged to submit feedback on the technologies to help TDOT determine the most reliable occupancy detection technology.
TDOT said the technologies will be evaluated over the coming months to determine the recommended technologies and standards for future statewide scaling across all truck parking facilities.
TDOT deployed four methods of monitoring technology:
- Magnetometers — to detect the number of trucks entering and exiting the Welcome Center’s eastbound lot.
- Radar-Camera Fusion Sensor — to detect the number of trucks entering and exiting the Welcome Center’s eastbound lot, and to detect the number of available parking spaces in the Welcome Center’s westbound lot.
- Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) — to detect the number of available parking spaces in the Welcome Center’s westbound lot.
- Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) cameras — to detect the number of available parking spaces in the Welcome Center’s westbound lot.
TDOT said the technology helps provide real-time availability information to truck drivers through roadside signage and in-cab alerts through Electronic Logging Devices.
Similar to TDOT Smartway cameras, any camera deployed at the I-40 Welcome Center to monitor parking will not be recorded or used for enforcement purposes.
TDOT said truck drivers often cannot find safe or official parking spaces and opt for parking on the shoulders and ramps, posing a “serious safety hazard” to not only themselves, but the public.
“A shortage of commercial truck parking continues to be an issue across the country, and TDOT is implementing this program to find viable solutions in Tennessee,” TDOT said. “By providing advanced notification of anticipated parking availability, drivers can make informed decisions on whether they can stretch to their hours-of-service limits or need to stop before reaching the I-40 Welcome Center to find adequate parking.”

articles.title: Fair game: Restoring technology neutrality through plug-in hybrid utility factor adjustment
articles.description: Fair game: Restoring technology neutrality through plug-in hybrid utility factor adjustment International Council on Clean Transportation
articles.description_html: Fair game: Restoring technology neutrality through plug-in hybrid utility factor adjustment  International Council on Clean Transportation
articles.article_title: Fair game: Restoring technology neutrality through plug-in hybrid utility factor adjustment - International Council on Clean Transportation
articles.heading: Fair game: Restoring technology neutrality through plug-in hybrid utility factor adjustment
articles.summary: Analyzes the impact of the EU’s utility factor curve correction on the gap between real-world and official CO2 emissions of plug-in hybrid electric vehicles and suggests a methodology to regularly update the utility factor curve using real-world data.
articles.content:
Working Paper
Fair game: Restoring technology neutrality through plug-in hybrid utility factor adjustment
The utility factor (UF) curve is the central variable used for calculating the official CO2 emissions for plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) in Europe. It defines the assumed real-world share of kilometers PHEVs are driven in charge-depleting mode—that is, in a mode using mostly electricity. The UF curve hence determines how low a PHEV’s official CO2 emissions can be.
Previous research has shown that real-world CO2 emissions from PHEVs substantially exceed official type-approval values used for manufacturer compliance, due to overly optimistic assumptions about real-world usage. The European Commission has acknowledged this fault and took a first step in 2025 in correcting the UF curve, with a second adjustment scheduled for 2027.
To clarify the discrepancies between the official and real-world CO2 emissions of PHEVs, this working paper uses on-board fuel and energy consumption monitoring (OBFCM) data from approximately 920,000 PHEVs registered in Europe between 2021 and 2023 to answer three questions:
- Will the European Commission’s scheduled 2027 correction to the UF curve be sufficient to close the gap between real-world and type-approval CO2 emissions?
- Will the higher electric range of new PHEV modes entering the market be enough to narrow the gap without UF curve adjustments?
- How can OBFCM data be used to maintain the UF curve to ensure that it reflects developments in PHEV technology and real-world usage?
Key Findings
The analysis finds that there was a substantial and fast-growing gap between real-world and type-approval CO2 emissions for PHEVs registered in 2021–2023. Fleet-average CO2 emissions during real-world driving were 3.5 times higher than type-approval values in 2021 and 4.6 times higher in 2023.
Two reinforcing trends drive this divergence. Real-world CO2 emissions are increasing as drive shares in charge-depleting mode are declining despite increasing electric ranges, leaving PHEV CO2 emissions only around 18% lower than those of internal combustion engine vehicles and conventional hybrids (ICVEs). At the same time, official PHEV CO2 emission values continue to drop rapidly, as the UF curve assumes that a longer electric range translates into greater electric use in practice. However, the analysis finds that the gap between real-world and type-approval emissions doesn’t decrease as electric range increases—on the contrary, the higher the electric range, the wider the gap.
This divergence between official and real-world emissions currently gives PHEVs an unfair advantage compared with ICEVs in the calculation of manufacturer emissions compliance. It furthermore misleads consumers about expected energy costs and unduly provides PHEVs privileges in incentive and taxation schemes. The report therefore presents a methodology for adjusting official PHEV CO2 emissions by updating the UF curve based on OBFCM data.
The analysis points to two priority actions for policymakers:
- Retain the 2027 UF curve adjustment in order to achieve a realistic representation of PHEVs in the EU CO2 standards. Even after the 2025 correction, type-approval CO₂ values for PHEVs will remain well below real-world levels, giving them an undue compliance advantage over ICEVs. The 2027 correction is expected to bring the PHEV gap closer to that observed for ICEVs; weakening or postponing it would perpetuate this discrepancy.
- Update the UF curve regularly using real-world OBFCM emissions data, beginning after the 2027 correction takes effect. To ensure that official PHEV CO2 emissions more accurately reflect real-world emissions, and, thereby, are treated equally as ICEVs with regards to CO2 standards, the European Commission can commit to a regular review of the UF curve with the reference distance recalibrated based on OBFCM data, as per the methodology proposed in this paper.

Real-world CO2 emissions are increasing as drive shares in charge-depleting mode are declining despite increasing electric ranges, leaving PHEV CO2 emissions only around 18% lower than those of internal combustion engine vehicles and conventional hybrids (ICVEs). At the same time, official PHEV CO2 emission values continue to drop rapidly, as the UF curve assumes that a longer electric range translates into greater electric use in practice. However, the analysis finds that the gap between real-world and type-approval emissions doesn’t decrease as electric range increases—on the contrary, the higher the electric range, the wider the gap.

This divergence between official and real-world emissions currently gives PHEVs an unfair advantage compared with ICEVs in the calculation of manufacturer emissions compliance. It furthermore misleads consumers about expected energy costs and unduly provides PHEVs privileges in incentive and taxation schemes. The report therefore presents a methodology for adjusting official PHEV CO2 emissions by updating the UF curve based on OBFCM data.

The analysis points to two priority actions for policymakers:

  • Retain the 2027 UF curve adjustment in order to achieve a realistic representation of PHEVs in the EU CO2 standards. Even after the 2025 correction, type-approval CO₂ values for PHEVs will remain well below real-world levels, giving them an undue compliance advantage over ICEVs. The 2027 correction is expected to bring the PHEV gap closer to that observed for ICEVs; weakening or postponing it would perpetuate this discrepancy.
  • Update the UF curve regularly using real-world OBFCM emissions data, beginning after the 2027 correction takes effect. To ensure that official PHEV CO2 emissions more accurately reflect real-world emissions, and, thereby, are treated equally as ICEVs with regards to CO2 standards, the European Commission can commit to a regular review of the UF curve with the reference distance recalibrated based on OBFCM data, as per the methodology proposed in this paper.

articles.heading: Policymakers, tech leaders discuss AI growth, workforce needs at G20 event in Chapel Hill
articles.summary: Global policymakers, technology executives and business leaders gathered in Chapel Hill on Wednesday for the second day of the G20 Innovation Ministerial.
articles.content:
Wednesday, September 2, 2026 10:02PM
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. (WTVD) -- Global policymakers, technology executives and business leaders gathered in Chapel Hill on Wednesday for the second day of the G20 Innovation Ministerial, where discussions focused on artificial intelligence, economic growth and the challenges of supporting the technology's rapid expansion.
The conference at the Carolina Inn brought together commerce officials from around the world to explore ways emerging technologies can strengthen national economies and improve competitiveness.
"For this Innovation Ministerial, Chapel Hill is interesting because it's a critical corner of what we call here the Research Triangle. It's built on one of the great innovation economies in America because it couples world-class universities, advanced manufacturing with technology, skilled workers, and together with public and private investment," said US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
Artificial intelligence remained at the center of the discussions, with leaders examining how governments and businesses can address issues ranging from regulation and cybersecurity to labor shortages and rising energy demands.
DAY 1 | G20 Innovation Ministerial talks spotlight AI, data centers as Musk, Zuckerberg weigh in virtually
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said countries may pursue different approaches to regulating and adopting artificial intelligence but argued the technology's economic potential makes participation essential.
"Many of you are going to take many different approaches of how you regulate AI, how you welcome it into your country, how you use it, but for sure I think it is non-negotiable that you have to use it," Altman said. "The economic growth and benefit to people that can come from this, the value to a country is too high to ignore."
The event also featured discussions on the infrastructure required to support AI development.
"We have this incredible industrial build-out of the likes of which we've never seen in the history of humanity, even more than the railroads of the 1800s," said Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang echoed calls for countries to invest in AI infrastructure.
"In the end, what every single country will have to do is you need to recognize this is infrastructure," Huang said. "Just as with water, roads, electricity, the internet, every single country needs to build infrastructure, so that you can support your own local economy."
The conversation comes as data center proposals continue to generate debate in communities across North Carolina, including in the Triangle. Supporters argue the facilities are critical to AI development and economic growth, while opponents have raised concerns about environmental impacts and energy use.
"The Ratepayer (Protection) Pledge is something we signed up to, as have the other major labs," Brown said. "And that makes it that we bring on power behind the grid, behind the meter, and we can give it back to the grid as well."
Job impacts also remained a major topic.
A May survey from Bentley University and Gallup found that 79% of Americans said they believe artificial intelligence will reduce the number of jobs over the next decade, while 6% said they believe it will increase employment opportunities.
Technology leaders at the conference argued that AI is already driving hiring in several industries, particularly those tied to infrastructure development.
During a discussion with Lutnick, Huang said AI investment is creating employment opportunities across multiple sectors.
"AI is now generating jobs across every single sector, from chip fabs to computer plants to AI factories," Huang said. "Just the number of jobs that we're creating is just hundreds of thousands. And as you know, this year alone, we're going to invest close to $1 trillion into the world's, into the United States infrastructure. And that's generating enormous economic growth and, of course, a lot of jobs."
"I think this will be the greatest boom in entrepreneurship, and the creation of small businesses the world has ever seen," Altman added.
Outside the private sector, artificial intelligence is also being embraced by government agencies. OpenAI has launched a pilot program with the North Carolina Department of Commerce focused on redevelopment and economic recovery in communities affected by Hurricane Helene. The company is also working with the State Treasurer's Office on issues involving unclaimed property.

articles.title: St. Johns County removing license plate readers from state roads following FDOT directive
articles.description: St. Johns County removing license plate readers from state roads following FDOT directive News4JAX
articles.description_html: St. Johns County removing license plate readers from state roads following FDOT directive  News4JAX
articles.article_title: St. Johns County removing license plate readers from state roads following FDOT directive
articles.heading: St. Johns County removing license plate readers from state roads following FDOT directive
articles.summary: The St. Johns County Sheriff’s Office is removing license plate reader technology from certain roadways following a directive from the Florida Department of Transportation.
articles.content:
ST. JOHNS COUNTY, Fla. – The St. Johns County Sheriff’s Office is removing license plate reader technology from certain roadways following a directive from the Florida Department of Transportation.
The removal is in response to an FDOT Memo requiring that license plate reader, or LPR, technology be taken out of the right of way of roads on the State Highway System in St. Johns County. The agency said it is complying with the order but did not say that all LPR cameras in the county would come down.
Recommended Videos
St. Johns County has roughly 180 of them.
Sheriff Robert A. Hardwick emphasized his confidence in the technology while acknowledging the need to follow the state directive.
“The St. Johns County Sheriff’s Office remains confident in the effectiveness and overwhelming success of license plate reader technology,” Hardwick said. “In addition, I am humbled by the trust the community has shown for our agency’s use of this valuable tool.”
“As your Sheriff, it is my responsibility to protect you, the citizens and visitors of St. Johns County,” he continued. “As technology evolves, we will continue to pursue the best balance between public safety and personal privacy.”
The agency also signaled its intent to work toward formal policy around LPR use. The SJSO said it supports the development of legislation that addresses concerns surrounding the technology and establishes clear standards for its use.
The office said it looks forward to continued collaboration with the Florida Sheriffs Association, state legislators and local stakeholders in shaping that policy.
Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office responds to FDOT directive
On Monday, Jacksonville Sheriff T.K. Waters announced JSO would discontinue the use of LPR technology following FDOT’s directive.
“As the elected Sheriff of Duval County, it is my responsibility to listen to the concerns of our citizens and act accordingly,” the sheriff said.
“LPR technology has proven to be an enormously valuable investigative tool, assisting our agency in solving serious crimes and locating missing and vulnerable individuals,” the sheriff said. “However, given the decision made at the state level and the concerns expressed by members of our community, I have determined that discontinuing the use of this technology is the appropriate course of action at this time.”
“The Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office remains fully committed to providing the highest level of public safety services to the people of Jacksonville,” the sheriff said. “We will continue to use every tool, resource, and technology available to prevent crime, solve cases, and protect our community.”
RELATED: ‘It matters what we think’: Jacksonville residents voice opinions on surveillance technology, Flock cameras | Have you been Flocked? This website may show whether police have searched your plates
Clay County Sheriff’s Office cites crime-fighting impact
The Clay County Sheriff’s Office has used LPR technology since 2018, and officials say the tools have made a measurable difference in public safety outcomes.
In the past year alone, the CCSO said license plate readers helped investigators find a missing 76-year-old woman from South Carolina whose vehicle was located in Middleburg using an automated license plate reader (ALPR). The technology also helped identify and locate a homicide suspect in a deadly stabbing, and safely recover a 10-year-old taken in a child custody interference case. In that case, the vehicle was located and stopped near the Florida-Alabama state line, leading to three arrests, the sheriff’s office reported in its statement about the discontinuation of Flock cameras.
Sheriff Michelle Cook said the removal of the technology will not slow the agency’s mission.
“As always, our commitment to fostering a safe community where families and businesses can thrive remains our top priority,” Cook said. “This decision does not hinder, nor sway, our efforts to prevent and fight crime, solve cases, hold offenders accountable and maintain public trust.”
Nassau County Sheriff’s Office eyes future of technology in law enforcement
Nassau County Sheriff Bill Leeper said his office will also comply with FDOT’s directive while keeping an eye on how law enforcement technology continues to evolve.
The sheriff’s office said it would stop using 34 Flock cameras across Nassau County.
Leeper struck a forward-looking tone, calling for collaboration between local and state partners on the responsible use of emerging tools.
“As technology continues to evolve, we welcome the opportunity to work with our local and state partners to ensure these tools are used appropriately, responsibly, and as intended to assist in solving serious crimes, locating missing or endangered persons, and recovering stolen property while also protecting the rights and privacy of our citizens,” Leeper said.

articles.description_html: Why Credo Technology Stock Plunged 20% Today  The Motley Fool
articles.article_title: Why Credo Technology Stock Plunged 20% Today | The Motley Fool
articles.heading: Why Credo Technology Stock Plunged 20% Today
articles.summary: Credo Technology crushed its earnings estimates. So why did the stock drop 20%?
articles.content:
Credo Technology (CRDO -20.04%) is having a difficult Wednesday. The company reported Q1 2027 results on Tuesday evening, smashing Wall Street's estimates and offering rosy guidance for the next quarter. But the stock was priced for perfection, and Credo gave the bears enough to feast on. The stock closed Wednesday's trading 20% lower.
NASDAQ: CRDO
Key Data Points
A beat-and-raise report with a catch
Let's start with the headline figures. Revenue more than doubled, with a 115% year-over-year jump to $479 million. Adjusted earnings landed at $1.20 per diluted share, up 131% from $0.52 per share in the year-ago period. Credo's active electric cables (AECs) are shipping to five hyperscalers, and the newer optical business is catching up fast. Q2 guidance pointed to roughly $530 million of top-line revenue, up from $268 million in last year's second quarter and well above the current analyst consensus at $517 million.
So it's a classic beat-and-raise report, but there's one uncomfortable wrinkle. Credo's business is incredibly concentrated on a handful of customers. The three largest clients accounted for 74% of total revenues.
That might have been alright for a calmer stock, but Credo is a volatile ticker and it headed into this report at sky-high valuation ratios. After today's sharp drop, the beta value is a massive 3.2, and the stock still trades at 59 times trailing earnings.
Why the sell-off makes sense (and why you might like Credo's stock anyway)
The price cut makes sense. Nobody likes intense customer concentration, and Credo's stock is still quite expensive. Credo's sales growth could hit a rock wall if one or more of those mega-buyers slow their orders.
However, the company is growing at nitro-boosted rates in the current economy. Credo remains an effective alternative investment in the data center construction boom. Adding optical components to the copper-based AEC foundation lowers the risk of one technology falling out of favor.

articles.title: Manifest Prosthetics blends craftsmanship and technology to help restore independence
articles.description: Manifest Prosthetics blends craftsmanship and technology to help restore independence FOX 13 Tampa Bay
articles.description_html: Manifest Prosthetics blends craftsmanship and technology to help restore independence  FOX 13 Tampa Bay
articles.article_title: Manifest Prosthetics blends craftsmanship and technology to help restore independence
articles.heading: Manifest Prosthetics blends craftsmanship and technology to help restore independence
articles.summary: The veteran-owned business combines hands-on craftsmanship with modern technology to help people living with limb loss.
articles.content:
Manifest Prosthetics blends craftsmanship and technology to help restore independence
TAMPA, Fla. - A step across the room. A return to a favorite activity. The freedom to do more on your own.
At Manifest Prosthetics, Orthotics & Bionics in Tampa, those everyday possibilities are the goal behind the custom devices its team builds and fits.
The veteran-owned business combines hands-on craftsmanship with modern technology to help people living with limb loss.
All under one roof
What we know:
Manifest’s Tampa location houses both its clinic and fabrication lab. That puts the people evaluating patients in the same building as the technicians making their custom prosthetic sockets — the portion of a prosthesis that fits around the remaining limb.
Keeping those steps together allows the team to work on the device where the patient receives care.
The clinic serves people throughout Tampa Bay and beyond.
Services offered
Dig deeper:
According to Manifest, its services include upper and lower-limb prosthetics, pediatric devices, custom orthotic braces and silicone restorations.
The team uses digital scanning as well as traditional casting, choosing the approach based on the patient’s needs.
Care also includes follow-up adjustments and repairs as patients continue using their devices.
A personal connection
What they're saying:
For co-founder Gordon Maniere, the work has a personal connection.
Maniere tells FOX 13 he grew up around his father’s prosthetic lab.
His father was a prosthetist, giving Maniere an early view of the craft and the people it serves.
As a teenager, Maniere began learning to laminate prosthetic limbs. Today, his practice also incorporates digital scanning and has fitted patients with prostheses.
That combination of experience and evolving technology reflects his emphasis on individualized care and addressing problems with fit.
Learn more
What's next:
Manifest Prosthetics’ Tampa clinic is located at 5109 N. Armenia Ave. Listed hours are Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
For information or to schedule a consultation, visit manifestpo.com or call 813-801-9110.
The Source: Information was gathered for this story from an interview with Manifest Prosethetics in Tampa.

articles.title: Every technological revolution has its Luddites. AI is no different
articles.description: Every technological revolution has its Luddites. AI is no different Northeastern Global News
articles.description_html: Every technological revolution has its Luddites. AI is no different  Northeastern Global News
articles.article_title: Every technological revolution has its Luddites. AI is no different
articles.heading: Every technological revolution has its Luddites. AI is no different
articles.summary: Debate is intensifying over the impacts of AI products and the data centers powering them — and new technologies, such as flock cameras.
articles.content:
What would Ned Ludd have to say about artificial intellgience?
Times of technological change, such as the present AI revolution, have a way of summoning old anxieties. Lately, that has meant the return of a lexical boogeyman that harkens back to a bygone era: the Luddites.
Times of technological change, such as the present AI revolution, have a way of summoning old anxieties — and with them, old antagonists.
Lately, that has meant the return of a lexical boogeyman that harkens back to a bygone era of techno-pessimism: the Luddites, those people over the years thought to fiercely oppose new technologies.
The Wall Street Journal recently declared 2026 “Hot Luddite Summer.” Gen Z’s growing skepticism about AI — documented in a recent Gallup poll, among other places — has led to comparisons with anti-tech resistance movements of yore. Some, such as the group of New York youth who call themselves the Luddite Club, embrace the label. Others, such as tech investor David Friedberg, use it to cast stones.
As debate intensifies over the economic, societal and environmental impacts of artificial intelligence products and the data centers powering them, and new and potentially invasive technologies, such as flock cameras, trigger street protests in communities across the U.S., a new and far messier cultural divide is emerging between proponents and opponents of the transformative tech, said Steven Vallas, an emeritus professor of sociology at Northeastern, who studies the technological transformation of work and the struggles that follow.
At stake is not simply whether these technologies will transform society, but who will regulate and ultimately bear the consequences of a transformation that is set to drastically redefine everything from work, authorship and creativity to scientific research, drug discovery and healthcare.
There’s no question that AI and associated technologies have become highly politicized, with some analysts saying the 2026 midterms could be a referendum on the technology. A recent Pew Research Center survey found that 71% of Americans believe AI will lead to fewer jobs in the United States over the next two decades, up from 64% in 2024. A separate YouGov poll found that 46% oppose police license-plate cameras like those made by Flock, compared with 38% who support them.
“It could be an important issue, especially where the economy isn’t working and technology is resonating with people’s homes and their jobs,” Vallas said.
Central to the pro or anti-tech discourse is a label, one that — depending on who you ask — can seem like a playful jab at a group of old fogeys, or an accusation to be hurled at opponents of “progress,” and thus a rallying cry for specific forms of political resistance, Vallas said.
“Over time, ‘Luddism’ has become a cudgel used to tarnish critics of technology, who are often portrayed as irrational opponents of progress,” however it is defined, Vallas said. Such a derogatory use of the term relies on a “narrow and selective interpretation” of the history of the movement.
The Luddites were a group of 18th century textile workers, who protested the industrialization of the textile industry and the mechanization of their work, brought about by the industrial revolution that began the same century. This period of radical change bore technologies that would transform the textile industry, including power looms and knitting frames, which allowed manufacturers to produce goods much faster and with less reliance on skilled labor, Vallas said.
The workers were not happy and as the legend goes some resorted to sabotage, including Ned Ludd, a mythical figure who — the story goes — is said to have destroyed textile machinery. His supporters invoked him as their fictional leader and used his name as a pseudonym for their cause.
Over decades, Luddism has been invoked in a variety of contexts — and used to scapegoat people more recently. The microwave once inspired kitchen-born skepticism as well as supermarket self-checkout lines, which met resistance when they were introduced, Vallas said.
Even the internet initially struck some as disconcertingly complex and dystopian, though early browsers such as Netscape and online service providers such as AOL and CompuServe helped make it more accessible, he said.
The point, according to Vallas, is that technologies that initially provoke knee-jerk resistance oftentimes become “more convivial” over time, once they’re adopted.
Like revolutions past, Vallas sees today’s AI revolution as something of a convergence of forces: the internet, the rise of what he called an “algorithmic society” and the “digitization of work” through the so-called platform economy, where much of day to day commerce now takes place on digital platforms.
“There are reasonable debates over the history of this movement,” he said. “But many accounts question the idea that the movement was a reactionary rejection of new technology, since it harbored lessons that we would do well to consider, like the idea that technologies develop most effectively when they incorporate the knowledge and interests of the workers themselves, and that violent conflicts are inevitable when large scale changes are imposed in the absence of democratic channels.”
Adam Cooper, a teaching professor of linguistics at Northeastern, said the term has grown from an “in-group label” used to describe oneself or one’s own community, to one directed at the “out-group,” or those perceived as outside the community, “with negative connotations.”
“Whether Luddite is dismissive or derogatory is, I’d expect, in the eye of the beholder,” he said.

articles.heading: Why Credo Technology Stock Plunged 20% Today
articles.summary: Credo Technology crushed its earnings estimates. So why did the stock drop 20%?
articles.content:
Why Credo Technology Stock Plunged 20% Today
Credo Technology (NASDAQ: CRDO) is having a difficult Wednesday. The company reported Q1 2027 results on Tuesday evening, smashing Wall Street's estimates and offering rosy guidance for the next quarter. But the stock was priced for perfection, and Credo gave the bears enough to feast on. The stock closed Wednesday's trading 20% lower.
A beat-and-raise report with a catch
Let's start with the headline figures. Revenue more than doubled, with a 115% year-over-year jump to $479 million. Adjusted earnings landed at $1.20 per diluted share, up 131% from $0.52 per share in the year-ago period. Credo's active electric cables (AECs) are shipping to five hyperscalers, and the newer optical business is catching up fast. Q2 guidance pointed to roughly $530 million of top-line revenue, up from $268 million in last year's second quarter and well above the current analyst consensus at $517 million.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
So it's a classic beat-and-raise report, but there's one uncomfortable wrinkle. Credo's business is incredibly concentrated on a handful of customers. The three largest clients accounted for 74% of total revenues.
That might have been alright for a calmer stock, but Credo is a volatile ticker and it headed into this report at sky-high valuation ratios. After today's sharp drop, the beta value is a massive 3.2, and the stock still trades at 59 times trailing earnings.
Why the sell-off makes sense (and why you might like Credo's stock anyway)
The price cut makes sense. Nobody likes intense customer concentration, and Credo's stock is still quite expensive. Credo's sales growth could hit a rock wall if one or more of those mega-buyers slow their orders.
However, the company is growing at nitro-boosted rates in the current economy. Credo remains an effective alternative investment in the data center construction boom. Adding optical components to the copper-based AEC foundation lowers the risk of one technology falling out of favor.

Before you buy stock in Credo Technology Group, consider this:
The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Credo Technology Group wasn't one of them. The 10 stocks that made the cut are built for long-term growth and could produce monster returns in the coming years.
Consider when Netflix made this list on December 17, 2004... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $435,803!* Or when Nvidia made this list on April 15, 2005... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $1,334,577!*
That performance is why people listen. With a track record of beating the S&P 500 by nearly 5x, Stock Advisor offers a distinct advantage. Don't miss the latest top 10 list, available with Stock Advisor, and join an investing community built for the long haul.

articles.article_title: Building foundations that last
articles.heading: Building foundations that last
articles.summary: Assistant Professor Iwnetim Abate creates space for ambitious research and sustainable growth for his graduate students.
articles.content:
How do you build something that lasts? For MIT Assistant Professor Iwnetim "Tim" Abate, the answer is the same whether he’s reimagining how the materials beneath our feet can store energy and manufacture essential chemicals, or mentoring MIT’s future researchers: focus on the foundation.
Rocks provide an unexpected thread connecting Abate’s research and his approach to mentorship. His research brings together electrochemistry, materials science, and Earth sciences to explore how the materials that make up our planet can be harnessed to address some of society’s most pressing challenges in energy and sustainable manufacturing.
In one line of inquiry, his group uses Earth-abundant elements found in rocks, such as manganese and iron, to develop high-energy, low-cost, and more sustainable batteries. In another, they are exploring how the Earth’s subsurface itself could function as a chemical factory. By harnessing naturally reactive rocks, geothermal heat, and injected fluids, they seek to pioneer new ways of producing valuable fuels and chemicals underground, with lower external energy requirements and emissions than conventional industrial processes.
Although batteries and subsurface chemical manufacturing operate at vastly different scales, they share a common philosophy: understanding the intrinsic chemistry of Earth’s materials deeply enough to harness it for useful transformations.
While Abate's research spans a broad range of scientific disciplines, his approach to mentorship is guided by a simple principle: helping students lay the groundwork for their careers after graduate school. Rather than measuring success solely through publications or technical accomplishments, he strives to equip students with the scientific skills, resilience, curiosity, and perspective needed to navigate any path their career may take.
"I often think about mentorship through the image of a rock," Abate explains. "A structure built on rock can withstand storms and the test of time. In the same way, I believe the most important role of a mentor is not simply to help students complete a project or publish papers, but to help them build a strong foundation."
Abate puts this philosophy into practice through his investment in his students' growth as researchers, professionals, and individuals.
In celebration of his exemplary mentorship, Abate has been recognized through MIT's Committed to Caring initiative, a student-driven program that honors graduate mentors who foster supportive and inclusive research environments.
Building holistic relationships
Students often arrive at graduate school with different ambitions. Whether they hope to pursue academia, industry, entrepreneurship, or public service, Abate begins by learning about each person's long-term goals.
Each time a new student joins his group, he meets with them individually to discuss their aspirations and helps tailor aspects of their PhD experience accordingly. Students say these conversations continue throughout their time in the lab, with regular one-on-one meetings focused on both research progress and career development, homing in on their opportunities beyond MIT.
For students interested in entrepreneurship, Abate leverages his own network, introducing them to venture capital firms, philanthropic organizations, and collaborators working across academia and industry. He encourages his students to pursue internships, recognizing that experiences outside the university can strengthen both their research perspective and their future careers.
Students also emphasize his ability to connect them with the expertise they need to push research forward. Whether facilitating access to specialized instrumentation or identifying researchers with complementary knowledge, Abate actively builds the relationships that allow his students and their projects to thrive.
Despite leading a growing research group while balancing teaching responsibilities and launching a startup, nominators wrote that Abate "consistently [shows] up for his students."
He makes time for individual chats with students, subgroup discussions, and weekly lab meetings, all while actively seeking their perspectives on research challenges. "Tim is often curious [to hear] our point of view on research problems and actively looks for our feedback," reflected one nominator.
This openness creates a synergistic environment where students are encouraged to help shape the direction of the group's work.
Creating space for ambitious ideas
Innovation, Abate believes, depends on more than technical expertise.
"Students need to know that it is OK to pursue ideas that may not work, and that setbacks are part of discovery, rather than signs of failure," he says. "My goal is to create an environment where ambitious ideas are welcomed, careful thinking is valued, and students know they have someone who believes in them through both successes and disappointments."
Students say this philosophy is reflected in the way that Abate approaches advising. Rather than directing every decision, he encourages them to think independently, remaining available whenever guidance is needed. His vast professional network often becomes an extension of that mentorship, opening doors to partnerships and expertise that help students tackle increasingly ambitious research questions.
This commitment to building strong foundations extends beyond his own research group. Since graduate school, Abate has worked to expand access to STEM education through his nonprofit Sci-Fro, which supports educational outreach across Africa. He has also contributed to broader efforts to strengthen scientific infrastructure and research institutions across the continent.
For Abate, these efforts reflect the same philosophy that guides his mentorship: lasting scientific progress depends not only on individual discoveries, but also on investing in people, communities, and institutions that enable future generations of scientists to thrive.
Supporting the person behind the PhD
Abate regularly checks in during one-on-one meetings, asking how his students are doing and what support they need. He believes these conversations are an essential part of advising.
"Graduate school is one of the most formative periods of a person's life," he says. "While research is important, I don't think success should come at the expense of health, relationships, or personal growth."
He encourages students to build lives that remain meaningful beyond the laboratory, recognizing that the habits, friendships, and perspectives developed during graduate school often shape them just as much as their scientific accomplishments.
Through steady guidance, meaningful connections, and genuine care for each student's well-being, Abate demonstrates a passion for developing exceptional researchers.
"I hope they leave MIT with a strong foundation — both scientifically and personally — that enables them to navigate future challenges, lead with integrity, and build fulfilling lives wherever their careers take them."

articles.heading: PPL Electric is investing in technology to help keep the lights on as demand rises. Here’s a look inside
articles.summary: With more demand than ever for power, what is PPL Electric Utilities doing to make sure its customers can keep their lights, computers and air conditioning running?
articles.content:
With more demand than ever for power, what is PPL Electric Utilities doing to make sure its customers can keep their lights, computers and air conditioning running?

On Wednesday morning, PPL hosted U.S. Assistant Energy Secretary Katie Jereza at its Walbert Training Center in South Whitehall Township. Company President Christine Martin gave a tour and PPL employees provided demonstrations on how the utility is using technology to prevent blackouts and keeping rates down for customers.

Jereza is traveling nationwide to see how technology is being advanced through a grant from the department’s Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships program. GRIP supports projects that strengthen and modernize the nation’s electric grid.

“Conditions that used to be predictable are now shifting in real time,” Jereza said, “pushing infrastructure beyond what it was designed to handle. The affordability and reliability of our electric grid is no longer just a technical matter. It is a lifeline for our communities.”

PPL is executing a $100 million grid resilience project co-funded by a 50% Energy Department grant that is about halfway completed, Martin said. Overall, PPL plans to invest about $8 billion into its transmission and distribution grid through 2029.

“Since 2015, that technology has helped us be able to restore power and avoid sustained outages for customers more than 3.7 million times,” Martin said. “That’s a real result for real customers. That matters, because during a power outage, every second counts.”

In a large barn-like building at the training center, spectators watched a worker install a single-phase recloser on a pole from a bucket truck, while PPL engineers Rawan Abu-Zaineh, Connor Duffy and Eric Rosenberger explained how the technology worked.

Another sensor device allows for predictive asset monitoring that tracks early physical signs for equipment failure or vegetation encroachment. The data is analyzed using artificial intelligence to alert PPL monitors and allow for preventive maintenance before outages can happen.

“What we’re targeting are issues that can kind of start developing over time, and we can take up all those early signs of failure before they cause an outage to our customers,” Duffy said.

Dynamic line rating is done through sensors on the transmission lines that calculate real-time capacity based on factors such as wind or temperature. This allows PPL to optimize power routing, integrate cheaper generation and avoid transmission line rebuilds.

“By doing that, we saved a lot of cost to customers, and we avoided having to go rebuild transmission lines, which would be very expensive and take many years to get done,” Rosenberger said.

When asked about data centers during a news conference, Martin said that PPL has 11 gigawatts under electric service agreements and more than 30 gigawatts under advanced agreements. She said large energy companies are drawn to PPL’s region because of the grid’s reliability.

Martin said to protect residential and small business ratepayers, PPL established a dedicated rate class for large load customers that use more than 50 megawatts. These customers pay for their required infrastructure growth, she said, ensuring that increased system volume helps keep general rates lower. PPL also signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge alongside other industry partners.

“PPL Electric Utilities is the only utility in Pennsylvania who has instituted a completely separate rate class for large load customers, those customers 50 megawatts and above,” Martin said. “What that means is those customers are paying for their growth, they’re paying for the investments we are making to serve them.”

With more demand than ever for power, what is PPL Electric Utilities doing to make sure its customers can keep their lights, computers and air conditioning running?

On Wednesday morning, PPL hosted U.S. Assistant Energy Secretary Katie Jereza at its Walbert Training Center in South Whitehall Township. Company President Christine Martin gave a tour and PPL employees provided demonstrations on how the utility is using technology to prevent blackouts and keeping rates down for customers.

Jereza is traveling nationwide to see how technology is being advanced through a grant from the department’s Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships program. GRIP supports projects that strengthen and modernize the nation’s electric grid.

“Conditions that used to be predictable are now shifting in real time,” Jereza said, “pushing infrastructure beyond what it was designed to handle. The affordability and reliability of our electric grid is no longer just a technical matter. It is a lifeline for our communities.”

PPL is executing a $100 million grid resilience project co-funded by a 50% Energy Department grant that is about halfway completed, Martin said. Overall, PPL plans to invest about $8 billion into its transmission and distribution grid through 2029.

“Since 2015, that technology has helped us be able to restore power and avoid sustained outages for customers more than 3.7 million times,” Martin said. “That’s a real result for real customers. That matters, because during a power outage, every second counts.”

articles.heading: Consumer Technology Association Ends Lobbying with McDermottPlus
articles.summary: Consumer Technology Association terminates McDermottPlus lobbying contract effective August 31, 2026. Details on healthcare innovation representation change.
articles.content:
Why It Matters
The Consumer Technology Association terminated its lobbying contract with McDermottPlus LLC effective August 31, according to a termination filing signed on August 28. McDermottPlus LLC represented Consumer Technology Association on healthcare innovation issues, including digital health and artificial intelligence, from 2024 through August 2026.
McDermottPlus charged Consumer Technology Association $30,000 for the third quarter of 2026. Quarterly filings from 2024 through the second quarter of 2026 showed $0 amounts.
The Consumer Technology Association was among McDermottPlus's smaller clients by disclosed lobbying value. The Rural Referral Center and Sole Community Hospital Coalition generated $330,000 in disclosed lobbying value across five filings. Several other McDermottPlus clients, including Ascension, the Association for Community Affiliated Plans, Connections Health Solutions LLC, and the Urgent Care Association, each accounted for $280,000 in disclosed lobbying value.
The firm had been exploring a merger with a private equity-owned competitor that did not materialize, and McDermottPlus closed after approximately a dozen years in business.

articles.title: Google defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech sale
articles.description: Google defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech sale The Guardian
articles.description_html: Google defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech sale  The Guardian
articles.article_title: Google defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech sale
articles.heading: Google defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech sale
articles.summary: Judge declines to make Google sell AdX in win for firm against US antitrust enforcers’ attempts to break up big tech
articles.content:
Alphabet’s Google escaped a breakup of its advertising technology business on Wednesday, when a judge in Virginia rejected US antitrust enforcers’ attempt to force a sale of Google’s online advertising exchange.
While the ad exchange is a small part of Google’s business, the ruling is the second powerful symbolic victory against the US Department of Justice in its efforts to force Google to sell assets to address illegal monopolies.
US judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, declined to make Google sell AdX, where publishers pay Google a 20% fee to sell ads in auctions that happen instantly when users load websites. She accepted most of the parties’ proposed behavioral remedies.
The justice department and a broad coalition of states sued Google in 2023 over its dominance in markets for advertising technology used by online publishers and websites.
In April 2025, Brinkema ruled that Google holds illegal monopolies on servers that host publisher ads and ad exchanges which sit between buyers and sellers. Google unlawfully locked publishers on its ad server into using its AdX, the judge found.
The tech company’s anticompetitive conduct “substantially harmed Google’s publisher customers, the competitive process, and, ultimately, consumers of information on the open web”, Brinkema said at the time.
At a trial last year on remedies in the case, the justice department argued that Google cannot be trusted to run AdX, given its past behavior.
Google argued that a forced sale would be technically difficult and result in a long and painful transition that would hurt customers. The company also sought to show the justice department’s demand was different from Google’s own previous offer to sell AdX to end an EU antitrust investigation, which Reuters reported in 2024.
Ad Manager represented 4.1% of Google’s overall revenue and 1.5% of operating profit in 2020, according to Wedbush research and analysis of court documents. More recent figures were redacted from court documents.
The ruling is the third time in a row that a judge has rejected a bid by US antitrust enforcers to break up big tech in a crackdown that started during Donald Trump’s first term. It is likely to fuel questions about whether courts are up to the task of checking the industry’s unprecedented power over the US economy.
A federal judge in Washington last year rejected the Federal Trade Commission’s attempt to make Meta Platforms sell off Instagram and WhatsApp, saying the agency failed to prove that Meta holds a monopoly in a social media landscape that has shifted drastically since the case was brought in 2020.
Likewise, another judge in Washington, who previously ruled that Google holds an illegal monopoly in online search, rejected the justice department’s attempt to make the company sell its Chrome browser, citing rising competition from generative artificial intelligence companies such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT.
US antitrust cases against Amazon and Apple, which involve big smartphone and online retail markets, will not go to trial until 2027 at the earliest.

articles.title: NCMC opens new Martin Jahn Technology Center in Petoskey
articles.description: NCMC opens new Martin Jahn Technology Center in Petoskey 9and10News.com
articles.description_html: NCMC opens new Martin Jahn Technology Center in Petoskey  9and10News.com
articles.article_title: NCMC opens new Martin Jahn Technology Center in Petoskey
articles.heading: NCMC opens new Martin Jahn Technology Center in Petoskey
articles.summary: The 11,750-square-foot facility expands hands-on learning opportunities in advanced manufacturing, engineering technology and skilled trades.
articles.content:
Classes are scheduled to begin in the new technology center later this fall semester. — PETOSKEY - North Central Michigan College hosted a ribbon-cutting ceremony Monday, to celebrate the opening of the new Martin Jahn Technology Center.
The 11,750-square-foot facility expands hands-on learning opportunities in advanced manufacturing, engineering technology and skilled trades.
The new building serves as the centerpiece of North Central’s $22 million Career and Technical Education Enhancement initiative, marking the college’s largest campus expansion in more than 50 years. As part of the initiative, the project also includes a 7,200-square-foot expansion of the Jack and Dorothy Harris Health Education and Science Center to support nursing and allied health programs.
The 11,750-square-foot center features dedicated space for hands-on instruction in several technical fields, including welding, CNC machining and HVACR.
The facility was funded through state and federal investments alongside private donations made through the NCMC Foundation. The center received its name following a lead gift from the Martin and Patricia Jahn Foundation.
North Central Michigan College President David Roland Finley praised the community collaboration behind the new facility during the ceremony. “Today’s celebration represents the culmination of thoughtful planning, strong public-private partnerships and the unwavering support of our elected officials, donors, business leaders and community members,” Finley said. “Together, you’ve invested not only in this facility, but in our students, our workforce and the future of Northern Michigan.”
Classes are scheduled to begin in the new technology center this fall.

articles.content:
Bipartisan legislation passes in unanimous vote

Washington, DC, Sept. 02, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The Engine Technology Forum (ETF) today praised the House Energy and Commerce Committee's passage of H.R. 2140, the Diesel Emissions Reduction Act (DERA) of 2025.

In a unanimous vote, the House Energy and Commerce Committee took the next step toward reauthorizing H.R. 2140 by adopting legislation to amend the Energy Policy Act of 2005 and reauthorize the Diesel Emissions Reduction Act.

"We recognize and thank Representatives Matsui (D-CA) and Langworthy (R-NY) for their leadership in sponsoring the legislation, and all the House Energy and Commerce Committee members who supported it," said Allen Schaeffer, executive director of ETF.

"DERA has been a bipartisan success story from the very beginning because of its structure and competitive process, successful implementation, ongoing need, and continued funding support. As outlined in the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Sixth Report to Congress , it's a program that has upgraded a wide range of technologies across the country, from marine and locomotive engines, port drayage trucks, and school buses to fire trucks and industrial stationary generators in Tribal communities."

DERA provides funding assistance to accelerate the upgrade or retirement of older diesel engines, prioritizing projects that reduce emissions in nonattainment or maintenance areas for particulate matter (PM) and ozone. DERA competitive grant applications are evaluated based on how projects benefit areas with poor air quality and the extent to which they engage community stakeholders. The DERA program also prioritizes goods movement projects because these projects tend to take place in communities impacted by higher levels of diesel exhaust, such as those near ports, rail yards, and distribution centers.

Since the inception of DERA, funding requests have exceeded available funding in each fiscal year (FY). In FYs 2019 and 2020 alone, grant and rebate applicants requested $220 million more in funds than were available from DERA appropriations. This legislation – H.R. 2140 – reauthorizes the DERA program through 2029.

The DERA program promotes an array of diesel emissions reduction strategies by working with manufacturers, fleet operators, air quality professionals, environmental and community organizations, and Tribal, state, and local officials. Together, EPA and others work to achieve emissions reductions in areas experiencing diminished air quality from diesel fleets. DERA has separate national and state award programs.

According to the EPA, more than 76,900 engines in vehicles, vessels, locomotives, and other pieces of equipment were replaced or retrofitted with DERA funds during FYs 2008 to 2020. DERA projects during these years are estimated to have reduced approximately 499,000 tons of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and 16,600 tons of PM over the lifetime of the replaced engines. These diesel emissions reduction projects are also estimated to have reduced approximately 19,400 tons of hydrocarbons (HC) and 66,600 tons of carbon monoxide (CO) and are expected to save over 572 million gallons of diesel fuel over the lifetime of the affected engines.

Approximately 58% of projects included school bus replacements. Additionally, there were more than 240 port and multi-sector projects, more than 90 municipal projects, and more than 90 construction projects. About 95% were diesel engines and vehicles. About 5% were natural gas, propane, gasoline, zero-emission, or hybrid engines and vehicles.

"We look forward to the consideration of H.R. 2140 by the full House of Representatives," noted Schaeffer.

About the Engine Technology Forum Founded on the principles of fact-based education, science, outreach and collaboration, the Engine Technology Forum is dedicated to promoting a greater understanding of the benefits of advanced engines and the fuels that they use, as well as how these contribute to a sustainable future. Plan A Technologies Acquires Stealth AI Assessment Technology to Expand Technical M&A Due Diligence Capabilities
PR Newswire
LAS VEGAS, Sept. 2, 2026
Proprietary technology helps Plan A evaluate complex technology environments faster—and uncover technical risks, patterns, and opportunities that traditional assessment tools may miss
LAS VEGAS, Sept. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Plan A Technologies, an award-winning AI and software engineering company specializing in providing technology advice and custom software and agent development, today announced the acquisition of a stealth AI assessment tool to enhance its technical M&A due diligence practice.
Plan A has become a trusted technical due diligence partner for private equity firms, strategic acquirers, enterprise companies, and private investors evaluating technology-intensive transactions. Its teams are brought in to answer some of the most important questions surrounding an acquisition: Is the underlying technology as strong as it appears? What risks may not be evident from management presentations? How difficult will the platform be to scale, integrate, modernize, or secure? And what additional investment may be required after closing?
The newly acquired technology gives Plan A another proprietary layer of analysis to help answer those questions.
"Good technical due diligence isn't about producing a longer list of issues. It's about distinguishing ordinary, fixable technical debt from something that can fundamentally change the cost or risk profile of a transaction," said Slav Kulik, Co-Founder of Plan A Technologies. "We help our clients to understand what is really happening underneath the surface of a technology platform and translate that into business implications. Technical due diligence has traditionally relied on expert interviews, manual code review, architecture analysis, documentation, and commercially available code scanning tools. Plan A will continue to use all of those approaches, but this new technology will help us analyze exceptionally large and fragmented technology ecosystems with greater speed and consistency while looking for patterns or anomalies that conventional approaches may miss."
Plan A believes this type of deeper analysis will become increasingly crucial as more and more code is created by AI, often resulting in company leaders who don't understand their own technology nearly as well as they did in the past.
Kulik added, "AI is not a substitute for senior technical judgment. The advantage comes from combining AI with people who have spent years building, scaling, fixing, integrating, and evaluating real production systems. That combination allows us to ask better questions and give our clients a more complete picture of what they're actually buying."
The tool's creator, Serhii Melnychuk, has joined Plan A Technologies as an architect to lead its integration and future development.
"I wanted to build something that could help experts do their job more effectively and connect signals scattered across different systems," said Serhii Melnychuk, lead developer of the technology. "It's incredibly exciting to see how Plan A integrated my tool into its broader approach and is bringing it to clients around the world."
The acquisition also reflects a broader strategy at Plan A: developing and acquiring proprietary technology that makes its engineers, architects, data specialists, and technology advisors more effective.
While technical M&A due diligence is an important and growing part of Plan A's business, it represents only one component of the company's broader work. Plan A also helps clients design and build new software products from scratch, deploy proprietary AI agents and agentic systems, modernize legacy applications, build data platforms, migrate infrastructure to the cloud, integrate enterprise systems, and solve large-scale engineering challenges.
That breadth is particularly valuable during M&A engagements because Plan A's diligence teams are not simply professional auditors who only evaluate technology—they are practitioners who build and operate it. The same engineering leaders assessing whether a platform can scale or be modernized have experience executing those initiatives in complex environments.
For clients, that means an assessment can go beyond identifying what is wrong. Plan A also helps define the optimal path forward, and if needed, can deploy the engineering teams required to execute the roadmap following the transaction.
About Plan A Technologies
Plan A Technologies was created to solve the toughest tech challenges facing today's businesses. Plan A helps organizations analyze their tech ecosystem to identify exactly what needs to be improved across their products and infrastructure—and then builds the solutions to fix it.
Rather than offering theoretical ideas or software that never launches, Plan A Technologies combines elite engineering talent with custom-built, proprietary AI agents to deliver fast, secure, production-ready solutions. Its capabilities span proprietary AI agent deployment, custom software development, application modernization, data platforms, cloud migrations, systems integration, and practical technical advice.
With more than 500 successful product deployments completed worldwide, Plan A helps organizations of every size—from ambitious startups to global enterprises—modernize their systems, automate complex operations, and stay ahead of the technology curve.
To see how Plan A turns complex technical challenges into real-world solutions, visit PlanATechnologies.com,

Donor & Partner Impact

Shaping Futures

Youth from 31 different states had a chance to explore STEM careers at this year's academy, hosted and organized by Middle Tennessee University.

Sep 2, 2026

3 min read

Check out this full story posted by Middle Tennessee University here!

Almost 60 Civil Air Patrol cadets from 31 states were selected to attend this year’s CAP National Cadet Engineering Technology Academy hosted and organized by Middle Tennessee State University’s colleges of Basic and Applied Sciences and Behavioral and Health Sciences, featuring majors ranging from aerospace to public health and mechatronics to criminal justice.

Fifty-four cadets, selected by CAP for the MTSU academy through a competitive application process, took part in classroom lectures, academic projects, hands-on learning and computer simulations during activities by the two science colleges, as well as supplemental opportunities provided by the Scott Borchetta College of Media and Entertainment and the College of Education.

Civil Air Patrol cadets in the U.S. Air Force Auxiliary’s National Cadet Engineering Technology Academy held July 18-25, 2026, at Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro, Tenn., use patient simulators to conduct drills in the School of Nursing in the College of Behavioral Sciences. (MTSU Photo by James Cessna)

Civil Air Patrol cadets in the National Cadet Engineering Technology Academy. tour the university’s School of Concrete and Construction Management Building. (MTSU Photo by James Cessna)

"The state-of-the-art facilities and outstanding faculty create exceptional learning experiences for the cadets,” said Missouri Wing’s Maj. Christina Ragain, director of the academy and lead for the 14 adults who guided the cadet activity. "Each year, the (James E. Walker Library) MakerSpace projects, aviation simulations, BAJA rovers, and meeting (retired) Lt. Gen. (Keith) Huber are highlights of the week.”

Going ALL In

Activities during the academy covered aerospace, agriculture, engineering technology, physics and astronomy, concrete and construction management, horse science, biology, chemistry, military science and mechatronics in Basic and Applied Sciences; fashion studies, social work, criminal justice, public health, physician assistant studies, athletics training and exercise science in Behavioral and Health Sciences.

Andrew Oppmann, MTSU’s vice president for marketing and communications and a CAP lieutenant colonel, urged cadets to take full advantage of the educational opportunities faculty crafted for the week.

“We at MTSU are honored to welcome you to our campus and congratulate you in your selection in this very selective academy,” Oppmann, a member of CAP’s Board of Governors, said during opening ceremonies.

Andrew Oppmann, at podium, Middle Tennessee State University’s vice president for marketing and communications and a Civil Air Patrol lieutenant colonel, welcomes CAP cadets attending the National Cadet Engineering Technology Academy on the MTSU campus in Murfreesboro, Tenn. Seated on stage, from left, are Greg Van Patten, dean of the College of Basic and Applied Sciences; Beth Loughry, public relations specialist in Marketing and Communications; and retired Lt. Gen. Keith Huber, senior adviser for veterans and leadership initiatives at MTSU. (MTSU Photo by James Cessna)

Making Mov(i)es

Cadets also learned about the recording industry in Media and Entertainment and used the television production studio shared by MTSU’s True Blue TV in the College of Education’s Center for Educational Media for video interviews. Also, Huber, the university’s senior adviser for veterans and leadership initiatives, conducted a leadership seminar for the cadets.

“The MTSU faculty has carefully curated every facet of this week to ensure that cadets not only learn about engineering but also experience the full scope of opportunities MTSU has to offer,” said Cadet Lt. Col. Ava Zendejas of Washington Wing, the academy’s cadet commander.

CAP’s national commander and CEO, Maj. Gen. Regena Aye thanked MTSU for hosting the annual event, acknowledging that the university was also deployed that same week to Oshkosh, Wisconsin, for EAA AirVenture, the world’s largest aviation experience.

“Such a joy to get to speak about the great work that Middle Tennessee State University does, and our partnership with them, which is very impactful in the lives of our cadets,” Aye told Flying Magazine during an interview at the 2026 EAA AirVenture.

“We have about 60 cadets there now, learning about the aviation career field,” she added. “And when you are on a college campus, and you get to experience what college students get to see and do on a daily basis, that inspires you to see yourself in that environment.”

Civil Air Patrol, founded in 1941 just before the start of America’s involvement in World War II, has more than 70,000 volunteer members. Congress chartered the organization to support the Air Force, and it is best known for its aerial search-and-rescue missions; cadet program for youths ages 12 through 18; and commitment to aerospace education.

Civil Air Patrol cadets in the National Cadet Engineering Technology Academy construct projects in the MakerSpace in the James E. Walker Library. (MTSU Photo by James Cessna)

MTSU and CAP have been partners in aerospace education for cadets since 2014 and have hosted the academy since 2017. The two entities first partnered from 1948 to 1953, when CAP’s Middle Tennessee State College Squadron was organized by students taking flight training at the on-campus airport.

Ragain said CAP was already looking ahead to coming back to campus for next year’s academy. "We look forward to continuing to work with MTSU into the future,” she said.

Learn more about Civil Air Patrol and how you can shape not only your future, but those around you as well.

Christina Ragain, director of the academy and lead for the 14 adults who guided the cadet activity. "Each year, the (James E. Walker Library) MakerSpace projects, aviation simulations, BAJA rovers, and meeting (retired) Lt. Gen. (Keith) Huber are highlights of the week.”

Going ALL In

Activities during the academy covered aerospace, agriculture, engineering technology, physics and astronomy, concrete and construction management, horse science, biology, chemistry, military science and mechatronics in Basic and Applied Sciences; fashion studies, social work, criminal justice, public health, physician assistant studies, athletics training and exercise science in Behavioral and Health Sciences.

Andrew Oppmann, MTSU’s vice president for marketing and communications and a CAP lieutenant colonel, urged cadets to take full advantage of the educational opportunities faculty crafted for the week.

“We at MTSU are honored to welcome you to our campus and congratulate you in your selection in this very selective academy,” Oppmann, a member of CAP’s Board of Governors, said during opening ceremonies.

Andrew Oppmann, at podium, Middle Tennessee State University’s vice president for marketing and communications and a Civil Air Patrol lieutenant colonel, welcomes CAP cadets attending the National Cadet Engineering Technology Academy on the MTSU campus in Murfreesboro, Tenn. Seated on stage, from left, are Greg Van Patten, dean of the College of Basic and Applied Sciences; Beth Loughry, public relations specialist in Marketing and Communications; and retired Lt. Gen. Keith Huber, senior adviser for veterans and leadership initiatives at MTSU. (MTSU Photo by James Cessna)

Making Mov(i)es

Cadets also learned about the recording industry in Media and Entertainment and used the television production studio shared by MTSU’s True Blue TV in the College of Education’s Center for Educational Media for video interviews. Also, Huber, the university’s senior adviser for veterans and leadership initiatives, conducted a leadership seminar for the cadets.

“The MTSU faculty has carefully curated every facet of this week to ensure that cadets not only learn about engineering but also experience the full scope of opportunities MTSU has to offer,” said Cadet Lt. Col. Ava Zendejas of Washington Wing, the academy’s cadet commander.

CAP’s national commander and CEO, Maj. Gen. Regena Aye thanked MTSU for hosting the annual event, acknowledging that the university was also deployed that same week to Oshkosh, Wisconsin, for EAA AirVenture, the world’s largest aviation experience.

“Such a joy to get to speak about the great work that Middle Tennessee State University does, and our partnership with them, which is very impactful in the lives of our cadets,” Aye told Flying Magazine during an interview at the 2026 EAA AirVenture.

“We have about 60 cadets there now, learning about the aviation career field,” she added. “And when you are on a college campus, and you get to experience what college students get to see and do on a daily basis, that inspires you to see yourself in that environment.”

Civil Air Patrol, founded in 1941 just before the start of America’s involvement in World War II, has more than 70,000 volunteer members. Congress chartered the organization to support the Air Force, and it is best known for its aerial search-and-rescue missions; cadet program for youths ages 12 through 18; and commitment to aerospace education.

Civil Air Patrol cadets in the National Cadet Engineering Technology Academy construct projects in the MakerSpace in the James E. Walker Library. (MTSU Photo by James Cessna)

MTSU and CAP have been partners in aerospace education for cadets since 2014 and have hosted the academy since 2017. The two entities first partnered from 1948 to 1953, when CAP’s Middle Tennessee State College Squadron was organized by students taking flight training at the on-campus airport.

Ragain said CAP was already looking ahead to coming back to campus for next year’s academy. "We look forward to continuing to work with MTSU into the future,” she said.
