articles.heading: Orange acquires Obvios’ Dome private 5G core technology
articles.summary: Orange has acquired Dome, a private 5G core technology developed by French company Obvios, as it looks to deepen its sovereign connectivity portfolio for defense, public safety and critical infrast | Orange is deepening its sovereign connectivity play with private 5G core tech aimed at defense, public safety and critical infrastructure customers.
articles.content:
Orange has acquired Dome, a private 5G core technology developed by French company Obvios, as it looks to deepen its sovereign connectivity portfolio for defense, public safety and critical infrastructure customers.
The cloud-native software platform is designed to help organizations deploy secure, resilient private mobile networks that can operate independently of public telecom infrastructure. Orange said the Dome technology will support low-latency communications, high resilience, full operational control and sovereign deployment for users in critical environments.

The deal also brings the experts behind Dome into Orange’s teams and strengthens Orange Business’s Defense & Security division, which was created to serve defense, homeland security and other sensitive sectors.


Nassima Auvray, head of Orange Business’s Defense & Security business unit, called the acquisition “a strategic milestone” for strengthening the company’s expertise in hybrid network solutions. She said it will accelerate Orange’s private 5G development and help the company deliver sovereign services tailored to European defense and critical infrastructure operators.
Potential use cases include drone and autonomous system operations, private connectivity for military bases, deployable tactical networks in remote or contested areas, surveillance at ports and airports, emergency services communications and real-time monitoring of energy, transportation and other critical infrastructure assets.
Read the full press release here.

articles.summary: Hoboken, N.J. – The Stevens Institute of Technology men's tennis team will compete in three events during the fall portion of its 2026-27 schedule, including the
articles.content:
Hoboken, N.J. – The Stevens Institute of Technology men's tennis team will compete in three events during the fall portion of its 2026-27 schedule, including the ITA Atlantic South Region Championship.
The Ducks open the fall at the Haverford/Swarthmore Invitational on Sept. 12-13. Stevens will compete at Haverford College on the opening day of the tournament before traveling to Swarthmore College for the second day of competition. Action is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. on both days.
Stevens will then travel to Fredericksburg, Va., for the four-day ITA Atlantic South Region Championship, hosted by the University of Mary Washington. The regional championship is scheduled for Oct. 1-4 and will feature both singles and doubles competition. The Ducks conclude their fall slate on Oct. 17 with a pair of MAC Freedom matches at the Bayonne Tennis Courts. Stevens will face Misericordia University and King's College (Pa.), with match times to be announced.
The remainder of the 2026-27 schedule, including the Ducks' spring championship season, will be announced at a later date.

articles.summary: INFUSE Bone Graft for TLIF receives eligibility for Medicare New Technology Add-on Payment, Advancing Reimbursement Support for Hospitals and Spine Surgeons – Ortho Spine News Ortho Spine News
articles.content:
GALWAY, Ireland, September 2, 2026 – Medtronic (NYSE: MDT), a global leader in healthcare technology announced that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) has granted a New Technology Add-on Payment (NTAP) for INFUSE™ Bone Graft for TLIF, effective October 1, 2026.
NTAP is a Medicare Fee For Service inpatient reimbursement mechanism designed to help support hospital adoption of qualifying new technologies during the period before standard payment rates are updated. By providing additional reimbursement for certain cases when the cost of a new technology exceeds the standard payment amount, NTAP can help reduce hospital financial barriers to early adoption and support patient access.
“This NTAP reflects the clinical value of INFUSE™ Bone Graft for TLIF and reinforces the importance of reimbursement support in helping hospitals adopt innovative technologies,” said Dave Breiter, vice president of Clinical, Medical, Regulatory Affairs and Health Economics for the Cranial & Spinal Technologies business. “For surgeons, hospitals, and patients, this milestone helps strengthen access to a proven biologic option for spine procedures while supporting the realities of inpatient care delivery.”
INFUSE™ bone graft is the first and only growth factor technology approved for use in spine fusion procedures. Earlier this year, Infuse™ bone graft received FDA premarket approval for TLIF following Breakthrough Device Designation (BDD) and a prioritized review timeline, underscoring the strength of the clinical evidence supporting its use. NTAP builds on that momentum by helping support hospital access to this important innovation.
The NTAP program is particularly relevant for hospital administrators and revenue cycle leaders, who evaluate not only clinical value, but also the reimbursement environment that can influence investments in new technologies.
This milestone underscores Medtronic’s commitment to advancing clinically meaningful innovation and helping expand access to important technologies in the hospital setting.
About NTAP
NTAP, or New Technology Add-on Payment, is a Medicare Fee For Service reimbursement mechanism for qualifying technologies used in the inpatient hospital setting. It is intended to help bridge the gap between the introduction of a new technology and the time when hospital payment rates are recalibrated to reflect its cost.
For more information about the NTAP designation for Infuse™ bone graft for TLIF: medtronic.com/SpineLine
About the Cranial & Spinal Technologies Business at Medtronic
As the global market leader, Medtronic Cranial and Spinal Technologies is transforming the standard of care in spine and cranial surgery by putting patients first and addressing the complex challenges faced by spine and neurosurgeons. With a portfolio of 150 products covering more than 20 pathologies, we serve over 4 million patients annually. Building on a legacy of innovation, our AiBLE™ ecosystem integrates advanced technologies, data, and AI with a patient-centric approach, offering customizable solutions to enhance surgical precision, improve workflow efficiency, and achieve better outcomes, before, during, and beyond surgery.
About Medtronic
Bold thinking. Bolder actions. We are Medtronic. Medtronic plc, headquartered in Galway, Ireland, is the leading global healthcare technology company that boldly attacks the most challenging health problems facing humanity by searching out and finding solutions. Our Mission — to alleviate pain, restore health, and extend life — unites a global team of 95,000+ passionate people across more than 150 countries.
Our technologies and therapies treat 70 health conditions and include cardiac devices, surgical robotics, insulin pumps, surgical tools, patient monitoring systems, and more. Powered by our diverse knowledge, insatiable curiosity, and desire to help all those who need it, we deliver innovative technologies that transform the lives of two people every second, every hour, every day. Expect more from us as we empower insight-driven care, experiences that put people first, and better outcomes for our world. In everything we do, we are engineering the extraordinary.
For more information on Medtronic, visit www.Medtronic.com and follow Medtronic on LinkedIn.
Any forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties such as those described in Medtronic’s periodic reports on file with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Actual results may differ materially from anticipated results.

articles.article_title: The technology reckoning: New priorities for IT leaders
articles.heading: The technology reckoning: New priorities for IT leaders
articles.summary: What a year of AI, quantum, cyber risk, and infrastructure constraints reveals about the next era of enterprise leadership
articles.content:
What a year of AI, quantum, cyber risk, and infrastructure constraints reveals about the next era of enterprise leadership
In the past year, enterprise technology risk has become more systemic, more physical and more entangled with policy and economics. It’s no longer possible to plan technology strategy in isolation – it must now account for the coverage of capital strategy, geopolitical strategy, workforce strategy, sustainability strategy and operational resilience.
The next twelve months will be less about discovering entirely new technologies and more about absorbing the consequences of the technologies that have already been deployed, writes Kris Lovejoy, Chief Strategy Officer, Kyndryl. In this new era, enterprises will discover that the hardest part of technology transformation is not invention; it is control.
Key takeaways
AI is moving from experimentation to economic discipline.
The pilot phase of generative AI is ending, and it is now becoming a run-rate expense, an operational dependency, and in some cases, a source of budget volatility. Agentic AI changes the nature of consumption, as a single user can trigger dozens or hundreds of model operations in a single business interaction. In addition to token consumption, conversations about open-weight models raise questions about whether every AI engagement must run through a “metered” service.
The enterprise is creating an ungoverned AI estate.
Unlike shadow IT, AI agents are full actors within the enterprise environment who can retrieve data, initiate transactions, generate code and more. Yet in recent research from Kyndryl, just 27% of executives told us they had a central registry and monitoring system for all AI operating in their environments. Without visibility into what agents exist, who owns them, what they can access and more, enterprises will struggle to answer essential and basic governance questions.
Digital growth is becoming constrained by physical resources.
Physical constraints, including power, water and community acceptance, are increasingly limiting AI adoption. This shift will change enterprise technology procurement as buyers begin asking cloud and AI providers the questions once reserved for utility providers, environmental teams and local governments.
Quantum is becoming a governance problem before becoming a compute advantage.
Quantum’s near-term impact begins with governance. Organizations must prepare for a future in which cryptographic assumptions change, optimization methods improve, and industry-specific quantum use cases begin moving from research partnerships toward early workflow integration. Waiting for a dramatic breakthrough could leave enterprises unprepared and cost them the opportunity to gain first-mover advantage.

articles.article_title: Plan A Technologies Acquires Stealth AI Assessment Technology to Expand Technical M&A Due Diligence Capabilities
articles.heading: Plan A Technologies Acquires Stealth AI Assessment Technology to Expand Technical M&A Due Diligence Capabilities
articles.summary: /PRNewswire/ -- Plan A Technologies, an award-winning AI and software engineering company specializing in providing technology advice and custom software and...
articles.content:
Proprietary technology helps Plan A evaluate complex technology environments faster—and uncover technical risks, patterns, and opportunities that traditional assessment tools may miss
LAS VEGAS, Sept. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Plan A Technologies, an award-winning AI and software engineering company specializing in providing technology advice and custom software and agent development, today announced the acquisition of a stealth AI assessment tool to enhance its technical M&A due diligence practice.
Plan A has become a trusted technical due diligence partner for private equity firms, strategic acquirers, enterprise companies, and private investors evaluating technology-intensive transactions. Its teams are brought in to answer some of the most important questions surrounding an acquisition: Is the underlying technology as strong as it appears? What risks may not be evident from management presentations? How difficult will the platform be to scale, integrate, modernize, or secure? And what additional investment may be required after closing?
The newly acquired technology gives Plan A another proprietary layer of analysis to help answer those questions.
"Good technical due diligence isn't about producing a longer list of issues. It's about distinguishing ordinary, fixable technical debt from something that can fundamentally change the cost or risk profile of a transaction," said Slav Kulik, Co-Founder of Plan A Technologies. "We help our clients to understand what is really happening underneath the surface of a technology platform and translate that into business implications. Technical due diligence has traditionally relied on expert interviews, manual code review, architecture analysis, documentation, and commercially available code scanning tools. Plan A will continue to use all of those approaches, but this new technology will help us analyze exceptionally large and fragmented technology ecosystems with greater speed and consistency while looking for patterns or anomalies that conventional approaches may miss."
Plan A believes this type of deeper analysis will become increasingly crucial as more and more code is created by AI, often resulting in company leaders who don't understand their own technology nearly as well as they did in the past.
Kulik added, "AI is not a substitute for senior technical judgment. The advantage comes from combining AI with people who have spent years building, scaling, fixing, integrating, and evaluating real production systems. That combination allows us to ask better questions and give our clients a more complete picture of what they're actually buying."
The tool's creator, Serhii Melnychuk, has joined Plan A Technologies as an architect to lead its integration and future development.
"I wanted to build something that could help experts do their job more effectively and connect signals scattered across different systems," said Serhii Melnychuk, lead developer of the technology. "It's incredibly exciting to see how Plan A integrated my tool into its broader approach and is bringing it to clients around the world."
The acquisition also reflects a broader strategy at Plan A: developing and acquiring proprietary technology that makes its engineers, architects, data specialists, and technology advisors more effective.
While technical M&A due diligence is an important and growing part of Plan A's business, it represents only one component of the company's broader work. Plan A also helps clients design and build new software products from scratch, deploy proprietary AI agents and agentic systems, modernize legacy applications, build data platforms, migrate infrastructure to the cloud, integrate enterprise systems, and solve large-scale engineering challenges.
That breadth is particularly valuable during M&A engagements because Plan A's diligence teams are not simply professional auditors who only evaluate technology—they are practitioners who build and operate it. The same engineering leaders assessing whether a platform can scale or be modernized have experience executing those initiatives in complex environments.
For clients, that means an assessment can go beyond identifying what is wrong. Plan A also helps define the optimal path forward, and if needed, can deploy the engineering teams required to execute the roadmap following the transaction.
About Plan A Technologies
Plan A Technologies was created to solve the toughest tech challenges facing today's businesses. Plan A helps organizations analyze their tech ecosystem to identify exactly what needs to be improved across their products and infrastructure—and then builds the solutions to fix it.
Rather than offering theoretical ideas or software that never launches, Plan A Technologies combines elite engineering talent with custom-built, proprietary AI agents to deliver fast, secure, production-ready solutions. Its capabilities span proprietary AI agent deployment, custom software development, application modernization, data platforms, cloud migrations, systems integration, and practical technical advice.
With more than 500 successful product deployments completed worldwide, Plan A helps organizations of every size—from ambitious startups to global enterprises—modernize their systems, automate complex operations, and stay ahead of the technology curve.
To see how Plan A turns complex technical challenges into real-world solutions, visit PlanATechnologies.com,

It's about distinguishing ordinary, fixable technical debt from something that can fundamentally change the cost or risk profile of a transaction," said Slav Kulik, Co-Founder of Plan A Technologies. "We help our clients to understand what is really happening underneath the surface of a technology platform and translate that into business implications. Technical due diligence has traditionally relied on expert interviews, manual code review, architecture analysis, documentation, and commercially available code scanning tools. Plan A will continue to use all of those approaches, but this new technology will help us analyze exceptionally large and fragmented technology ecosystems with greater speed and consistency while looking for patterns or anomalies that conventional approaches may miss."

Plan A believes this type of deeper analysis will become increasingly crucial as more and more code is created by AI, often resulting in company leaders who don't understand their own technology nearly as well as they did in the past.

Kulik added, "AI is not a substitute for senior technical judgment. The advantage comes from combining AI with people who have spent years building, scaling, fixing, integrating, and evaluating real production systems. That combination allows us to ask better questions and give our clients a more complete picture of what they're actually buying."

The tool's creator, Serhii Melnychuk, has joined Plan A Technologies as an architect to lead its integration and future development.

"I wanted to build something that could help experts do their job more effectively and connect signals scattered across different systems," said Serhii Melnychuk, lead developer of the technology. "It's incredibly exciting to see how Plan A integrated my tool into its broader approach and is bringing it to clients around the world."

The acquisition also reflects a broader strategy at Plan A: developing and acquiring proprietary technology that makes its engineers, architects, data specialists, and technology advisors more effective.

While technical M&A due diligence is an important and growing part of Plan A's business, it represents only one component of the company's broader work. Plan A also helps clients design and build new software products from scratch, deploy proprietary AI agents and agentic systems, modernize legacy applications, build data platforms, migrate infrastructure to the cloud, integrate enterprise systems, and solve large-scale engineering challenges.

That breadth is particularly valuable during M&A engagements because Plan A's diligence teams are not simply professional auditors who only evaluate technology—they are practitioners who build and operate it. The same engineering leaders assessing whether a platform can scale or be modernized have experience executing those initiatives in complex environments.

For clients, that means an assessment can go beyond identifying what is wrong. Plan A also helps define the optimal path forward, and if needed, can deploy the engineering teams required to execute the roadmap following the transaction.

About Plan A Technologies

Plan A Technologies was created to solve the toughest tech challenges facing today's businesses. Plan A helps organizations analyze their tech ecosystem to identify exactly what needs to be improved across their products and infrastructure—and then builds the solutions to fix it.

Rather than offering theoretical ideas or software that never launches, Plan A Technologies combines elite engineering talent with custom-built, proprietary AI agents to deliver fast, secure, production-ready solutions. Its capabilities span proprietary AI agent deployment, custom software development, application modernization, data platforms, cloud migrations, systems integration, and practical technical advice.

With more than 500 successful product deployments completed worldwide, Plan A helps organizations of every size—from ambitious startups to global enterprises—modernize their systems, automate complex operations, and stay ahead of the technology curve.

To see how Plan A turns complex technical challenges into real-world solutions, visit PlanATechnologies.com,

articles.title: John Deere Showcases Hands-Free Baling Technology at Farm Progress
articles.description: John Deere Showcases Hands-Free Baling Technology at Farm Progress RFD-TV
articles.description_html: John Deere Showcases Hands-Free Baling Technology at Farm Progress  RFD-TV
articles.article_title: John Deere Showcases Hands-Free Baling Technology at Farm Progress
articles.heading: John Deere Showcases Hands-Free Baling Technology at Farm Progress
articles.summary: John Deere showcases hands-free baling technology at Farm Progress Show, designed to reduce operator activity, fatigue, and unnecessary movement.
articles.content:
BOONE, IOWA (RFD NEWS) — The largest outdoor agricultural event in the United States is underway, with thousands of farmers and ranchers gathering in Boone, Iowa, for the Farm Progress Show. RFD-TV is on the ground at the show, where John Deere is highlighting new technology designed to make hay and forage operations more efficient while reducing operator fatigue.
Kaylene Ballesteros, John Deere Hay and Forage Market Manager, joined FarmHER + RanchHER host Kirbe Schnoor at the show to discuss the company’s new hands-free baling technology.
Automation Takes on More of the Baling Process
John Deere’s hands-free baling system builds on automation features many farmers may already have on their equipment.
Ballesteros said existing technologies such as AutoTrac, AutoTurn and tractor-baler automation can now work alongside new Weave Automation on John Deere’s RB baler.
The system is designed to allow the operator to bale with less hands-on involvement, reducing in-cab operator activity by up to 76%, according to John Deere.
“This is really just an extension of current automation that we have with our customers today,” Ballesteros said.
Building on Existing Equipment Investments
The technology is designed for operations baling materials such as corn stalks and wheat straw, while building on precision technology farmers may already have invested in.
Ballesteros said the goal is to help producers get more value from their existing equipment rather than requiring them to completely change their operations.
Testing has shown improvements in productivity and fuel efficiency while reducing operator activity.
Reducing Fatigue During Long Baling Windows
For farmers and ranchers facing narrow windows to get hay baled, reducing fatigue can be especially important.
Ballesteros said producers told John Deere they wanted less mental fatigue, denser and more consistent bales, and greater value from their existing investments.
The automation can help maintain a more consistent path while baling, potentially improving fuel efficiency by reducing unnecessary movement.
“We’re just trying to help them have more tools in their toolbox so that when they do need them, they can pull them out and use them,” Ballesteros said.
Giving Operators More Flexibility
The technology is also designed to give experienced operators more flexibility and help less-experienced operators achieve more consistent results.
Ballesteros acknowledged that highly experienced operators can already produce consistent, square-shouldered bales. The benefit of automation, she said, is giving those operators the ability to focus on other responsibilities while the equipment handles more of the baling process.
That could mean monitoring another field, making a phone call or simply freeing up time during demanding stretches of the season.
For operations where baling sometimes extends into the early morning hours, reducing the mental and physical demands on the operator could be particularly valuable.
FarmHER + RanchHER at Farm Progress Show
RFD-TV is also highlighting the women working across agriculture during the Farm Progress Show.
FarmHER + RanchHER’s Kirbe Schnoor is leading a panel discussion featuring four finalists for the Women in the Field “Producer of the Year” Award. The winner will be announced at 2 p.m. during the show.

articles.title: Owen Thiele, Este Haim, Kate Berlant, Lisa Gilroy, Joel Kim Booster Join Variety’s Entertainment & Technology Summit
articles.description: Owen Thiele, Este Haim, Kate Berlant, Lisa Gilroy, Joel Kim Booster Join Variety’s Entertainment & Technology Summit Variety
articles.description_html: Owen Thiele, Este Haim, Kate Berlant, Lisa Gilroy, Joel Kim Booster Join Variety’s Entertainment & Technology Summit  Variety
articles.article_title: Owen Thiele, Este Haim, Kate Berlant, Lisa Gilroy, Joel Kim Booster Join Variety’s Entertainment & Technology Summit
articles.heading: Owen Thiele, Este Haim, Kate Berlant, Lisa Gilroy, Joel Kim Booster Join Variety’s Entertainment & Technology Summit
articles.summary: Leadership from WPP Media, NBCUniversal Entertainment, Netflix, Amazon, Paramount, Hallmark, and more are scheduled to speak.
articles.content:
Variety has announced additional programming for its Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY on Sept. 17 in Los Angeles. This includes actor and host of “In Your Dreams” podcast Owen Thiele; musician, composer and music supervisor Este Haim; actress and comedian Kate Berlant; actor, writer and comedian Lisa Gilroy; writer and comedian Joel Kim Booster; Nancy Hall, U.S. CEO of WPP Media; and Liz Jenkins, chief business officer of NBCUniversal Entertainment.
Thiele, Haim, Berlant, Gilroy and Booster are scheduled to headline the “Storytelling Vanguards” panel, which will explore the creative processes driving today’s most dynamic storytellers and hear their perspectives on where film, television, music, podcasting and more are headed.
Popular on Variety
WPP’s Hall will join Tom McKenna, global head of media, operations & business development, Audible for the discussion “When Stories Speak: Reaching Audiences in the Next Era of Entertainment.”
In other highlights, the fireside chat “Behind the Business: Netflix Comedy and the Return of ‘A Different World’” will feature Tracey Pakosta, VP comedy original series, Netflix and Felicia Pride, creator, executive producer and showrunner, of the upcoming Netflix series “A Different World.”
Joining them will be a distinguished group of industry leaders shaping the future of media and entertainment, including Jeremy Helfand, Global VP, head of Prime Video Advertising at Amazon; Marie Marks, SVP, global experiences at Paramount; Darren Abbott, president of Hallmark Media and chief brands officer of Hallmark; Billy Parks, head of FOX Creator Studios; and Christina Kothari, global head of consumer marketing at Reddit.
Helfand joins “The New Era of the TV Business” panel alongside Puja Vohra, chief marketing officer and EVP, advertising sales, Fox Corporation; Jimmy White, managing director and head of large customer sales, Samsung Ads; Gina Reduto, EVP, strategy, advertising & partnerships, NBCUniversal; Josh Mattison, EVP, digital revenue pricing, planning & operations, Disney Advertising; and Matty Beckerman, CEO & founder, IRCODE. The panel will explore innovations behind driving business across media platforms and will be moderated by Variety’s business editor, Todd Spangler.
Marie Marks and Darren Abbott will be alongside Natalia Premovic, chief consumer products & experiences officer, Mattel, Ed Bobrin, Microsoft AI and data leader, EY Americas, and Ivo Gerscovich, head of SEGA Brands and chief business & brand officer, “Sonic the Hedgehog”, in the “The Future of IRL: Trends in Event and Experiential Entertainment” panel. The panel will be moderated by Jay Tucker, executive director, Center for Media, Entertainment and Sports, UCLA Anderson School.
“We’re entering a new era where AI is transforming how content is created, discovered, monetized and experienced,” said Vamsi Duvvuri, EY Americas Technology, Media & Entertainment and Telecommunications AI Leader. “What excites me most is the opportunity to help creators and media companies get more value from their IP, tell richer stories, and create more personal relationships with audiences. We’re moving beyond simply watching content to experiencing it across digital and physical worlds. Variety‘s Entertainment & Technology Summit brings together the people who are helping define what’s next.”
Parks and Kothari join the “Titans of Innovation Roundtable” panel, which will talk about cutting-edge initiatives and flashes of insight that move the entertainment business forward. The pair join Sean Atkins, CEO, Dhar Mann Studios, Maya Rogers, CEO, Tetris, and Nicole Wyskoarko, president and head of Urban A&R, Interscope Geffen A&M Records. The panel will be moderated by Sammi Cohen, CEO, Social Currency Media & host, “Social Currency with Sammi Cohen” podcast.
Ernst & Young is the presenting partner of the event. Official partners are Comscore and WPP Media. AMC Global Media, Havas Play, IRCODE, Spotify, and Teads are supporting partners of the summit.
Space is limited, reserve your ticket at variety.com/enttech.

articles.title: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation’s Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools
articles.description: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation’s Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools NYC.gov
articles.description_html: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation’s Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools  NYC.gov
articles.source: The official website of the City of New York
articles.article_title: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation’s Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools
articles.heading: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation’s Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools
articles.summary: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation’s Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools NYC.gov
articles.content:
What you should know
- Representing the most expansive student-facing AI policy in the country, the Mamdani administration prioritizes student safety and real, human instruction
NEW YORK – Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels today announced a moratorium on student-facing generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) use in schools, alongside a new screen time policy, a decision that will impact nearly 600,000 public school students, or two-thirds of the system’s total enrollment. The policy establishes a one-year moratorium, effective in the 2026-2027 school year, on student-facing generative AI for children in 2-K through 8th grade. It also introduces twice-yearly AI critical thinking modules for high schoolers, limited AI pilots for a small number of high school classrooms and age-appropriate screen time restrictions.
“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow. They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators and wrestle with tough problems on their own,” said Mayor Mamdani. “The tech industry wants us to believe that A.I.-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary. We do not see it that way. That’s why we’re implementing a moratorium on generative AI for students in 2-K through 8th grade and spending the next year studying the impacts of this technology.”
“We have a responsibility to ensure that rapidly-changing technology supports our children and their learning, rather than getting in the way of it,” said Governor Kathy Hochul. “New York State has been leading the way in our efforts to keep kids focused on learning and growing — not clicking and scrolling — and I commend Mayor Mamdani for building on this work and pushing our shared commitment to supporting New York’s kids forward.”
“As Chancellor and as a parent, I believe our job is to protect what makes learning work, while ensuring every child has the critical thinking skills they need before graduating,” said Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels. “We’re putting guardrails in place to protect the human connection, curiosity and creativity that help children grow. We’re standing firmly in our belief that innovation does not mean more technology, and over the next year, we will lead with evidence to make sure technology serves learning — not the other way around.”
“As artificial intelligence rapidly expands into students’ lives, our city government has a responsibility to ensure this technology is serving, and not hurting, their development,” said Public Advocate Jumaane D. Williams. “This ban on student-facing AI for our youngest students, as well as age-appropriate screen time restrictions, are important steps in the right direction. Using this as a foundation but not a final word, we must continue to thoroughly review technologies that are entering the classroom and institute guardrails that promote the safety and well-being of New Yorkers.”
Representing the most expansive student-facing AI moratorium in the nation, the new policy eliminates AI use for students in grades 2-K through 8th grade. This includes all software that uses student-facing generative AI. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades.
Throughout the 2026-27 school year, a new Technology in Schools Coalition, made up of students, educators, parent leaders, elected officials, advocates, union partners and experts in the field will convene to assess the impact of the moratorium and limited pilots. The coalition will publish a report with recommendations for future school years.
For a maximum of 50,000 high school students in general education classes, or approximately 5% of the public-school student body, five limited AI pilots will be introduced. All high school students will also have access to twice-yearly AI literacy classes designed to help them think critically about AI before they begin to rely on it.
The two 45-minute modules will introduce students to what AI is and is not, as well as AI-related bias, risks, ethical considerations and impacts on careers and future skills.
The limited pilots will be offered at a maximum of five classes per high school. All use will take place under the direct supervision of a trained educator and will involve carefully vetted AI tools. The pilots were selected based on rigorous safety and data privacy standards, their focus on teacher-guided instruction and their commitment to keeping students as the primary thinker in the classroom.
Pilot programs include:
- Quill: Accessed by English language arts classrooms, Quill is designed to support close reading, text analysis and the use of evidence to support claims. Students will use Quill for no more than 15 minutes per week.
- Edia: Accessed by math classrooms, Edia is designed to provide step-by-step coaching and prompt students to explain their reasoning. Students will use Edia for no more than 20 minutes per week.
- Brisk Teaching: Accessed through teacher-created activities, Brisk Teaching is designed to provide guided practice using teacher-selected texts or videos, with objectives and guardrails set by the teacher. Students will use Brisk Boost for 10 to 20 minutes once or twice per week.
- Playlab: To be used across multiple subjects, Playlab is designed to help students engage with assignment-specific applications and examine AI outputs for bias and reasoning. No more than two assignments per marking period will use Playlab.
- Intel AI-Ready Schools: To be used across multiple subjects, Intel AI-Ready Schools is designed to help students identify community problems and develop AI solutions through semester-long projects. Students will use the tool for one period per week.
Teachers will continue to be permitted to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks, provided all tools comply with NYCPS safety standards. Exceptions to the policy will be granted for assistive technology usage by students with disabilities, multilingual learners and students participating in career readiness programs, like computer science.
With this new policy, students in 2nd grade and below will see restricted 1:1 screen time, with recommended caps of 30 minutes a day for students in 3rd grade through 5th grade and 45 minutes for students in 6th grade through 8th grade.
Under the new policy, all technology tools used in NYCPS will undergo an exhaustive review and will be barred if their functionality is ultimately determined not to be mission-critical to learning. The review will include vendor accountability for safety and transparency standards, ethics, evidence of learning design and instructional impact, prior research and the continuous collection of user feedback.
“Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Chancellor Kamar Samuels are taking a thoughtful and responsible approach to AI in our schools. Early-grade education must be rooted in building foundational skills through evidence-based practices, not experimenting on children with rapidly evolving technology. As Chair of the New York State Assembly Committee on Libraries and Education Technology, I introduced similar legislation, and I’m proud to serve on the advisory panel that will help New York City determine where AI can genuinely improve education while protecting students and preserving appropriate exceptions for children with disabilities,” said Assemblymember Robert Carroll, Chair of the Assembly Committee on Libraries and Education Technology.
“The AI policy set forth today protects the city’s youngest learners and prepares high school students to tackle the changing landscape they will graduate into. This policy is appropriately careful and responsive to community voices. I look forward to working closely with the Technology in Schools Coalition to further develop this policy and ensure accountability. As the coming wave of technology emerges, young people will be on the forefront — it will be their creativity, and ingenuity will lead the way. Our responsibility is to establish guardrails, such as these, to help them do it responsibly. This is a good step in that direction,” said Councilwoman Rita Joseph, Higher Education Chair.
“As a former middle school teacher, I'm so pleased to see that our Mayor is taking a nuanced approach to a new and rapidly changing educational tool. We took too long to respond to the effects of social media and smart phones on our youth. This combination of a 1-year ban with select pilot programs allows us to take a serious look at AI usage in schools and find a path that allows our students to adapt to our changing world in a safe manner,” said State Senator Jabari Brisport.
“This one-year ban on student-facing artificial intelligence technology use and restrictions on screen time through eighth grade are the right policies for optimal student learning and development,” said Council Member Lincoln Restler. “Credit to Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for listening to students, parents, teachers and administrators and protecting our young people from the potentially harmful effects of untested technology. This pause alongside a commitment to meaningfully engage stakeholders in the months ahead will allow us to craft long term policies amid a rapidly changing technology landscape.”
“We should never confuse a machine’s ability to produce an answer with a child’s ability to arrive at one. There is something sacred in the struggle to understand: the question asked twice, the page wrestled with, the mistake that becomes discovery, the teacher who sees possibility before a student sees it in themselves,” said State Senator Robert Jackson. “That is where intellect is formed and independence begins. In a democracy, we educate children not simply to know things, but to question, discern, imagine, and ultimately think for themselves. I commend Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for recognizing that progress must earn its place in the classroom. Technology will continue to change, but our obligation must remain constant: childhood must never be the price we pay for innovation.”
“Tech companies have forced their way into every corner of kids' lives with big promises of benefits but little evidence to back them up. Enough is enough,” said State Senator Andrew Gounardes. “These new rules are an important step toward ensuring our kids' needs come before Big Tech's profits. By putting smart, thoughtful guardrails around the use of tech in schools, we can ensure learning comes first. Thanks to Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for working to give our children the education they need and deserve.”
“AI is changing how we learn and work, and our kids need to be prepared to use it safely, think critically, and interrogate the information it produces,” said Council Member Gale A. Brewer. “I am encouraged that NYC Public Schools is taking a comprehensive approach, with age-appropriate AI literacy in K–8 and more focused instruction in high school, and I look forward to the program being shared with parents and staff. Thank you to Chancellor Kamar Samuels and Mayor Mamdani for preparing our students for a rapidly changing world.”
“The recent METR OpenAI report demonstrated how easily AI models can run amok, literally learning how to lie and cheat while covering their tracks to evade being caught deviating from their original code. Our ability to use generative AI with confidence that it won’t turn on our kids and do something else is tenuous at best. The policies announced today are well thought out, age-appropriate, and comprehensive — allowing for carefully chosen pilots for high schoolers and for those AI tools that provide access for students with disabilities and English language learners. Thank you, Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels, for pumping the brakes and creating this detailed policy,” said Assemblymember Jo Anne Simon.
“As a 14-year public school special education teacher and Chair of the City Council's Education Committee, I've seen how quickly new technology can outpace a school system's ability to manage it responsibly,” said Council Member Eric Dinowitz. “My committee's recent oversight hearing made clear the DOE needs a deliberate, evidence-based approach before AI tools reach classrooms unchecked. I applaud Chancellor Samuels' work on this policy and look forward to continuing our work together to ensure our students are kept safe and that technologies support and enhance learning.”
“AI and technology are central to New York’s economic future, as underscored by last week’s CBRE report showing that New York City now has more tech jobs than the Bay Area. We’re encouraged that high schoolers will have access to AI career readiness tools that can help prepare them for the workforce, and we recommend expanding this access beyond one hour per week in the future. At the same time, strong guardrails should enable age-appropriate learning that puts safety first, even at younger grades. Preparing youth for adult life and workplaces that rely on technology will require students to understand AI, question it, and use it safely, under the guidance of teachers. These are incredibly complex issues, and we give Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels credit for listening to all sides and creating a task force, which I am proud to serve on, to help shape what comes next,” said Tech:NYC President & CEO Julie Samuels.
###

“As artificial intelligence rapidly expands into students’ lives, our city government has a responsibility to ensure this technology is serving, and not hurting, their development,” said Public Advocate Jumaane D. Williams. “This ban on student-facing AI for our youngest students, as well as age-appropriate screen time restrictions, are important steps in the right direction. Using this as a foundation but not a final word, we must continue to thoroughly review technologies that are entering the classroom and institute guardrails that promote the safety and well-being of New Yorkers.”

Representing the most expansive student-facing AI moratorium in the nation, the new policy eliminates AI use for students in grades 2-K through 8th grade. This includes all software that uses student-facing generative AI. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades.

Throughout the 2026-27 school year, a new Technology in Schools Coalition, made up of students, educators, parent leaders, elected officials, advocates, union partners and experts in the field will convene to assess the impact of the moratorium and limited pilots. The coalition will publish a report with recommendations for future school years.

For a maximum of 50,000 high school students in general education classes, or approximately 5% of the public-school student body, five limited AI pilots will be introduced. All high school students will also have access to twice-yearly AI literacy classes designed to help them think critically about AI before they begin to rely on it.

The two 45-minute modules will introduce students to what AI is and is not, as well as AI-related bias, risks, ethical considerations and impacts on careers and future skills.

The limited pilots will be offered at a maximum of five classes per high school. All use will take place under the direct supervision of a trained educator and will involve carefully vetted AI tools. The pilots were selected based on rigorous safety and data privacy standards, their focus on teacher-guided instruction and their commitment to keeping students as the primary thinker in the classroom.

Pilot programs include:

  • Quill: Accessed by English language arts classrooms, Quill is designed to support close reading, text analysis and the use of evidence to support claims. Students will use Quill for no more than 15 minutes per week.
  • Edia: Accessed by math classrooms, Edia is designed to provide step-by-step coaching and prompt students to explain their reasoning. Students will use Edia for no more than 20 minutes per week.
  • Brisk Teaching: Accessed through teacher-created activities, Brisk Teaching is designed to provide guided practice using teacher-selected texts or videos, with objectives and guardrails set by the teacher. Students will use Brisk Boost for 10 to 20 minutes once or twice per week.
  • Playlab: To be used across multiple subjects, Playlab is designed to help students engage with assignment-specific applications and examine AI outputs for bias and reasoning. No more than two assignments per marking period will use Playlab.
  • Intel AI-Ready Schools: To be used across multiple subjects, Intel AI-Ready Schools is designed to help students identify community problems and develop AI solutions through semester-long projects. Students will use the tool for one period per week.

Teachers will continue to be permitted to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks, provided all tools comply with NYCPS safety standards. Exceptions to the policy will be granted for assistive technology usage by students with disabilities, multilingual learners and students participating in career readiness programs, like computer science.

With this new policy, students in 2nd grade and below will see restricted 1:1 screen time, with recommended caps of 30 minutes a day for students in 3rd grade through 5th grade and 45 minutes for students in 6th grade through 8th grade.

Under the new policy, all technology tools used in NYCPS will undergo an exhaustive review and will be barred if their functionality is ultimately determined not to be mission-critical to learning. The review will include vendor accountability for safety and transparency standards, ethics, evidence of learning design and instructional impact, prior research and the continuous collection of user feedback.

“Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Chancellor Kamar Samuels are taking a thoughtful and responsible approach to AI in our schools. Early-grade education must be rooted in building foundational skills through evidence-based practices, not experimenting on children with rapidly evolving technology. As Chair of the New York State Assembly Committee on Libraries and Education Technology, I introduced similar legislation, and I’m proud to serve on the advisory panel that will help New York City determine where AI can genuinely improve education while protecting students and preserving appropriate exceptions for children with disabilities,” said Assemblymember Robert Carroll, Chair of the Assembly Committee on Libraries and Education Technology.

“The AI policy set forth today protects the city’s youngest learners and prepares high school students to tackle the changing landscape they will graduate into. This policy is appropriately careful and responsive to community voices. I look forward to working closely with the Technology in Schools Coalition to further develop this policy and ensure accountability. As the coming wave of technology emerges, young people will be on the forefront — it will be their creativity, and ingenuity will lead the way. Our responsibility is to establish guardrails, such as these, to help them do it responsibly. This is a good step in that direction,” said Councilwoman Rita Joseph, Higher Education Chair.

“As a former middle school teacher, I'm so pleased to see that our Mayor is taking a nuanced approach to a new and rapidly changing educational tool. We took too long to respond to the effects of social media and smart phones on our youth. This combination of a 1-year ban with select pilot programs allows us to take a serious look at AI usage in schools and find a path that allows our students to adapt to our changing world in a safe manner,” said State Senator Jabari Brisport.

“This one-year ban on student-facing artificial intelligence technology use and restrictions on screen time through eighth grade are the right policies for optimal student learning and development,” said Council Member Lincoln Restler. “Credit to Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for listening to students, parents, teachers and administrators and protecting our young people from the potentially harmful effects of untested technology. This pause alongside a commitment to meaningfully engage stakeholders in the months ahead will allow us to craft long term policies amid a rapidly changing technology landscape.”

“We should never confuse a machine’s ability to produce an answer with a child’s ability to arrive at one. There is something sacred in the struggle to understand: the question asked twice, the page wrestled with, the mistake that becomes discovery, the teacher who sees possibility before a student sees it in themselves,” said State Senator Robert Jackson. “That is where intellect is formed and independence begins. In a democracy, we educate children not simply to know things, but to question, discern, imagine, and ultimately think for themselves. I commend Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for recognizing that progress must earn its place in the classroom. Technology will continue to change, but our obligation must remain constant: childhood must never be the price we pay for innovation.”

“Tech companies have forced their way into every corner of kids' lives with big promises of benefits but little evidence to back them up. Enough is enough,” said State Senator Andrew Gounardes. “These new rules are an important step toward ensuring our kids' needs come before Big Tech's profits. By putting smart, thoughtful guardrails around the use of tech in schools, we can ensure learning comes first. Thanks to Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for working to give our children the education they need and deserve.”

“AI is changing how we learn and work, and our kids need to be prepared to use it safely, think critically, and interrogate the information it produces,” said Council Member Gale A. Brewer. “I am encouraged that NYC Public Schools is taking a comprehensive approach, with age-appropriate AI literacy in K–8 and more focused instruction in high school, and I look forward to the program being shared with parents and staff. Thank you to Chancellor Kamar Samuels and Mayor Mamdani for preparing our students for a rapidly changing world.”

“The recent METR OpenAI report demonstrated how easily AI models can run amok, literally learning how to lie and cheat while covering their tracks to evade being caught deviating from their original code. Our ability to use generative AI with confidence that it won’t turn on our kids and do something else is tenuous at best. The policies announced today are well thought out, age-appropriate, and comprehensive — allowing for carefully chosen pilots for high schoolers and for those AI tools that provide access for students with disabilities and English language learners. Thank you, Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels, for pumping the brakes and creating this detailed policy,” said Assemblymember Jo Anne Simon.

“As a 14-year public school special education teacher and Chair of the City Council's Education Committee, I've seen how quickly new technology can outpace a school system's ability to manage it responsibly,” said Council Member Eric Dinowitz. “My committee's recent oversight hearing made clear the DOE needs a deliberate, evidence-based approach before AI tools reach classrooms unchecked. I applaud Chancellor Samuels' work on this policy and look forward to continuing our work together to ensure our students are kept safe and that technologies support and enhance learning.”

“AI and technology are central to New York’s economic future, as underscored by last week’s CBRE report showing that New York City now has more tech jobs than the Bay Area. We’re encouraged that high schoolers will have access to AI career readiness tools that can help prepare them for the workforce, and we recommend expanding this access beyond one hour per week in the future. At the same time, strong guardrails should enable age-appropriate learning that puts safety first, even at younger grades. Preparing youth for adult life and workplaces that rely on technology will require students to understand AI, question it, and use it safely, under the guidance of teachers. These are incredibly complex issues, and we give Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels credit for listening to all sides and creating a task force, which I am proud to serve on, to help shape what comes next,” said Tech:NYC President & CEO Julie Samuels.

articles.article_title: Credo Technology Reports Q1 Results: Should Investors Hold or Fold?
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: CRDO's strong Q1 growth and AI demand face a key test as optical ramps, customer concentration and valuation raise risks.
articles.content:
- AVGO -2.74%

- CRDO -0.64%

- ALAB +3.17%

- MRVL +1.14%

Credo Technology Group Holding Ltd CRDO reported stellar performance for the first quarter of fiscal 2027 yesterday, but investors seem wary. Shares are down 10% in pre-market trading today, despite quarterly revenues surpassing management's guidance and the company maintaining an aggressive growth outlook for the year. Credo continues to benefit from the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, driving demand for its active electrical cables ("AEC"), optical solutions and retimers. However, the expectations now seem demanding as the next leg of growth hinges on a sharp ramp in the optical business. For investors evaluating CRDO today, the investment debate goes beyond the headline numbers and centers on whether its expanding opportunity set is sufficient to offset the associated execution risks.

CRDO's Q1 Earnings Snapshot

Credo reported fiscal first-quarter revenues of $479 million, up 10% sequentially and 115% year over year. It also beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 0.7%. The company has posted triple-digit year-over-year growth for seven consecutive quarters. Non-GAAP gross margin came in at 68%, compared with 67.6% in the prior-year quarter. Non-GAAP operating expenses increased to $95.2 million from $54.5 million in the prior-year quarter. The increase reflected continued investment in research and development Non-GAAP operating income rose to $230.6 million from $96.2 million, producing a non-GAAP operating margin of 48.2%. Non-GAAP net income margin reached 49.3% in the fiscal first quarter, compared with 44.1% in the year-ago quarter, underscoring the company's ability to convert top-line growth into bottom-line profitability. Non-GAAP earnings per share came in at $1.20, up 130.8% and beat the consensus estimate by 2.6%.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Cash flow from operations was $90.2 million, down from $92 million sequentially, primarily due to working-capital changes. Capital expenditures were $7.3 million, resulting in free cash flow of $82.9 million Cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments stood at $764.3 million, a decrease of $679 million from the previous quarter due to the cash outlay for the DustPhotonics acquisition. For the fiscal second quarter, management expects revenues between $525 million and $535 million. Non-GAAP gross margin is expected to be between 67% and 69%, and non-GAAP operating expenses are expected to be $100-$105 million. Credo continues to forecast more than 85% year-over-year revenue growth for fiscal 2027, aided by an expected second-half inflection

AI Connectivity Demand Remains a Major Tailwind

CRDO's focus on high-performance, energy-efficient connectivity solutions gives it strategic relevance as hyperscalers and cloud service providers overhaul their network architectures. As AI clusters grow to hundreds of thousands of GPUs, connectivity is emerging as a critical constraint. Management highlighted that the challenge is no longer just bandwidth, but also reliability, power efficiency, signal integrity, telemetry and serviceability. Credo believes its system-level approach, which combines silicon, firmware, manufacturing tests and qualification, remains a key differentiator. AEC is a system-level product for CRDO and its core growth engine. The company now has deep relationships with five hyperscalers, alongside expanding engagement with Neocloud customers. Credo continues to see higher AEC penetration within existing customers as deployments scale, while the shift toward 200-gig-per-lane 1.6T ports provides another growth opportunity.

Optics Could Become CRDO's Next Big Opportunity

The most significant shift in Credo's business mix is unfolding in its optical segment. Management continues to project more than $600 million in optical revenues, with ZeroFlap optics, silicon photonics PICs and optical DSPs each contributing more than $100 million. Credo added that its optical DSP business generated "record revenues" in the fiscal first quarter. The company also recognized its first silicon-photonics PIC revenues following the DustPhotonics acquisition, with initial wins involving 800-gig and 1.6T optical transceivers. ZeroFlap Optics represents another important opportunity. Management noted that production shipments are underway, and it expects additional fiscal 2027 customer ramps across both 800-gig and 1.6T products involving hyperscalers and Neocloud operators. Beyond AEC and optics, the retimer business is another lucrative opportunity. Management noted that the retimer business also delivered record quarterly revenues, supported by scale-up deployments of Screaming Eagle at 100-gig-per-lane and initial contributions from its 200-gig-per-lane Blue Heron retimer. Longer-term opportunities include Active LED Cables and OmniConnect. Credo continues to expect initial ALC revenues in fiscal 2028. Further, management added that OmniConnect could represent "thousands of dollars of Credo content per GPU", with revenues also expected to begin in fiscal 2028.

Customer Concentration and other Challenges

CRDO's growth does not come without meaningful risks. In the fiscal first quarter, four customers generated roughly 84% of quarterly revenues. Customer concentration is a major concern as it exposes the company to shifts in customer spending decisions and could materially affect results. Execution risk is another risk factor. Much of the expected growth in fiscal 2027 is dependent on a successful ramp in the optical business. Any delay in deployment or broader industry transitions could affect this ramp. Macroeconomic uncertainties and exposure to the AI investment cycle amid increasing market competition from the likes of Broadcom AVGO, Marvell Technology MRVL and Astera Labs ALAB may also impact CRDO's growth trajectory.

CRDO's Premium Valuation: Another Concern

CRDO is trading at a forward 12-month price/earnings ratio of 30.09X, higher than the Electronic-Semiconductors sector's multiple of 13.31X.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

The market is pricing in the explosive revenue momentum, strong profitability and expanding hyperscaler relationships. However, this leaves very little room for error. Any execution missteps or demand-supply chain troubles could lead to heavy volatility in the stock. In comparison, Broadcom trades at a forward 12-month P/E multiple of 20.64X, while Astera Labs and Marvell are trading at a multiple of 50.99X and 36.69X, respectively. Over the past year, CRDO has gained 65.6%. In comparison, the Electronic-Semiconductors industry, the broader Computer and Technology sector and the S&P 500 are up 46.1%, 27.2% and 19.7%, respectively.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Investor enthusiasm around AI buildout has benefited other semiconductor stocks as well. Marvell Technology, Broadcom and Astera Labs have gained 237.7%, 22.3% and 58.5%, respectively.

Should You Hold or Fold CRDO After Q1?

Credo's fiscal first-quarter performance reinforces the strength of its fundamental growth story. The company is aligned with one of the most powerful and durable trends in technology, the rise of AI-driven infrastructure. The expanding portfolio is particularly encouraging. Optical DSPs, silicon-photonics PICs, ZeroFlap Optics, retimers, ALCs and OmniConnect could steadily broaden Credo's addressable market and reduce its dependence on a single product category over time. However, customer concentration, increasing expenses and the need to execute a substantial second-half optical ramp leave little room for disappointment. The long-term growth opportunity remains compelling, but the near-term risk-reward warrants some caution. Existing investors may stay put, but new investors would be better off waiting for a favorable entry point. At present, CRDO carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). articles.heading: Creative Technology Group Founder Graham Andrews Sets Year-End Exit
articles.summary: Tom See joins NEP Group unit as president and will take day-to-day reins on Jan. 1
articles.content:
Creative Technology Group Founder Graham Andrews Sets Year-End Exit
Tom See joins NEP Group unit as president and will take day-to-day reins on Jan. 1
LAS VEGAS—Live-events technology firm Creative Technology Group has set a leadership change for next year, with founder and CEO Graham Andrews to step down from day-to-day duties at year-end, succeeded by Tom See as the company’s president.
See, who was most recently chief strategy officer for Live Nation International Venues, the hospitality division of Live Nation Entertainment, joins the NEP Group unit on Sept. 14.
Andrews will join the NEP board as a nonexecutive director effective Jan. 1, 2027.
Creative Technology provides video, audio, lighting and networking solutions for live sports, entertainment and corporate events.
“When I founded Creative Technology 40 years ago, I wasn’t sure where it would take me—but I always knew that, if we were successful, it would be important to develop leaders who, at the right moment, could take our company to the next level,” Andrews said. “This is that moment, for me personally and for CT.”
NEP Group CEO Martin Stewart described Andrews as an “entrepreneur at heart” who has strong insights into what customers want.
“I’m grateful for Graham’s leadership and the legacy he leaves,” Stewart said. “I couldn’t be more pleased that we’ll continue to benefit from his perspective as a board member next year.”
The professional video industry's #1 source for news, trends and product and tech information. Sign up below.
At Live Nation, See led a hospitality division that comprised more than 120 venues, 15,000 events per year and more than 30,000 employees. From 2015 to 2021, he was president of Live Nation Ampitheaters, overseeing facilities, operations and marketing for more than 50 venues.
“I have tremendous respect for Graham and the legacy he’s built at Creative Technology,” See said. “What he and the team have created is incredibly special—a company with world-class capabilities, deep client relationships and a culture built around delivering at the highest level. I’m grateful for the opportunity to build on that foundation and excited about what we can accomplish together in the next chapter of CT’s growth.”
For more on Creative Technology, visit its website or the NEP Group website.
Mike Demenchuk is content manager of TV Tech and content director of the NAB Show Daily, taking on those roles after serving as content manager of Broadcasting+Cable and Multichannel News since 2017. After stints as reporter and editor at Adweek, The Bond Buyer and local papers in New Jersey, he joined the staff of Multichannel News in 1999 as assistant managing editor and had served as the cable trade publication's managing editor since 2005. He edits copy and writes headlines for both the TV Tech print magazine and website, and manages content and production of the NAB Show Daily and other special projects.

articles.content:
PublicFile Pro is a new, patent-pending compliance platform from Summit Technology Group.
It is an “all in one” cloud-based offering that Summit says uses a single dashboard yet can help stations conduct a public-file health check; keep political advertising paperwork under control; bring EAS logging and weekly review into the cloud; get practical help with the FCC’s new cybersecurity requirements; see what is due before it becomes urgent; keep EEO records; make quarterly reporting easier; and manage for one station or an entire group.
The tool is for commercial and noncommercial AM, FM and TV broadcasters in the United States. It replaces spreadsheets, paper logs, shared drives and reminders with an organized compliance workspace.
PublicFile Pro inspects and manages a station’s FCC-hosted records, identifying any that may be missing, late or incomplete, and preserving a dated review history.
A free tier provides each station with a public-file review per year. Retention controls track how long records should remain available and flag any items, such as political files, eligible for removal.
Cloud EAS logging collects records from Sage and Digital Alert Systems units, organizes tests and alerts, highlights missing or unsuccessful activity, and creates weekly reports for review and signatory approval. The Political File Manager follows candidate and issue-advertising orders from request through airing, invoicing and final reconciliation.
Its equipment-security workspace includes an encrypted password vault, unique password generation, password-reuse prevention and credential-rotation management. It tracks security updates and documents firewall or network-separation protections associated with FCC 26-38.
An interactive regulatory calendar brings public-file, political, license-renewal, EEO and Quarterly Issues/Programs deadlines into a station-specific view.
Automated EEO management and Quarterly Issues/Programs reporting modules are pending.
Additional utilities address Chief Operator designations, ownership information, station-website public-file links, legal-ID review, license-renewal announcements and corrective-action records.

articles.title: Linxup Survey Finds Safety Technology Outweighs Privacy Concerns
articles.description: Linxup Survey Finds Safety Technology Outweighs Privacy Concerns Pest Control Technology
articles.description_html: Linxup Survey Finds Safety Technology Outweighs Privacy Concerns  Pest Control Technology
articles.article_title: Linxup Survey Finds Safety Technology Outweighs Privacy Concerns
articles.heading: Linxup Survey Finds Safety Technology Outweighs Privacy Concerns
articles.summary: Nearly half of drivers say they or a coworker have benefited from dash cam evidence in an accident dispute, contrasting with fleet leaders’ previous privacy and resistance concerns.
articles.content:
ST. LOUIS — A new survey of 267 commercial fleet professionals from Linxup found that 77% of drivers say the benefits of fleet safety tools outweigh privacy concerns, and that drivers value the protection it provides and the accidents it prevents. The findings also point to the broader role of safety culture, with employer safety practices influencing retention, customer trust and day-to-day confidence, the company said.
When asked what would make the biggest difference in their day-to-day work, 29% of drivers ranked "protection if something goes wrong" as their top choice, followed by 27% who chose "fewer accidents.” Nearly half (44%) of field service professionals say they or a coworker have been involved in an accident where dash cam footage or GPS tracking worked in their favor during an insurance claim or legal dispute. The finding reflects a broader shift in perception. As more drivers see the technology work in their favor, they're increasingly viewing it as a tool that protects them rather than one that monitors them, Linxup said.
"Safety technology is often viewed through the lens of reducing accidents, but drivers are telling us they value technology that can provide an objective record when something goes wrong," said Naeem Bari, founder and chief product officer at Linxup. "Fleet drivers want greater confidence every time they get behind the wheel; that isn’t and shouldn’t be an impossible ask. Our findings show that protection, accountability, and knowing your company has your back all matter to today's workforce, reinforcing that safety programs work best when technology is positioned as a tool that supports employees, not just company operations.”
The research found the impact of fleet safety extends well beyond driver behavior. More than three-quarters (76%) of respondents said how their employer approaches safety influences their decision to stay with a company, while 61% said customers have mentioned their company's safety practices as a reason for doing business with them. Additionally, 42% reported their employer has become more serious about safety over the past year, highlighting safety's growing role in both employee retention and customer confidence.
The survey also found that organizations with formal safety programs see stronger engagement with safety initiatives. Respondents at companies with formal programs reported higher adoption of GPS tracking (80%) and dash cameras (68%) and were more likely to say safety makes them want to stay with their employer compared to those without a formal safety program (49% compared to 38%). Those with a formal safety program also reported more consistent driver feedback and proactive monitoring of accidents and near misses than those at organizations with informal or no safety programs, the company said.
Compared with Linxup's 2025 fleet safety research, the company said this year's survey highlights greater alignment between managers and drivers on the value of fleet safety technology. While last year's survey found fleet leaders believed driver privacy concerns were a significant barrier to dash cam adoption, this year's driver survey found that 77% believe the benefits of fleet safety tools outweigh privacy or resistance concerns.
Additional key findings from the survey include:
- Safety incentives matter. Eighty-two percent of respondents say tying pay or bonuses to safety scores would motivate them to improve their driving performance, with cash bonuses ranking as the top motivator.
- Operational pressures remain a challenge. More than (73%) say real-world job demands make it hard to drive efficiently at least some of the time, including 44.6% who say it happens sometimes and 28.5% who say it happens often. Leadership shares the blame too. 22.5% say management sets safety rules but doesn’t follow through, and another 22.5% say rules only change after an incident.
- Drivers want communication, not just technology. More than 72% say their employer has explained how GPS tracking or dash cameras affect insurance coverage, reinforcing the importance of transparency around fleet safety tools.
- Women were even more likely than men to view fleet safety technology positively. More than 91% of women agreed the benefits of fleet safety tools outweigh privacy or driver resistance concerns, compared to 75% of men. Women were also significantly more likely to say "protection if something goes wrong" would make the biggest difference in their day-to-day work (41% vs. 28%).
This survey was conducted by Centiment on behalf of Linxup in June 2026. It is based on a survey of 267 field service professionals who are part of a commercial fleet in the United Stat

articles.title: Novel Spatial Technology May Improve the Understanding of Cancer Biology
articles.description: Novel Spatial Technology May Improve the Understanding of Cancer Biology news.feinberg.northwestern.edu
articles.description_html: Novel Spatial Technology May Improve the Understanding of Cancer Biology  news.feinberg.northwestern.edu
articles.article_title: Novel Spatial Technology May Improve the Understanding of Cancer Biology - News Center
articles.heading: Novel Spatial Technology May Improve the Understanding of Cancer Biology
articles.summary: Northwestern Medicine scientists have developed a novel high-resolution 3D spatial genomics platform that may enhance future research about how genome organization and genetic alterations contribute to the development of disease, including cancer, as detailed in a recent study published in Nature Methods.
articles.content:
Northwestern Medicine scientists have developed a novel high-resolution spatial genomics platform that may enhance future research about how genome organization and genetic alterations contribute to the development of disease, including cancer, as detailed in a recent study published in Nature Methods.
“What is particularly exciting is that we can simultaneously profile 3D genome organization and chromatin accessibility while preserving the native spatial context of cells and tissues, and we can also detect genomic alterations such as copy-number changes and structural variations in cancer,” said co-corresponding author Feng Yue, PhD, the Duane and Susan Burnham Professor of Molecular Medicine and a professor of Biochemistry and Molecular Genetics and of Pathology.
Nearly all biological processes depend on the spatial organization of different types of cells within the tissue microenvironment, and the location and interactions of individual cells influence the function of these processes, which include protein localization, chromatin accessibility and histone modifications.
Recent advances in spatial “omics” techniques have enabled scientists to profile different molecular features, such as the transcriptome, proteome and epigenome while preserving their spatial context within tissues, but the techniques do not capture 3D genome folding.
Imaging-based approaches have also been used to study the genome organization and its relationship to biological processes such as immune response and disease progression. However, these approaches typically interrogate selected loci or regions in the genome, underscoring the need for complementary sequencing-based technologies that can map the entire genome.
To address this gap, Yue’s team developed Spatial-ATAC-Hi-C, a microfluidic-based spatial platform that can profile both 3D genome organization and chromatin accessibility within native tissue samples.
To validate their approach, the scientists applied Spatial-ATAC-Hi-C to adult mouse brain tissue and adult human brain tissue samples, revealing unique chromatin architecture features and gene regulatory programs in both neuronal and non-neuronal cell populations.
In glioblastoma and astrocytoma patient samples, Spatial-ATAC-Hi-C was also able to detect spatially resolved 3D genome alterations, in addition to genetic copy number variations and structure variations in certain regions of the tumors.
“We showed even within the same tumor, different regions can harbor distinct copy number alterations or structural variations,” said Yue, who is also director of the Center for Advanced Molecular Analysis. “Being able to detect these genomic differences while preserving their spatial context could help us better understand tumor heterogeneity.”
Overall, Spatial-ATAC-Hi-C provides a new technology for studying genome organization and gene regulation in cancer and developmental biology, according to Yue.
“This integrated approach provides a powerful tool to systematically explore the dynamic interplay between 3D chromatin structure, accessibility and spatiotemporal gene regulation within a complex biological context while preserving native spatial organization,” the authors wrote.
Ping Wang, PhD, research assistant professor of Biochemistry and Molecular Genetics; Juang Wang, PhD, a postdoctoral fellow in the Yue laboratory; Qixuan Wang, a student in the Driskill Graduate Program in Life Sciences (DGP); Mark Youngblood, MD, PhD, assistant professor of Neurological Surgery, were co-first authors of the study.
Rong Fan, PhD, Harold Hodgkinson Professor of Biomedical Engineering at Yale University, was co-corresponding author of the study.
Co-authors of the study include Alok Swaroop, ‘19 MD, ‘19 PhD, ’21 GME, instructor in the Department of Medicine, Division of Hematology and Oncology; Khizar Nandoliya, a medical student; Hinda Najem, PhD, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Neurological Surgery; Amy Heimberger, MD, PhD, the Jean Malnati Miller Professor of Brain Tumor Research and vice chair for research in the Department of Neurological Surgery; and Adam Sonabend, MD, the Etka Frimerman Professor of Neurosurgery.
Yue, Heimberger and Sonabend are members of the Robert H. Lurie Comprehensive Cancer Center of Northwestern University.
This work was supported by National Institute of Health grants R35GM124820, 1R01HG009906, and R01HG011207, T32 CA009560 and T32 CA070085; a Neurosurgery Research and Education Foundation Fellowship; the United States Department of Defense (CA230856); American Brain Tumor Association Basic Research Fellowship (fully supported by Tap Cancer Out); and the Society of Neurological Surgeons.
