articles.title: Ad Tech Analyst CartographAI Is Now Helping Vendors Market Themselves
articles.description: Ad Tech Analyst CartographAI Is Now Helping Vendors Market Themselves AdExchanger
articles.description_html: Ad Tech Analyst CartographAI Is Now Helping Vendors Market Themselves  AdExchanger
articles.article_title: Ad Tech Analyst CartographAI Is Now Helping Vendors Market Themselves
articles.heading: CartographAI Launched To Help Advertisers Pick The Right Tech Vendors. Now, It’s Helping Vendors Market Themselves, Too
articles.summary: The company, which helps advertisers pick the right tech partners, is also launching an accelerator program to help tech vendors market their solutions.
articles.content:
With so many ad tech vendors to choose from, where should brands and agencies begin?

CartographAI, a new startup from two buy-side veterans, wants to help advertisers pick the right tech partners by using assessment criteria that weigh what media buyers actually care about, rather than publicly-available marketing materials.

CartographAI is the brainchild of former Goodway Group CEO Jay Friedman and Danilo Tauro, a former McKinsey analyst who also previously headed up Procter & Gamble’s vendor analysis and risk assessments. They told AdExchanger they launched the endeavor earlier this year to disrupt the industry’s traditional consultancies that advise advertisers on tech strategy as well as the analyst model that anoints certain companies as leaders in their categories.

Instead of compiling a one-size-fits-all list of what it believes are the top tech vendors in the industry like other analysts, Friedman said, CartographAI helps individual brands and agencies find the right fit for them, which might not always be the industry-consensus category leaders.

In addition to helping buyers compare different competitive solutions, a big part of the company’s value prop is simply breaking down what various tech vendors do in a more straightforward way than you can find on their websites. According to Tauro, some agencies who have tested the solution said, “It’s like the Lumascape , but you can double-click the logos.”

CartographAI’s vendor-ranking solution started as a brand- and agency-focused product, and those groups will remain its core constituencies, Friedman and Tauro said.

But the company is also launching an accelerator program to help tech vendors more effectively market their solutions to advertisers, it announced this week.

Marketing to marketers

The accelerator program has already assembled a roster of ad tech vendors, including The Trade Desk, Viant, MNTN, Adelaide, Optable, Chalice, Gamera, Clinch, Evertune, Eulerity, TAU, Bright Mountain, Version2, NativeAds, QRate and Narrative.

For between $1,000 and $3,000 a month, depending on the company’s size and growth stage, Friedman said, vendors can sign up to get “deep, analyst-level intel on your subcategory” on a monthly call with CartographAI and its team of subject-matter experts. These experts are drawn from Friedman’s and Tauro’s industry contacts, including from the Procter & Gamble digital alumni forum.

The experts give vendors insight, sourced from direct conversations with buyers, into what advertisers are looking for in their tech solutions, Tauro said. These insights can inform not only the vendors’ product road maps but how they market their solutions.

Plus, CartographAI will promote accelerator program participants on social media and in podcasts and newsletters, and vendors also get access to co-marketing opportunities with CartographAI at ad industry events.

The accelerator program is particularly valuable for helping an ad tech startup like Gamera , a media quality platform that launched in 2022, get its product in front of the right people, said its CEO and co-founder, Gareth Glaser. “It helps us identify the right contacts at brands, agencies, trading desks and everything in between without going through a long series of false starts, while also providing an objective, concise way to communicate what our product does and why it matters.”

Having that clear path into the buy-side market is one thing, Glaser said, but it also comes “with guidance from people who understand how to create the right conversations and, just as importantly, avoid the unproductive ones.”

Attention measurement platform Adelaide is early in its journey with CartographAI’s accelerator program, Adelaide CEO Marc Guldimann said, but the company already received plenty of valuable feedback on its go-to-market strategy during the onboarding process.

“Jay has a [Charlie-]Munger-like command of incentives in the ecosystem and Danilo is super strategic,” Guldimann said. “Advice and blunt feedback from a team with this kind understanding of the market is invaluable.”

In addition, later this year, CartographAI plans to launch an AI analyst solution grounded on its industry expertise that will advise advertisers on which vendors can help them solve particular challenges or drive certain KPIs.

Given that planned rollout, Glaser said, “CartographAI is laying important groundwork for a future in which buyers increasingly use AI to discover, evaluate and engage with new technology partners.”

Ranking the vendors

Until the AI analyst launches, advertisers can access CartographAI’s vendor rankings through its website, which is live with about 1,000 rankings today and about 20 new company profiles added per month. The website rankings are free to access; clients just have to sign up for a login.

CartographAI groups ad tech vendors into different vertical market categories. For example, it has a category for DSPs and another for identity resolution/ID graph providers/DMPs.

It then ranks the vendors according to five criteria that are unique to their vertical market, labeling their offerings as either “emerging,” “capable” or “advanced” in each of those five criteria. For instance, the identity solution category’s criteria include match quality, coverage and portability, privacy and consent mechanics, activation utility and commercial and dependency risk.

On top of using the free site rankings, brands and agencies can also sign up for a more traditional white glove consulting service. Each of these deals is priced on a custom basis, with CartographAI charging between five and six figures for consulting, Friedman said, although it’s still solidifying the economics of this offering.

Once the company’s AI analyst is ready for market, it should help further streamline how brands and agencies run their RFPs when onboarding new vendors, Tauro said.

In his experience, he said, buyers can spend six-plus months evaluating new partners, with about two months spent simply learning everything they can about the particular product category. That’s why CartographAI prioritizes connecting advertisers with experts who are already knowledgeable about the different vertical ad tech markets – and why it’s training its AI on their expertise.

“It’s almost a marketplace of knowledge,” Tauro said. “The point is helping that translation between how marketers think, talk and operate, and how tech companies do.”

According to Tauro, some agencies who have tested the solution said, “It’s like the Lumascape, but you can double-click the logos.”

CartographAI’s vendor-ranking solution started as a brand- and agency-focused product, and those groups will remain its core constituencies, Friedman and Tauro said.

But the company is also launching an accelerator program to help tech vendors more effectively market their solutions to advertisers, it announced this week.

Marketing to marketers

The accelerator program has already assembled a roster of ad tech vendors, including The Trade Desk, Viant, MNTN, Adelaide, Optable, Chalice, Gamera, Clinch, Evertune, Eulerity, TAU, Bright Mountain, Version2, NativeAds, QRate and Narrative.

For between $1,000 and $3,000 a month, depending on the company’s size and growth stage, Friedman said, vendors can sign up to get “deep, analyst-level intel on your subcategory” on a monthly call with CartographAI and its team of subject-matter experts. These experts are drawn from Friedman’s and Tauro’s industry contacts, including from the Procter & Gamble digital alumni forum.

The experts give vendors insight, sourced from direct conversations with buyers, into what advertisers are looking for in their tech solutions, Tauro said. These insights can inform not only the vendors’ product road maps but how they market their solutions.

Plus, CartographAI will promote accelerator program participants on social media and in podcasts and newsletters, and vendors also get access to co-marketing opportunities with CartographAI at ad industry events.

The accelerator program is particularly valuable for helping an ad tech startup like Gamera, a media quality platform that launched in 2022, get its product in front of the right people, said its CEO and co-founder, Gareth Glaser. “It helps us identify the right contacts at brands, agencies, trading desks and everything in between without going through a long series of false starts, while also providing an objective, concise way to communicate what our product does and why it matters.”

Having that clear path into the buy-side market is one thing, Glaser said, but it also comes “with guidance from people who understand how to create the right conversations and, just as importantly, avoid the unproductive ones.”

Attention measurement platform Adelaide is early in its journey with CartographAI’s accelerator program, Adelaide CEO Marc Guldimann said, but the company already received plenty of valuable feedback on its go-to-market strategy during the onboarding process.

“Jay has a [Charlie-]Munger-like command of incentives in the ecosystem and Danilo is super strategic,” Guldimann said. “Advice and blunt feedback from a team with this kind understanding of the market is invaluable.”

In addition, later this year, CartographAI plans to launch an AI analyst solution grounded on its industry expertise that will advise advertisers on which vendors can help them solve particular challenges or drive certain KPIs.

Given that planned rollout, Glaser said, “CartographAI is laying important groundwork for a future in which buyers increasingly use AI to discover, evaluate and engage with new technology partners.”

Ranking the vendors

Until the AI analyst launches, advertisers can access CartographAI’s vendor rankings through its website, which is live with about 1,000 rankings today and about 20 new company profiles added per month. The website rankings are free to access; clients just have to sign up for a login.

CartographAI groups ad tech vendors into different vertical market categories. For example, it has a category for DSPs and another for identity resolution/ID graph providers/DMPs.

It then ranks the vendors according to five criteria that are unique to their vertical market, labeling their offerings as either “emerging,” “capable” or “advanced” in each of those five criteria. For instance, the identity solution category’s criteria include match quality, coverage and portability, privacy and consent mechanics, activation utility and commercial and dependency risk.

On top of using the free site rankings, brands and agencies can also sign up for a more traditional white glove consulting service. Each of these deals is priced on a custom basis, with CartographAI charging between five and six figures for consulting, Friedman said, although it’s still solidifying the economics of this offering.

Once the company’s AI analyst is ready for market, it should help further streamline how brands and agencies run their RFPs when onboarding new vendors, Tauro said.

In his experience, he said, buyers can spend six-plus months evaluating new partners, with about two months spent simply learning everything they can about the particular product category. That’s why CartographAI prioritizes connecting advertisers with experts who are already knowledgeable about the different vertical ad tech markets – and why it’s training its AI on their expertise.

“It’s almost a marketplace of knowledge,” Tauro said. “The point is helping that translation between how marketers think, talk and operate, and how tech companies do.”

articles.title: Hemant Desai Appointed as ACCGov CIO/IT Department Director
articles.description: Hemant Desai Appointed as ACCGov CIO/IT Department Director Athens-Clarke County
articles.description_html: Hemant Desai Appointed as ACCGov CIO/IT Department Director  Athens-Clarke County
articles.article_title: Hemant Desai Appointed as ACCGov CIO/IT Department Director
articles.heading: Hemant Desai Appointed as ACCGov CIO/IT Department Director
articles.summary: Athens-Clarke County Unified Government (ACCGov) Manager Bob Cowell has appointed Hemant Desai to serve as the new Chief Information Officer (CIO) and Information Technology (IT) Department Director b
articles.content:
Athens-Clarke County Unified Government (ACCGov) Manager Bob Cowell has appointed Hemant Desai to serve as the new Chief Information Officer (CIO) and Information Technology (IT) Department Director beginning September 28, 2026.
Desai has more than 20 years of technology leadership experience across the nonprofit, government, and education environments.
"Hemant brings an impressive combination of local government experience, technical expertise, and a genuine understanding of how technology can better serve an organization and its community," said Cowell. "His previous public sector roles have given him valuable perspectives on the opportunities and challenges facing communities like ours. We’re excited to welcome him to Athens-Clarke County and to our leadership team."
In his most recent information technology role, Desai served for nearly five years as the CIO for the International City/County Management Association (ICMA) based in Washington, DC. In this position, he led initiatives related to cloud modernization, identity management, AI governance, and digital transformation for the global nonprofit serving local government professionals worldwide.
Prior to his work at ICMA, Desai worked for over a decade for the Guilford County Government in Greensboro, NC as Project Manager, Director of Client Services, and for nearly eight years, as CIO. As CIO, he directed a team of 52 IT professionals in enterprise IT operations, cybersecurity, data governance, infrastructure modernization, and digital transformation initiatives for North Carolina’s third-largest county government serving more than 540,000 residents across 20 departments.
"I'm honored to join Athens-Clarke County as Chief Information Officer," said Desai. "Technology works best when it's invisible to the people it serves, quietly making government more responsive, more secure, and more connected to the community. I look forward to building that kind of technology foundation alongside the Mayor and Commission and staff to earn the trust of the residents we serve every day."
Prior to his government work, Desai held the positions of president and CIO of a regional computer learning center. He holds a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering from Maharaja Sayajirao University in India and an MBA in Technology Management from the University of Phoenix. He holds certifications from the Project Management Institute (PMI) as a Program and Project Management Professional and is a Microsoft certified trainer and IT professional.
The Athens-Clarke County IT Department provides high-quality computer services, state-of-the-art computer networks and software applications, reliable equipment and system access, proficient technical support, and assistance that encourages the application of technology to improve the efficiency and productivity of ACCGov operations.
For more information on the ACCGov IT Department, visit www.accgov.com/it.

articles.description: Letters to the Editor: Trump is setting us back in categories far beyond military technology Los Angeles Times

articles.article_title: Letters to the Editor: Trump is setting us back in categories far beyond military technology
articles.heading: Letters to the Editor: Trump is setting us back in categories far beyond military technology
articles.summary: An L.A. Times reader writes that a recent headline about a regression in military technology 'can be applied to President Trump spending money on programs in environmental destruction, lawlessness in justice and rewriting history.'
articles.content:
Letters to the Editor: Trump is setting us back in categories far beyond military technology
- Click here to listen to this article
- Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
To the editor: Contributing writer Jon Duffy’s headline applies to so many other areas besides reverting to old technologies for aircraft carrier launches (“Trump is spending billions to reverse American progress,” Aug. 31).
Examine the federal budget and policies. The same headline can be applied to President Trump spending money on programs in environmental destruction, lawlessness in justice and rewriting history. It can apply to the spurning of allies and diplomatic collaboration and initiating and fighting spurious wars. Then there’s the defunding of health programs and spreading confusion about vaccines.
There are countless other examples: slashing federal aid to education, legalizing discrimination, exploding the national debt, promoting fossil fuels at the expense of green energy, defanging civil and human rights laws, undermining gun control laws, increasing the power of billionaires and corporations to buy elections and establishing limits on voting. The weakening of Congress and the curtailing of the power of lower courts, the building of personal monuments and the destruction of others and the cuts to scientific research grants are all further examples of how our tax dollars are at work reversing American programs that we have fought so long and hard to establish.
Duffy’s description barely represents the “tip of the iceberg,” as most recently exposed by the melting of a glacier in Nepal, while the Trump administration denies climate change.
Joel Pelcyger, Los Angeles

WIESBADEN, HESSEN, GERMANY

09.01.2026

Story by Natalie Simmel

U.S. Army Garrison Wiesbaden

CLAY KASERNE, Germany — U.S. Army Garrison Wiesbaden is exploring two innovative ways to empower their Directorate of Public Works personnel with technological support: robotic lawn mowers 2.0 and upper-body exoskeletons.

The upgrades come as part of an existing effort to modernize garrison workflows and support frontline personnel, integrating practical automation directly into daily operations.

“I think it's very exciting for each of our directorates, especially DPW, with the amount of manual and physical labor that is done, to look for innovative ways to assist the workforce as well as better accomplish the mission before us,” said Col. Ringo Midles, U.S. Army Wiesbaden Garrison commander.

Upgraded autonomous mowers DPW is experimenting with an updated version of autonomous lawnmowers. While the garrison already uses automated models in several areas across the installation, the upgraded system brings additional operational benefits.

The new model delivers consistent endurance, running continuously for up to eight hours on a single charge. Multi-map storage lets the units transition between designated work zones. Its cutting mechanism features millimeter-precise height adjustments designed for optimal turf health across varied terrain.

As with the previous model, safety remains a priority. The mowers maintain a strict 1.7-meter (about 5.5-foot) perimeter around obstacles and adjust their path when encountering moving objects. Sensors detect people, pets, and small wildlife such as rabbits and hedgehogs, while adaptive learning algorithms refine navigation routes and situational awareness over time.

These autonomous systems free up DPW maintenance teams to reallocate staffing elsewhere on the installation. Where broad-area mowingrequired three- to four-person crews, teams can now scale down to two workers per zone.

“It makes us more efficient,” Midles said. “We are not trying to exchange our staff with new technology; we are trying to support them with it. I would rather see that lawn mower do 80 percent of the work and our skilled workers do the last 20 percent that the robot cannot do and have our manpower directed at other, more pressing matters. We have plenty of work to do.”

During a loan period, DPW is testing the upgraded autonomous lawnmower to evaluate its suitability for use in the installation.

“You have to try them out in order to find where to place investments,” Midles said. “The way this enables a team of DPW workers to be more places and provide better services is exciting to me.”

Exoskeleton support for physical labor DPW purchased one upper-body exoskeleton, deployed in field trials across several DPW departments.
“We are testing the exoskeleton with our painters, gardeners, masons, and electricians to identify where it delivers the greatest impact,” said Martin Hallbauer, Deputy Director of DPW.

While the automated lawnmowers alleviate the overall workload, the exoskeleton’s purpose is to support the physical health of the personnel performing the work.

“From a safety and ergonomics standpoint, our priority is safeguarding the long-term health of our workforce,” Hallbauer added. “By delivering measurable ergonomic relief during repetitive tasks, overhead work, and heavy lifting, this technology protects our frontline operators.”

The core benefit of the exoskeleton is physical endurance and injury prevention rather than artificial strength amplification. Designed to support the arms, shoulders, and back, the unit redistributes mechanical load away from vulnerable joints.

This significantly reduces physical fatigue and repetitive stress injuries during sustained heavy lifting and extended overhead tasks, such as streetlight maintenance and warehouse repairs.

articles.heading: Real Time Automation's John Rinaldi Accepted into Forbes Technology Council; Champions Scalable, Open Smart Manufacturing
articles.summary: /PRNewswire/ -- Real Time Automation (RTA), a global leader in industrial networking solutions, today announced that John Rinaldi, Founder and Chief Strategist...
articles.content:
Industrial networking expert and author joins invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs, and technology executives.
PEWAUKEE, Wis., Sept. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Real Time Automation (RTA), a global leader in industrial networking solutions, today announced that John Rinaldi, Founder and Chief Strategist of Creating Industrial connectivity products, has been accepted into the Forbes Technology Council.
John was selected by a review committee based on the depth and diversity of his experience. Criteria for acceptance include a proven track record of successfully impacting business growth metrics, recognized technical leadership, and substantial personal and professional achievements in industrial automation and communication technologies.
As a pioneer in industrial networking, John has authored six industry-standard books—including Industrial Ethernet, Modbus, and OPC UA: The Everyman's Guide—along with more than 100 articles on industrial communications. Through his leadership at RTA, he has dedicated decades to simplifying plant-floor connectivity, eliminating proprietary vendor lock-in, and helping manufacturers of all sizes modernize legacy systems into connected, smart operations.
"We are pleased to welcome John Rinaldi into the community," said Scott Gerber, founder of Forbes Councils, the collective that includes the Forbes Technology Council. "The Forbes Councils' mission is to bring together recognized leaders in their industry, creating a curated, social capital-driven network that helps every member grow professionally and achieve a greater impact on the business world."
As an accepted member of the Council, John will collaborate with senior technology leaders in a private forum and work with a professional editorial team to share expert thought leadership via original business articles on Forbes.com. His contributions will focus on data modeling, industrial AI prerequisites, interoperability, and practical digital transformation strategies for discrete and process manufacturing.
"I am honored to join the Forbes Technology Council," said John S. Rinaldi. "True digital transformation and industrial AI cannot succeed without addressing the real challenge on the factory floor: standardizing and contextualizing data at the edge. I look forward to collaborating with fellow technology executives and contributing practical, reality-grounded insights on how manufacturers can build reliable, scalable architectures."
About Real Time Automation
Headquartered in Pewaukee, Wisconsin, Real Time Automation (RTA) has been delivering industrial connectivity solutions since 1989. RTA specializes in making industrial networking simple, reliable, and accessible through protocol gateways, embedded software, and expert consultation. Backed by its commitment to world-class customer support and tailored solutions, RTA helps manufacturers and OEMs worldwide move vital operational data seamlessly across legacy and modern automation ecosystems. For more information, visit rtautomation.com.
About Forbes Councils
Forbes Councils is a collective of invitation-only communities created in partnership with Forbes and the expert community builders who founded Young Entrepreneur Council (YEC). In Forbes Councils, exceptional business owners and leaders come together with the people and resources that can help them thrive. For more information about Forbes Technology Council, visit forbestechcouncil.com.

articles.description_html: GF announces customer availability of UX platform technologies for intelligent edge, connectivity and Physical AI applications  GlobalFoundries
articles.article_title: GF announces customer availability of UX platform technologies for intelligent edge, connectivity and Physical AI applications | GlobalFoundries
articles.heading: GlobalFoundries announces customer availability of UX platform technologies for intelligent edge, connectivity and Physical AI applications
articles.summary: New CMOS platforms combine ultra-low power connectivity, sensing and mixed-signal innovation for next-generation edge devices
articles.content:
Newest feature-rich CMOS platform family combines ultra-low power connectivity, sensing and mixed-signal innovation with cost-efficient manufacturing for next-generation edge devices
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Sept. 2, 2026 – Today at its annual GF Technology Summit (GTS) in North America, GlobalFoundries (Nasdaq: GFS) (GF) announced process design kit (PDK) availability for its UX platform family, two new feature-rich CMOS technologies purpose-built for next-generation intelligent edge devices and advanced sensing systems. First introduced on stage at GTS last year, the UX family includes 40nm (40UX) and 22nm (22UX) technologies, providing customers with a scalable roadmap for ultra-low power microcontrollers, wireless connectivity devices, sensor interfaces, imaging systems and edge AI applications. Built on proven technology modules and supported by GF’s design ecosystem and global manufacturing footprint, UX technologies will help customers accelerate development of AI devices and intelligent systems while balancing performance, power, cost and supply requirements.
As intelligence moves from the cloud into billions of connected devices, designers need semiconductor technologies that combine precise sensing, always-on connectivity and energy-efficient processing within tight power and form factor constraints. The UX family expands GF’s portfolio of differentiated technologies for Physical AI, giving customers a scalable path for solutions enabling connected microcontrollers (MCUs), highly integrated sensing and mixed-signal systems. 40UX brings proven, cost-efficient integration to MCUs and always-on-edge devices, while 22UX provides a higher level of analog, sensing, and mixed-signal performance for more complex intelligent systems.
The 40UX platform is optimized for secure, smart and connected microcontrollers and systems-on-a-chip (SoCs) serving wearable, IoT and wireless connectivity applications. Based on GF’s high-volume 40nm platform with high-endurance eFlash technology that has shipped more than one million wafers to date, 40UX combines ultra-low leakage transistors and SRAM, low-noise analog capabilities, integrated embedded flash with built-in self-test functionality and advanced RF enablement to support long battery life, high reliability and compact form factors. The platform is particularly well suited for Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) devices, wireless connectivity products, low-noise sensor interfaces and other power-sensitive edge applications.
The 40UX platform is set to ramp to volume production at GF’s Singapore site by 2027, with future production planned though its site in Malta, New York. The technology’s roadmap includes optimizations embedded processing, including high-voltage and noise enablement, Automotive Grade 1 qualification and enhanced embedded non-volatile memory options.
For applications that require higher levels of analog integration and sensing performance, the 22UX platform delivers an analog-optimized 22nm solution for edge AI, imaging and mixed-signal systems. The platform combines ultra-low power operation with low-noise analog devices, improved device matching, wafer-scale Random Telegraph Signal (RTS) noise characterization, bonding-ready wafers for advanced 3D integration and a roadmap for ultra-low leakage, analog compute-in-memory and embedded memory capabilities. The platform is ideally suited for stacked CMOS image sensor readout ICs with a 1/f flicker noise and low-noise 3.3V analog FET for precise measurement. The platform’s improved device matching and higher voltage headroom make it an optimal choice for cost-optimized mixed-signal SoCs, sensor interfaces and power sensitive edge devices that require superior analog performance.
The 22UX platform integrates analog-optimized features including ultra-low power capabilities for exceptional energy-efficiency and third generation fill cells for faster product-level block/module integration. The platform is industry-compatible, offering easy porting from other bulk CMOS platforms, and was developed using high-volume proven modules and GF’s successful 28nm technology that has shipped over one million wafers to date. 22UX will be manufactured at GF’s advanced manufacturing facility in Dresden, Germany with a roadmap to reach multi-site production through GF’s global footprint.
“Intelligence is moving into more of the devices people and businesses rely on every day, creating new demands for power efficiency, precise sensing, connectivity and cost-effective integration,” said Ed Kaste, senior vice president of GF’s CMOS business. “Our new UX platform family gives customers a scalable path to develop differentiated products for the intelligent edge, backed by proven technology and GF’s global manufacturing capabilities. By expanding our feature-rich CMOS portfolio with 40UX and 22UX, we are helping customers bring the next generation of connected and Physical AI systems to market.”
Both platforms are available for customer engagement and prototyping through GF’s GlobalShuttle™ multi-project wafer program with quarterly shuttles scheduled through 2027.
About GF
GlobalFoundries (GF) is a leading manufacturer of essential semiconductors the world relies on to live, work and connect. We innovate and partner with customers to deliver more power-efficient, high-performance products for the automotive, smart mobile devices, internet of things, communications infrastructure and other high-growth markets. With our global manufacturing footprint spanning the U.S., Europe, and Asia, GF is a trusted and reliable source for customers around the world. Every day, our talented global team delivers results with an unyielding focus on security, longevity, and sustainability. For more information, visit www.gf.com.

articles.title: GF and RAAAM Memory Technologies announce the joint development of next-generation GCRAM technology and test chip on FDX platform
articles.description: GF and RAAAM Memory Technologies announce the joint development of next-generation GCRAM technology and test chip on FDX platform GlobalFoundries
articles.description_html: GF and RAAAM Memory Technologies announce the joint development of next-generation GCRAM technology and test chip on FDX platform  GlobalFoundries
articles.article_title: GF and RAAAM Memory Technologies announce the joint development of next-generation GCRAM technology and test chip on FDX platform | GlobalFoundries
articles.heading: GlobalFoundries and RAAAM Memory Technologies announce the joint development of next-generation GCRAM technology and test chip on FDX platform
articles.summary: Collaboration enabling densest standard CMOS on-chip memory solution for FDX platform widely used for advanced AI chips
articles.content:
Collaboration targets to enable the densest standard CMOS on-chip memory solution for the FDX platform widely used for advanced AI chips, by delivering 40% area shrink and up to 60% power reduction compared to commodity SRAM
MALTA, N.Y., and Peta Tikva, Israel, Sept. 2, 2026 – GlobalFoundries (Nasdaq: GFS)(GF) and RAAAM Memory Technologies, a pioneer in advanced on-chip memory solutions, today announced a strategic collaboration to develop and qualify Gain-Cell RAM (GCRAM) technology. The partnership has reached a major milestone with the successful tape-out of a GCRAM test vehicle on GF’s industry-leading FDX™ FD-SOI platform.
As edge AI, automotive, and IoT devices continue to demand unprecedented amounts of data, on-chip memory has become a critical bottleneck and often constitutes the majority of the silicon area. Designers are looking for innovative on-chip memory solutions offering higher-density and lower-power consumption compared to commodity SRAM.
Leveraging RAAAM’s patented GCRAM, the companies have co-designed the GCRAM bitcell using “pushed” design rules on FDX technology, achieving 40% memory area shrink and up to 60% memory power reduction compared to SRAM. The companies have jointly designed and taped out a GCRAM test chip. At the next step, the companies will start providing GCRAM design access to lead customers in early 2027.
“The successful tape-out of our GCRAM test vehicle on GF’s FDX platform is a testament to the powerful synergy between RAAAM’s memory innovations and GlobalFoundries’ manufacturing excellence,” said Robert Giterman, CEO and co-founder of RAAAM Memory Technologies. “Our GCRAM technology allows semiconductor companies to significantly increase their on-chip memory capacity or reduce the silicon area while keeping the same amount of on-chip memory, while the ultra-low leakage of FD-SOI technology extends data retention, enabling designers to unlock substantial energy savings for edge AI devices”
“At GlobalFoundries, we are continuously pushing the boundaries of what is possible on our FDX platform and keep enhancing our IP offering to meet our customers’ needs,” said Sudipto Bose, vice president of FD-SOI product management at GlobalFoundries. “Partnering with RAAAM Memory Technologies allows us to offer our customers an incredibly compelling on-chip memory solution that redefines the power-performance-area (PPA) equation for advanced AI and other applications.”
The semiconductor ecosystem is already recognizing the potential of this joint development. NXP Semiconductors, a leader in intelligent systems at the edge, is closely evaluating the benefits of the GCRAM solution.
“The industry needs a paradigm shift in on-chip memory. The GCRAM solution developed by RAAAM and GF offers immense potential,” said Victor Wang, VP of front end innovation at NXP Semiconductors. “The projected area shrink and power reductions provide a clear path to increasing on-chip memory capacities, which is vital for reducing off-chip data movement and driving greater system-level efficiency.”
About GF
GlobalFoundries (GF) is a leading manufacturer of essential semiconductors, enabling AI at scale from the cloud to the physical world. Through deep partnerships with customers, GF delivers differentiated, power-efficient and high-performance solutions for automotive, aerospace and defense, data center, smart mobile devices, internet of things and other high-growth markets. With global manufacturing operations across the U.S., Europe and Asia, GF is a trusted and holistic technology partner for customers around the world. GF’s talented, global team remains focused every day on security, longevity and sustainability.
For more information, visit www.gf.com.
About RAAAM Technologies
RAAAM Memory Technologies is a fabless semiconductor IP company providing the most cost-effective on-chip memory technology in the industry. RAAAM’s patented Gain-Cell RAM (GCRAM) technology provides up to 50% silicon area reduction and up to 3X reduced power consumption over traditional SRAM. GCRAM can serve as a drop-in SRAM replacement in SoCs and is fully compatible with standard CMOS fabrication flows, allowing designers to integrate more memory in a smaller die area with lower power consumption.
For more information, visit www.raaam-tech.com.

articles.content:
Linkhome Establishes AI Computing Subsidiary Linkhome Technologies and Begins Preliminary Evaluation of a Proposed European AI Computing Project That Could Involve Up to 144 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs
Linkhome says its proposed European AI computing plan—potentially up to 144 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs—has no assurance it will proceed or reach that scale.
Rhea-AI Summary
Linkhome Holdings (LHAI) formed a wholly owned subsidiary, Linkhome Technologies, to focus on AI computing infrastructure, enterprise AI solutions, robotics and high‑performance computing services. The company’s board approved the subsidiary and authorized further evaluation and preliminary development activities for a proposed European AI computing project.
The proposed project, if pursued, could involve deploying up to 144 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs to serve cloud providers, enterprise AI, high‑performance computing and robotics workloads. Linkhome has prepared a preliminary internal budget, obtained non‑binding equipment quotations and started early discussions with potential European data center operators, cloud providers and prospective customers. No counterparties have committed, no binding agreements have been signed, and no final investment decision or capital commitment has been made. The company cautions that there is no assurance the project will proceed or reach the currently contemplated scale, location or timeline.

articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Rajes will lead the company’s technology strategy across architecture, systems integration, data and AI.
articles.content:
Merit Financial Advisors has appointed John Rajes as chief technology officer (CTO), adding a new senior executive as the firm expands its leadership structure.
Rajes will lead the company's technology strategy across architecture, systems integration, data and AI, with responsibility for efforts to create a more consistent digital environment for advisors and staff.
Rajes has previously worked in senior roles at LPL Financial, UBS, Barclays and Goldman Sachs.
Most recently, he ran an independent consulting practice.
While at LPL Financial, where he served as head of strategic partnerships, he oversaw a fintech partner network of around 90 providers and managed investment product relationships involving asset managers, insurance companies and separately managed account providers.
At Merit, one of his initial tasks will be to set out a technology roadmap aimed at improving integration, scale and simplicity.
This includes linking data and functions across the firm's existing technology systems so advisors spend less time switching between platforms.
The new role is also intended to separate responsibilities within the firm's technology and product operations.
Rajes will oversee technology strategy, infrastructure and execution, while chief product officer Brian Green remains focused on product strategy and development. Both report to Lee.
Merit said advisors will be involved during the development of new technology initiatives, with feedback gathered as projects are designed rather than after completion.
Rajes is based in Charlotte, North Carolina, and will also spend substantial time at the firm's headquarters in Alpharetta, Georgia.
The move follows Merit's acquisition of the $900m Bridgeway Group in Southern California.
The appointment comes alongside other recent management changes at Merit.
Earlier this year, the firm named Doug Moore as chief financial officer and appointed Sarah Mouser as executive vice president of financial planning. It also added Alex Hansen as chief advisor success officer.
The firm has more than $30.1bn in assets and operates through over 55 offices nationwide.
It has completed 61 acquisitions so far, including nine partnerships in 2026.

articles.summary: Reflow Medical recently shared that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has granted the Spur peripheral retrievable stent system a new technology add-on payment (NTAP), providing additional reimbursement for eligible fee-for-service Medicare inpatient cases beginning 1 October 2026.  A company press release notes that, under the fiscal year 2027 NTAP programme, qualifying inpatient […]
articles.content:
Reflow Medical recently shared that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has granted the Spur peripheral retrievable stent system a new technology add-on payment (NTAP), providing additional reimbursement for eligible fee-for-service Medicare inpatient cases beginning 1 October 2026.
A company press release notes that, under the fiscal year 2027 NTAP programme, qualifying inpatient cases involving the Spur stent system are eligible for an incremental payment up to US$2,596.75, in addition to the applicable Medicare severity diagnosis-related group (MS-DRG) payment. Reflow states that actual payment is determined on a case-by-case basis in accordance with the applicable CMS and NTAP methodology used. The NTAP is available for a period of up to two years.
“NTAP is designed to help hospitals adopt new technology by reducing any financial barriers when introducing clinically meaningful innovations,” says Jill Joines, director of market access and health economics for Reflow Medical. “By recognising the added costs of qualifying new technologies, NTAP supports timely patient access for Medicare beneficiaries while hospitals gain experience with the technology,” she adds.
“This is an important milestone for Spur and for our continued efforts to support physicians treating patients with infrapopliteal arterial disease, a population with significant unmet clinical needs,” said Isa Rizk, CEO and co-founder of Reflow Medical.
The Spur stent system was granted De Novo classification by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in May 2025, following its earlier FDA Breakthrough Device designation. It is intended as an adjunct to percutaneous transluminal angioplasty to dilate stenoses in infrapopliteal arteries ranging in diameter from 2.5–4.5mm. The Spur stent provides temporary mechanical scaffolding and is retrieved following treatment, leaving no permanent implant behind.

articles.summary: The company, whose systems have been used by Israeli forces since October 7, has accumulated more than 500,000 operational flight hours. Its new funding will help expand technology developed through combat experience in Israel to the country’s allies.
articles.content:
AITAN raises $41 million to take Israeli combat drone technology global
The company, whose systems have been used by Israeli forces since October 7, has accumulated more than 500,000 operational flight hours. Its new funding will help expand technology developed through combat experience in Israel to the country’s allies.
Drone company AITAN, formerly known as eyesAtop, has raised $41 million in its first significant funding round. The round was co-led by Deep33 and Dell Technologies Capital, with participation from Gokul Rajaram, a board member at Pinterest and Coinbase. Other investors include Benjamin Ling of Bling Capital and Kevin Weil of Scribble Ventures. Including previous funding, AITAN has raised a total of $54 million.
AITAN develops artificial intelligence-based combat systems that have been used by Israeli forces since October 7 in highly challenging combat conditions. Its technology is designed to enable robotic forces to carry out complex combat missions while reducing the exposure of soldiers to risk.
The company was built on the technology of eyesAtop, a small veteran startup founded more than a decade ago by Yinon Atzmon, Idan Yitzhak, Ben Barkay, and Einav Harazi. In 2025, entrepreneurs Udi Oster and Daniel Almog acquired the company’s technology, seeking to capitalize on the surge in demand for drone technologies following the war in Israel. The two serve as AITAN’s joint CEOs, and the company employs about 50 people at its offices in Ramat Gan.
A few months ago, the company changed its name to AITAN in memory of Oster’s younger brother, Eitan, an Egoz officer who was killed in Lebanon in September 2024.
Oster and Almog met while serving together in Unit 8200 and, after leaving the military in 2014, founded the startup Tapingo. The company developed an online food-ordering management platform and was sold to U.S. delivery company Grubhub for $150 million in 2018.
AITAN’s main product is an operating system for drones that allows militaries to deploy and operate robotic combat systems at scale while maintaining operational continuity even when supply chains are disrupted.
The experience of the wars in Israel and Ukraine has highlighted the operational and logistical challenges involved in deploying robotic combat systems on a large scale. Unlike traditional weapons systems, which can be manufactured and stored for years, robotic systems can evolve during a conflict, sometimes from week to week, in response to changing battlefield requirements and disruptions to supply chains.
Militaries must also be able to manufacture the systems in large volumes, operate them in complex combat environments and make different platforms work together as a coordinated force rather than as a collection of separate systems.
“With the outbreak of the Swords of Iron War, it was clear to us that the only goal before us was to help our friends and family win and return safely from captivity and the battlefield. Three years later, with our technology already having a broad operational impact in the field, it is the right time to expand our reach and bring these capabilities to Israel’s allies around the world,” Oster said.
AITAN’s systems are in daily use by the IDF and the Ministry of Defense and have accumulated more than 500,000 operational flight hours across a wide range of robotic combat missions.
The company recently won a joint tender to develop the IDF’s command-and-control platform for the next generation of attack drones, as well as major design contracts for robotic weapons systems.
Many of AITAN’s employees are reservists and veterans of Israel’s defense establishment, bringing significant operational experience to the company. Its close proximity to day-to-day military operations allows the system to be regularly updated based on feedback and lessons from the battlefield.
“Robotic warfare is becoming a central part of the ability of countries to maintain their security independence, and more and more of them understand that they must develop and maintain these capabilities themselves,” said Lior Prosor, general partner at Deep33.
“To this end, control of the entire process is required, from supply and production chains, through software development and force training, to the operation of the systems in the field, their maintenance and their ongoing adaptation to operational needs. Israel and Ukraine are among the few countries in the world that have gained significant operational experience operating robotic systems, along with many flight hours in combat conditions. This experience gives AITAN a unique advantage and allows it to expand its activities and offer its technology and capabilities to Israel’s allies,” he said.
“We believe that Physical AI will be one of the most significant technological areas in the coming decade,” said Yair Snir, managing director at Dell Technologies Capital. “One of the key challenges on the way there is the ability to connect complex autonomous systems and allow them to operate together in a coordinated manner, even in complex terrain conditions.”
AITAN, he said, recognized early that the future of the security industry depends on the ability to connect different systems and smart networks so they can communicate, make decisions and act together. “The technology it has developed has already proven itself in security environments on the ground, and illustrates the growing importance of these capabilities,” Snir said.

The company was built on the technology of eyesAtop, a small veteran startup founded more than a decade ago by Yinon Atzmon, Idan Yitzhak, Ben Barkay, and Einav Harazi. In 2025, entrepreneurs Udi Oster and Daniel Almog acquired the company’s technology, seeking to capitalize on the surge in demand for drone technologies following the war in Israel. The two serve as AITAN’s joint CEOs, and the company employs about 50 people at its offices in Ramat Gan.

A few months ago, the company changed its name to AITAN in memory of Oster’s younger brother, Eitan, an Egoz officer who was killed in Lebanon in September 2024.

Oster and Almog met while serving together in Unit 8200 and, after leaving the military in 2014, founded the startup Tapingo. The company developed an online food-ordering management platform and was sold to U.S. delivery company Grubhub for $150 million in 2018.

AITAN’s main product is an operating system for drones that allows militaries to deploy and operate robotic combat systems at scale while maintaining operational continuity even when supply chains are disrupted.

The experience of the wars in Israel and Ukraine has highlighted the operational and logistical challenges involved in deploying robotic combat systems on a large scale. Unlike traditional weapons systems, which can be manufactured and stored for years, robotic systems can evolve during a conflict, sometimes from week to week, in response to changing battlefield requirements and disruptions to supply chains.

Militaries must also be able to manufacture the systems in large volumes, operate them in complex combat environments and make different platforms work together as a coordinated force rather than as a collection of separate systems.

“With the outbreak of the Swords of Iron War, it was clear to us that the only goal before us was to help our friends and family win and return safely from captivity and the battlefield. Three years later, with our technology already having a broad operational impact in the field, it is the right time to expand our reach and bring these capabilities to Israel’s allies around the world,” Oster said.

AITAN’s systems are in daily use by the IDF and the Ministry of Defense and have accumulated more than 500,000 operational flight hours across a wide range of robotic combat missions.

The company recently won a joint tender to develop the IDF’s command-and-control platform for the next generation of attack drones, as well as major design contracts for robotic weapons systems.

Many of AITAN’s employees are reservists and veterans of Israel’s defense establishment, bringing significant operational experience to the company. Its close proximity to day-to-day military operations allows the system to be regularly updated based on feedback and lessons from the battlefield.

“Robotic warfare is becoming a central part of the ability of countries to maintain their security independence, and more and more of them understand that they must develop and maintain these capabilities themselves,” said Lior Prosor, general partner at Deep33.

“To this end, control of the entire process is required, from supply and production chains, through software development and force training, to the operation of the systems in the field, their maintenance and their ongoing adaptation to operational needs. Israel and Ukraine are among the few countries in the world that have gained significant operational experience operating robotic systems, along with many flight hours in combat conditions. This experience gives AITAN a unique advantage and allows it to expand its activities and offer its technology and capabilities to Israel’s allies,” he said.

“We believe that Physical AI will be one of the most significant technological areas in the coming decade,” said Yair Snir, managing director at Dell Technologies Capital. “One of the key challenges on the way there is the ability to connect complex autonomous systems and allow them to operate together in a coordinated manner, even in complex terrain conditions.”

AITAN, he said, recognized early that the future of the security industry depends on the ability to connect different systems and smart networks so they can communicate, make decisions and act together. “The technology it has developed has already proven itself in security environments on the ground, and illustrates the growing importance of these capabilities,” Snir said.

articles.content:
- CRDO -20.04%

Credo Technology Group Holding Ltd. (NASDAQ: CRDO ) stock fell Wednesday despite better-than-expected fiscal first-quarter results, as shrinking margins, rising costs and lofty investor expectations overshadowed the earnings and revenue beats .

Credo shares had gained 43.6% this year through Tuesday's close. That rally may have also left the stock vulnerable to profit-taking .

After Tuesday's closing bell, Credo reported fiscal 2027 first-quarter revenue of $479 million. That beat the analyst estimate of $471.77 million. Adjusted earnings of $1.20 per share topped the $1.17 consensus .

Revenue increased 10% from the prior quarter and 115% from a year earlier. It exceeded the high end of Credo's guidance. The period also marked its seventh straight quarter of triple-digit annual growth.

Margins Narrow As Costs Surge

GAAP gross margin fell to 64.5% from 68.2% in the prior quarter. It was also down from 67.4% a year earlier.

GAAP operating income rose to $120.7 million from $60.7 million a year ago. However, it declined from $155.8 million in the previous quarter.

The GAAP operating margin narrowed to 25.2%. That compared with 35.7% in the prior quarter and 27.2% a year earlier.

GAAP operating expenses more than doubled to $188.4 million from $89.6 million. Research and development spending climbed to $114.5 million from $52.4 million. Selling, general and administrative expenses rose to $73.9 million from $37.2 million.

Credo Profit More Than Doubles

Net income increased to $129.4 million, or 67 cents per share. That compared with $63.4 million, or 34 cents per share, a year earlier.

Adjusted net income surged 140% to $236.3 million. Adjusted operating income rose to $230.6 million from $96.2 million. The adjusted operating margin reached 48.2%.

Operating cash flow totaled $90.2 million, while free cash flow reached $82.9 million. Credo ended the quarter with $764.3 million in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments.

AI Demand Drives Connectivity Growth

Credo said rising AI infrastructure investment continues to fuel demand. Larger computing clusters, faster data rates and more complex networks are creating opportunities across optical and copper products.

The active electrical cable business remains Credo's largest segment. Growth came from deeper ties with five hyperscalers, rising demand from neo-cloud companies and the shift toward 200-gig-per-lane and 1.6-terabit ports.

View more earnings on CRDO

Optical digital signal processor revenue reached a first-quarter record. Credo expects its first 1.6-terabit DSP revenue later in fiscal 2027.

The company also secured two major design wins for next-generation products. Those projects should ramp in fiscal 2028, although some activity could begin late in fiscal 2027.

Following its DustPhotonics acquisition, Credo recorded its first silicon photonics photonic integrated circuit revenue. The company expects its 800-gigabit and 1.6-terabit transceiver products to ramp.

Near-package optics design wins should begin ramping in fiscal 2028. Meanwhile, Zero Flap Optics has started production shipments. Credo plans additional 800-gigabit and 1.6-terabit ramps during fiscal 2027.

The retimer business also posted record first-quarter revenue. Screaming Eagle led demand at 100 gigabits per lane, while Blue Heron began contributing at 200 gigabits per lane.

Credo Issues Strong Outlook

For the second quarter, Credo expects revenue of $525 million to $535 million. That topped the $515.79 million analyst estimate .

The company projected an adjusted gross margin of 67% to 69%. It expects its full-year adjusted gross margin to remain broadly in line with fiscal 2026.

Credo expects ZeroFlap Optics, silicon photonics PICs and optical DSPs to each contribute more than $100 million in fiscal 2027. Together, those businesses should generate more than $600 million in fiscal 2027 optical revenue.

The company also expects fiscal 2027 total revenue growth of more than 85%.

Credo's Omni Connect SerDes and Weaver gearbox products target rising memory bandwidth and capacity needs. The opportunity is especially large in AI inference systems. Credo sees potential content worth thousands of dollars per GPU, with revenue expected from fiscal 2028.

articles.summary: When the engine sound disappears in an EV, what is an NVH engineer to do? Randy Rozema, director of acoustics and vibration at ACS, tells SAE Expert Insight that even when the elimination of ICE noise exposes new, high-frequency, and structural sounds, engineers have plenty of strategies to provide expected customer comfort.
articles.content:
Future of NVH Technology: Adapting to New Industry Demands
Key points
Electric cars lack engine noise, exposing quiet cabin distractions like tire tread and rattles.
Acoustic testing chambers use foam or fiberglass to measure high-frequency vehicle sounds accurately.
Automation and robotics help less experienced technicians perform precise and repeatable tests.
When the engine sound disappears in an EV, what is an NVH engineer to do? Randy Rozema, director of acoustics and vibration at ACS, tells SAE Expert Insight that even when the elimination of ICE noise exposes new, high-frequency, and structural sounds, engineers have plenty of strategies to provide expected customer comfort. The discussion also explores NHV brain drain as the industry loses senior engineers, how real-world sensor data can 'calibrate' a digital twin so engineers can actually trust its virtual acoustic predictions and how to update testing chambers for an exhaust-free world.
Transcript
00:00:01 Hello everyone, welcome to another SAE Expert Insight. My name is Sebastian Blanco, I'm the editor of Automotive Engineering Magazine, and I'm talking today with Randy Rozenboom, director of acoustics and vibration at ACS, about the future of NVH technology. Randy, how are you doing?
>> Great, how are you?
>> Good. This is an interesting topic
00:00:21 because NVH is changing so rapidly, and we want to talk today about how to adapt to the industry demands. Um, what can you tell me about how the elimination or the reduction or the changes that are happening with the internal combustion engine noise, and how that exposes new sounds that are happening coming from today's new vehicles?
>> Yeah, sure. So, you know, historically
00:00:43 combustion engine noise has been a masking agent, if you will, in the automotive industry, and what we're seeing is with the advent of electric vehicles or EVs, we're seeing new noises pop up in the in the driver cabin and in the passenger areas. So, you know, some of the things that we're seeing today are
00:01:05 an increase in notice of tire noise. And there's some parameters there that are influencing the tire noise. It's the the the tread design, the the material compound of the tire, and factors like that, and those are things that can be tested in the lab and and can be evaluated, and changes can be made. Other things though
00:01:28 to account for are interior noises such as as the industry terms it, buzz, squeak, and rattle, where we're seeing plastic on plastic surfaces that are now generating noises, and a real good example, related to a project recently done, was um airbags have a capsule in them that has an accelerant that makes the explosion,
00:01:54 if you will, when the airbag deploys. Well, with the quieter interiors, those little pellets that make that reaction are being heard in the dashes of the vehicles while they're going down the road. So, we're we're seeing these quieter environments in the automotive sector or in the the vehicles, I guess you should say.
00:02:16 And as a result, we now are looking at needing to align test facilities that can deal with this.
>> So, it sounds like what you're saying is when designing or when developing EVs, if you if you're working on NVH, you know, aspects of a vehicle, you're really this is the expert mode. You're not playing at the beginner level anymore where you have some background
00:02:37 to kind of cover the noises. What are some of the things that you need to do in a lab? Like what from the design perspective, from the machine perspective, that anticipate vehicle design changes, you know, in the in the 10 15 years down the road. Do we need to totally rebuild our labs for this sort of testing?
00:02:55
>> No, not necessarily. We're we're doing a couple of different things. When we're when we're looking at utilizing an existing lab space, we need to keep in mind a NVH lab is designed to have a life cycle of 30 to 40 years. I mean, it's not made up of components that are going to go obsolete or or wear out over time.
00:03:17 Yeah, you're going to you're going to do maintenance. You're going to buy new data acquisition systems, but the chambers that are used in and of themselves largely are the same. But, historically, you know, in the the '80s, '90s, early 2000s, the chambers have been getting fabricated or built with perforated metal wedges.
00:03:40 And over the years, there's been a lot of debate over are the high-frequency noises that we would be seeing from EVs, as an example, being measured correctly. And and the reason for that question is the the the feeling with the experts is you're getting reflection of sound off of that metal surface, and it's getting reflected right back to where the sound
00:04:06 is generating from, and it's resulting in sound levels that are potentially skewed or greater than what they should be. So, in today's environment, we're now seeing a lot of applications where if a new chamber is being built, they're going to use a fabric-wrapped fiberglass, or they're going to use some
00:04:29 type of a foam compound to undertake that absorption. And therefore, they're getting rid of that reflection, and we're getting more accurate data. So, really, it's just a matter of, you know, what does the internal of the room looking like? And the other piece to keep in mind is
00:04:50 back when we had IC engines, we had to deal with engine exhaust. That's not a thing today. Now we have batteries. So, we have chambers that have features that really aren't necessary. They They aren't needed. And that's okay. They can still be in the room. The rooms have been qualified to perform with those things
00:05:12 in there, and we can still use the room as it is. Or if if people really want to get into the the the nitty-gritty, we can go in, make a small retrofit, and remove some of those potentially reflective surfaces that comprise engine exhaust or things of that nature.
>> One of the things that that brings up is the idea of sort of, um, knowledge
00:05:35 within the people who are doing the testing and the engineers who are who are working on all this. Um, if you know the way the things worked in the '80s, '90s, and 2000s, you can adapt them to today. But the industry is losing, um, a lot of NVH engineers, you know, just the normal cycle of people retiring and everything. And we have a lot of new tools from
00:05:55 robotics and machine learning and automated auto automation. How are these new tools helping some of the younger, less tech experienced technicians successfully run these tests that you're talking about?
>> Yeah, there there's a couple of benefits here. Like you say, we have these new tools,
00:06:11 we have technologies, we have robots. So, we can automate tests now, meaning a technician can be brought in who understands the product that's being tested more so than the test that's being run because a a knowledgeable engineer can come in, program the measurement surface that needs to be scanned, or program whatever the test cycle is, and then the
00:06:37 technician literally can come in, put the product in, get it operational, set the sensors where they need to be, and push a button and let the the automated test run, let the data be collected. And on the back end, then the the knowledgeable engineer can evaluate, analyze, and post-process that data. And the other piece of it is, you know, like you say, we have robots and things
00:07:00 like that. That that really helps in terms of we have, say, a sound intensity measurement where you have to move a sensor probe over discrete locations or across a dis uh continuous path, you have a an automated repeatable means to do that now, whereas in the past, it's been all
00:07:23 human interaction, and you know, technician A may may line up on the center of a square, whereas technician B might line up on the intersection between two squares. So, all of the randomness and variable kind of goes away, and your data becomes a higher quality output as well.
>> Yeah, I never trusted uh technician B. I I thought they were looking a little
00:07:47 shady, you know, they didn't know quite what they were doing.
>> That was the intern.
>> Um Yeah, exactly. Um so you we have these new tools. Um what about something in the realm where we're dealing with virtual um you know, projects and things and how that it interacts with the real world. Um an AI
00:08:04 system an AI system, for example, could you know, look at the data and design an acoustically perfect part in a computer, but that doesn't then lead to something you can actually manufacture. How do you deal with some of these, you know, fanciful ideas or things that could be done in the virtual space then then converting them over to to real world technologies?
00:08:23
>> I think before we get into that question, we want to actually look at how do you know or how do you trust the output that's coming from that digital and you know, they they refer to it as a digital twin because at some point along the line you're going to build the prototype. You're going to measure that prototype and really the crux of it are taking that real world data, that real
00:08:46 sensor data and using that to calibrate your digital image. And now when you run those those simulations on that digital image, you're going to say, "Hey, I have an output I can trust." But to your point, AI and or or the the the virtual model isn't necessarily something that's manufacturable. And so there does need to be a human review aspect to this to
00:09:13 say, "Is what is being optimized or what is being designed something that we can physically produce, whether it be through 3D printing or some other uh existing process such as stamping or or you know, machining, things of that nature. But at the end of the day, you do need to be able to break the part that is a virtual part into components
00:09:38 that is manufacturable and assemblable.
>> Mhm. I think if we have any takeaway point from this discussion today is that, you know, the institutional knowledge is very important as well as understanding how the new technologies can blend and lead us towards better NVH systems in the future. So, Randy, thank you so much for speaking with us today and we'll see
00:09:59 everyone next time on Expert Insights.
>> Great. Thank you. Appreciate the invite to join you today.

00:04:29 type of a foam compound to undertake that absorption. And therefore, they're getting rid of that reflection, and we're getting more accurate data. So, really, it's just a matter of, you know, what does the internal of the room looking like? And the other piece to keep in mind is

How do you deal with some of these, you know, fanciful ideas or things that could be done in the virtual space then then converting them over to to real world technologies?

You're going to measure that prototype and really the crux of it are taking that real world data, that real

00:08:46 sensor data and using that to calibrate your digital image. And now when you run those those simulations on that digital image, you're going to say, "Hey, I have an output I can trust." But to your point, AI and or or the the the virtual model isn't necessarily something that's manufacturable. And so there does need to be a human review aspect to this to

But at the end of the day, you do need to be able to break the part that is a virtual part into components

So, Randy, thank you so much for speaking with us today and we'll see

articles.title: Palantir CEO Alex Karp backs ousted Ukraine defense minister's new defense tech startup
articles.description: Palantir CEO Alex Karp backs ousted Ukraine defense minister's new defense tech startup CNBC
articles.description_html: Palantir CEO Alex Karp backs ousted Ukraine defense minister's new defense tech startup  CNBC
articles.article_title: Palantir CEO Alex Karp backs ousted Ukraine defense minister's new defense tech startup
articles.heading: Palantir CEO Alex Karp backs ousted Ukraine defense minister's new defense tech startup
articles.summary: Fedorov is launching a defense tech company backed by Palantir CEO Alex Karp, aiming to turn Ukraine’s wartime experience into new technologies.
articles.content:
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov is launching a defense technology company backed by Palantir CEO Alex Karp, as the former government official looks to turn Ukraine's wartime technology experience into products for Kyiv and its allies.
Karp is set to become the company's first lead investor, according to Fedorov's press office. The size of the investment was not disclosed.
In a video posted by Fedorov on X on Tuesday, Karp said the company could bring Ukraine's knowledge and experience of warfare "as a product to allied countries."
"You and your colleagues are launching a company that I think will be defining for the world," Karp said.
Few other details about the venture have been disclosed, including its name, the technologies it plans to develop or the extent of Karp's involvement. Fedorov's press office declined to provide further information but said they planned to announce the next stages of cooperation with Palantir gradually. Palantir didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
The venture comes as Ukraine's war with Russia has accelerated the development and deployment of technologies including drones, artificial intelligence and battlefield software.
Fedorov, a longtime advocate of using technology to transform Ukraine's military, said the company would seek to apply lessons learned during the war to technologies that could be used both by Ukraine and its allies.
"During the full-scale war, our team gained unique experience working with defense technologies in Ukraine and seeing firsthand how technology is transforming modern warfare," Fedorov said in a statement.
Fedorov, 35, was removed as defense minister by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in July as part of a major government reshuffle, after just six months in the role. His dismissal prompted protests in Ukraine.
Since leaving government, Fedorov has been courting U.S. investors and technology executives as he pursues a series of projects focused on Ukraine's defense sector.
He is also seeking U.S. backing for a separate defense technology investment fund focused on areas including battlefield robotics, interceptor drones and AI-enabled missiles, the Financial Times reported last week.
The former defense minister had cultivated relationships with prominent U.S. tech executives during the war. Last month, he called Elon Musk "the most important tech person and entrepreneur in the world for our country," praising Starlink's move to prevent Russian forces from using the satellite internet service.

articles.title: NYC schools ban AI for students through 8th grade under sweeping new policy
articles.description: NYC schools ban AI for students through 8th grade under sweeping new policy ABC7 New York
articles.description_html: NYC schools ban AI for students through 8th grade under sweeping new policy  ABC7 New York
articles.article_title: No AI until high school: NYC schools announce major classroom technology overhaul
articles.heading: No AI until high school: NYC schools announce major classroom technology overhaul
articles.summary: Mayor Mamdani says children need "human connection" in the classroom as NYC launches a one-year AI moratorium for students through 8th grade.
articles.content:
Wednesday, September 2, 2026 4:25PM
NEW YORK CITY (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other city officials announced a sweeping new policy Wednesday imposing a one-year ban on student use of generative artificial intelligence in New York City public schools from 2-K through 8th grade, while limiting screen time for younger students and launching AI literacy lessons for high schoolers.
The moratorium, which takes effect during the 2026-27 school year, will affect nearly 600,000 students, roughly two-thirds of the city's public school enrollment.
"This moratorium is a commitment to getting the future right," Mamdani said. "We will embrace new technology, but only when it serves our students."
City officials said student-facing AI tools and companion chatbots will be prohibited for younger grades while a coalition of educators, parents, experts and elected officials studies the technology's impact and recommends next steps.
A limited number of high school classrooms will be allowed to participate in closely monitored AI pilot programs, and all high school students will receive twice-yearly lessons focused on AI literacy, bias, ethics and critical thinking.
Officials said teachers will still be permitted to use AI for lesson planning and administrative work that meets city safety standards.
The policy also introduces new screen time guidelines, including restrictions on one-to-one device use for the youngest students and recommended daily caps of 30 minutes for grades 3-5 and 45 minutes for grades 6-8.
Mayor Mamdani called the move necessary to protect "human connection" in classrooms, arguing children should develop problem-solving and social skills alongside teachers and peers rather than relying on AI tools.
School leaders have been awaiting the guidance for months. Principals were instructed in July to pause software purchases while the administration finalized its policy. Earlier guidance released in March did not include grade-based AI restrictions or limits on digital devices.
The crackdown comes amid growing concerns from parents, educators and lawmakers about the impact of artificial intelligence and screen-based learning on children. Parent advocacy groups have pushed for an AI moratorium in schools, while more than half of the City Council signed a letter urging City Hall and the Department of Education to halt expanded AI use in classrooms.
UFT President Michael Mulgrew said parents' concerns about artificial intelligence helped fuel calls for stricter guardrails.
"Parents are getting very, very upset with A.I. because all they hear are these horror stories about A.I. and they're rightfully protective of their children," Mulgrew said during a recent appearance on Up Close.
Mulgrew called AI "a very dangerous thing" and said schools should avoid using new products until they have been properly vetted. He also noted that teachers and principals lacked clear guidance on the policy just weeks before the start of the school year.
Supporters of the restrictions argue that many AI-powered educational programs offer questionable academic value and can encourage students to rely on technology rather than critical thinking. Some instructional apps have been criticized for resembling video games and making it easier for students to circumvent traditional learning.
The concerns mirror those that fueled New York City's bell-to-bell cellphone ban, which took effect at the start of the last school year as educators and parents sought to reduce distractions and improve student engagement.
"The tech industry wants us to believe that A.I.-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary. We do not see it that way," Mamdani said in a statement ahead of the announcement.
