articles.title: Russia secretly assists Iran with supersonic cruise missiles - FT
articles.description: Russia secretly assists Iran with supersonic cruise missiles - FT Iran International
articles.description_html: Russia secretly assists Iran with supersonic cruise missiles - FT  Iran International
articles.article_title: Russia secretly assists Iran with supersonic cruise missiles - FT
articles.heading: Russia secretly assists Iran with supersonic cruise missiles - FT
articles.summary: Russia has secretly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missile technology that experts say could give Tehran a new way to threaten US Navy vessels in the Middle East, the Financial Times reported, citing leaked Russian correspondence, travel records and military patents.
articles.content:
Russia secretly assists Iran with supersonic cruise missiles - FT
Russia has secretly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missile technology that experts say could give Tehran a new way to threaten US Navy vessels in the Middle East, the Financial Times reported, citing leaked Russian correspondence, travel records and military patents.
The program, codenamed C430L, began in 2023 and continued during this year's war with the United States and Israel, the FT said.
Its main focus is a ramjet propulsion system that would allow a cruise missile to sustain flight at several times the speed of sound, reducing the time available for US and allied defenses to detect and intercept it.
“For the Iranians, this would give them a qualitatively new strategic weapon system that could threaten US Navy vessels,” Jim Lamson, a former CIA military analyst focused on Iran, told the FT.
Iran has built and flight-tested the propulsion system, but there is no evidence that a Russian-assisted supersonic cruise missile has entered service, the newspaper said.
Russian technical support
The FT said Russia's state arms exporter Rosoboronexport arranged the program with missile developer NPO Mashinostroyenia.
Russian engineers made repeated trips to Iran before a contract was signed with Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics in November 2023, according to records reviewed by the newspaper.
By 2025, Russian specialists were analyzing Iranian flight-test data and advising Tehran on the ramjet's fuel system, combustion stability, air intake and engine nozzle.
“This is the transfer of a highly strategically sensitive military technology from Russia that the Iranians have wanted to acquire for decades,” Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst with Conflict Armament Research, told the FT.
“A programme like this would require political clearance from the very top in Russia,” he said.
The Kremlin, Rosoboronexport, NPO Mashinostroyenia and the Iranian government did not respond to requests for comment from the FT.
Potential naval impact
Supersonic cruise missiles combine high speed with low-altitude flight, making them harder for air and missile defenses to detect and engage quickly.
That could be particularly significant in the Persian Gulf, where the United States and its regional allies operate advanced land- and sea-based defenses.
Hinz said Russian engineering support could be especially valuable because it would help Iran solve technical problems rather than simply provide finished weapons.
“Getting a 60-year-old engineer to fly over and problem-solve, using their experience, is hugely valuable,” he said.
The FT said the program continued into 2026, with Russia preparing technical reports and both sides discussing a further phase of development.
A June 2026 Rosoboronexport letter showed talks were still under way over that next stage, though it was unclear whether it had begun.
Deeper military ties
The program points to a deeper form of military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran, with Russia helping Iran acquire the know-how to develop an advanced weapon system of its own.
Iran previously supplied Russia with Shahed attack drones used in Ukraine and helped Moscow establish domestic production.
The FT has also reported that Russia agreed to supply Iran with Verba shoulder-fired air defense systems, while Tehran acquired a high-resolution Chinese satellite later used to monitor US military facilities in the region.
“If the Russians are able to help the Iranians fix their technical problems, I think this would be one of the more impactful areas of Russian military-technical assistance to Iran in recent years,” Lamson said.
Peru severed diplomatic relations with Iran on Tuesday, accusing Tehran of escalating conflicts in the Middle East, restricting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and obstructing nuclear inspections.
“The government of the Republic of Peru has decided to sever diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” the Foreign Ministry said.
Lima cited what it described as Iran’s repression of peaceful protests, restrictions on press freedom, discrimination against women and girls, and persecution of political opponents.
“Within the framework of its firm commitment to defending democracy, a fundamental principle of its foreign policy, Peru has observed with growing concern the deterioration of democracy in Iran, as documented by various United Nations mechanisms, particularly regarding the repression of peaceful protests, violations of press freedom, discrimination against women and girls, and the persecution of political opponents,” read the statement.
The ministry said Iranian restrictions and disruptions to international trade through Hormuz since March violated freedom of navigation, harmed energy markets and threatened global supply chains.
“The government of Peru views with deep concern the severe restrictions imposed by the Iranian regime, as well as the disruption of international trade through the Strait of Hormuz since March 2026, because they contravene principles such as freedom of navigation and the right of passage through straits used for international maritime transit, which cannot be subject to unilateral conditions, while also affecting navigational safety, the protection of human life at sea and the preservation of the marine environment, in addition to their repercussions for energy prices and the stability of global supply chains,” the foreign ministry said.
Lima also linked the diplomatic rupture to broader security concerns, accusing Tehran of fueling regional violence and denying UN nuclear inspectors’ access to facilities needed to verify that Iran was not developing nuclear weapons.
“The government of Peru also strongly rejects Iran’s incitement to violence and the escalation of conflicts in the Middle East, as well as its obstruction of the work of the International Atomic Energy Agency,” it said.
Peru will maintain consular relations to protect the two countries’ citizens and interests. The decision was communicated to Tehran through Iran’s embassy in Ecuador, which also covers Peru.
Iranian authorities did not immediately respond to Peru’s decision.
An Iranian court has sentenced Ali Zarei Doozdarresi, a protester shot by security forces and blinded in one eye during the 2022 protests, to death after he returned from Germany and was arrested upon arrival in Iran, US-based rights outlet HRANA reported.
Branch 23 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court convicted Zarei of “corruption on Earth,” based on alleged acts including extensive political activity, producing false news, propaganda against the establishment, disrupting security and unauthorized entry into and exit from the country, according to HRANA.
The death sentence was communicated to him on August 23, HRANA said.
Zarei, around 27 and from Tehran, was arrested by Intelligence Ministry agents on April 28 after returning to Iran. His case was initially handled by Branch 3 of Tehran Prosecutor’s Office District 33, known as the Security Prosecutor’s Office, before he was transferred to Qezel Hesar Prison in Karaj on June 30.
He is currently being held in Unit 3, Ward 37 of the prison, according to HRANA.
Zarei lost sight in his right eye after being shot during the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests. He was later detained in December 2023 while visiting the graves of protesters killed in the crackdown at Tehran’s Behesht-e Zahra cemetery and spent 33 days in solitary confinement in Evin Prison.
He subsequently left Iran and reached Germany on a humanitarian visa.
While in Germany, Zarei appeared on stage at a February 14 rally in Munich held on the sidelines of the Munich Security Conference alongside exiled Prince Reza Pahlavi who had called for the gathering.
Iranian authorities have increasingly used the death penalty against protesters and political dissidents. Amnesty International has accused authorities of continuing to “weaponize the death penalty to repress dissent,” saying politically motivated death sentences have followed grossly unfair trials.
Last month, Norway-based Iran Human Rights said 29 people arrested in connection with the January 2026 protests had been executed since March 19, in addition to two protesters from the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom movement. The group said hundreds of protesters were facing the death penalty and warned of an escalation in executions of political prisoners.
The US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran has also said authorities are increasingly using fast-tracked group prosecutions to sentence protesters to death, describing the practice as part of a strategy to punish those who joined protests and deter future dissent.
Iran’s latest strikes on American forces have brought threats of further US retaliation, but Washington increasingly sees Tehran’s military escalation as a sign of economic vulnerability rather than strategic strength.
After Iran launched missiles at US bases in Jordan in response to an American strike on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, President Donald Trump promised another response.
“We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump told Fox News. “There will be a response.”
At the same time, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent offered a different measure of who has the advantage.
“I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically,” Bessent said, arguing that Tehran is feeling the effects of Washington’s expanding pressure campaign.
Iran’s economy does not have to collapse, he said. “We just have to have the regime come to their senses.”
That leaves a central question hanging over the latest exchange: can Iran’s military retaliation actually improve its position as economic pressure mounts?
“Keep firing on Jordan, keep firing on Kuwait and Bahrain and UAE, but does that solve your problem at home?” Kamran Bokhari, Strategic Forecaster and Senior Resident Fellow with the Middle East Policy Council in Washington, told Iran International.
Bokhari believes Washington has little incentive to escalate into a larger war when it can respond to specific Iranian actions while maintaining the blockade and economic pressure.
“Keep the blockade,” he said. “If they try to mine, do what they did yesterday, but don’t escalate anything, and just keep the pressure up on the economic front.”
In that scenario, Iran retains the ability to retaliate, but its attacks do little to relieve the broader pressures facing the Islamic Republic.
Can economic pressure lead to something bigger?
Ali Dadpay, an Iranian American economist from Texas, said Washington’s stated objective is to change the Islamic Republic’s behavior rather than openly pursue regime change.
“Right now, they officially and legitimately say change of behavior,” Dadpay said.
But he argued that the economic deterioration Iran is experiencing could ultimately produce a more consequential outcome than Washington’s stated goal.
Dadpay pointed to the Soviet Union, East Germany and communist Poland as examples of political systems that collapsed without being invaded by a foreign power.
“A similar set of socio-economic factors can create a similar outcome,” he said of Iran.
Dadpay also said the combination of military and economic pressure could alter calculations among groups within the Islamic Republic and push the system toward what he described as a “new equilibrium.”
The immediate question is how far Washington is prepared to go with that economic pressure.
Max Meizlish, a former senior policy adviser at the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, said a key test will be whether the US targets financial institutions facilitating Iranian trade with China.
Iran may still have oil to sell. The bigger question is whether Tehran can get paid. Unless financial channels through Hong Kong, the UAE and elsewhere are constrained, Meizlish said, “the regime is still going to have pathways for rearming itself.”
The pressure reaches ordinary Iranians
The expanding campaign is also having consequences beyond the regime. On August 24, OFAC suspended General License G, which had permitted certain educational services and academic exchanges involving Iranians.
ETS told Iran International it has since paused TOEFL and GRE testing inside Iran. Iranian nationals can still take the tests outside the country.
Dadpay called the impact on testing a “side effect” of the broader restrictions. Meizlish said the administration may be trying to prevent regime-linked individuals from using educational opportunities abroad.
But he acknowledged the wider cost.
“There could be an unintended effect here where ordinary Iranians are caught in the crossfire, so to speak,” Meizlish said.
Iran’s missiles have shown Tehran can still strike back. What remains unclear is whether those attacks can ease the pressure building on the Islamic Republic — or whether Washington’s economic squeeze can change the regime’s behavior without increasingly hurting the Iranians it is meant to pressure Tehran on behalf of.
Iran’s IRGC intelligence arm is recruiting non-Iranian operatives to carry out attacks on ships, waterways and ports in East Asia, including two major Chinese ports, sources familiar with the plans told Iran International.
Iran International has obtained information about three alleged recruits and an operation being developed by Unit 4000, the Special Operations Division of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Intelligence Organization.
According to the sources, the unit recruited the three individuals through Shiite clerics in Thailand and Indonesia and has begun planning attacks in the Malacca and Bangka straits, as well as at Tanjung Priok Port in Indonesia and the Ningbo-Zhoushan and Shanghai ports in China.
The operations are being overseen by Brigadier General Rahman Moghaddam, commander of Unit 4000, according to Iran International’s sources.
Moghaddam was reported killed in an Israeli strike in Tehran on March 3, during the opening days of the war. Israeli security agencies identified him among senior Iranian intelligence figures killed in Israeli attacks.
Two days later, drones struck Nakhichevan in Azerbaijan in an attack Baku blamed on Iran, although Tehran denied responsibility. CNN later reported that Iranian officials believed the drone attack was retaliation for Moghaddam’s killing, which Tehran suspected had been carried out with Israeli assistance from Azerbaijan.
Iran International has now obtained information indicating that those reports of Moghaddam’s death were incorrect. According to the new information, he survived the strike and is now overseeing what the sources describe as a new phase of Unit 4000’s overseas maritime operations.
Moghaddam, a former deputy coordinator at the Defense Ministry’s Protection and Intelligence Organization, took charge around three years ago of Unit 4000, which has been linked to assassination and sabotage operations targeting opponents of the Islamic Republic and Israeli interests abroad.
Plans to target ships in Indonesian and Chinese waters
Two sources familiar with the IRGC’s activities said Moghaddam is overseeing a new program aimed at expanding Unit 4000’s operations into East Asian waters.
The sources said the unit is considering attacks on commercial, military and privately owned vessels transiting the Malacca Strait, one of the world’s most important shipping routes, as well as the Bangka Strait.
Operatives recruited by the unit have also developed plans targeting Tanjung Priok, Indonesia’s busiest port, and the major Chinese ports of Ningbo-Zhoushan and Shanghai, the sources said.
The plans would represent a significant geographical expansion of Iran’s maritime pressure campaign.
Since the war began on February 28, Iran has sought to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have disrupted maritime traffic around the Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea.

Russia secretly assists Iran with supersonic cruise missiles - FT

AI-generated editorial illustration depicting missile development, regional military technology and the potential threat to US naval forces. Image created for illustrative purposes.

Russia has secretly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missile technology that experts say could give Tehran a new way to threaten US Navy vessels in the Middle East, the Financial Times reported, citing leaked Russian correspondence, travel records and military patents.

The program, codenamed C430L, began in 2023 and continued during this year's war with the United States and Israel, the FT said.

Its main focus is a ramjet propulsion system that would allow a cruise missile to sustain flight at several times the speed of sound, reducing the time available for US and allied defenses to detect and intercept it.

“For the Iranians, this would give them a qualitatively new strategic weapon system that could threaten US Navy vessels,” Jim Lamson, a former CIA military analyst focused on Iran, told the FT.

Iran has built and flight-tested the propulsion system, but there is no evidence that a Russian-assisted supersonic cruise missile has entered service, the newspaper said.

Russian technical support

The FT said Russia's state arms exporter Rosoboronexport arranged the program with missile developer NPO Mashinostroyenia.

Russian engineers made repeated trips to Iran before a contract was signed with Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics in November 2023, according to records reviewed by the newspaper.

By 2025, Russian specialists were analyzing Iranian flight-test data and advising Tehran on the ramjet's fuel system, combustion stability, air intake and engine nozzle.

“This is the transfer of a highly strategically sensitive military technology from Russia that the Iranians have wanted to acquire for decades,” Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst with Conflict Armament Research, told the FT.

“A programme like this would require political clearance from the very top in Russia,” he said.

The Kremlin, Rosoboronexport, NPO Mashinostroyenia and the Iranian government did not respond to requests for comment from the FT.

Potential naval impact

Supersonic cruise missiles combine high speed with low-altitude flight, making them harder for air and missile defenses to detect and engage quickly.

That could be particularly significant in the Persian Gulf, where the United States and its regional allies operate advanced land- and sea-based defenses.

Hinz said Russian engineering support could be especially valuable because it would help Iran solve technical problems rather than simply provide finished weapons.

“Getting a 60-year-old engineer to fly over and problem-solve, using their experience, is hugely valuable,” he said.

The FT said the program continued into 2026, with Russia preparing technical reports and both sides discussing a further phase of development.

A June 2026 Rosoboronexport letter showed talks were still under way over that next stage, though it was unclear whether it had begun.

Deeper military ties

The program points to a deeper form of military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran, with Russia helping Iran acquire the know-how to develop an advanced weapon system of its own.

Iran previously supplied Russia with Shahed attack drones used in Ukraine and helped Moscow establish domestic production.

The FT has also reported that Russia agreed to supply Iran with Verba shoulder-fired air defense systems, while Tehran acquired a high-resolution Chinese satellite later used to monitor US military facilities in the region.

“If the Russians are able to help the Iranians fix their technical problems, I think this would be one of the more impactful areas of Russian military-technical assistance to Iran in recent years,” Lamson said.

Peru severed diplomatic relations with Iran on Tuesday, accusing Tehran of escalating conflicts in the Middle East, restricting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and obstructing nuclear inspections.

“The government of the Republic of Peru has decided to sever diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” the Foreign Ministry said.

Lima cited what it described as Iran’s repression of peaceful protests, restrictions on press freedom, discrimination against women and girls, and persecution of political opponents.

“Within the framework of its firm commitment to defending democracy, a fundamental principle of its foreign policy, Peru has observed with growing concern the deterioration of democracy in Iran, as documented by various United Nations mechanisms, particularly regarding the repression of peaceful protests, violations of press freedom, discrimination against women and girls, and the persecution of political opponents,” read the statement.

The ministry said Iranian restrictions and disruptions to international trade through Hormuz since March violated freedom of navigation, harmed energy markets and threatened global supply chains.

“The government of Peru views with deep concern the severe restrictions imposed by the Iranian regime, as well as the disruption of international trade through the Strait of Hormuz since March 2026, because they contravene principles such as freedom of navigation and the right of passage through straits used for international maritime transit, which cannot be subject to unilateral conditions, while also affecting navigational safety, the protection of human life at sea and the preservation of the marine environment, in addition to their repercussions for energy prices and the stability of global supply chains,” the foreign ministry said.

Lima also linked the diplomatic rupture to broader security concerns, accusing Tehran of fueling regional violence and denying UN nuclear inspectors’ access to facilities needed to verify that Iran was not developing nuclear weapons.

“The government of Peru also strongly rejects Iran’s incitement to violence and the escalation of conflicts in the Middle East, as well as its obstruction of the work of the International Atomic Energy Agency,” it said.

Peru will maintain consular relations to protect the two countries’ citizens and interests. The decision was communicated to Tehran through Iran’s embassy in Ecuador, which also covers Peru.

Iranian authorities did not immediately respond to Peru’s decision.

An Iranian court has sentenced Ali Zarei Doozdarresi, a protester shot by security forces and blinded in one eye during the 2022 protests, to death after he returned from Germany and was arrested upon arrival in Iran, US-based rights outlet HRANA reported.

The death sentence was communicated to him on August 23, HRANA said.

Zarei, around 27 and from Tehran, was arrested by Intelligence Ministry agents on April 28 after returning to Iran. His case was initially handled by Branch 3 of Tehran Prosecutor’s Office District 33, known as the Security Prosecutor’s Office, before he was transferred to Qezel Hesar Prison in Karaj on June 30.

He is currently being held in Unit 3, Ward 37 of the prison, according to HRANA.

He subsequently left Iran and reached Germany on a humanitarian visa.

Iranian authorities have increasingly used the death penalty against protesters and political dissidents. The US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran has also said authorities are increasingly using fast-tracked group prosecutions to sentence protesters to death, describing the practice as part of a strategy to punish those who joined protests and deter future dissent.

Iran’s latest strikes on American forces have brought threats of further US retaliation, but Washington increasingly sees Tehran’s military escalation as a sign of economic vulnerability rather than strategic strength.

After Iran launched missiles at US bases in Jordan in response to an American strike on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, President Donald Trump promised another response.

“We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump told Fox News. “There will be a response.”

At the same time, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent offered a different measure of who has the advantage.

“I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically,” Bessent said, arguing that Tehran is feeling the effects of Washington’s expanding pressure campaign.

Iran’s economy does not have to collapse, he said. “We just have to have the regime come to their senses.”

That leaves a central question hanging over the latest exchange: can Iran’s military retaliation actually improve its position as economic pressure mounts?

“Keep firing on Jordan, keep firing on Kuwait and Bahrain and UAE, but does that solve your problem at home?” Kamran Bokhari, Strategic Forecaster and Senior Resident Fellow with the Middle East Policy Council in Washington, told Iran International.

Bokhari believes Washington has little incentive to escalate into a larger war when it can respond to specific Iranian actions while maintaining the blockade and economic pressure.

“Keep the blockade,” he said. “If they try to mine, do what they did yesterday, but don’t escalate anything, and just keep the pressure up on the economic front.”

In that scenario, Iran retains the ability to retaliate, but its attacks do little to relieve the broader pressures facing the Islamic Republic.

Can economic pressure lead to something bigger?

Ali Dadpay, an Iranian American economist from Texas, said Washington’s stated objective is to change the Islamic Republic’s behavior rather than openly pursue regime change.

“Right now, they officially and legitimately say change of behavior,” Dadpay said.

But he argued that the economic deterioration Iran is experiencing could ultimately produce a more consequential outcome than Washington’s stated goal.

Dadpay pointed to the Soviet Union, East Germany and communist Poland as examples of political systems that collapsed without being invaded by a foreign power.

“A similar set of socio-economic factors can create a similar outcome,” he said of Iran.

Dadpay also said the combination of military and economic pressure could alter calculations among groups within the Islamic Republic and push the system toward what he described as a “new equilibrium.”

The immediate question is how far Washington is prepared to go with that economic pressure.

Max Meizlish, a former senior policy adviser at the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, said a key test will be whether the US targets financial institutions facilitating Iranian trade with China.

Iran may still have oil to sell. The bigger question is whether Tehran can get paid. Unless financial channels through Hong Kong, the UAE and elsewhere are constrained, Meizlish said, “the regime is still going to have pathways for rearming itself.”

The expanding campaign is also having consequences beyond the regime. On August 24, OFAC suspended General License G, which had permitted certain educational services and academic exchanges involving Iranians.

ETS told Iran International it has since paused TOEFL and GRE testing inside Iran. Iranian nationals can still take the tests outside the country.

Dadpay called the impact on testing a “side effect” of the broader restrictions. Meizlish said the administration may be trying to prevent regime-linked individuals from using educational opportunities abroad.

But he acknowledged the wider cost.

“There could be an unintended effect here where ordinary Iranians are caught in the crossfire, so to speak,” Meizlish said.

Iran’s missiles have shown Tehran can still strike back. What remains unclear is whether those attacks can ease the pressure building on the Islamic Republic — or whether Washington’s economic squeeze can change the regime’s behavior without increasingly hurting the Iranians it is meant to pressure Tehran on behalf of.

articles.article_title: The terror threat no one saw coming after the 9/11 attacks
articles.heading: The Terror Threat No One Saw Coming After 9/11
articles.summary: New technologies have both increased the ability of militants to carry out attacks and expanded the number of potential targets.
articles.content:
The plot to commit the deadliest act of terrorism in modern history was surprisingly low-tech. The crucial element of the operation carried out by 19 Al-Qaeda militants on September 11, 2001, wasn’t the multimillion-dollar passenger planes, but the simple box cutters they used to hijack them.
The critical lesson for counterterrorism in the aftermath of those attacks was that such catastrophic acts of violence did not require sophisticated tools nor vast resources, only malicious determination, careful planning and the ability to exploit vulnerabilities hidden in plain sight.
However, in the 25 years since that tragedy which forever changed the course of the United States, and much of the world, the rapid evolution of the kinds of technology now widely available to anyone with an internet connection has scaled those vulnerabilities dramatically. The proliferation of drones, artificial intelligence and other innovations that were in their nascent stages during 9/11 has given bad actors ready access to many more instruments of mass destruction.
“The most significant shift hasn’t been in a single technology,” Kerry Chávez, an international security expert specializing in the use of emerging technology by nonstate actors, told Newsweek. “It has been in a supply-side inversion that has opened new or upleveled ways of war to violent nonstate actors (VNSAs).” Whether a drone attack dispersing lethal chemical agents over a crowded stadium or an AI-empowered hacker bringing down critical infrastructure—both scenarios Chávez often sees in wargames and simulations—she says, “It’s not a specific threat that most concerns me. It’s a posture that both attackers and defenders will take into the near future that will determine the degree of asymmetry and advantage that these tools afford.”
In the past, Chávez said, resource constraints and export controls meant most militant groups simply could not access military-grade systems or technology. Now, markets for drones and AI are more accessible to everyday consumers, and those tasked with intercepting threats are struggling to keep pace.
“The implication is that the threat landscape has become thicker as dual-use technologies enable the democratization of destruction,” Chávez told Newsweek. “In other words, it enables more VNSAs to wage violence by lowering the entry threshold and bolstering them beyond previous levels. By more, I mean in number, size, capability, variety and motivation/ideology.”

Or the continued threat of Islamism?” he added. “It’s a fair debate, and good points exist on all sides, but it needs to be more explicit.”
After all, he pointed out, counterterrorism is not just about preserving life. Some 20,000 people were killed in the U.S. in 2024, “yet the attacks on the Twin Towers weigh more heavily on our collective mind. And for good reason.”
“The September 11th attacks were also attacks on the American way of life and our society from an organized group that wished us harm,” Kallenborn said. “That should be our focus going forward: countering organized, hostile ideologies that can plan and orchestrate complex, coordinated attacks like those on September 11th.”

articles.title: Russia secretly aiding Iran in development of supersonic cruise missile technology - report

articles.article_title: Russia assisting Iran in development of supersonic cruise missiles | The Jerusalem Post
articles.heading: Russia secretly aiding Iran in development of supersonic cruise missile technology - report
articles.summary: The program, codenamed C430L, began in 2023 and was arranged by Russia's state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, in coordination with the US-sanctioned NPO Mashinostroyenia.
articles.content:
Russia has been secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles, London-based outlet The Financial Times reported on Wednesday morning, which experts say would likely have been intended for anti-ship and land attacks.
The program, codenamed C430L, began in 2023 and was arranged by Russia's state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, in coordination with the US-sanctioned NPO Mashinostroyenia, FT reported.
According to FT, Russian arms export officials and senior NPO Mashinostroyenia engineers traveled to Iran repeatedly in 2023.
Among the engineers who conducted these trips were Alexander Dergachev, chief designer for sea-launched missiles and cruise missile complexes; Alexander Chebakov, head of NPO Mashinostroyenia’s design department for air-breathing propulsion units and a specialist in supersonic ramjet propulsion for cruise missiles; and Yuri Prokhorchuk, head of the aerodynamics and ballistics department.
FT also learned that Vladislav Kuzmichev, head of Rosoboronexport’s department of defense technologies and space, accompanied the delegation on its third trip to Iran, and later negotiated the C430L contract with Iran.
By 2025, NPO Mashinostroyenia had received various Iranian technical materials, which Russian engineers analyzed and responded to with various questions.
In correspondence seen by FT from April 2025, Rosoboronexport proposed sending a delegation of Russian specialists to Iran and asked Tehran to answer the engineers' questions before the trip.
“People often think about technology transfers as being solely about sending blueprints, parts, or entire missiles," Fabian Hinz, an Iranian missiles expert and senior analyst with Conflict Armament Research, a UK-based weapons-tracing organization, told FT, "but getting a 60-year-old engineer to fly over and problem-solve, using their experience, is hugely valuable.”
Iranian president thanks Putin for support against United States
On Tuesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow's position on the war in Iran and resulting sanctions, and said that together, Moscow and Tehran can resist what he called US "unilateralism."
The two leaders spoke on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek.
During the meeting, Putin told Pezeshkian that Moscow stood in solidarity with the Iranian people in the fight for their interests.
Putin also said that Russia and Iran will maintain their economic and trade relationship despite the current military and political environment.
“During this difficult period, we are striving to provide you with the necessary assistance - as we have discussed - and are supplying you with essential goods,” Putin said.
Pezeshkian accuses US of violating international law
Pezeshkian, in turn, said that the US does not have the right to impose sanctions "whenever they please," and accused them of violating international law and committing acts of aggression.
Russia and Iran, he said, would find ways to circumvent the US sanctions.
"Within frameworks like the SCO and other organizations, we can bypass unilateral measures and cooperate on a multilateral basis,” he stated.
Notably, the US sanctions Pezeshkian was referring to, including Washington’s latest measures targeting Iranian financial networks and IRGC-linked assets, are not in themselves prohibited under international law. Economic sanctions also do not constitute an “act of aggression” under the UN definition.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Editorial: Sometimes the best classroom technology is no technology at all
articles.description: Editorial: Sometimes the best classroom technology is no technology at all reflector.com
articles.description_html: Editorial: Sometimes the best classroom technology is no technology at all  reflector.com
articles.article_title: Editorial: Sometimes the best classroom technology is no technology at all
articles.heading: Editorial: Sometimes the best classroom technology is no technology at all
articles.summary: If a muscle atrophies, our bodies weaken. We can’t walk very far, we can’t lift things.
articles.content:
If a muscle atrophies, our bodies weaken. We can’t walk very far, we can’t lift things.
When your ability to think atrophies, well, that’s arguably a whole lot worse. “Cogito, ergo sum,” or — “I think, therefore I am,” as René Descartes put it.
Thinking, thus, is as elemental as breathing. Universities should create the conditions for students to learn how to do it well, and the University of Chicago has struck an important blow to that end.
Leaning on the convenience of artificial intelligence for writing assignments comes at a cognitive cost: a reduction in critical thinking, according to a 2025 study from researchers at MIT, Wellesley and the Massachusetts College of Art and Design.
A new policy for the U. of C.’s social sciences core aims to return the classroom to an analog experience in which students must generally read, write and analyze without AI’s assistance.
“At UChicago, we train students to use both reason and specialized knowledge in preparation for life as a free person,” the memo from Social Sciences Collegiate Division Master Jenny Trinitapoli reads. “… we first equip students to read, write, and think without dependence on AI, just as we equip students to read, write, and think beyond the bounds of conventional views or leading ideologies.”
In other words, this is about challenging students to think for themselves before introducing the life-altering capabilities of artificial intelligence into the equation.
Note, this memo is explicitly not anti-AI. Trinitapoli notes that technology can be “used for good scholarly purposes in other parts of the curriculum.”
It simply recognizes the proper sequence of things — think first, leverage tools after.
The same restraint applies to professors, who will not be permitted to employ AI to write syllabuses or course materials. AI use in grading is also tightly restricted.
This effort to cultivate our own minds, as Trinitapoli puts it, is noble and worthwhile, and absolutely in keeping with the university’s long and hallowed reputation as an institution where rigorous instruction and deep intellectual engagement are considered table stakes.
Notably, this policy does not apply to the whole school but to a set of discussion-based social science courses. U. of C. President Paul Alivisatos has made his broader philosophy known, too, and it comes across as entirely sensible, acknowledging the powerful assistance AI can offer when, say, doing data analysis while at the same time reinforcing the need for independent thought.
“The University has a duty of care to ensure that the education offered to you is responsive to these technological developments by teaching you how to think with machines, how to think without them, and how to think about them,” Alivisatos said in a June statement.
The U. of C. is not alone in reckoning with how to lasso AI in academic settings. Duke University earlier this month updated its AI guidance, reinforcing that students are expected to do their own work, unless authorized, and sharing the expectation that professors should come up with guidance on the use of AI in the classroom to be included in their syllabuses. All while firmly supporting AI literacy.
Columbia University, too, “embraces generative AI tools” while also demanding its students rely on the use of their own critical thinking skills in the pursuit of their education, meaning students are expected to do their assignments and exams without AI assistance unless expressly permitted.
These universities are among our nation’s top schools, and what they do resonates far beyond the confines of campus. We expect others will follow suit.

articles.title: Tech Briefs: Warner, Griffith talk drone technology for Iran — and the Radford arsenal
articles.description: Tech Briefs: Warner, Griffith talk drone technology for Iran — and the Radford arsenal Cardinal News
articles.description_html: Tech Briefs: Warner, Griffith talk drone technology for Iran — and the Radford arsenal  Cardinal News
articles.article_title: Tech Briefs: Warner, Griffith talk drone technology for Iran — and the Radford arsenal
articles.heading: Tech Briefs: Warner, Griffith talk drone technology for Iran — and the Radford arsenal
articles.summary: Warner says White House turned down Ukraine’s offer of drone assistance; Griffith floats a plan to have Virginia Tech drone program monitor Radford Army Ammunition Plant.
articles.content:
Drones are going to be ubiquitous in the coming years, Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said last week. The onetime cellphone entrepreneur told a group gathered at Virginia Tech’s Kentland Farm that if he had to start his investing career over, he would be a drone guy.
I wrote about the event in question, a ribbon-cutting for a new counter-drone testing and research facility on the university-owned farm, for Monday’s Cardinal News. For today’s Tech Briefs, I’m writing up some interesting stuff that Warner and U.S. Rep. Morgan Griffith, R-Salem, said during gaggles set up after the ribbon-cutting.
There wasn’t enough room for it in Monday’s piece, which focused on the $5 million research contract the university signed with the Army. And with drone-centric wars happening internationally, in Ukraine and Iran, it’s a topic that will be top of mind for a long time.
But first, remember that I’m always up for tips, questions and suggestions, so feel free to email me: tad@cardinalnews.org.
Warner says White House turned down Ukraine’s offer of drone assistance before Iran war
Warner, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told reporters on Friday that the Trump administration in December turned down Ukraine’s offer of drone technology.
“Ukrainians, because of the existential threat [from Russia] have been able to turn around their technology at record speed,” he said.
Meanwhile, the U.S. is wasting valuable munitions shooting down the cheap drones that Iran is using to attack its Middle Eastern bases and intelligence, he said.
“What’s really angered me is, in four years, we’ve had people testify before the intelligence committee saying, ‘Oh, absolutely, we’ve learned these lessons, and then we start this war of choice with Iran, and we’re using missiles that cost more than $2 million a pop to shoot down Iranian drones.
“And we have only brought the price point down of our counter-drone technology to roughly 60, 70, $80,000 [apiece]. That cannot be done at scale.”
Meanwhile, Ukraine is building counter-drones at $5,000 each, he said. While the British and some Persian Gulf states are flying them, “we are behind,” he said.
“We ought to be able to do the same. … If you’re going to start a war of choice, wouldn’t you want the best in the world to protect your soldiers? We turned it down, so we’re using up more munitions at a record pace.”
Griffith, in a separate interview, deferred to Warner’s understanding about whether the White House turned down Ukrainian help, but said that Ukraine is the clear leader in drone warfare tech, and that “obviously, in retrospect, it might have been an error” to turn down the assistance.
Plenty of Iranian drones and missiles have hit important targets, and multiple news sources have reported destruction in the air and on the ground, including a key Navy logistical hub in Bahrain. Just past the six-month mark in the war, both sides have recently resumed firing at each other.
Griffith floats plan to have Virginia Tech drone program monitor Radford Army Ammunition Plant
Multiple dignitaries took to the dais at Kentland Farm before the ribbon-cutting. Griffith walked up with an idea: Use Virginia Tech’s drone program for occasional patrols over the Radford Army Ammunition Plant.
“Even if we can’t provide 24/7 security over the arsenal right now, anybody who’s looking at that as a target, as a bad guy, has to worry about … maybe they have the Virginia Tech folks flying over doing some experiments,” he told the group.
Later, he told reporters that he has gotten some good feedback about the idea, though it would require cutting the red tape involved with getting permission to fly over the plant just across the river from Kentland.
“I come up with lots of ideas, and every now and then one of them’s good,” he said. “I think this is a good one.”
It would require the Army’s permission, he said. But with the university’s drone library built out and the plant’s location within view, it makes sense to occasionally fly over there, as a deterrent to potential attacks, he added.
“Apply a few test runs through there,” Griffith said. “See what they can detect with their defense systems. Let them [the plant] know in advance they’re doing it. You wouldn’t have to be 24/7, but if you’re using it as a test ground, then the bad guys don’t know … particularly if you didn’t do it on a regular set every Tuesday at 3, but you just did it, whenever. You call them and say, ‘OK, we got them coming in 15 minutes,’ and boom, there they are.”
Maybe the researchers could learn things about patrolling military sites, he said. The Radford plant is mostly civilian-staffed, but there is a small military presence at a “major asset,” he said.
“It’s not like they have to ship all the equipment across the country,” he said. “It’s right there.”
A Virginia Tech spokeswoman said the university didn’t have a comment.

articles.article_title: TDK to showcase smart javelin technology as official global supporter of World Athletics Ultimate Championship | News  | Budapest 26 | World Athletics Ultimate Championships
articles.heading: TDK to showcase smart javelin technology as official global supporter of World Athletics Ultimate Championship
articles.summary: Top athletes from around the world will throw a 'TDK smart javelin' equipped with TDK sensors during a special demonstration session
articles.content:
TDK's smart javelin technology
• Top athletes from around the world will throw a 'TDK smart javelin' equipped with TDK sensors during a special demonstration session at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, Hungary, from September 11-13.
• Throwing data collected by sensors will be analysed in real time, and visualisations of the data will be showcased at the venue.
TDK Corporation has been announced as an official global supporter of the World Athletics Ultimate Championship. As part of the partnership, TDK will provide a 'TDK Smart Javelin' – a javelin equipped with TDK sensors – to visualise performance data during a special javelin-throw demonstration session at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship, to be held in Budapest, Hungary, from September 11-13.
Ahead of the World Athletics Championships Tokyo 25, TDK worked with World Athletics on a project to visualise javelin throw data using sensor technology. The project explored how previously unseen performance data could be captured and presented to enhance understanding of the event for athletes and spectators.
Since then, improvements to the sensor module and software have enabled TDK to analyse and visualise the javelin’s movement in real time. While conventional competition results record the distance of each throw, the sensor technology can provide additional data on factors such as release angle, rotation, speed, height and flight trajectory. This information can give athletes greater insight into their technique and performance, while the visualisations can also help spectators better understand the technical and physical demands of javelin throwing.
Top javelin throwers from around the world will participate in the demonstration session. Data collected from the javelins – including release angle, rotation, speed, height and flight trajectory – will be analysed in real time, with visualisations displayed at the venue. The technology will give spectators a new way to understand the technique and performance behind elite javelin throwing.
Session details
• Date / time: Friday 11 September 2026, 9:00am-1:00pm local time (scheduled)
• Venue: Training & warm-up venue at The Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre
Athletes scheduled to participate
• Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage (Sri Lanka): Ranked No.1 in the world in the men’s javelin in 2026
• Keshorn Walcott (Trinidad and Tobago): 2025 world champion; 2012 Olympic champion; 2016 Olympic bronze medallist
• Haruka Kitaguchi (Japan): 2024 Olympic champion; 2023 world champion; Japanese record holder
(Note: Kitaguchi will attend the session to discuss the sensor technology but will not throw)
• Máté Horváth (Hungary): 2025 Hungarian champion; 2022 European U18 silver medallist
• Fanni Kövér (Hungary): 2024 Hungarian champion; 2023 European U20 bronze medallist
• Máté Járvás (Hungary): 2026 Hungarian bronze medallist
The project forms part of TDK’s long-term vision, ‘TDK Transformation’ and its ‘In Everything, Better.’ brand identity. Through its ‘TDK Sensing Within’ concept, TDK is working with partners to apply its sensor technology to products and solutions across a range of areas.
TDK has been an official partner of World Athletics since 1983 and has supported the development of athletics for more than four decades. The partnership has increasingly included projects that use TDK technology to provide new insights into athlete performance and the sport.
The World Athletics Ultimate Championship is a brand-new global championship that is set to transform the athletics calendar and settle the debate over which athlete is the best of the best every two years. It will pit world champions, Olympic champions, Wanda Diamond League winners and the year’s top-ranked athletes against each other to crown the champion of champions. The Ultimate, which will take place in Budapest, Hungary, on 11-13 September, features a historic prize pot of US$10 million.

articles.title: AnalySwift wins NASA award to develop robotic space welding technology
articles.description: AnalySwift wins NASA award to develop robotic space welding technology Engineer Live
articles.description_html: AnalySwift wins NASA award to develop robotic space welding technology  Engineer Live
articles.article_title: AnalySwift wins NASA award to develop robotic space welding technology - Engineer Live
articles.heading: AnalySwift wins NASA award to develop robotic space welding technology
articles.summary: AnalySwift and Purdue University's two-year project is intended to address a major challenge for long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond
articles.content:
AnalySwift, a Purdue University-affiliated engineering software company, has received an $899,738 Phase II Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) award from NASA to develop robotic technology for welding and unwelding thermoplastic composite structures in space.
The two-year project is intended to address a major challenge for long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond: the cost and physical constraints associated with transporting large infrastructure from Earth. By enabling structures to be disassembled, reconfigured and reused, the technology could reduce the need to launch new construction materials and overcome spacecraft launch-fairing limitations.
Allan Wood, president and CEO of AnalySwift, said the activity will focus on enabling disassembly and reassembly of large truss structures through thermoplastic composite joints.
“This capability allows the repurposing of spacecraft components for other missions, achieving multiuse structures and assembling large structures without the limit of launch-fairing dimensions,” he said.
The project combines composite materials development, robotics and simulation. Its objectives include developing thermoplastic composite joints incorporating embedded resistance heaters, building robotic manipulators for welding and unwelding, demonstrating robotic disassembly and reassembly of a prototype truss, and assessing the feasibility of repurposing full-scale structures.
Kawai Kwok, associate professor in Purdue University’s School of Aeronautics and Astronautics, is principal investigator. His team will develop joints incorporating a resistance heater made from the same thermoplastic matrix as the composite struts, alongside a thin-film resistor.
“The embedded heater provides in situ heating to bring the thermoplastic matrix to the processing temperature for bonding and debonding the joint-strut interface by mechanical forces,” he said. “Intelligent robotic systems will perform the welding operation and structural reassembly to achieve reconfiguration of a truss.”
Robotics development will be led by Yu She, assistant professor in Purdue’s Edwardson School of Industrial Engineering. His team will develop a dual-arm system incorporating vision, tactile sensing, and force and thermal feedback.
“My team will develop a dual-arm robotic system that uses vision, tactile sensing, and force and thermal feedback to locate composite joints, activate their embedded heaters, and carefully separate or reconnect the structural components,” he said.
The project follows AnalySwift’s Phase I NASA STTR award in 2024. The company will contribute its composite simulation expertise to modelling the materials and structures required, including assessing the feasibility of repurposing full-scale trusses.
“Long-duration crewed missions to the moon, Mars and beyond require infrastructure to be constructed sustainably on these surfaces,” Wood said.

articles.title: Charlotte Pulica | Technology is making us boring
articles.description: Charlotte Pulica | Technology is making us boring The Daily Pennsylvanian
articles.description_html: Charlotte Pulica | Technology is making us boring  The Daily Pennsylvanian
articles.source: Charlotte Pulica | Technology is making us boring - The Daily Pennsylvanian
articles.article_title: Charlotte Pulica | Technology is making us boring
articles.heading: Charlotte Pulica | Technology is making us boring
articles.summary: Columnist Charlotte Pulica argues that while “no-tech” classes may seem like a nuisance, they are the best solution to getting the most out of an education.
articles.content:
What happens when you put 30 Ivy League students in a classroom and ask them a question? Apparently, nothing.
Whether it’s a first-year seminar with 10 students or a lecture hall with over 100, we’ve all watched as our professor posed a question and was met with an awkward silence. We’ll stare at our computers, pretending we’re deep in thought or entrenched in our notes, and wait for someone to break the tension. It may not be every question or every class, but it’s enough to create an environment where we’ve simply gotten used to not responding. Humanities and seminar-based classes are supposed to thrive off of conversation, discussion, and even contention. But unfortunately, none of that can happen if students don’t feel the need to participate.
It’s hard to believe that Penn students have nothing to say or no opinions to share. As a matter of fact, it seems that Penn students always have something to say. The dead air isn’t necessarily caused by a lack of interesting thoughts or comments, but rather the ever-present technology we can’t seem to go without anymore, and with it comes an increasingly accurate idea: technology has made us boring.
It’s not that Penn students are unintelligent or unable to answer a question if a computer is in front of them. But the presence of tech in class — even if it’s just for note taking — has been proven to produce worse outcomes for students. The result is often a combination of increased distractions, decreased satisfaction with the class, and an overall lack of understanding when it comes to the course material. It’s becoming clear that classes have become a competition between the course material and our screens, and everybody is losing in the process.
Penn’s solution? An increase in professors creating a “no-tech” policy for their classroom. No phones, no iPads, no laptops — a completely analog transformation. I’ve experienced my fair share of tech-free classes in both humanities and STEM courses. And although I’ve noticed a general disapproval from students (including, occasionally, myself), I’ve also noticed something much more thought-provoking: everyone and everything seemed less boring. Without the physical barrier of a screen taking up everyone’s view, the only thing left to focus on was the class itself.
It’s easy to buy into the justification of foundational or major requirements and only see a class as a means to an end. When you have your laptop right in front of you, why not finish that problem set or reply to that email? Sometimes it can feel more efficient to treat a class like a study hall, and we’re all guilty of it. But in those moments when your focus is on a screen instead of the professor, a whole possibility of education is lost.
The reason we don’t just take online classes, sequester ourselves in our dorms, and bury ourselves in self-produced research in order to graduate is because that’s not the point of Penn. We’re meant to collaborate and converse with people who have completely different experiences and backgrounds under the mentorship of world class professors. And the truth is, that’s harder to do when there’s a screen blocking your view and constantly fighting for your attention.
Sure, it might take a little extra effort to take notes with a pen and paper rather than typing on a laptop. But it’s definitely not without reward. Students do much better on exams and with information retention in general when they handwrite their notes compared to using tech, and without the added distraction, you’re able to focus on the class at hand rather than the screen in front of you. And if all we care about is trying to minimize the amount of time and work we put into everything, why even bother coming to Penn? If not to educate and better ourselves, are we really paying $100,000 a year just to reorganize our Google Calendar during a lecture?
SEE MORE FROM CHARLOTTE PULICA:
No-tech classes might feel over the top or annoying, but when it comes to a discussion-based class or a seminar, they’re starting to feel essential. Participating in discussions, answering questions, retaining and interacting with the content — these are the qualities that make a course truly educational. Yes, technology is always going to be a part of our lives and our education, and yes, it might feel easier in the moment to rely on it, but we have an opportunity to take classes that are meant to expand our perspectives and challenge our ideas, which seems a lot more valuable than whatever is on our screen.
Classes can feel boring. Discussions can feel boring. Required readings can feel boring. But in a world where we have a constant stream of dopamine-inducing content inches away from our faces, being forced to confront that feeling might be the only way to realize that it was really us being boring the entire time.
CHARLOTTE PULICA is a College sophomore studying Cognitive Science from Enoch, Utah. Her email is cpulica1@sas.upenn.edu.
Charlotte Pulica is a College first year studying communications and consumer psychology from Enoch, Utah. Her column focuses on student life and administrative policy. She currently serves as a Deputy Opinion Editor and can be reached at cpulica1@sas.upenn.edu .

articles.summary: West Fargo police are sharing a new method aimed at combating point-of-sale transaction fraud.
articles.content:
West Fargo Police debut skim scan technology to fight card fraud
WEST FARGO, N.D. (Valley News Live) - West Fargo police are sharing a new method aimed at combating point-of-sale transaction fraud. The technology, called Skim Scan technology, detects hidden skimmers or shimmers on payment terminals at retailers and gas pumps.
How the technology works
Police say the device allows them to be proactive by inspecting point-of-sale systems at businesses to check whether devices have been compromised.
“We want to do some prevention of fraud-type activities,” said Sgt. Craig Danielson of the West Fargo Police Department.
“Prevention in the form of inspecting those point-of-sale devices for businesses to ensure them that the devices they have are not being compromised.”
The department has one device, which costs about $500.
A nationwide trend
Police say skimming fraud is prevalent nationwide and describe the new technology as a way to get ahead of the trend. In 2025, law enforcement across the country removed more than 400 illegal skimming devices, preventing an estimated potential fraud loss of more than $428 million.
“The trend nationwide is a lot of fuel stations, a lot of pumps where they’re away from those point-of-sale locations and front counter areas,” Danielson said.
Consumer reaction
Aaron Niehaus, a consumer, said fraud is something he keeps in mind, especially at the pump.
“I think it’s something you need to be constantly aware of in a digital world, where your payment is always on your person and all your financial assets are sitting in your pocket, you know?” Niehaus said.
Niehaus said he thinks the new technology is warranted.
“Digital systems are not necessarily owned by that place of business. It’s part of a broader network, a broader financial network of credit card transactions. If it means preventing people from getting scammed then information is used responsibly, it’s a good thing to me,” Niehaus said.
How to get terminals scanned
A link to request a terminal scan can be found, here.
Police also recommend using caution when using payment terminals, including checking for anything loose, crooked, damaged or scratched. They recommend using tap-to-pay.

“Digital systems are not necessarily owned by that place of business. It’s part of a broader network, a broader financial network of credit card transactions. If it means preventing people from getting scammed then information is used responsibly, it’s a good thing to me,” Niehaus said.

How to get terminals scanned

A link to request a terminal scan can be found, here.

Police also recommend using caution when using payment terminals, including checking for anything loose, crooked, damaged or scratched. They recommend using tap-to-pay.

articles.heading: China approves string of ‘telepathy’ devices amid push to leapfrog Elon Musk
articles.summary: Chinese regulators have approved a group of brain-technology products this year, as local start-ups push to surpass Musk’s Neuralink.
articles.content:
China approves string of ‘telepathy’ devices amid push to leapfrog Elon Musk
Chinese regulators have approved a group of brain-technology products this year, as local start-ups push to surpass Musk’s Neuralink
China’s health regulators have granted approvals for a string of brain-technology products this year, as domestic start-ups push to transform the treatment of conditions ranging from paraplegia to Alzheimer’s and depression.
The approvals come as Beijing bids to lead the world in brain-computer interfaces – devices that allow patients to control digital devices using thought alone – offering generous policy support to help Chinese firms compete with overseas players such as Elon Musk’s Neuralink.
Among the brain tech products to win Chinese market approval recently is a system developed by a domestic firm named Tiankai Suishi (Tianjin) Intelligent Technology, which helps doctors assess whether a patient’s cognitive functions have been impaired.
The device is a cap studded with electrodes that fits over a patient’s scalp and can be used to read the electrical signals given off by the brain, according to an article posted to the company’s official WeChat feed. It was approved by China’s National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) on August 19, official records show.
Tiankai Suishi also sells BCI devices that aid early diagnosis of cognitive dysfunction linked to conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and schizophrenia. It is currently seeking regulatory approval for a product to assist with diagnosing depression.
The company, founded in 2023, has registered capital of 10.67 million yuan (US$1.59 million), according to the corporate database Qichacha. It is led by Gu Bin, who completed a doctoral degree at Tianjin University’s medical school, according to Chinese media reports.

articles.title: Fake 10 Downing Street listing exposes 'unfit' Booking.com, says consumer group
articles.description: Fake 10 Downing Street listing exposes 'unfit' Booking.com, says consumer group BBC
articles.description_html: Fake 10 Downing Street listing exposes 'unfit' Booking.com, says consumer group  BBC
articles.article_title: Which? says fake 10 Downing Street listing exposes 'unfit' Booking.com checks
articles.heading: Fake 10 Downing Street listing exposes 'unfit' Booking.com, says consumer group
articles.summary: Booking.com said the "limited test" was "not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings or reviews".
articles.content:
Fake 10 Downing Street listing exposes 'unfit' Booking.com, says consumer group
Consumer group Which? says it was able to create a fake listing for 10 Downing Street on travel giant Booking.com.
The UK watchdog said its researchers were able to book a bogus stay at the prime minister's address - as well as leave a fake review noting "hanging out" with resident mouser Larry the cat as a highlight.
It said despite clear signs it was fake, Booking.com did not remove the listing until two months after it was uploaded.
"This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings or reviews published on our platform," a Booking.com spokesperson told the BBC.
They said because Which?'s listing was not "live" on its site across the two months it was present, "some of our automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the closed listing".
People could only see the listing and request to book the property during a 20-minute window opened by Which? so its researchers could try to book it.
Booking.com's spokesperson added "a range of checks and verification measures" help secure the site, and technologies such as AI "help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours".
But Which? Travel editor Rory Boland said its checks had been shown to be "unfit for purpose".
"If Booking.com's so-called sophisticated AI systems can't spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it's no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily," he said.
"It would be laughable that we were able to list the UK's most famous address for rent, if the consequences weren't so devastating for holidaymakers, who risk losing thousands of pounds to bogus listings and phishing links."
It is not the first time the site has faced criticism over its security efforts and customer service.
'Prime city centre location'
Which?'s listing, uploaded to Booking.com on 18 June, advertised a "1 bedroom apartment in the heart of London".
It used images of the iconic 10 Downing Street front door, listed at its address - with a description referring to the one bedroom space as "a prime city centre location".
In the 20 minutes that Which? permitted customers to request a stay at its fake 10 Downing Street property, it said 14 people asked to do so.
Only the booking request from a person known to be a Which? researcher was accepted.
The watchdog's team also sent the researcher a message within Booking.com's system asking them to click an external link to confirm their payment details - something booking sites typically block to prevent customers being scammed.
But Which? said that in this instance, Booking.com did not flag or remove the external link it sent.
Booking.com said it had "visible reminders to not click on links customers are not confident about, and booking confirmations also provide further guidance, including details of the agreed payment schedule".
The fake review left by Which? also seemingly passed the site's checks, despite bearing all the hallmarks of a joke.
"It was unbelievable that Booking.com let us stay at 10 Downing Street - the home of the UK PM!" it said.
The listing itself was removed by the platform on 27 August.
Some customers have previously accused the firm of failing to protect them from falling victim to cyber-criminals.
"Fraud affects many industries, and 80% of UK adults believe scams are becoming more sophisticated," said Booking.com's spokesperson - adding it was continuing to strengthen its defences in the face of this challenge.
Which?, meanwhile, said more should be done to force booking sites to swiftly remove false listings under the Online Safety Act (OSA).
The Act requires firms which have identified illegal content, including fraudulent material, on their sites to show they are committed to removing it.
Boland said Ofcom, which enforces the OSA, should be encouraged use it to "crack down on irresponsible online platforms that leave consumers wide open to fraud".
"For illegal content generated by users, platforms have existing legal duties that mean they must take it down swiftly once they become aware of it," an Ofcom spokesperson told Which?.

articles.title: G20 Innovation Ministerial kicks off in Chapel Hill with AI, emerging technology as centerpieces of discussion
articles.description: G20 Innovation Ministerial kicks off in Chapel Hill with AI, emerging technology as centerpieces of discussion The Daily Tar Heel
articles.description_html: G20 Innovation Ministerial kicks off in Chapel Hill with AI, emerging technology as centerpieces of discussion  The Daily Tar Heel
articles.article_title: G20 Innovation Ministerial kicks off in Chapel Hill with AI, emerging technology as centerpieces of discussion
articles.heading: The Daily Tar Heel
articles.summary: Guest speakers like Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and David Sachs discuss AI boosting global economies — and a new industrial revolution.
articles.content:
The G20 Innovation Ministerial kicked off this Tuesday in Chapel Hill, with science and technology ministers from the world’s most powerful economies gathering at the Carolina Inn to discuss the future of technology-driven growth.
Michael Kratsios, President Donald Trump’s science and technology advisor, opened with an overview of the two-day event’s mission: to share best practices and shape the future of technology-driven growth for global economies. He also unveiled the “Carolina Principles for Emerging Technology,” a framework that the G20 Innovation Working Group has finalized over the past several months.
Kratsious said that North Carolina being home to the Research Triangle, the first public university and being the “first in flight” made Chapel Hill the right place to host these conversations.
The event has culminated in an increased security presence and community opposition to the speakers, which has led to planned protests throughout the week.
In adopting the Carolina Principles, Kratsios said that G20 members commit to three general goals: investing in foundational research to accelerate discovery, strengthening development and commercialization pathways, driving trusted adoption and deployment by applying existing sector-specific rules where appropriate — reserving new regulation for novel considerations.
Kratsios mentioned that these principles don’t require countries to harmonize their legal systems or standardize regulatory institutions across nations. He said that every country will have its own approach in supporting discovery, development and deployment, but these shared principles will help G20 ministers to fully realize the benefits of technology for their people.
“As many of you know, AI is transforming so many parts of our economies. But I think one area that is underreported and one that we’ll be stressing today is AI for scientific discovery,” Kratsios said. “Applying artificial intelligence to material science, chemistry, math, physics — that is where the greatest breakthroughs are going to happen in the next five to 10 years, and that is where we can show the biggest impact to our people.”
‘Stockfish-level good’: Elon Musk discusses the future of artificial intelligence software
Appearing virtually as the event’s first guest speaker, Tesla and SpaceX CEO and OpenAI co-founder Elon Musk told ministers that countries should expect to continue seeing significant productivity gains from digital AI and emerging humanoid robotics. Scaling this gain, he estimated that AI will increase the total global economy by 20 to 30 percent, meaning about $20 to $30 trillion per year.
Musk added that by the end of next year, AI will likely be able to do anything digital that doesn’t require the “shaping of atoms by hand”. He referred to this level of AI as “Stockfish-level good,” pointing to the powerful Stockfish chess engine, which can easily beat the world’s best chess players. He said that this software will be so advanced that it will be “impossible for a human to compete in writing software with AI.”
Using this AI software alongside powerful chips and electromechanical dexterity, Musk said that humanoid robotics will grow at an explosive rate.
“This is one I would be willing to put serious money betting on, that there will be at least a billion robots in 10 years, and that those robots will be at least five times the output of a human,” Musk said. “Meaning that a billion humanoid robots will be more productive than all humans combined.”
Musk’s closing message concerned electricity. Regarding data centers, he told ministers that industry consensus points to a power shortfall of roughly 15 gigawatts in 2027, saying “there actually is quite a crisis of power” because AI chip production is growing far faster than electricity supply can keep up with. He said that the gap is already severe enough that SpaceX built its own power plants to run AI infrastructure.
‘It’s a new industrial revolution’: Leaders talk upgrading power
David Sacks, former White House “AI Czar” and co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, also attended virtually. Sacks pointed to roughly $800 billion being invested in the United States’ AI capacity this year. Sacks added he expects that number to rise to $1.4 trillion next year.
“It’s a new industrial revolution, and I think that if we harness this correctly, it’s an opportunity for the U.S. to reindustrialize, to upgrade its power grid, to bring back some manufacturing in these cutting-edge areas, which has been a priority of President Trump,” Sacks said.
Bob Mumgaard, CEO of Commonwealth Fusion Systems, discussed accelerating development timelines in physical technology sectors via video call. He emphasized that tools like large-scale computing, AI, and advanced materials allow for much faster progress than previously possible, and said that if AI companies are allowed to generate their own power, they can contribute excess electricity back to local residents and decrease electrical prices for residents.
He said his company is transitioning from completing a facility in Massachusetts to starting construction on its first commercial power plant in Virginia.
Virtual speaker Demis Hassabis, chairman and co-founder of Google DeepMind, said with the aid of AI tools like AlphaFold, the drug discovery process can be shortened from the span of years to months, and maybe even one day.
‘Hands of billions of people’: Mark Zuckerberg talk AI empowerment
Mark Zuckerberg, founder, chairman and CEO of Meta, joined virtually. He said his philosophy is made up of three principles: empowering individuals as a source of prosperity, using AI and superintelligence for invention — not automation — and having technology diffused into a system of checks and balances.
“We’re working on agents at Meta that we want to put in the hands of billions of people, where they just understand your goals and can work 24/7 on your behalf to help you achieve them,” Zuckerberg said.
The final virtual speaker of the day was Michael Crow, president of Arizona State University, who talked through how ASU is rethinking higher education to keep pace with rapid industrial transformation. He said that AI has been an “unbelievably empowering” force used to accelerate, enhance and deepen learning.
Day 2 of the G20 Innovation Ministerial will take place on Wednesday, and will include fireside chats with Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang at the Carolina Inn.
