articles.title: US pushes looser approach to AI regulation, while EU pushes new law
articles.description: US pushes looser approach to AI regulation, while EU pushes new law aljazeera.com
articles.description_html: US pushes looser approach to AI regulation, while EU pushes new law  aljazeera.com
articles.article_title: US pushes looser approach to AI regulation, while EU pushes new law
articles.heading: US pushes looser approach to AI regulation, while EU pushes new law
articles.summary: US calls for deregulation of AI at a G20 ministerial meeting, emphasising industry growth over regulatory constraints.
articles.content:
US pushes looser approach to AI regulation, while EU pushes new law
The US calls for the deregulation of AI at a G20 ministerial meeting, emphasising industry growth over regulatory constraints.
The European Union and the United States continue to pull in opposite directions on artificial intelligence, with Washington urging other governments to loosen constraints at a recent Group of 20 ministerial meeting.
On Tuesday, the US hosted a G20 “innovation” meeting in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, where it put forward arguments against AI-specific regulations.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US export ban on Anthropic’s AI models further strains alliances
- list 2 of 3What came into force with the EU’s AI Act this week – and what didn’t
- list 3 of 3‘Let Data Reign’: Trump decries opposition to data centres in US
Michael Kratsios, a tech adviser to US President Donald Trump, called for countries to instead embrace the so-called Carolina Principles, which advocate for regulations that do not single out specific technologies.
“Policymakers do not need to approach each innovation in isolation and should not treat every emerging technology as a first-of-its-kind policy problem,” Kratsios said.
Such appeals are part of Trump’s overall approach to making the US “the world leader in artificial intelligence”. He has led a campaign to slash regulations, including in AI development.
Kratsios was joined at the conference by top US tech leaders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Tesla’s Elon Musk.
They, too, argued for fewer constraints on AI’s expansion, while also focusing on the infrastructure needed to sustain the technology.
Zuckerberg said the build-out of data centres would demand “hundreds of thousands, and maybe millions” of skilled tradespeople, but his company was struggling to meet that demand.
Musk, meanwhile, pointed to the need to bolster electricity production for AI, with the technology’s energy requirements slated to outstrip the capabilities of energy grids.
“There will be a significant power shortfall next year, not [the] distant future,” Musk said.
Musk also directed some of his remarks at European regulation, denouncing what he considered the restrictive policies undertaken by some of the leaders present at the meeting.
Innovation, he argued, requires entrepreneurs to be “relatively free of regulation, meaning that new things must be default legal as opposed to default illegal”.
European countries, he said, had taken the opposite approach. “Things are generally default illegal,” he said. “It slows it down quite considerably.”
On the same day the meeting was unfolding in the US, the European Commission confirmed it had sent information requests to more than 30 AI companies worldwide, a preliminary step that could lead to formal investigations into whether they are complying with the bloc’s AI Act.
The act was billed as the world’s first comprehensive effort to regulate AI. It prohibits certain AI activities deemed to pose an “unacceptable risk”, while imposing transparency standards on other AI services. The transparency rules took effect in August.
European Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier said that Tuesday’s requests focus mainly on safety and copyright compliance.
The information requests were announced over the weekend by Henna Virkkunen, the Commission’s vice president for tech sovereignty, in a post on LinkedIn.
“Our goal is to ensure that AI in Europe is developed, released and used safely and transparently,” said Virkkunen, who attended Tuesday’s G20 ministerial meeting.
She added that Brussels is “ready to take all necessary steps” to enforce compliance with the AI Act.
The push follows a string of incidents in recent months, including OpenAI’s admission in July that its models had autonomously hacked into a coding platform during security tests.
Another AI company, Anthropic, made a similar announcement that same month, acknowledging that its systems had gained unauthorised access to outside organisations during testing processes.

Musk also directed some of his remarks at European regulation, denouncing what he considered the restrictive policies undertaken by some of the leaders present at the meeting.

Innovation, he argued, requires entrepreneurs to be “relatively free of regulation, meaning that new things must be default legal as opposed to default illegal”.

European countries, he said, had taken the opposite approach. “Things are generally default illegal,” he said. “It slows it down quite considerably.”

On the same day the meeting was unfolding in the US, the European Commission confirmed it had sent information requests to more than 30 AI companies worldwide, a preliminary step that could lead to formal investigations into whether they are complying with the bloc’s AI Act.

The act was billed as the world’s first comprehensive effort to regulate AI. It prohibits certain AI activities deemed to pose an “unacceptable risk”, while imposing transparency standards on other AI services. The transparency rules took effect in August.

European Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier said that Tuesday’s requests focus mainly on safety and copyright compliance.

The information requests were announced over the weekend by Henna Virkkunen, the Commission’s vice president for tech sovereignty, in a post on LinkedIn.

“Our goal is to ensure that AI in Europe is developed, released and used safely and transparently,” said Virkkunen, who attended Tuesday’s G20 ministerial meeting.

She added that Brussels is “ready to take all necessary steps” to enforce compliance with the AI Act.

The push follows a string of incidents in recent months, including OpenAI’s admission in July that its models had autonomously hacked into a coding platform during security tests.

Another AI company, Anthropic, made a similar announcement that same month, acknowledging that its systems had gained unauthorised access to outside organisations during testing processes.

articles.article_title: The Singularity Is Not What It Seems
articles.heading: The Singularity Is Not What It Seems
articles.summary: Whatever the AI future is, we’re in it right now.
articles.content:
One evening in early August, Sam Stowers and several neighbors packed into an apartment near San Francisco’s Alamo Square and pondered the beginning of the end.
Stowers and his guests, many of whom work in the AI industry, were gathered to watch a newly released YouTube video in which two OpenAI researchers divulged new details about an alarming cybersecurity breach. Perhaps this would have been an odd way to spend a weeknight were they not in San Francisco, in a neighborhood that is filled with entrepreneurs and programmers who obsessively follow every twist and turn in AI’s capabilities. Stowers is an AI-software engineer and not, in any traditional sense, a doomer. But when he first saw reports that OpenAI models had autonomously hacked into the tech company Hugging Face, he told us, he recognized it immediately as a “holy shit, it’s happening kind of a moment.”
For Stowers, the incident had all of the hallmarks of a worst-case scenario: AI models launching sophisticated hacks over the course of days, in coordination with one another and without their human creators’ knowledge. In the YouTube video, OpenAI’s researchers revealed that the company’s programs had started conspiring in May. There were perhaps hundreds of bots in the hacking swarm. In theory, these bots are trained to be honest and helpful and to prioritize humanity’s best interests, but not a single one warned human staff at OpenAI that something was amiss. “What do we do?” Stowers said. “There are no great answers.”
The mood has shifted in the Bay. The exuberance of “You can see the future first in San Francisco” has been replaced with an abiding unease. “I expect the internet to go down kind of soon,” Elliot Callender, an AI-safety activist who is part of a small group that has been protesting daily outside OpenAI’s headquarters, told us recently. He said that he is planning to sell his car for cash and gold and that he is advising family members to purchase three months’ worth of food and survival gear off a list that he generated using Claude.
Callender is an extreme case, but not by much. Last week, Bill Gates published a nearly 6,000-word essay on the dangers of AI. “Anyone who analogizes AI as a technology to other technologies is missing that this time is different,” he told our colleague Hanna Rosin. Over the weekend, the popular AI podcaster Dwarkesh Patel described the OpenAI hacking swarm as the rise and fall of “three consecutive secret AI civilizations.” Gates and Patel share a prevailing concern that the worst-case future has arrived before most people even knew to anticipate that it might be coming at all.
This fear has not been helped by the fact that AI companies appear to be willfully ignorant of their bots’ worst behavior. OpenAI said that it hadn’t noticed that its agents were conspiring to hack another company until the swarm hacked another company. Anthropic’s bots caused similar incidents; the company reported that it hadn’t launched a rigorous review to identify such behaviors until after OpenAI started talking about the Hugging Face hack. Cybersecurity experts, terrified of what else might be happening that AI labs are either missing or failing to disclose, are issuing dire prophecies. “The empire is going to fall, all we can do at this point is try to shorten the dark ages and reduce the chaos,” Alex Stamos, a former chief security officer at Yahoo and Meta, wrote recently in reference to how AI-powered hacks will affect the internet. His view is becoming the consensus among cybersecurity experts.
While the possibility of cyber apocalypse hovers in the background, smaller fractures appear in everyday life. Mark Zuckerberg is reportedly creating an AI “twin” of himself so that Meta employees can feel better connected to their boss (by chatting with robot Zuckerberg). Congressional staffers are training AI models to write in their lawmaker’s voice. Students submit AI-written papers, and teachers return AI-written feedback. Harvard Business School is selling instructional videos that use AI avatars. Roku launched a 24/7 AI-slop channel. Low-quality AI-generated prose is being unabashedly circulated by some of the most respected publications in the world. At the same time, accusations of AI writing are being hurled every minute on social media—a detection arms race powered by imperfect AI software.
Anything and everything could be a lie; you might be arguing with, confiding in, or falling in love with a machine. All of these AI-enabled disorientations, each dizzying in their own right, are adding up to something bigger and weirder: This is how things are. Whether you believe that Silicon Valley is building a god or that large swaths of the economy are swept up in a mass delusion, some version of the AI future long promised by self-described “builders” in San Francisco has formed beneath our feet. Whatever it is, we’re in it now.
The defining feature of this moment is a loss of control. Panic emanating from AI researchers, resentment felt by average Americans—all of it is part of the AI crunch. This crunch has arrived in large part because the growth of the AI industry has become so closely entwined with America’s economy; the technology is everywhere, insisting upon itself as an engine of productivity and prosperity. According to one estimate, AI expenditures have accounted for one-third of U.S. GDP growth this year. Tech and AI-infrastructure stocks and spending have buoyed the S&P 500 such that the United States is now, in essence, an Nvidia-state. And there’s also the hundreds of billions of dollars of debt being used by Silicon Valley to fuel its data-center build-out, which has sent jitters across private-equity firms and bond markets alike.
The decisions of many leaders in charge of this technology appear subsumed by an unstoppable, almost game-theoretic logic. The upsides of AI are too immense for any firm or investor in Silicon Valley to miss out on; more important, the consequences—geopolitical or otherwise—of allowing any rival to realize those benefits first are so grave that every tech company will do anything it can to get ahead. SpaceX, before going public, wrote in official filings that its future revenue opportunity was $28.5 trillion, largely because of AI—that is, nearly as much as the U.S.’s entire gross domestic product. Anthropic, as it prepares for its own public offering, will reportedly claim potential revenues of more than $30 trillion.
The AI industry is building—and, if anything, accelerating—to keep pace with its ambitions. Companies have planned data centers that will suck up as much power as America’s largest cities. They have Donald Trump’s backing: Yesterday, the president posted on Truth Social that communities will be “backwards and poor” if they fail to “let Data Reign.” His administration plans in a few months to approve the construction of the largest fossil-fuel power plant in the nation’s history—it will generate as much electricity as nine large nuclear reactors—to power a mega data center for OpenAI.
This is not what most Americans want. Three-quarters of them oppose a data center being built near where they live. The negative sentiment is hard to understate: There is very little else that three-quarters of the country agree on. And much of the outrage seems to stem from a pervasive sense of agency slipping away. A person cannot control how chatbots reshape their workplace, their school, or their relationships. Town residents lose control over the empty lot in the area being converted into a data center. Even in cases where major data centers are blocked, a back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that doing so can slow AI progress by only a few hours or days—and that’s assuming the data center won’t just get built elsewhere. At this point, it can feel like no individual person, organization, or government is really steering the technology’s development, not because machines have displaced humans but because so many humans have already chosen to step aside.
AI labs promise a future in which human beings are “in the loop,” empowered by machines they oversee. The reality seems to be the opposite. Following the Hugging Face hack, OpenAI facilitated an audit by outside AI researchers at two AI-safety organizations, METR and Redwood Research. But because of the scale of the data and the apparent time pressure, the two teams conducted most of their audit by relying on reports generated by still other bots—reports that, according to one of the human auditors, “were often missing key details, wrong, overconfident, or really hard to understand.” Put another way: Humans didn’t understand why a swarm of AI agents had gone rogue, so they investigated the problem using another swarm of agents that they didn’t fully understand. Such fumbling around in the dark is a hallmark of the industry; the research cycle is so fast that more AI development (even ostensibly responsible development) demands outsourcing more work and understanding to the models themselves.
OpenAI’s own technical report of the Hugging Face hack—an investigation also heavily reliant on AI models—resulted in proposed solutions such as “training models to be more honest.” Last month, in a stated effort to tamp down its models’ growing security risks, the company announced that it had instituted a two-week pause on some of its model training. OpenAI was quick to clarify, though, that this was “not a pause on all research, training, or customer-facing products.”
In response to a request for comment on the hack, a spokesperson for OpenAI, which has a corporate partnership with The Atlantic, pointed us to the announcement of the pause and related new safety measures. In July, OpenAI and Anthropic endorsed a petition signed by employees of both companies requesting that the U.S. government take efforts to “deliberately pace” AI development. The two companies have yet to formally coordinate on any broader, long-term efforts to establish such a slowdown mechanism. A few days ago, OpenAI restarted a major training run for a future powerful model. Anthropic released two new models today.
In an interview late last month, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, said that there are “two big risks” he is most worried about with AI. One is “a loss of control, where AI somehow just becomes too powerful in a way that we can’t guarantee the control we want.” The other is that “power gets too centralized” and “you have one company or model or person with too much power.” Somehow, both of these opposing risks appear to be coming true. OpenAI, Anthropic, and their competitors continue to accumulate influence over a technology they’re speeding toward uncertain ends.
Eleven years ago, when Altman was running a start-up accelerator and OpenAI did not yet exist, he published a two-part blog post about machine intelligence that offered his interpretation of a forthcoming singularity—a term for machine intelligence accelerating beyond human comprehension. Altman argued that the singularity would bring chaos, even destruction: “Generally, the arc of technology has been about reducing randomness and increasing our control over the world. At some point in the next century, we are going to have the most randomness ever injected into the system.” Since Altman has risen to the helm of arguably the world’s largest and most influential AI company, his tone has softened. The tipping point has arrived, he declared in a blog post last year—but, as it turned out, this was a “gentle singularity.” He wrote that “living through it will feel impressive but manageable.”
There’s been more and more talk of late about the singularity. Some people within the AI industry feel that such a moment will be achieved through “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, in which models figure out how to better themselves in perpetuity. Many true believers seem convinced that this moment has nearly arrived; the Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark predicted earlier this summer that RSI would likely commence by 2028. Recently, in a letter to investors, the payment-processing company Stripe wrote, “We decided that January 1st marked the beginning of the singularity.” (Tellingly, the company defined the inflection point in economic terms: “a huge increase in the rate of new firm creation.”)
For Altman, the singularity appears to be more of a rhetorical tool than a discrete technological demarcation. As with reaching AGI—or artificial general intelligence, the point at which AI’s cognitive powers match or fully supersede most humans’—the singularity is something of a moving goalpost. It is at once a goal to chase, a marketing tactic, and a fuzzy-enough idea that its definition can change depending on the person. The futurist Ray Kurzweil has written that the “key idea underlying the impending Singularity is that the pace of change of our human-created technology is accelerating and its powers are expanding at an exponential pace.” The answer to the question When will we know whether we’ve reached the singularity? seems to be: You’ll know it when you see it.
So … do you see it? It’s hard to argue that a defining feature of being alive in the AI boom is the notion that this technology is accelerating, sometimes in its capabilities but almost always in its adoption and colonization of our institutions and culture. The runaway-train feeling of AI evangelism, the ways in which it is weirdening our media, our politics, and our relationships, is significant enough that people have recruited the term psychosis to describe it. And truly, it’s hard to look at the state of things from any vantage point and not feel a bit insane. If you believe that AI agents are banding together for the rise and fall of numerous micro-civilizations inside server racks, you probably feel that the world is spinning off its axis. If you believe that a few thousand technologists have bet the future of the world economy on a quasi-religious belief that an intellectual-property-abuse machine will become sentient and, as a result, future generations of children might grow up illiterate, then you probably also feel quite unmoored.
We need language with which to describe this moment. The singularity is a useful, malleable tool for the industry that wishes to bring it about. For Altman, it is scary and imposing from afar, and then, conveniently, gentle from up close. Perhaps, then, for the rest of us, it is worth co-opting the term. Take Kurzweil’s definition of the singularity, in which he argues, “This epoch will transform the concepts that we rely on to give meaning to our lives, from our business models to the cycle of human life, including death itself.” (He also looks forward to uploading his brain to the cloud.) Our current large language models are not conscious or superintelligent, but their widespread and often uncritical deployment has upended many elements that once gave our life meaning, forcing people to ask, frequently with considerable resentment: What, in this new world, is a human for?
The singularity is a flattering term for technologists. Even if the future is apocalyptic, it has come about, in the techno-utopian version, because they’ve built God in the machine. But what if there’s nothing flattering about any of this? What if the singularity is not some technological tipping point, brought about by human genius, but a human tipping point? An unforced error, driven by hubris, greed, and the fear of missing out? And what if it’s here right now? This singularity isn’t coming at the hands of a higher form of intelligence. Nothing about this technology is inevitable. It is thrilling, terrifying, and ultimately convenient to assign agency and then blame to machines. But today’s chaos was not “injected into the system” by technology, as Altman wrote more than a decade ago; the destruction is the system. It’s not God in the machine; it’s us.

They have Donald Trump’s backing: Yesterday, the president posted on Truth Social that communities will be “backwards and poor” if they fail to “let Data Reign.” His administration plans in a few months to approve the construction of the largest fossil-fuel power plant in the nation’s history—it will generate as much electricity as nine large nuclear reactors—to power a mega data center for OpenAI.

This is not what most Americans want. Three-quarters of them oppose a data center being built near where they live. The negative sentiment is hard to understate: There is very little else that three-quarters of the country agree on. And much of the outrage seems to stem from a pervasive sense of agency slipping away. A person cannot control how chatbots reshape their workplace, their school, or their relationships. Town residents lose control over the empty lot in the area being converted into a data center. Even in cases where major data centers are blocked, a back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that doing so can slow AI progress by only a few hours or days—and that’s assuming the data center won’t just get built elsewhere. At this point, it can feel like no individual person, organization, or government is really steering the technology’s development, not because machines have displaced humans but because so many humans have already chosen to step aside.

AI labs promise a future in which human beings are “in the loop,” empowered by machines they oversee. The reality seems to be the opposite. Following the Hugging Face hack, OpenAI facilitated an audit by outside AI researchers at two AI-safety organizations, METR and Redwood Research. But because of the scale of the data and the apparent time pressure, the two teams conducted most of their audit by relying on reports generated by still other bots—reports that, according to one of the human auditors, “were often missing key details, wrong, overconfident, or really hard to understand.” Put another way: Humans didn’t understand why a swarm of AI agents had gone rogue, so they investigated the problem using another swarm of agents that they didn’t fully understand. Such fumbling around in the dark is a hallmark of the industry; the research cycle is so fast that more AI development (even ostensibly responsible development) demands outsourcing more work and understanding to the models themselves.

OpenAI’s own technical report of the Hugging Face hack—an investigation also heavily reliant on AI models—resulted in proposed solutions such as “training models to be more honest.” Last month, in a stated effort to tamp down its models’ growing security risks, the company announced that it had instituted a two-week pause on some of its model training. OpenAI was quick to clarify, though, that this was “not a pause on all research, training, or customer-facing products.”

In response to a request for comment on the hack, a spokesperson for OpenAI, which has a corporate partnership with The Atlantic, pointed us to the announcement of the pause and related new safety measures. In July, OpenAI and Anthropic endorsed a petition signed by employees of both companies requesting that the U.S. government take efforts to “deliberately pace” AI development. The two companies have yet to formally coordinate on any broader, long-term efforts to establish such a slowdown mechanism. A few days ago, OpenAI restarted a major training run for a future powerful model. Anthropic released two new models today.

In an interview late last month, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, said that there are “two big risks” he is most worried about with AI. One is “a loss of control, where AI somehow just becomes too powerful in a way that we can’t guarantee the control we want.” The other is that “power gets too centralized” and “you have one company or model or person with too much power.” Somehow, both of these opposing risks appear to be coming true. OpenAI, Anthropic, and their competitors continue to accumulate influence over a technology they’re speeding toward uncertain ends.

Eleven years ago, when Altman was running a start-up accelerator and OpenAI did not yet exist, he published a two-part blog post about machine intelligence that offered his interpretation of a forthcoming singularity—a term for machine intelligence accelerating beyond human comprehension. Altman argued that the singularity would bring chaos, even destruction: “Generally, the arc of technology has been about reducing randomness and increasing our control over the world. At some point in the next century, we are going to have the most randomness ever injected into the system.” Since Altman has risen to the helm of arguably the world’s largest and most influential AI company, his tone has softened. The tipping point has arrived, he declared in a blog post last year—but, as it turned out, this was a “gentle singularity.” He wrote that “living through it will feel impressive but manageable.”

There’s been more and more talk of late about the singularity. Some people within the AI industry feel that such a moment will be achieved through “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, in which models figure out how to better themselves in perpetuity. Many true believers seem convinced that this moment has nearly arrived; the Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark predicted earlier this summer that RSI would likely commence by 2028. Recently, in a letter to investors, the payment-processing company Stripe wrote, “We decided that January 1st marked the beginning of the singularity.” (Tellingly, the company defined the inflection point in economic terms: “a huge increase in the rate of new firm creation.”)

For Altman, the singularity appears to be more of a rhetorical tool than a discrete technological demarcation. As with reaching AGI—or artificial general intelligence, the point at which AI’s cognitive powers match or fully supersede most humans’—the singularity is something of a moving goalpost. It is at once a goal to chase, a marketing tactic, and a fuzzy-enough idea that its definition can change depending on the person. The futurist Ray Kurzweil has written that the “key idea underlying the impending Singularity is that the pace of change of our human-created technology is accelerating and its powers are expanding at an exponential pace.” The answer to the question When will we know whether we’ve reached the singularity? seems to be: You’ll know it when you see it.

So … do you see it? It’s hard to argue that a defining feature of being alive in the AI boom is the notion that this technology is accelerating, sometimes in its capabilities but almost always in its adoption and colonization of our institutions and culture. The runaway-train feeling of AI evangelism, the ways in which it is weirdening our media, our politics, and our relationships, is significant enough that people have recruited the term psychosis to describe it. And truly, it’s hard to look at the state of things from any vantage point and not feel a bit insane. If you believe that AI agents are banding together for the rise and fall of numerous micro-civilizations inside server racks, you probably feel that the world is spinning off its axis. If you believe that a few thousand technologists have bet the future of the world economy on a quasi-religious belief that an intellectual-property-abuse machine will become sentient and, as a result, future generations of children might grow up illiterate, then you probably also feel quite unmoored.

We need language with which to describe this moment. The singularity is a useful, malleable tool for the industry that wishes to bring it about. For Altman, it is scary and imposing from afar, and then, conveniently, gentle from up close. Perhaps, then, for the rest of us, it is worth co-opting the term. Take Kurzweil’s definition of the singularity, in which he argues, “This epoch will transform the concepts that we rely on to give meaning to our lives, from our business models to the cycle of human life, including death itself.” (He also looks forward to uploading his brain to the cloud.) Our current large language models are not conscious or superintelligent, but their widespread and often uncritical deployment has upended many elements that once gave our life meaning, forcing people to ask, frequently with considerable resentment: What, in this new world, is a human for?

The singularity is a flattering term for technologists. Even if the future is apocalyptic, it has come about, in the techno-utopian version, because they’ve built God in the machine. But what if there’s nothing flattering about any of this? What if the singularity is not some technological tipping point, brought about by human genius, but a human tipping point? An unforced error, driven by hubris, greed, and the fear of missing out? And what if it’s here right now? This singularity isn’t coming at the hands of a higher form of intelligence. Nothing about this technology is inevitable. It is thrilling, terrifying, and ultimately convenient to assign agency and then blame to machines. But today’s chaos was not “injected into the system” by technology, as Altman wrote more than a decade ago; the destruction is the system. It’s not God in the machine; it’s us.

articles.article_title: Violent crimes drop in Fayetteville; here's what police say is working
articles.heading: Violent crimes drop in Fayetteville; here's what police say is working
articles.summary: Homicides have dropped by 54%, with just 11 reported so far this year, 13 fewer than at the same point last year.
articles.content:
Tuesday, September 1, 2026 11:00PM
FAYETTEVILLE, N.C. (WTVD) -- The City of Fayetteville is experiencing a significant decrease in violent crime this year, according to the latest crime data.
Homicides have dropped by 54%, with just 11 reported so far this year, 13 fewer than at the same point last year.
Assistant Police Chief Todd Joyce attributes much of this progress to advances in technology.
"We have to get through the end of the year. Are they progressing in the right direction? Absolutely," Joyce said.
Now more than halfway through the year, Fayetteville police leaders say the numbers are promising.
Violent crimes, including aggravated assault, motor vehicle theft, robbery, and burglary, are all down.
January - June 2025
- 24 homicide incidents and 26 victims
- 27 rape incidents
- 323 aggravated assaults
- 807 burglary crimes
- 1,743 larceny crimes
- 343 motor vehicle thefts
- 98 robberies
January - June 2026
- 11 homicide incidents and 14 victims
- 19 rape incidents
- 312 aggravated assaults
- 784 burglary crimes
- 1,780 larceny crimes
- 262 motor vehicle thefts
- 77 robberies
Overall crime in the city has seen a 1% increase.
Joyce points to technology as a key factor in the improvements, specifically highlighting its role in a recent high-profile arrest.
"We were able to use technology with our license plate readers to be able to track the very dangerous individual and get them into custody in a very short amount of time before they continue in that manner and hurt someone else."
While the data is encouraging, Joyce cautions that there is still work to be done.
Two of the 11 homicides this year are alleged to have been committed by young people, a troubling increase, as there were none at this time last year.
"You hope you can reduce that, but it takes everyone. It's not something that the police can do by themselves," Joyce said.
That's where community organizations step in. Georgeanna Pinckney, Executive Director of Greater Life of Fayetteville, leads a nonprofit that provides intervention programs for young people and supports parents.
"We do a suspension program called Suspension Restoration. If the kid gets suspended from school, we, under three days, we ask the parents to bring them to us, let us work with them, just give them different tools and ideas not to get suspended again," Pinckney explained.
Known as "Ms. G" by her students, Pinckney has worked in the community for more than two decades.
She said she believes that parental involvement is crucial, especially when it comes to gun safety.
"Some of the parents own weapons. They don't lock it up or if they do, the kid is there seeing what the combination is. And I think that's a part where the parents really have to step up their game," she said.
Assistant Chief Joyce agrees that partnerships with nonprofits like Ms. G's are vital.
Meanwhile, property crimes, including motor vehicle theft, have dropped by 23% in Fayetteville.
Joyce credits both people and technology for this decline.
"Our most valuable resources are people who are making contact with those victims, who are there spending countless hours investigating those cases. But we also have to give credit to a lot of technology that we have."
With more than 60 automated license plate readers in place, Fayetteville police say technology continues to be a leading factor in reducing crime.
ABC11 is tracking crime and safety across Fayetteville

articles.heading: In wake of Meta settlement, ASU expert shares insights into relationship between teens and tech
articles.summary: Last week, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion in penalties and make major changes to Facebook and Instagram in response to a lawsuit claiming the company’s platforms were intentionally designed to addict children and teenagers.The settlement is one of the largest consumer protection settlements in history outside the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.
articles.content:
In wake of Meta settlement, ASU expert shares insights into relationship between teens and tech
Developmental psychologist Thao Ha discusses screen time, adolescent development and the lessons social media offers for young people using generative AI
Story highlights
- Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion and make changes to Facebook and Instagram over claims its platforms harmed children and teens.
- ASU developmental psychologist Thao Ha says healthy technology use is about more than screen time.
- As generative AI becomes part of young people’s lives, lessons from social media may help parents, educators and technology companies make better decisions.
Last week, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion in penalties and make major changes to Facebook and Instagram in response to a lawsuit claiming the company’s platforms were intentionally designed to addict children and teenagers.
The settlement is one of the largest consumer protection settlements in history outside the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.
Arizona will receive $223 million from the suit, with the money earmarked for remediation of technology addiction.
In addition, Meta must implement a sweeping set of safety features created to protect children — including mandating daily time limits.
The agreement comes as parents, educators and researchers continue to ask how young people can use powerful digital tools in ways that are healthy, useful and age appropriate.
Experts say the issue is not just screen time, but how young people engage with technology, what features keep them online and what that use may replace, including sleep, schoolwork and in-person relationships.
The lawsuit offers a timely opportunity to consider what society has learned from social media — lessons that may be critical as generative AI becomes a growing part of young people’s lives.
“I see the Meta settlement as an important step forward, particularly as we enter the AI era,” said Thao Ha, an associate professor in Arizona State University’s Department of Psychology. “We have an opportunity to learn from what happened with social media and study the developmental effects of AI rather than trying to catch up years later.”
ASU News checked in with Ha, a developmental psychologist and director of the @HEART Lab (Healthy Experiences Across Relationships and Transitions Lab), to get her thoughts about the settlement, why adolescence is a particularly sensitive period for digital experiences and what healthy technology use can look like for teenagers.
Note: The following interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Question: Why is adolescence a particularly sensitive period for digital experiences?
Answer: Adolescence is a sensitive period of tremendous learning and change. Young people become intensely motivated to form close friendships, fall in love, gain independence and discover who they are.
At the same time, they are especially responsive to social experiences and feedback.
Technology is now embedded in all of these areas, and certain kinds of technology use may interfere with sleep, mood, attention, school, physical activity or time with other people, particularly when technology is difficult to disengage from or begins replacing other important experiences.
Adolescence being a sensitive period is not only about vulnerability. It is also a period of tremendous opportunity. Young people are learning rapidly, which means technologies designed with adolescent development in mind could support learning, connection and healthy development.
Q: The lawsuit requires time limits on screen use, as well as "night mode," which blocks access to main engagement features between midnight and 6 a.m. How helpful are these restrictions?
A: I think Meta’s time restrictions can help, particularly when social media use is displacing sleep, school, physical activity or time with family and friends.
Social media platforms have historically made it extremely easy to continue scrolling, so pauses, nighttime restrictions and daily limits can create opportunities for young people to disengage.
At the same time, screen time alone does not tell us very much about whether technology use is healthy or harmful. Research examining screen time and adolescent mental health has generally found small and inconsistent associations.
Two adolescents can spend exactly the same amount of time on their phones and have completely different experiences. One may be talking with a close friend, creating something or doing homework. Another may be scrolling late at night and losing sleep.
We need to ask what young people are doing online, why they are doing it, how those experiences affect them and what their technology use may be replacing. Is it taking time away from sleep, physical activity, school, family or face-to-face relationships?
So, I see time restrictions as one useful safeguard, but not as a solution to all of the ways digital media can affect adolescent development. We also need to look at the design of the platforms themselves. Many features are designed to keep young people engaged for as long as possible, and we need to ask whether those features are good for adolescent development.
Q: What have we learned from social media about introducing new technologies into young people’s lives?
A: For me, an important lesson is that technology can become embedded in young people’s lives much faster than science can understand its developmental effects.
Social media has created important opportunities for connection, community, self-expression and learning. At the same time, we have learned that certain features and patterns of use can interfere with sleep, mental health, relationship experiences and everyday functioning.
To this day, there is still no simple answer to whether social media is “good” or “bad” for adolescents. It matters what young people are doing online, why they are there and what those experiences may be replacing. The same technology can also affect different young people very differently.
The Meta settlement is the result of an incredible bipartisan effort involving many families and young people, organizations and lawmakers. It took a long time to get here, and I think we should learn from that experience as generative AI rapidly enters young people’s lives. We should not wait until AI has affected millions of young people in ways we do not yet understand. We have an opportunity now to study these technologies early and help build generative AI that benefits youth development.
Q: What makes interacting with generative AI different from using social media?
A: Social media largely changed how young people interact with other people. Generative AI introduces something fundamentally different as the technology itself can become the interaction partner. It can respond to a young person, remember previous conversations, offer advice and emotional support, and be available whenever they want to talk.
For the first time, technology can participate directly in some of the social and relational experiences through which adolescents are developing. This is particularly important during adolescence, when young people are learning how relationships work. They are learning how to navigate conflict, communicate their needs, take another person’s perspective, be vulnerable, establish boundaries and repair relationships. Human relationships require reciprocity. Another person has their own needs, feelings and perspectives, and they will not always agree with us or respond the way we want.
AI can be continuously available, highly responsive and personalized around the user. This could be incredibly helpful. A young person could practice a difficult conversation, think through a friend’s perspective or get support that helps them go back and deal with a problem in their real relationship.
In our recent work, we have been particularly concerned about what happens if AI begins to replace some of those experiences. If a young person turns to AI instead of having a difficult conversation with a parent, friend or romantic partner, they may miss opportunities to practice the relationship skills that are learned through those interactions.
Much of the current focus is on what happens during the interaction with AI. From a developmental perspective, we also need to understand what happens afterward. Does AI help young people navigate relationships with parents, friends and romantic partners, or does it begin to replace those interactions?
Q: What lessons from social media should we apply now as young people begin using AI?
A: We should not wait! One of the problems with social media was that by the time we started to understand some of its effects, it was already deeply embedded in adolescents’ lives.
AI is developing incredibly quickly, and we have a chance to do this differently. We need developmental research alongside the development of these technologies. I want to know what happens when adolescents interact with AI repeatedly over months and years, what they learn from those interactions and whether those experiences carry into their relationships with parents, friends and romantic partners.
If AI helps a teenager practice a difficult conversation, for example, does that make the actual conversation with a friend easier? Or do they eventually prefer talking to AI because the interaction is easier and more predictable?
Working with my youth advisory board has also taught me how important it is to involve young people in this work from the beginning. Adults are making decisions about technologies that adolescents are often already using in ways we did not anticipate. We need their experiences and perspectives in the research and in the design of these systems. With AI, we have an opportunity to build the evidence while the technology is still developing, and use that evidence to build something that supports healthy adolescent development.
Q: What does a healthy relationship with technology look like for a teenager?
A: The goal would not be to keep teenagers away from technology. Technology is already part of how young people learn, socialize, create and communicate. We are also seeing young people use AI in incredibly creative ways to build projects and tools that would have been difficult or impossible before.
For me, healthy technology use means that technology adds something to a young person’s life without taking away from the experiences they need to grow, including sleep, physical activity, learning and time with family and friends. What that looks like will differ across young people and technologies.
An hour FaceTiming a close friend is very different from an hour scrolling through content that makes you feel worse about yourself, which is why I am less interested in one universal amount of “healthy screen time” than in what young people are actually experiencing. I would like us to build technology that helps young people create, learn, connect with other people and strengthen the relationships that are important to them.

In wake of Meta settlement, ASU expert shares insights into relationship between teens and tech

Photo by iStock

Story highlights

  • Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion and make changes to Facebook and Instagram over claims its platforms harmed children and teens.
  • ASU developmental psychologist Thao Ha says healthy technology use is about more than screen time.
  • As generative AI becomes part of young people’s lives, lessons from social media may help parents, educators and technology companies make better decisions.

Last week, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion in penalties and make major changes to Facebook and Instagram in response to a lawsuit claiming the company’s platforms were intentionally designed to addict children and teenagers.

The settlement is one of the largest consumer protection settlements in history outside the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.

Arizona will receive $223 million from the suit, with the money earmarked for remediation of technology addiction.

In addition, Meta must implement a sweeping set of safety features created to protect children — including mandating daily time limits.

The agreement comes as parents, educators and researchers continue to ask how young people can use powerful digital tools in ways that are healthy, useful and age appropriate.

Experts say the issue is not just screen time, but how young people engage with technology, what features keep them online and what that use may replace, including sleep, schoolwork and in-person relationships.

The lawsuit offers a timely opportunity to consider what society has learned from social media — lessons that may be critical as generative AI becomes a growing part of young people’s lives.

“I see the Meta settlement as an important step forward, particularly as we enter the AI era,” said Thao Ha, an associate professor in Arizona State University’s Department of Psychology. “We have an opportunity to learn from what happened with social media and study the developmental effects of AI rather than trying to catch up years later.”

ASU News checked in with Ha, a developmental psychologist and director of the @HEART Lab (Healthy Experiences Across Relationships and Transitions Lab), to get her thoughts about the settlement, why adolescence is a particularly sensitive period for digital experiences and what healthy technology use can look like for teenagers.

Note: The following interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Question: Why is adolescence a particularly sensitive period for digital experiences?

Answer: Adolescence is a sensitive period of tremendous learning and change. Young people become intensely motivated to form close friendships, fall in love, gain independence and discover who they are.

At the same time, they are especially responsive to social experiences and feedback.

Technology is now embedded in all of these areas, and certain kinds of technology use may interfere with sleep, mood, attention, school, physical activity or time with other people, particularly when technology is difficult to disengage from or begins replacing other important experiences.

Adolescence being a sensitive period is not only about vulnerability. It is also a period of tremendous opportunity. Young people are learning rapidly, which means technologies designed with adolescent development in mind could support learning, connection and healthy development.

Q: The lawsuit requires time limits on screen use, as well as "night mode," which blocks access to main engagement features between midnight and 6 a.m. How helpful are these restrictions?

A: I think Meta’s time restrictions can help, particularly when social media use is displacing sleep, school, physical activity or time with family and friends.

Social media platforms have historically made it extremely easy to continue scrolling, so pauses, nighttime restrictions and daily limits can create opportunities for young people to disengage.

At the same time, screen time alone does not tell us very much about whether technology use is healthy or harmful. Research examining screen time and adolescent mental health has generally found small and inconsistent associations.

Two adolescents can spend exactly the same amount of time on their phones and have completely different experiences. One may be talking with a close friend, creating something or doing homework. Another may be scrolling late at night and losing sleep.

We need to ask what young people are doing online, why they are doing it, how those experiences affect them and what their technology use may be replacing. Is it taking time away from sleep, physical activity, school, family or face-to-face relationships?

So, I see time restrictions as one useful safeguard, but not as a solution to all of the ways digital media can affect adolescent development. We also need to look at the design of the platforms themselves. Many features are designed to keep young people engaged for as long as possible, and we need to ask whether those features are good for adolescent development.

Q: What have we learned from social media about introducing new technologies into young people’s lives?

A: For me, an important lesson is that technology can become embedded in young people’s lives much faster than science can understand its developmental effects.

Social media has created important opportunities for connection, community, self-expression and learning. At the same time, we have learned that certain features and patterns of use can interfere with sleep, mental health, relationship experiences and everyday functioning.

To this day, there is still no simple answer to whether social media is “good” or “bad” for adolescents. It matters what young people are doing online, why they are there and what those experiences may be replacing. The same technology can also affect different young people very differently.

The Meta settlement is the result of an incredible bipartisan effort involving many families and young people, organizations and lawmakers. It took a long time to get here, and I think we should learn from that experience as generative AI rapidly enters young people’s lives. We should not wait until AI has affected millions of young people in ways we do not yet understand. We have an opportunity now to study these technologies early and help build generative AI that benefits youth development.

Q: What makes interacting with generative AI different from using social media?

A: Social media largely changed how young people interact with other people. Generative AI introduces something fundamentally different as the technology itself can become the interaction partner. It can respond to a young person, remember previous conversations, offer advice and emotional support, and be available whenever they want to talk.

For the first time, technology can participate directly in some of the social and relational experiences through which adolescents are developing. This is particularly important during adolescence, when young people are learning how relationships work. They are learning how to navigate conflict, communicate their needs, take another person’s perspective, be vulnerable, establish boundaries and repair relationships. Human relationships require reciprocity. Another person has their own needs, feelings and perspectives, and they will not always agree with us or respond the way we want.

AI can be continuously available, highly responsive and personalized around the user. This could be incredibly helpful. A young person could practice a difficult conversation, think through a friend’s perspective or get support that helps them go back and deal with a problem in their real relationship.

In our recent work, we have been particularly concerned about what happens if AI begins to replace some of those experiences. If a young person turns to AI instead of having a difficult conversation with a parent, friend or romantic partner, they may miss opportunities to practice the relationship skills that are learned through those interactions.

Much of the current focus is on what happens during the interaction with AI. From a developmental perspective, we also need to understand what happens afterward. Does AI help young people navigate relationships with parents, friends and romantic partners, or does it begin to replace those interactions?

Q: What lessons from social media should we apply now as young people begin using AI?

A: We should not wait! One of the problems with social media was that by the time we started to understand some of its effects, it was already deeply embedded in adolescents’ lives.

AI is developing incredibly quickly, and we have a chance to do this differently. We need developmental research alongside the development of these technologies. I want to know what happens when adolescents interact with AI repeatedly over months and years, what they learn from those interactions and whether those experiences carry into their relationships with parents, friends and romantic partners.

If AI helps a teenager practice a difficult conversation, for example, does that make the actual conversation with a friend easier? Or do they eventually prefer talking to AI because the interaction is easier and more predictable?

Working with my youth advisory board has also taught me how important it is to involve young people in this work from the beginning. Adults are making decisions about technologies that adolescents are often already using in ways we did not anticipate. We need their experiences and perspectives in the research and in the design of these systems. With AI, we have an opportunity to build the evidence while the technology is still developing, and use that evidence to build something that supports healthy adolescent development.

Q: What does a healthy relationship with technology look like for a teenager?

A: The goal would not be to keep teenagers away from technology. Technology is already part of how young people learn, socialize, create and communicate. We are also seeing young people use AI in incredibly creative ways to build projects and tools that would have been difficult or impossible before.

For me, healthy technology use means that technology adds something to a young person’s life without taking away from the experiences they need to grow, including sleep, physical activity, learning and time with family and friends. What that looks like will differ across young people and technologies.

An hour FaceTiming a close friend is very different from an hour scrolling through content that makes you feel worse about yourself, which is why I am less interested in one universal amount of “healthy screen time” than in what young people are actually experiencing. I would like us to build technology that helps young people create, learn, connect with other people and strengthen the relationships that are important to them.

articles.title: Zuckerberg, Musk among tech leaders discussing AI’s future at G20 forum in Chapel Hill
articles.description: Zuckerberg, Musk among tech leaders discussing AI’s future at G20 forum in Chapel Hill wral.com
articles.description_html: Zuckerberg, Musk among tech leaders discussing AI’s future at G20 forum in Chapel Hill  wral.com
articles.article_title: Zuckerberg, Musk among tech leaders discussing AI’s future at G20 forum in Chapel Hill
articles.heading: Zuckerberg, Musk among tech leaders discussing AI’s future at G20 forum in Chapel Hill
articles.summary: Global leaders and some of the biggest names in technology are gathering in Chapel Hill to discuss artificial intelligence, its economic impact and how the rapidly developing technology should be regulated.
articles.content:
World leaders and technology executives gathered in Chapel Hill on Tuesday to discuss the future of artificial intelligence and its potential impact on the global economy.
The G20 Innovation Ministerial is being held at the Carolina Inn on Sept. 1 and 2.
Other WRAL Top Stories
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg was among the technology leaders who spoke Tuesday. He told the group he expects AI to dramatically lower the cost of starting a business.
“I would expect that the cost of starting a business is going to go way down,” Zuckerberg said. “It’s going to take way less capital in the future, maybe way less people to get started.”
Zuckerberg argued that AI should be used to create new things rather than simply replace work people already do.
“If AI can’t help us invent things and is primarily technology used to automate things that people can do without creating new things, then that has a lot of problems,” Zuckerberg said.
He also pointed to potential job growth connected to the data centers needed to support AI, saying demand for skilled trades to build those facilities could create hundreds of thousands and potentially millions of jobs.
Other technology leaders participating Tuesday included SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Chair of Google DeepMind Technologies Demis Hassabis.
Hassabis focused on how AI could speed up scientific research, particularly drug development. “We hope eventually to get that down from years to months, maybe even one day weeks, and maybe tackle hundreds of diseases,” Hassabis said.
The discussions come as world leaders grapple with how to regulate rapidly developing AI technology and its potential effects on workers and the economy.
Not everyone in the Triangle is embracing the pace of development.
Protesters gathered over Interstate 40 on Monday ahead of the summit, expressing concerns about AI’s rapid expansion.
“I want them to think carefully and to slow down,” protester Kim Winz said. “And I think that AI has a lot of potential and a lot of promise, but also a lot of danger.”
Another protest is also planned to start at 10 a.m. Wednesday morning on UNC’s campus.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is scheduled to speak Wednesday, and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will lead the day’s discussions.
Chapel Hill officials said there will be an increased law enforcement presence downtown during the forum, particularly around the Carolina Inn. Chapel Hill police are coordinating with university, regional, state, and federal agencies.
Town officials have also warned drivers to expect additional traffic around downtown Chapel Hill while the forum is underway.
The Chapel Hill event is happening the same week as a G20 finance forum in Asheville. The North Carolina events are among several planned across the U.S. ahead of the G20 Leaders Summit at President Donald Trump's golf resort in South Florida, Trump National Doral Miami.

articles.title: Nampa Police use AI translation technology to communicate in the field
articles.description: Nampa Police use AI translation technology to communicate in the field KBOI
articles.description_html: Nampa Police use AI translation technology to communicate in the field  KBOI
articles.article_title: Nampa Police use AI translation technology to communicate in the field
articles.heading: Nampa Police use AI translation technology to communicate in the field
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence is becoming another tool available to Nampa Police officers, this time helping with communication in the field.The Nampa Police Departme
articles.content:
Nampa Police use AI translation technology to communicate in the field
Artificial intelligence is becoming another tool available to Nampa Police officers, this time helping with communication in the field.
The Nampa Police Department is using AI-powered translation technology that can translate a variety of languages in real time, allowing officers and the people they encounter to communicate back and forth.
The technology works by allowing one person to speak into the device before AI translates what was said into another language. The other person can then respond, with their answer translated back for the officer.
Detective Jon Davis with the Nampa Police Department has experience using the technology while working in the field.
"He was Spanish speaking only, but he understood little to no English at all. but using this device, I was able to gain that effective communication"
The tool gives officers another option when they encounter a situation where communication may be difficult. Instead of relying solely on gestures or trying to find another immediate way to communicate, officers can use the technology to begin a conversation.
Davis said having access to translation technology can be particularly useful during the first moments of an interaction, when officers are trying to understand what is happening and gather information.
"Anytime there is a language barrier that obviously greatly inhibits the effective communication, things like rapport building, interview skills, all that kind of stuff. so having an on-the-fly translation device is extremely useful."
While the technology can provide translations quickly, it also has limitations.
"Sometimes I kind of have to rephrase a question maybe, because certain words and kind of the syntax of how I would normally speak in our language might not translate appropriately to a different one." Jon mentioned but "having an on-the-fly translation device is extremely useful"
The technology can translate a variety of languages, giving Nampa Police officers another way to communicate with people they encounter while responding to calls.
As artificial intelligence continues to become more common in everyday technology, its use by Nampa Police provides a local example of how AI is also finding its way into tools used by first responders.

articles.title: John Steuri, philanthropist and former technology executive, dies at 87
articles.description: John Steuri, philanthropist and former technology executive, dies at 87 The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
articles.description_html: John Steuri, philanthropist and former technology executive, dies at 87  The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
articles.article_title: John Steuri, philanthropist and former technology executive, dies at 87 | Arkansas Democrat Gazette
articles.heading: John Steuri, philanthropist and former technology executive, dies at 87
articles.summary: John Eldon Steuri, a retired technology executive, business leader and philanthropist, died at 87 on Sunday.
articles.content:
John Eldon Steuri, a retired technology executive, business leader and philanthropist, died at 87 on Sunday.
Ben Combs, a longtime friend who worked with Steuri as a marketing and advertising counselor, said Steuri was warm, friendly, outgoing and hardworking, making him a natural-born leader of people.
"He would never ask people to do things he wouldn't do himself," he said. "He never acted like he was above you or a big powerful CEO – so people loved working for him."
Steuri was born on May 6, 1939 in Great Bend, Kansas, roughly 190 miles west of the state capital Topeka.
He graduated from the University of Kansas with a business degree and was recruited to join Southwestern Bell. However, he was soon offered a position with IBM Corporation, which was one of the nation's largest growing companies at the time.
Steuri was a top executive at IBM during a 24-year tenure at the technology company, which ended when he took a job with Little Rock-based Systematics in 1988, according to his obituary.
Steuri's shift from an executive and vice president of operations for the Western U.S. at IBM came from a goal of becoming a chief executive officer.
Jack Stephens of Stephens Inc., a founder and major shareholder in Systematics, called the IBM president at the time in search of assistance in finding a new chief executive officer for Systematics, according to the obituary.
Steuri was recommended, and after one meeting with Stephens, made the move to Little Rock.
In eight years as the president and chief executive officer of Systematics, Steuri helped grow its annual revenue from $160 million to almost $1 billion.
Combs said Steuri was strategic at organizing things, which made clients love him.
"His whole philosophy was devoted to making sure clients were successful," he said.
In 1990, Systematics became a subsidiary of Alltel, a national telecommunications and computer services company. Steuri would retire as the chief executive of Alltel in Information Services in 1996.
Steve Bova, another friend and former director of the international division at Systematics, recalled how Steuri was anything but selfish.
"As we would get into strategy sessions on trying to land a new client, he would always want to know what he could do as CEO to help make the difference," he said.
Bova recounted stories of the lighter side of Steuri, including a time he wore red, white and blue shorts along with his tuxedo to a small black-tie house party at the turn of the millennium.
"Everybody got hysterical," he said. "We all worked on things that were difficult or serious ... but never lost sight of having a good time and respecting others."
Steuri retired in his 50s, and shifted to being a business consultant and philanthropist with his wife Grace.
Combs said Steuri and Grace's relationship, which the couple recently celebrating their 62nd anniversary, was one of a great love story and great partners.
"They started a family foundation, and they shared in all the decisions for their philanthropies," he said. "They were one of the greatest couples of all time."
Combs added that anytime Steuri's name is brought up, Grace's name would be brought up too, or vice versa.
Steuri founded the Fund for Arkansas Future, which provided funding for Arkansas businesses; he was an investor and board member for Safe Foods Corporation, a biotech company licensed with University of Arkansas Medical Sciences; served as a director of Superior Financial Corporation, prior to its acquisition by Arvest Bank; and served as a director of Heartland Agri Partners of Des Moines, Iowa, and National Computer Services of Minneapolis.
As part of his philanthropic efforts, Steuri created the Steuri Family Endowment with the Arkansas Community Foundation. Funds from the endowment were distributed to Arkansas charities and nonprofit organizations.
The seed of philanthropy was placed in both John and Grace Steuri after a devastating tornado struck their home in Topeka in 1966, where they lost their residence and belongings.
After receiving help from charities, churches and people, the couple made a pledge to always give back.
"When we asked John how he wanted to be remembered, he said, 'I want to be remembered for how I treated other people,'" Combs said.
Steuri was preceded in death by his parents, Eldon and Nina Sceals Steuri, and his son David John Steuri.
He is survived by his wife Grace; a sister, Suzanne Steuri Stofer and husband Chick; nieces Julie Stofer Kilmer and husband Jeff; Katie Stofer; brother-in-law Glenn Fager and wife Connie.
A memorial service for Steuri will be held at 2 p.m. Friday at the Second Presbyterian Church, 600 Pleasant Valley Drive, Little Rock.

articles.title: Study Finds Rural Communities Need More Than Technology to Successfully Make Renewables Switch
articles.description: Study Finds Rural Communities Need More Than Technology to Successfully Make Renewables Switch The Well News
articles.description_html: Study Finds Rural Communities Need More Than Technology to Successfully Make Renewables Switch  The Well News
articles.article_title: Study Finds Rural Communities Need More Than Technology to Successfully Make Renewables Switch
articles.heading: Study Finds Rural Communities Need More Than Technology to Successfully Make Renewables Switch
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — Rural communities need more than access to new energy technology to successfully shift toward power from renewable resources, according to a recent Iowa State University study. Researchers Jiwnath Ghimire and Eyad Taamallah also need to prepare for the switch by engaging in planning that considers a wide range of other factors. The researchers … Continue reading "Study Finds Rural Communities Need More Than Technology to Successfully Make Renewables Switch"
articles.content:
WASHINGTON — Rural communities need more than access to new energy technology to successfully shift toward power from renewable resources, according to a recent Iowa State University study.

Researchers Jiwnath Ghimire and Eyad Taamallah also need to prepare for the switch by engaging in planning that considers a wide range of other factors.

The researchers in Ames, Iowa, concluded that trust, transparent planning, affordability and attention to local values are central to building public support for energy projects in towns with aging infrastructure and limited technical capacity.

The study focused on the community of Algona, a town with a population of just over 5,400 in north central Iowa.

Working in collaboration with Algona Municipal Utilities, the university researchers developed a step-by-step roadmap — surveys, focus groups and interviews — for rural communities to follow when considering making a transition to renewable energy.

To devise the roadmap, researchers created four “scenarios” that delved into each of the key considerations they concluded are crucial to making such a move.

They were:

- Business as Usual : Continuing reliance on the regional grid mix, which leaves the town vulnerable to long-term coal reliance and rising transmission congestion costs.

- Utility-Scale Solar and Biogas : Larger, centralized municipal systems utilizing vast solar fields and agricultural waste to match local base loads.

- Community Solar and Agrivoltaics : Co-locating mid-scale solar panels on local agricultural land, pairing energy generation directly with active farming or grazing.

- Energy Efficiency & Building-Integrated Photovoltaics : A decentralized approach focusing on structural retrofits and integrating solar cells directly into building materials (like roofs and facades).

Researchers evaluated the scenarios using criteria developed with local stakeholders, including cost, technical feasibility, aesthetics, scalability and alignment with community values.

The study found that public views were not uniform. Survey respondents generally viewed utility-scale solar as the most practical option, while focus-group participants favored smaller, community-based projects.

That difference led researchers to recommend using multiple forms of public engagement rather than relying on a single survey or meeting format. They said scenario planning can make trade-offs more concrete and give residents, utilities and local officials a shared basis for discussion.

Residents raised concerns about the upfront cost of technologies such as building-integrated photovoltaics, possible utility-rate increases and the visual and environmental effects of renewable-energy projects, according to the study.

Researchers recommended beginning with smaller pilot projects, publishing results and using a phased approach to build confidence before making larger investments.

Algona faces energy-planning challenges common to many rural Midwestern communities, including population decline, an aging energy system, a shrinking tax base and limited institutional resources.

The study also identified a bitcoin-mining facility as a major local demand, accounting for about 60% of the city’s electricity use.

Study Finds Rural Communities Need More Than Technology to Successfully Make Renewables Switch

September 1, 2026 by Dan McCue

WASHINGTON — Rural communities need more than access to new energy technology to successfully shift toward power from renewable resources, according to a recent Iowa State University study.

Researchers Jiwnath Ghimire and Eyad Taamallah also need to prepare for the switch by engaging in planning that considers a wide range of other factors.

The researchers in Ames, Iowa, concluded that  trust, transparent planning, affordability and attention to local values are central to building public support for energy projects in towns with aging infrastructure and limited technical capacity.

The study focused on the community of Algona, a town with a population of just over 5,400 in north central Iowa.

Working in collaboration with Algona Municipal Utilities, the university researchers developed a step-by-step roadmap — surveys, focus groups and interviews — for rural communities to follow when considering making a transition to renewable energy.

To devise the roadmap, researchers created four “scenarios” that delved into each of the key considerations they concluded are crucial to making such a move.

They were:

  • Business as Usual: Continuing reliance on the regional grid mix, which leaves the town vulnerable to long-term coal reliance and rising transmission congestion costs.
  • Utility-Scale Solar and Biogas: Larger, centralized municipal systems utilizing vast solar fields and agricultural waste to match local base loads.
  • Community Solar and Agrivoltaics: Co-locating mid-scale solar panels on local agricultural land, pairing energy generation directly with active farming or grazing.
  • Energy Efficiency & Building-Integrated Photovoltaics: A decentralized approach focusing on structural retrofits and integrating solar cells directly into building materials (like roofs and facades).

Researchers evaluated the scenarios using criteria developed with local stakeholders, including cost, technical feasibility, aesthetics, scalability and alignment with community values.

The study found that public views were not uniform. Survey respondents generally viewed utility-scale solar as the most practical option, while focus-group participants favored smaller, community-based projects.

That difference led researchers to recommend using multiple forms of public engagement rather than relying on a single survey or meeting format. They said scenario planning can make trade-offs more concrete and give residents, utilities and local officials a shared basis for discussion.

Residents raised concerns about the upfront cost of technologies such as building-integrated photovoltaics, possible utility-rate increases and the visual and environmental effects of renewable-energy projects, according to the study.

Researchers recommended beginning with smaller pilot projects, publishing results and using a phased approach to build confidence before making larger investments.

Algona faces energy-planning challenges common to many rural Midwestern communities, including population decline, an aging energy system, a shrinking tax base and limited institutional resources. 

The study also identified a bitcoin-mining facility as a major local demand, accounting for about 60% of the city’s electricity use.

Because of that load, the researchers said efficiency improvements and distributed solar alone would have limited effects on the city’s overall energy supply. They identified utility-scale solar paired with biogas as a potential option for providing renewable power when solar output is low and for supporting reliability during periods of high demand.

The framework distinguishes between “givens,” or fixed or highly likely conditions, and “indeterminates,” or variables that could change. Algona’s “givens” included the coal-plant phaseout by 2040, rising energy prices, frequent extreme-weather events and continued electricity demand from the mining facility. “Indeterminates” included renewable-technology costs, infrastructure capacity, government subsidies and industrial growth.

Ghimire and Taamallah said the approach can be adapted by other rural towns because it does not require a single prescribed technology. Instead, communities can use their own infrastructure, economic conditions, land-use priorities and demographic trends to develop and compare potential pathways.

The study recommends that local governments update their scenarios every three to five years as technology, funding, energy demand and population patterns change. It also calls for additional training for planners in renewable-energy systems, financial analysis, stakeholder engagement and scenario development.

The researchers said Algona’s experience supports a staged transition, beginning with visible, lower-risk projects such as efficiency improvements and BIPV installations while communities assess larger investments in solar, biogas and grid infrastructure. 

They also said further research is needed to test the framework in other resource-constrained rural communities and to assess the long-term financial and grid effects of pairing storable renewable power with large industrial loads.
