articles.content:
BORGER, Texas — OmniTRAX has introduced a new technology on a Texas short line that monitors dark territory for train presence, broken rails, and track temperatures 24 hours a day.
The Advanced Rail Condition Detector and TrueTemp Link, from Athena Industrial Services, have been deployed on the Panhandle Northern Railroad, a 31-mile former Santa Fe line between Borger and Panhandle, Texas.
“The Panhandle’s wide-ranging winter and summer temperatures pose serious environment challenges that require 24/7 attention to maintain operational integrity,” Sergio Sabatini, OmniTRAX president and chief operating officer, said in a press release. “Athena’s cutting-edge safety technology provides critical rail monitoring in the Texas Panhandle’s extreme temperatures. articles.heading: How AI plotted an interstellar journey to Alpha Centauri
articles.summary: The Fermi Explorer Mission plans to launch a spacecraft to our nearest star by the end of 2029, using a trajectory discovered by AI.
articles.content:
How AI plotted an interstellar journey to Alpha Centauri
The Fermi Explorer Mission plans to launch a spacecraft to our nearest star by the end of 2029, using a trajectory discovered by AI.
A nonprofit organization called the Fermi Explorer Mission announced today that it intends to launch a spacecraft to our nearest star system by the end of 2029.
It’s a hugely ambitious mission—if all goes well, the spacecraft could take up to 80,000 years to arrive at Alpha Centauri, which is 4.4 light-years away. And the spacecraft will follow a novel trajectory discovered by an AI system developed by Physical Superintelligence (PSI), an AI physics research lab. PSI is launching today with $58 million in funding led by Breakthrough Energy, a climate-focused investment group founded by Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates.
It’s not the first time this has been tried. In 2016, the billionaire tech investor Yuri Milner announced an interstellar mission called Breakthrough Starshot to launch humanity’s first spacecraft to Alpha Centauri. The plan was to use powerful lasers that would propel tiny probes to a fifth of the speed of light—fast enough to reach Alpha Centauri within 20 years. Milner pledged $100 million toward a proof of concept. But a decade later, nothing has launched.
“We didn’t want to do another Breakthrough Starshot,” says Philip Johnston, the cofounder and president of the Fermi Explorer Mission. “We’re dead set on something actually launching.” The new mission, currently funded by individual private donors, is expected to cost just $15 million.
To stick to that budget, “we are not constraining ourselves to doing it in a human lifetime,” says Johnston. “Let’s just figure out the way to get to another star.”
The spacecraft will carry cargo weighing at least one kilogram. That will include artistic and scientific payloads, messages, and a copy of the Golden Record, a gold-plated disc of Earth’s sounds and images that NASA attached to its two Voyager probes in 1977 as a message to any civilization that might find them.
Engineering an interstellar journey is extremely difficult. Alpha Centauri is about 25 trillion miles away from Earth. One of the fastest objects that humans have ever launched, the Voyager 1 probe, has been flying since 1977 and has covered less than 1% percent of that distance. At its speed, the trip would take more than 70,000 years.
Johnston and his team spent a year trying, and failing, to find a way for a small, solar-powered spacecraft costing only $15 million to reach Alpha Centauri. They kept running into the knotty problem of how to give the spacecraft enough power without making it too heavy (and thus more fuel-guzzling).
After the Fermi team struggled to find a workable route, Johnston mentioned the problem in a podcast hosted by Alex Wissner-Gross, a physicist who cofounded PSI. Wissner-Gross offered to run it through an AI system the lab developed, called Get Physics Done. It’s open-source software that takes a physics research question, breaks it into smaller tasks, and decides which simulations to run, using AI models including Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s GPT.
A week later, the AI system turned up a novel trajectory, to Johnston’s surprise. It combined well-known orbital maneuvers in a way the Fermi team had not considered, according to a paper that has not been peer-reviewed. It suggested that the spacecraft could first slow down so its orbit swings in close to the sun—closer than Mercury. On each close pass, it would fire its engine so that the solar panels get four times the light, and a burst of thrust delivered at high speed would buy more energy than the same burst anywhere else. Because the engine would run only near the sun, the solar panels could stay small and the spacecraft light.
The system conducted the research mostly on its own for three days, running on a billion tokens, says Matt Pines, the cofounder and CEO of PSI. An astrophysicist on PSI’s staff steered it to follow the mission’s requirements, asked for a cost analysis and clearer charts, and checked the output for errors.
“The fact that it came up with an entirely different mission profile, one that was creative and not one [the Fermi team] had considered—that was the more surprising aspect,” says Pines. Still, the model lacks a human researcher’s judgment and taste, he says. It has no reliable sense of which problems are interesting or which approaches are worth pursuing, so it often gets stuck chasing dead ends or failing to explore different approaches. “I don’t think we’ve yet figured out how these models can internally represent something like that,” he says of research judgment.
Even if the Fermi probe launches, “we’re pretty confident that we will not be the first to arrive” at Alpha Centauri, says Johnston, since he expects spacecraft technology to improve. If an engine a thousand years from now is even 20% faster than today’s, a spacecraft launched then would still beat Fermi’s probe to Alpha Centauri by more than 10,000 years.
But the Fermi project isn’t just an interstellar mission driven by engineering ambition. It’s also a quest to answer one of the oldest open questions in physics. In 1950, the physicist Enrico Fermi posed a puzzle: The galaxy has hundreds of billions of stars, most of them far older than our sun. Even a civilization traveling slowly between stars could spread across the whole galaxy in a few million years, which pales in comparison to how old the galaxy is. If there is intelligent life somewhere, we should have seen signs of its existence by now.
That means either reaching for another star is too difficult or other intelligent species simply haven’t bothered. But once the Fermi probe launches, we will become a civilization that can and wants to reach another star, meaning that neither explanation might be what’s keeping the galaxy unexplored. That could point us toward more unsettling possibilities, says Johnston. Maybe life like ours is almost unimaginably rare. Or maybe intelligent life is common but tends to die out before it can spread.
If the latter is true, “one of those reasons could be that once you hit superintelligence, that for some reason is self-destructive,” says Johnston. “Maybe in the next 50 years, there’s some great filter that we do not pass through. That all intelligent civilizations, for some reason, do not pass through.”

articles.heading: New Joint Incubator Backs Founders Building Dual-Use Technologies
articles.summary: Six companies founded by University of California San Diego students, faculty and alumni have been selected for the inaugural cohort of a new joint summer incubator from the UC San Diego Office of Innovation and Commercialization (OIC) and Bow Capital.
articles.content:
New Joint Incubator Backs Founders Building Dual-Use Technologies
Each selected team received $100,000 in investment funding to participate in a three-month sprint supporting technologies with defense, government, and commercial applications.
Published Date
Article Content
Six companies founded by University of California San Diego students, faculty and alumni have been selected for the inaugural cohort of a new joint summer incubator from the UC San Diego Office of Innovation and Commercialization (OIC) and Bow Capital, an early stage venture capital firm anchored by the University of California.
Launched in June, the incubator is tailored to founders developing dual-use technologies that can serve both national security and commercial markets, spanning sectors including defense, robotics, autonomy, space, digital biology and critical infrastructure. Each selected team receives $100,000 in upfront funding and participates in a three-month, full-time, in-person program at the Design and Innovation Building.
“UC San Diego is committed to building talent, partnerships and pathways needed to advance dual-use technologies,” said Paul Roben, associate vice chancellor of innovation and commercialization at UC San Diego. “By leveraging the strengths of our university and the San Diego region, we can build a national powerhouse for dual-use innovation while preparing the next generation of talent to contribute to it.”
The incubator further strengthens an existing ecosystem supporting dual-use innovation, drawing on Horizon, OIC’s accelerator program; FORGE, a dual-use national security innovation initiative anchored by Innovating for National Security (i4NS), a nationally ranked STEM workforce development program focused on experiential learning; and Accelerating Innovations to Market (AIM), a market-driven technology accelerator. Alongside Bow Capital, these programs provide founders with mentorship, strategic guidance, customer introductions and access to investors, operators and government partners as they work to advance their technologies toward commercialization.
“Many of the world's most important technologies begin in research labs but never make it into the hands of those who need it most,” said Andre Ranadivé, partner at Bow Capital and Army veteran. “Through our partnership with the OIC team, we're building a dual-use technology incubator that helps bridge that gap, connecting breakthrough science with both commercial markets and national security needs.”
This intersection of university resources and Bow Capital’s broader network gives these founders a unique combination of technical, business and industry support beyond capital alone.
“Founders need more than capital to move research and deep science-backed innovations to deployment — they need direct lines to operators, prime contractors and the government customers who validate how technologies perform in the field,” said Shane Moise, director of Horizon Accelerator, which facilitated the program’s creation. “Together, we built this program with FORGE and i4NS to strengthen national security and translational pieces founders can't access on their own. This cohort is the proof point.”
Stifel Bank also sponsored the program, setting up startup bank accounts for all six founders. DLA Piper, through Horizon board member Lisa Haile, PhD, provided legal expertise to help founders establish their companies, cap tables and other foundational documents for long-term growth.
“What’s exciting about this dual-use cohort is watching small, fast-moving teams take on problems once reserved for the largest prime contractors,” said Senior Vice President Sam Wogan of Stifel Venture Banking. “These founders are turning frontier science into real-world capabilities. Stifel Bank is proud to support Bow Capital and UC San Diego as they give these founders the resources to make that leap."
Meet the Cohort
The teams were selected from a competitive applicant pool based on technical depth and originality, team capability and speed of execution, and alignment with dual-use and national security priorities. Their technologies range from medical devices and advanced materials to artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, reflecting the breadth of translational research emerging from across the university.
ReBlood RX
Founders: Carlos Munoz, PhD and Christopher Caballero
ReBlood RX is creating a shelf-stable hemoglobin-based oxygen carrier designed to deliver oxygen when donor blood is unavailable.
Netra
Founders: Pranay Yalamanchali, William Stobaugh, Tanay Karumanchi and Landon Stobaugh
Netra is building an adaptable, distributed counter-unmanned aircraft system detection platform that combines radio frequency, acoustic and optical sensing into a self-healing mesh network.
Evaporion
Founders: Renkun Chen, PhD, Shengqiang Cai, PhD, Tony Tong, PhD and Raja Annapooranan, PhD
Evaporion has developed a breakthrough cooling technology, inspired by how sweat cools skin, that removes heat 10 times faster than today's liquid cooling while using a fraction of the energy. It's built for the world's most heat-intensive electronics — power inverters, defense systems, and AI chips — cutting energy costs and unlocking compute power that heat currently leaves on the table.
Valanor
Founders: Alex Battikha and Nicolas Dos Santos
Winner of the hardware track at the Bow Capital defense technology hackathon, Valanor builds integrated site security systems for airports, theme parks and stadium venues, pairing its software with ground robots and NDAA-compliant drones. Its platform unifies every camera, sensor, and robot in one dashboard, correlates alarms into a single incident, and lets an operator dispatch a robot or drone to verify, with every event logged and audit-ready.
AMRADTECH, Inc.
Founders: Alan Hirales, PhD candidate, and Jenna Hirales, PhD candidate
AMRADTECH is expanding radiation detection beyond the few large, costly installations that leave gaps at borders, ports, and critical infrastructure. Its networked detection architecture delivers persistent, real-time, distributed monitoring at a size, weight, power, and cost point conventional systems cannot reach.
Tessera Ceramics
Founders: Kent Griffith, PhD and Elena Sjoblom
Tessera Ceramics is engineering hierarchically stabilized, rare-earth-free advanced ceramics for extreme-temperature and high-stress environments, including jet engines, thermal barrier coatings, and ceramic matrix composites.
Together, the six companies reflect different paths for translating research into technologies with potential across the defense sector and beyond. The program meets them at different points along that path, from developing early-stage technologies to advancing products toward commercialization.
“This incubator catalyzed the commercialization of the advanced ceramic technologies developed in my materials chemistry laboratory,” said Founder Kent J. Griffith of Tessera Ceramics and assistant professor of Chemistry at UC San Diego. “The cumulative resources and connections have been immensely helpful in guiding the early stages of our journey.”
At Evaporion, founder and Jacobs School of Engineering faculty member Renkun Chen, PhD, is already seeing that support shape the company’s next steps.
“The funding, resources and mentorship are helping us accelerate our R&D, prototype development and customer discovery,” said Chen. “The Bow Capital team has advised us on technical development and business strategy while connecting us with potential partners, and UC San Diego's Horizon team has introduced us to potential customers, investors and other partnership opportunities. The support and connections we've gained through this program are helping us advance our technology toward commercialization.”
For Ranadivé, the program’s larger promise lies in what these companies can become beyond the incubator.
“Our ambition is to help build the next generation of enduring dual-use companies that strengthen American innovation, enhance our national security, and ensure the United States continues to be the world's technology leader,” added Ranadivé. “We're incredibly grateful to UC San Diego for being such an outstanding partner, and we're excited to see what this exceptional cohort accomplishes."
As the inaugural cohort moves beyond the incubator, the founders will keep developing their technologies and building relationships with the customers and partners who can take them to the next stage.

As the inaugural cohort moves beyond the incubator, the founders will keep developing their technologies and building relationships with the customers and partners who can take them to the next stage.

articles.article_title: IEEE President’s Note: Technology for Social Good
articles.heading: IEEE President’s Note: Technology for Social Good
articles.summary: IEEE humanitarian tech programs help improve lives worldwide
articles.content:
Across IEEE, our strength lies not only in the excellence of our individual communities but also in our ability to bring them together around shared problems that demand interdisciplinary solutions. Our mission as a public charity—to advance technology for the benefit of humanity—is becoming an increasingly powerful differentiator. It is more than a statement of principle; it is a strategic advantage. When engineers and technologists serve with purpose and lead with heart, they strengthen the future of our profession and demonstrate why IEEE is uniquely positioned to lead at the intersection of technology and societal impact.
IEEE Humanitarian Technologies is a consortium of programs and initiatives—supported by a global network of volunteers and technical professionals—working together to apply technology to solve the world’s most pressing problems. These include Empower a Billion Lives, EPICSinIEEE, MOVE, IEEE REACH, IEEE SIGHT, IEEE Smart Village, and IEEE Tech4Good. These programs embody our mission in action. They are not simply charitable activities; they are strategic assets that help IEEE lead globally, innovate boldly, and remain essential to technical professionals at every stage of their careers. While deeply human in purpose, humanitarian technologies are fundamentally engineering challenges, demanding the full depth of engineering rigor and realized through disciplined, deeply technical work.
Cultivating Technical Leaders
IEEE Humanitarian Technologies sits at the intersection of engineering excellence, societal need, and global opportunity. Its programs allow our members to show the world that engineering and technology are forces for good, capable of addressing urgent challenges with precision, creativity, and compassion. These programs do more than inspire; they strengthen the technical ecosystem that underpins IEEE’s leadership.
Bringing together experts from power and energy, communications, computing, robotics, biomedical engineering, and many other domains to address real-world problems, these interdisciplinary intersections are where breakthroughs emerge. When engineers and technologists collaborate with the right humanitarian frameworks across sectors and cultures, they illuminate new constraints, design pathways, and opportunities that traditional project environments rarely reveal. This is how humanitarian technologies help shape the future of engineering itself.
These efforts also illustrate a broader opportunity for IEEE. By identifying critical challenges that can be addressed only through collaboration across disciplines, IEEE can mobilize the power of its global community toward solving problems around the world. In doing so, we strengthen both our impact on society and the value we provide to members, partners, and future generations.
These programs also build the leadership capacity our profession needs. Engineers working in humanitarian contexts learn to navigate ambiguity, engage diverse stakeholders, manage constraints, and design for environments where failure has real human consequences. They develop systems thinking, ethical reasoning, and cross‑cultural fluency—competencies increasingly essential in a world where technology and society are deeply intertwined. They also learn to transition from R&D to implementation by engineering the support, manufacturing, and delivery systems that make solutions viable in specific countries, all while balancing competing requirements. In doing so, humanitarian programs equip professionals with the capabilities that define modern technical practice.
Humanitarian technologies also help prepare the future technical workforce. Students and young professionals increasingly seek meaningful, high‑impact work. By engaging in purpose‑driven projects, they can discover their own capacity to grow, strengthen their technical skills, and become the leaders and problem‑solvers who will guide our profession forward.
Purpose Inspires Engagement
Our members feel this deeply. Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining the organization and renewing their membership. Those with higher membership grades identify “participation in humanitarian technology efforts” as one of the most satisfying experiences IEEE offers. These are not just data points; they are also signals of what our community values and what it expects IEEE to champion.
Younger generations amplify this even more. Millennials view IEEE through a global lens, prioritizing “humanitarian impact” and “large-scale collaboration.” One millennial member shared that teaching robotics to children in under-resourced communities transformed them into a deeply engaged member. Gen Z members emphasize inclusivity, environmental responsibility, and purpose-driven engineering, recommending that IEEE offer humanitarian-based challenges and competitions to increase engagement.
These findings reveal something powerful: Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful; they also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact. They also create loyalty and develop the leadership pipeline IEEE needs for the decades ahead.
These programs also strengthen our brand. Members across segments describe IEEE as an organization that works hard to make real changes in the world. That perception is not just flattering, it is strategic. It positions IEEE as a global leader in responsible innovation that can be trusted to guide technology for the public good, catalyzing innovation that benefits society at scale.
As we look ahead, IEEE has an opportunity to become the world’s leading convening force for developing interdisciplinary technology solutions to solve humanity’s most important challenges. Our future relevance will be defined not only by the technologies we advance but also by the problems we choose to help solve.
Read more powerful stories about how technology is improving lives across global initiatives in the 2025 IEEE Social Impact Report at ieee.org/advancing-technology/building-better-world/social-impact-report.
—MARY ELLEN RANDALL
IEEE president and CEO
Please share your thoughts with me: president@ieee.org.

articles.title: Draft bill would provide more help to school districts for school technology
articles.description: Draft bill would provide more help to school districts for school technology WyomingNews.com
articles.description_html: Draft bill would provide more help to school districts for school technology  WyomingNews.com
articles.article_title: Draft bill would provide more help to school districts for school technology
articles.heading: Draft bill would provide more help to school districts for school technology
authors: Hector Martinez The Sheridan Press Via Wyoming News Exchange
articles.summary: SHERIDAN — A Wyoming Legislature bill draft would help provide additional funds to school districts for technology.
articles.content:
SHERIDAN — A Wyoming Legislature bill draft would help provide additional funds to school districts for technology.
The Wyoming school funding model currently funds school districts $250 per average daily membership for school technology. ADM accounts for the average number of students enrolled in a school or district each day during the academic year.
An increasing or decreasing trend of ADM can impact a school district in a variety of ways, primarily in revenue, according to previous reporting from the Sheridan Press.
Larry Picus, a school finance consultant for Picus, Odden and Associates, recommended a computer ratio of 1:3 for students in grades kindergarten through fifth and 1:1 in grades 6-12 and $398 per ADM.
Albany County School District 1 Chief Information and Cybersecurity Officer Shawn Hime said ACSD1 serves approximately 4,000 students and 800 employees. Its information technology staff consists of 10 employees managing about 2,250 devices.
As the Wyoming Legislature's Committee on School Finance Recalibration considers technology during recalibration, Hime said he encourages the legislators to keep one distinction in mind: the number of computers a district owns is not the same cost as operating its technology environment.
Hime said certainly student and staff devices are part of the cost, but behind those devices are costs such as networks and wireless infrastructure; cyber security; identity and account management; filtering and student safety systems; student information and learning management systems.
“There’s been some consideration of modifying the 1:1 model. I would caution against that. We’ve seen a clear operational benefit from maintaining a 1:1 student device model. When a Chromebook is assigned to an individual, that student has clear responsibility for the device and we maintain a complete history associated with that specific asset,” Hime said. “That accountability has helped us reduce device breakage because students are more likely to take care of equipment they know is assigned directly to them.”
Last year ACSD1 spent more than $25,000 on Chromebook repair and replacement. Hime said the school district has seen a 25% reduction in device damage over the last year because of its 1:1 ratio.
After hearing testimony, committee members voted to sponsor a draft bill that includes $395 per ADM for technology. The draft bill also includes minimums for staffing at districts for a 1.0 full-time equivalent tech director and a .5 student information system clerk.
While there was not an exact ratio specified in the drafting instructions, Sheridan County School District 1 Business Manager Jeremy Smith said in a text message to The Sheridan Press the $395 per ADM won’t get a school district 1:1 for K-12, but it provides the flexibility needed.
The next meeting will be Oct. 21-22 at 8:30 a.m. in Casper.

articles.title: A Message from Chief Sizemore Regarding ALPR Technology
articles.description: A Message from Chief Sizemore Regarding ALPR Technology Cape Coral Police Department
articles.description_html: A Message from Chief Sizemore Regarding ALPR Technology  Cape Coral Police Department
articles.article_title: A Message from Chief Sizemore Regarding ALPR Technology - Cape Coral Cops
articles.heading: A Message from Chief Sizemore Regarding ALPR Technology
articles.summary: (September 1, 2026) —For more than a decade, the Cape Coral Police Department has responsibly utilized Automated License Plate Reader […]
articles.content:
(September 1, 2026) —For more than a decade, the Cape Coral Police Department has responsibly utilized Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) technology as one of many tools available to our officers and investigators.
During that time, ALPR technology has helped us solve countless crimes and develop investigative leads that otherwise may not have existed. It has played a role in multiple homicide investigations, helping us identify and apprehend violent offenders who are now serving life sentences in prison.
It has helped us locate stolen vehicles, identify suspects, find missing people, and ultimately hold criminals accountable.
It is a tool. Nothing more—and nothing less.
It doesn’t replace good police work. It makes good police work more effective.
I also recognize that there are legitimate questions surrounding ALPR technology, including privacy, data retention, access, sharing, and accountability. Those questions deserve thoughtful answers and appropriate safeguards.
At the Cape Coral Police Department, we have spent more than a decade developing policies and practices designed to ensure this technology is used responsibly, and in a manner consistent with the constitutional rights of the people we serve.
But the environment in Florida has changed.
Our Governor has made his position on ALPR technology clear: He supports law enforcement and its mission, but wants the Legislature to establish safeguards and guardrails by drafting state law governing the use of this technology.
The Florida Department of Transportation has taken actions affecting the use of this technology on state roadways. At the same time, there remains a lack of clear and consistent statewide statutory guidance establishing the rules under which law enforcement agencies should operate.
I don’t believe local law enforcement should be left to navigate that uncertainty on its own.
For that reason, I have made the decision to discontinue the use of ALPR technology by the Cape Coral Police Department.
This is not because I believe the technology is inherently bad.
It is not because I believe it has been abused here.
And it certainly isn’t because I believe we should abandon a tool that has proven itself over and over again in solving crime and protecting our community.
I’m doing it because I believe the time has come for our elected officials in Tallahassee to establish a clear legal framework for the responsible use of this technology.
Give law enforcement the guardrails.
Establish the standards.
Define the accountability.
Protect individual constitutional rights.
Then let us do our jobs.
At some point, we have to stop asking local law enforcement agencies to navigate this issue in a vacuum. If the state believes this technology requires additional safeguards—and I believe reasonable safeguards are appropriate—then it is time for the Legislature to establish them.
That is what legislatures do. They establish the law. Law enforcement leaders then operate within that framework.
I don’t believe it serves Floridians to have a patchwork of policies and prohibitions developed independently by individual municipalities, often without the benefit of the operational experience necessary to understand how this technology is actually used.
Decisions about the operational use of law enforcement technology are best made by the law enforcement professionals responsible for public safety, within a clear legal framework established by the State Legislature.
I took an oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States, and I take that oath seriously. I would never implement a program, policy, or technology that runs afoul of that oath or the constitutional rights it protects.
Every sworn member of the Cape Coral Police Department takes that same oath.
And every officer who takes that oath in our department is administered that oath personally by me.
That matters.
Technology doesn’t change our obligation to the Constitution. It also doesn’t change our responsibility to protect the people we serve. And it doesn’t give us permission to compromise either.
So for now, we will step back.
We will wait for our lawmakers to establish the framework.
And when that framework is in place, we will evaluate it carefully and determine how—and whether—ALPR technology can be responsibly returned to service.
I remain hopeful that it will be.
Because I believe we can protect individual rights and give law enforcement the tools necessary to protect our communities.
We don’t have to choose between public safety and constitutional rights.
We have an obligation to protect both.
For more than ten years, we have demonstrated that ALPR technology can be used as a responsible law enforcement tool while respecting those principles.
I am confident that our policymakers will recognize that, establish the appropriate framework, and allow professional law enforcement leaders to do what we have been entrusted to do.
Protect our communities. Solve crime. Save lives. And uphold the Constitution.
That’s the job. And that’s what we’ll continue to do.
–Chief Anthony Sizemore, Cape Coral Police Department

articles.title: John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO after 15 years
articles.description: John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO after 15 years Al Jazeera

articles.article_title: John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO after 15 years
articles.heading: John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO after 15 years
articles.summary: Apple gears up for innovation under Ternus before a new product launch event that could include foldable phones.
articles.content:
John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO after 15 years
Apple gears up for innovation under Ternus before a new product launch event that could include foldable phones.
John Ternus has officially taken over as the chief executive officer of Apple, succeeding Tim Cook, who ended a 15-year tenure leading the tech giant.
Ternus, who took the helm on Tuesday, had been serving as the senior vice president for hardware engineering at the Cupertino, California-based company since 2021.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Apple regains top spot as world’s most valuable company
- list 2 of 4US stocks near record high, oil falls as Trump claims Iran talks under way
- list 3 of 4Telegram says Apple suspension followed content norms violation by one user
- list 4 of 4Google Maps renames Lake Ontario after Trump’s decree on ‘Lake America’
When Apple announced the transition in April, the company said that Cook will move into the role of executive chairman.
Ternus is an old hand at the company. He joined Apple’s product design team in 2001 and climbed the ranks. He was appointed vice president of hardware engineering in 2013 and was promoted in 2021 to the senior vice president role that he has now moved up from.
A graduate of the University of Pennsylvania, Ternus had previously worked on virtual reality headsets at a company called Virtual Research Systems.
Since joining Apple, Ternus has overseen the launch of a range of its most well-known product lines, including the iPad and AirPods.
Given Ternus’s background in hardware engineering, analysts saw his appointment as a sign that the company, best known for its iPhone, is pushing to double down on innovation across its device portfolio.
“The appointment of Ternus is Apple’s subtle way of [doubling down] on hardware innovation as a core strategy. It doesn’t refute the Tim Cook era; it marks a new stage in Apple’s history by intertwining AI with hardware, rather than treating AI as a standalone product,” Babak Hafezi, professor of international business at American University, told Al Jazeera.
Ternus’s task
Ternus is set to hit the ground running in the new role. On September 9, Apple is expected to unveil its latest iPhone as well as a foldable device, a new product in its lineup. The foldable phone market, although still niche, is a growing segment of the consumer phone sector that is currently dominated by Samsung, which launched it in 2019.
Analysts forecast that Apple will make headway quickly. Apple is expected to ship 17 million foldable iPhones and reach 40 percent of the market share by the end of next year, according to IDC research, a tech intelligence firm.
Apple is also slated to launch a new version of Siri, its personal assistant, with the newest version of its iOS software planned for release this month. It is intended to be more conversational and provide more personalised content for individual users, including scanning personal emails and text messages.
In a news statement announcing the new feature, the company used the example of using Siri “to find a restaurant recommendation a friend messaged them about, surface a hotel confirmation number from an old email”.
Ternus comes into his new role at a time that Apple has been criticised for a slower rollout in the generative AI space, falling behind companies like OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and Anthropic, the maker of Claude.
However, Aleksandar Tomic, associate dean for strategy, innovation, and technology at Boston College, argues that focusing on its core products could help Apple lead the AI boom in the long run.
“To use a metaphor, there were people during the gold rush mining for gold, and then there were those selling the picks and shovels for the prospectors. Apple has really stayed in the picks-and-shovels lane,” Tomic said.
“They have not done any kind of data centre, industrial-grade chips, but they have developed their own chips that they put into the Macs and MacBook Pros that allow people to run local LLMs [Large Language Models] and so on. The iPhone becomes kind of an AI access engine.”
In June, analysts at Morgan Stanley expressed concern that Apple may struggle with an AI Siri rollout because its older phones lack the capability to run advanced AI features.
This comes as Apple also faces supply chain strains. In June, the company raised the price on some MacBooks and iPads as the cost of computer memory increased due to AI companies driving up demand for chips and servers.
It also has to walk a tightrope between Washington, DC’s trade war with China, where it has a huge market and major supply chain, even as it has attempted in the last few years to diversify some of that to India and Vietnam. Apple has announced plans to invest billions of dollars in the US, and President Donald Trump wants the company to make its iPhones there.
For investors, Cook is a tough act to follow. Under his leadership, the company’s stock jumped 2,258 percent. Apple’s stock has grown steadily over the last year, too. It is up more than 37 percent since this time last year, and more than 16 percent since the beginning of 2026.
On Tuesday, the company’s stock rose by 2.2 percent in midday trading as Ternus took over his new role.

When Apple announced the transition in April, the company said that Cook will move into the role of executive chairman.

Ternus is an old hand at the company. He joined Apple’s product design team in 2001 and climbed the ranks. He was appointed vice president of hardware engineering in 2013 and was promoted in 2021 to the senior vice president role that he has now moved up from.

A graduate of the University of Pennsylvania, Ternus had previously worked on virtual reality headsets at a company called Virtual Research Systems.

Since joining Apple, Ternus has overseen the launch of a range of its most well-known product lines, including the iPad and AirPods.

Given Ternus’s background in hardware engineering, analysts saw his appointment as a sign that the company, best known for its iPhone, is pushing to double down on innovation across its device portfolio.

“The appointment of Ternus is Apple’s subtle way of [doubling down] on hardware innovation as a core strategy. It doesn’t refute the Tim Cook era; it marks a new stage in Apple’s history by intertwining AI with hardware, rather than treating AI as a standalone product,” Babak Hafezi, professor of international business at American University, told Al Jazeera.

Ternus’s task

Ternus is set to hit the ground running in the new role. On September 9, Apple is expected to unveil its latest iPhone as well as a foldable device, a new product in its lineup. The foldable phone market, although still niche, is a growing segment of the consumer phone sector that is currently dominated by Samsung, which launched it in 2019.

Analysts forecast that Apple will make headway quickly. Apple is expected to ship 17 million foldable iPhones and reach 40 percent of the market share by the end of next year, according to IDC research, a tech intelligence firm.

Apple is also slated to launch a new version of Siri, its personal assistant, with the newest version of its iOS software planned for release this month. It is intended to be more conversational and provide more personalised content for individual users, including scanning personal emails and text messages.

In a news statement announcing the new feature, the company used the example of using Siri “to find a restaurant recommendation a friend messaged them about, surface a hotel confirmation number from an old email”.

Ternus comes into his new role at a time that Apple has been criticised for a slower rollout in the generative AI space, falling behind companies like OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and Anthropic, the maker of Claude.

However, Aleksandar Tomic, associate dean for strategy, innovation, and technology at Boston College, argues that focusing on its core products could help Apple lead the AI boom in the long run.

“To use a metaphor, there were people during the gold rush mining for gold, and then there were those selling the picks and shovels for the prospectors. Apple has really stayed in the picks-and-shovels lane,” Tomic said.

“They have not done any kind of data centre, industrial-grade chips, but they have developed their own chips that they put into the Macs and MacBook Pros that allow people to run local LLMs [Large Language Models] and so on. The iPhone becomes kind of an AI access engine.”

In June, analysts at Morgan Stanley expressed concern that Apple may struggle with an AI Siri rollout because its older phones lack the capability to run advanced AI features.

This comes as Apple also faces supply chain strains. In June, the company raised the price on some MacBooks and iPads as the cost of computer memory increased due to AI companies driving up demand for chips and servers.

It also has to walk a tightrope between Washington, DC’s trade war with China, where it has a huge market and major supply chain, even as it has attempted in the last few years to diversify some of that to India and Vietnam. Apple has announced plans to invest billions of dollars in the US, and President Donald Trump wants the company to make its iPhones there.

For investors, Cook is a tough act to follow. Under his leadership, the company’s stock jumped 2,258 percent. Apple’s stock has grown steadily over the last year, too. It is up more than 37 percent since this time last year, and more than 16 percent since the beginning of 2026.

On Tuesday, the company’s stock rose by 2.2 percent in midday trading as Ternus took over his new role.

articles.article_title: Juno Propulsion wins $1.2M grant from NSF to advance non-toxic space propulsion system
articles.heading: Juno Propulsion wins $1.2M grant from NSF to advance non-toxic space propulsion system
articles.summary: The National Science Foundation has awarded a $1.2 million grant to Juno Propulsion to support work on a non-toxic space propulsion system.
articles.content:
The National Science Foundation has awarded a $1.2 million grant to Tukwila, Wash.-based Juno Propulsion to support the startup’s development of a non-toxic propulsion system for in-space applications.
The two-year Phase II project, funded through NSF’s Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program, will be conducted in partnership with the University of Washington and UW Professor Carl Knowlen’s lab. The focus of the funding is to support work on Juno’s Product Development Unit (PDU), which uses rotating detonation rocket engine technology.
By combining high-efficiency propulsion with non-toxic propellants, Juno aims to enable spacecraft to maneuver farther and faster while reducing the risks associated with traditional toxic propellants. Work on the PDU is intended to advance Juno’s system to Technology Readiness Level 8, positioning it near production-ready status on the standard 1-to-9 TRL scale.
“This award represents an important milestone in taking our rotating detonation propulsion technology from development and flight demonstration toward a production-ready product,” Juno Propulsion CEO Alexis Harroun said in a news release. “We’re excited to continue our collaboration with the University of Washington and Professor Knowlen’s lab as we take the next step toward delivering this technology to commercial and government customers.”
The Phase II grant, announced last week, follows up on a $275,000 Phase I SBIR grant that was awarded in 2024.
Juno Propulsion’s team is getting ready for Project Iris, an on-orbit demonstration of its propulsion technology that’s due to fly aboard Momentus’ Vigoride 8 satellite platform in 2027. The lessons learned from Project Iris will feed directly into work on the PDU.
The startup was founded in 2023 by Harroun and chief technology officer Ari Martinez, who met while earning their Ph.D.s at Purdue University. Harroun received her undergraduate degree in aeronautics and astronautics from UW and interned at Blue Origin, Boeing and NASA before heading to Purdue.
In June, Juno Propulsion announced the close of a $1.4 million pre-seed financing round, led by SOSV with participation from Hypernova Fund, Leslie Ventures, Activate, Collaborative Fund, Safar Partners and Cape Fear Ventures.

articles.title: Feature Article: Biometrics at the Border—Making Exit Secure and Efficient
articles.description: Feature Article: Biometrics at the Border—Making Exit Secure and Efficient Homeland Security (.gov)
articles.description_html: Feature Article: Biometrics at the Border—Making Exit Secure and Efficient  Homeland Security (.gov)
articles.article_title: Feature Article: Biometrics at the Border—Making Exit Secure and Efficient | Homeland Security
articles.heading: Feature Article: Biometrics at the Border—Making Exit Secure and Efficient
articles.summary: S&T recently brought industry partners to the Progreso International Bridge border crossing in Texas to demonstrate facial biometric capabilities for U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
articles.content:
The Science and Technology Directorate (S&T) recently brought industry partners to the Progreso International Bridge border crossing in Texas to demonstrate facial biometric capabilities for U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP). The effort supports S&T’s priority to help secure U.S. borders by identifying, testing, and transitioning technologies that strengthen security while facilitating efficient lawful travel. Hear from S&T, CBP, and our partners about this successful real-world test of secure, easy-to-use biometric technologies and how they capture essential data as pedestrians exit the country.
S&T has once again shown that strong technical expertise, trusted partnerships, technological precision, and sound science can operate at full throttle while delivering operational success across the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Each of these elements is equally important when supporting agencies like CBP, especially when assessing mission-critical technologies before they are selected for deployment.
“In October 2025, CBP approached S&T with a request for solutions that could securely, efficiently, and accurately confirm the departure of pedestrians exiting the U.S. at border crossings using biometrics,” said Arun Vemury, S&T Senior Advisor for Biometrics and Identity. “To meet long-standing legislative requirements and Administration priorities, S&T facilitated the technology demonstration to support CBP in testing cutting-edge technologies to efficiently perform its mission.”
CBP turned to S&T and its knowledge of the facial biometrics landscape to quickly assess the current state of the market and identify emerging technologies that could meet CBP’s specific needs and high standards for secure border operations.
To support the request, S&T coordinated with federal and industry partners through Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs). The goal was to provide analysis to support CBP’s near-term planning and broader border security objectives. By leveraging the CRADAs, S&T enabled the industry partners to work quickly, cover their own costs, and provide the greatest value for informed governmental decision-making.
In early 2026, S&T invited six companies to the Maryland Test Facility (MdTF) for basic capability demonstrations to determine which solutions should be operationally tested. These demonstrations led CBP and S&T to select three solutions for additional data collection: two from NEC National Security Systems (NSS) and one joint solution from Paravision and AiFi.
Before deployment, S&T built a replica of the pedestrian exit environment at MdTF so vendors could install and assess their prototypes before taking them to the Progreso border crossing. This helped reduce risk by identifying issues in a controlled environment before testing in an active border environment.
When the industry partners arrived at the Progreso International Bridge in May, they began setting up for the operational assessment that would support CBP’s planning.
For the testing to be successful, the technologies had to account for human factors such as travelers’ walking pace, as well as hats, sunglasses, umbrellas and other items people use or carry. Collecting usable facial images outdoors during the day and at night, at speed and scale, is challenging given the many variables.
The partners leveraged artificial intelligence (AI) and other technologies to perform tasks such as constructing a 3D digital environment of the image capture zone, observing pedestrian movement, and analyzing facial images to determine whether they were suitable for biometric matching in CBP’s Traveler Verification Service.
The industry partners installed their products in various configurations. Some cameras were mounted on poles at different heights to account for individuals of different statures.
Because ports of entry operate day and night, tests were also conducted after dark using external lighting configurations. S&T evaluated how lighting affected facial image collection using various camera alignments.
As pedestrians approached the border exits, signs in English and Spanish informed them that U.S. citizens could opt out of biometric exit collection if they did not wish to have their picture taken, since the biometric Entry/Exit mandate applies to non-U.S. citizen travelers.
“It is one thing for a technology to work in a lab like MdTF, but it is significantly more difficult when the tech is deployed operationally at the border. At Progreso, it had to work with limited infrastructure, in a challenging environment, and do it autonomously,” said Dr. Cameron Whitelam, director of S&T’s Biometric, Identity, and Advanced Computing Division. “And it did just that.”
The technologies’ use of AI and other autonomous systems enhances border security and efficiency. This enables CBP to allocate officers to higher-value tasks while increasing the number of travelers processed and helping CBP accurately confirm the arrival and departure of foreign visitors to the United States.
“We were extremely impressed with the technology and the vendors that S&T brought down to Progreso on our behalf,” said Larry Panetta, Director of CBP’s Biometrics Program Office. “The image capture capabilities of pedestrians walking through the border exit area exceeded expectations in both day and night conditions. This technology could prove to be a force multiplier and allow CBP to maximize deployment of resources.
“The fact that this went from concept to operational data collection in just a few months is amazing. It was a pleasure working with S&T and we’re looking forward to more collaborations with them in the near future.”
For related media inquiries, please contact STMedia@hq.dhs.gov.

articles.title: West Fargo police deploy new technology to detect card skimmers
articles.description: West Fargo police deploy new technology to detect card skimmers The Mighty 790 KFGO
articles.description_html: West Fargo police deploy new technology to detect card skimmers  The Mighty 790 KFGO
articles.article_title: West Fargo police deploy new technology to detect card skimmers
articles.heading: West Fargo police deploy new technology to detect card skimmers
articles.summary: WEST FARGO, N.D. (KFGO) - The West Fargo Police Department has deployed new technology designed to detect hidd...
articles.content:
WEST FARGO, N.D. (KFGO) – The West Fargo Police Department has deployed new technology designed to detect hidden credit card skimming devices on retail checkout terminals and fuel pumps.
The initiative aims to protect consumers from financial fraud caused by skimmers and shimmers, which are illegal devices attached to card readers that steal payment data wirelessly or store it internally for scammers to retrieve later. Local retailers and convenience stores can sign up online to request visits from the department’s Investigations Unit, where detectives will sweep equipment and educate business staff on detection.
Police Chief Pete Nielsen said the proactive measures are necessary following a surge in fraud-related service calls in recent years.
“Illegal credit card skimming can have devastating impacts on innocent, law-abiding citizens who are victimized by this fraud,” Nielsen said. “This technology is another tool our department is using to keep our residents informed while taking these scam devices off the street.”
Nationwide, law enforcement personnel removed more than 400 illegal skimming devices during similar operations in 2025, preventing an estimated $428 million in potential fraud losses.
Police advise residents to visually and physically inspect point-of-sale readers, ATMs, and gas pumps before inserting a card. Consumers should check for loose, crooked, or damaged components and refrain from using any machine that appears altered. Officials added that using contactless tap-to-pay options or chip-enabled cards offers the strongest protection against skimming fraud.

articles.title: Paperless Paducah: Barcode Tracking Lowers Costs, Accelerates Cleanup
articles.description: Paperless Paducah: Barcode Tracking Lowers Costs, Accelerates Cleanup Department of Energy (.gov)
articles.description_html: Paperless Paducah: Barcode Tracking Lowers Costs, Accelerates Cleanup  Department of Energy (.gov)
articles.article_title: Paperless Paducah: Barcode Tracking Lowers Costs, Accelerates Cleanup
articles.heading: Paperless Paducah: Barcode Tracking Lowers Costs, Accelerates Cleanup
articles.summary: Pens, paper and clipboards are becoming things of the past at the U.S. Department of Energy’s Paducah Site as employees use barcode scanning technology to swiftly inventory thousands of pieces of equipment in a 2.1-million-square-foot legacy facility being prepared for demolition, leading to more efficient cleanup.
articles.content:
Pens, paper and clipboards are becoming things of the past at the U.S. Department of Energy’s Paducah Site as employees use barcode scanning technology to swiftly inventory thousands of pieces of equipment in a 2.1-million-square-foot legacy facility being prepared for demolition, leading to more efficient cleanup.
Office of Environmental Management
September 1, 2026
Container Management Supervisor Jonathan Tucker scans a waste container for tracking, demonstrating one of the many uses of the Paducah Site’s barcode tracking system.
PADUCAH, Ky. — Pens, paper and clipboards are becoming things of the past at the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Paducah Site as employees use barcode scanning technology to swiftly inventory thousands of pieces of equipment in a 2.1-million-square-foot legacy facility being prepared for demolition, leading to more efficient cleanup.
DOE Office of Environmental Management (EM) deactivation and remediation contractor Four Rivers Nuclear Partnership (FRNP) originally employed the barcode scanning system to collect necessary information to track the inventory of waste containers, speeding up the process by eliminating manual paper input. Now, employees rely on the system to track components during deactivation of the C-337 Process Building.
"The expanded use of barcode technology is a significant step forward for inventory and data management at the site," Federal Project Director William Wessel said. "Using this technology to quickly and accurately capture information digitally, we not only reduce the potential for human error but also simplify our ability to manage and retrieve data in real time across various organizations at the site."
Going paperless with barcode scanning comes after the Paducah Site embraced a new technology at C-337 that enables workers to efficiently scan equipment for uranium deposits as they deactivate the former uranium enrichment process building. Both initiatives demonstrate how EM incorporates innovation and efficiency into cleanup, focusing on priorities and reining in costs without sacrificing safety or effectiveness.
The barcode scanning technology improves accuracy and streamlines processes by eliminating the transfer of data from paper to digital input. Data is collected in the field in real time, then uploaded into a database. Workers can easily gather information via digital applications or hand-held scanners.
Through an initiative in which contractors collaborate on lessons learned and best practices, FRNP shared the barcode scanning technology with operations and site mission support contractor Mission Conversion Services Alliance (MSCA) as a cost-savings tool. MSCA is evaluating its potential use in tracking the 43,000 remaining depleted uranium hexafluoride cylinders stored at the site, key to DOE’s work to transform liabilities into assets for the nuclear renaissance and future reindustrialization.
"Investing in technologies, collaborative knowledge and resource sharing is crucial for advancing the mission at the Paducah Site," Portsmouth Paducah Project Office Acting Deputy Manager April Ladd said. "It's about empowering the workforce to use new technology in the field to enhance efficiency, ensure accuracy and maintain the highest standards of safety and compliance across our operations."
-Contributor: Dylan Nichols

articles.title: A Framework for Mutually Beneficial U.S.-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation
articles.description: A Framework for Mutually Beneficial U.S.-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation J Street
articles.description_html: A Framework for Mutually Beneficial U.S.-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation  J Street
articles.article_title: A Framework for Mutually Beneficial U.S.-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation - J Street
articles.heading: A Framework for Mutually Beneficial U.S.-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation
articles.summary: A Framework for Mutually Beneficial U.S.-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation J Street
articles.content:
The U.S.-Israel Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) expires in 2028. Along with Israel’s actions in Gaza and the costly war with Iran, the MOU’s impending expiration has prompted a growing debate over the future of the bilateral relationship.
J Street has previously proposed five principles for a mutually beneficial and politically sustainable security partnership:
- The United States should maintain a strong security partnership with Israel where our interests align.
- The United States should phase out direct financial support for arms sales to Israel and treat Israel as it does other wealthy U.S. allies.
- U.S. arms sales and other forms of assistance to Israel should be fully consistent with American law.
- U.S. arms sales to Israel should be further conditioned to incentivize alignment with American interests and laws — as has been the case with other allies and partners — when their behavior is inconsistent with U.S. interests.
- The United States should continue to sell short-range air and ballistic missile defense (BMD) capabilities to Israel.
The first topic has drawn particular attention in recent months amid proposals that would significantly deepen defense, intelligence, and technology cooperation. A key concern is that expanded procurement, co-production, and joint development of new systems could simply replace the phased-out military subsidy with a different source of financing that is less visible to the American public and less subject to congressional scrutiny. In effect, this would deliver similar financial benefits to the Israeli government, while simply moving these funds from channels that can be leveraged and conditioned on Israeli behavior (in the State Department) to bureaucratic contracting channels (in the Department of Defense). Another concern is that jointly developed weapons could be used to carry out or enable actions that undermine U.S. interests or violate human rights and international humanitarian law.
At the same time, Israel can still be a valuable partner for the U.S. military, and access to its advanced technologies, weapons manufacturers, and human capital can serve America’s strategic interests. Historically, the U.S.-Israel security partnership has benefited both the United States and Israel in addressing several common threats on and off the battlefield. The two countries have worked closely together in the areas of counterterrorism strategy and cybersecurity. Also notable is their joint development of rocket and missile defense technologies. The two countries continue to work together to develop counter-unmanned aerial system (UAS) capabilities that both countries are likely to benefit from in the years ahead.
The goal should therefore be not to prevent all U.S.-Israel defense cooperation, but to ensure that it advances both countries’ interests, remains politically accountable, and does not enable violations of U.S. and international law. The following principles provide a framework for achieving that balance.
As long as Israel acts in contradiction of U.S. interests in Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon – and in a number of these cases, violates international humanitarian law – the United States should not expand military and defense technology cooperation with Israel. That does not mean existing programs – especially those focused on rocket and missile defense – should end.
J Street supports the Ceasefire Compliance Act, which ties Israel’s ability to use U.S. weapons in Gaza and the West Bank to its good-faith implementation of the 2025 Gaza ceasefire agreement it has already agreed to, and its adherence to Israeli and international law in the West Bank. Today, Israel is not meeting those conditions. Before the U.S. and Israel come to any new major defense-technology agreements, Israel should meet the conditions outlined in the Ceasefire Compliance Act, and should also engage constructively to implement a ceasefire and withdrawal agreement in Lebanon.
Israel’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon indicate a risk that weapons jointly developed by Israel and the United States – including those to which American manufacturers contribute proprietary technology – could be used to harm civilians in violation of international law.
Existing U.S. law already links eligibility for arms sales and many other forms of security assistance to the conduct of recipient governments and security forces through a number of legal provisions. Section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act prohibits security assistance to “any country the government of which engages in a consistent pattern of gross violations of internationally recognized human rights.” Section 620M (also known as the Leahy Law) bars assistance to specific units of foreign security forces if there is credible information that the unit has committed a gross violation of human rights. And Section 620I prohibits security assistance to any country that blocks or restricts U.S.-backed humanitarian aid.
Under current law, cooperative defense projects and the technology they develop appear to be subject to these same human rights restrictions as arms sales or other forms of security assistance; however, it is not fully clear whether they would be subject to all the same restrictions. The same conditions for eligibility for arms sales or other forms of security assistance should apply to any country that is benefiting from access to American technology through joint cooperative defense projects – including Israel. Therefore, any laws establishing new cooperative projects should make clear that these projects are subject to all relevant human rights conditions in the Foreign Assistance Act and other arms export laws.
These safeguards may reduce some countries’ desire to pursue cooperative projects with the United States. That is a price worth paying to ensure technology developed by America is used in accordance with U.S. law and values.
The Pentagon acquisition process – and the Armed Services committees that oversee it – evaluate procurement, co-production, and co-development decisions through the narrow lens of potential benefit to military capability, readiness, cost, schedule, and technical risk. Israeli technologies – and Israeli companies, engineers, and scientists – can indeed benefit the U.S. military. The Pentagon and Armed Services committees are therefore likely to view many arms purchases and joint projects with Israel favorably on their military merits.
But at a time when Israel’s far-right government is attempting to foreclose, rather than promote, the possibility of a lasting peace between Israelis and Palestinians – an outcome that is essential to America’s interest in regional stability – decisions to deepen cooperation with Israel must go beyond the narrow logic of military procurement and also consider America’s broader strategic interests in the region.
Agreements that deepen the military-to-military relationship should therefore be reviewed not only by the House and Senate Armed Services committees, but also by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee (SFRC) and the House Foreign Affairs Committee (HFAC). Existing law already recognizes that certain cooperative defense projects are also foreign policy decisions. Section 27 of the Arms Export Control Act requires advance foreign policy committee notification for certain cooperative defense agreements. The same review process should apply to all cooperative defense agreements – not just with Israel but with any country.
There is a strategic benefit to maintaining the U.S. military’s sovereign capabilities, where possible. Agreements that forgo that benefit by incorporating Israeli technology into the U.S. defense architecture should therefore be required to demonstrate a clear benefit to doing so. Israeli technology has directly benefited the American military in the past, including the Trophy system, which protects American tanks; enhancements Israel developed for the F-35; and the co-production of Iron Dome for the U.S. Marines. This principle ensures that American procurement of Israeli technology is in both countries’ interests, as it can and should be. It also ensures that procurement does not become a back door for the annual subsidy.
Joint initiatives should focus on shared challenges – including cyber, missile defense, and counter-UAS – and require genuine cost-sharing to ensure that both countries benefit. And the focus should be on weapons that both countries will field in the future. If a program is focused on systems that only Israel will field, Israel should cover the full cost. The executive branch should be able to certify to Congress that these conditions have been met before any new cooperative defense-technology program begins. Again, this bar should exist not just for Israel but for any wealthy security partner.

articles.title: Online entertainment sites in the context of U.S.-Israel business and technology
articles.description: Online entertainment sites in the context of U.S.-Israel business and technology The Jerusalem Post
articles.description_html: Online entertainment sites in the context of U.S.-Israel business and technology  The Jerusalem Post
articles.article_title: Online entertainment sites in the context of U.S.-Israel business and technology | The Jerusalem Post
articles.heading: Online entertainment sites in the context of U.S.-Israel business and technology
articles.summary: How American market scale and Israeli expertise in cybersecurity, AI, fintech and software are shaping the technology behind digital entertainment.
articles.content:
Online entertainment has become a revealing case study in American technology, as regulated digital platforms depend on software, payments, cybersecurity, data analysis, geolocation and identity systems.
You can see that connection clearly in Michigan, where regulated digital entertainment has developed into a large market with sophisticated technical requirements. That market also offers a useful way to understand U.S.-Israel commercial ties, as American companies bring scale, capital, consumers and regulatory experience and Israeli technology firms contribute expertise in cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, fintech and advanced software.
The interesting story sits behind the games, so you can think of digital entertainment as a technology business with entertainment at the customer-facing layer. As these industries become more interconnected, the relationship between U.S. markets and Israeli innovation becomes easier to understand.
Michigan's digital entertainment economy
If you look at Michigan online gambling sites, you can see how quickly regulated digital entertainment has matured, as Michigan had 15 authorized commercial and tribal operators offering legal iGaming as of May 2026.
The state reported $301.2 million in digital entertainment gross receipts during June, so the business remains substantial after a monthly decline from May. June online sports entertainment added $40.1 million in gross receipts, bringing combined internet entertainment and sports-related gross receipts to $341.3 million.
Operators also submitted $62.3 million in state taxes and payments for June, so the market carries significant public revenue alongside private activity. Bet365 entered Michigan in April with sports and digital entertainment products, adding another international operator to a large competitive and growing U.S. digital marketplace.
The U.S.-Israel business connection
The U.S.-Israel business relationship gives this technology story a wider context, as the two countries have maintained a free trade agreement since 1985.
As U.S. goods and services trade with Israel reached an estimated $55 billion in 2024, U.S. goods trade totaled $34.4 billion in 2025. That level of commerce matters for digital industries because technology companies can sell specialized capabilities across a relationship that supports investment, trade and connections.
Israel has built a strong high-tech sector, so its start-ups can develop products for demanding customers. The Israel Innovation Authority reported more than 1,500 active deep-tech companies in 2025, raising more than $28 billion between 2019 and 2025. That combination gives U.S. businesses technology access, and Israeli firms gain American market scale today.
Cybersecurity and digital trust
Cybersecurity becomes crucial when you consider what a digital account contains, as operators handle payment details, identification data, credentials, geolocation signals, transactions and behavior.
If a platform cannot detect suspicious activity quickly, fraud can become expensive and trust can deteriorate, so security systems have to operate continuously across transactions. The connection also extends into artificial intelligence, as machine-learning systems can flag unusual account activity and help security teams prioritize threats.
You can see digital entertainment as one use case for technologies that also serve banks, retailers, insurers and financial businesses. As transaction volumes rise, technical resilience becomes a commercial requirement affecting revenue, reputation, compliance and customer confidence.
Payments and identity systems
Payments and identity systems create another connection, as a transaction can involve services before money reaches a digital account.
A customer might interact with a digital entertainment interface as payment processing, identity verification, geolocation and banking can operate behind that screen. If any component fails, the customer can experience a declined transaction or delayed withdrawal, so operators have incentives to improve each stage.
Israeli fintech companies have developed expertise across digital finance, security and identity technologies, fitting naturally into American platforms under state rules. Michigan provides an illustration, as operators generated $289.21 million in adjusted digital entertainment gross receipts during June 2026. That scale means payment reliability and fraud detection can produce meaningful commercial effects, so technical efficiency becomes part of the customer experience directly.
American scale and Israeli innovation
American market scale gives technology companies a useful testing ground, as U.S. digital entertainment regulation varies by state and forces flexible systems.
A platform serving Michigan needs to satisfy state requirements, so another state can require different licensing, tax, geolocation, user-protection or technical rules. That fragmentation creates an engineering problem, but it also creates demand for modular software that can adapt without rebuilding systems.
Israeli technology firms can contribute specialized tools, and American operators contribute market knowledge, data, capital and distribution. The business logic becomes clear when you consider Michigan's 2025 results, as operators reported $3.1 billion in digital entertainment gross receipts and $671.3 million in internet sports-related receipts. Those figures show why adaptable infrastructure matters, as operational improvements can become valuable at national U.S. scale.
Where the technology goes next
The next phase of this relationship will focus on artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, payments and user protection, as each area combines technical complexity with commercial demand.
You can see the user-protection side in Michigan, where residents gained access to free Gamban licenses through a partnership to help people block digital entertainment sites and apps. That approach shows how technology can support consumer protection alongside digital entertainment, so innovation can serve operators and customers.
For U.S. companies, Israeli expertise can provide capabilities as American markets can provide scale. The result is a business model to watch, as digital entertainment connects consumer services with fintech, cybersecurity, software and regulation. If you look beyond the interface, you can see the U.S.-Israel technology relationship operating through infrastructure that makes modern commerce possible.
This article was written in cooperation with BAZOOM
