articles.content:
NEW HANOVER COUNTY — Parents and New Hanover County Schools staff members gathered for a superintendent-hosted town hall last week, though many people raised concerns on issues the district has no direct control over.
On Aug. 25, two days into the traditional school year, New Hanover County Schools Superintendent Chris Barnes hosted a forum for staff, followed by one for parents, to hear feedback and have district leadership respond to inquiries. Around 25 people attended each session.
The two groups had some distinctions — a chunk of the parent discussion was dedicated to screen time and technology use, while salaries was a major issue for the staff session. Both groups also raised similar issues over transportation, school funding, facilities, and arts education.
Barnes pointed out some limitations in addressing them, largely due to state-level funding decisions.
“I’ve tried not to do that game where I go and blame the state for what the county’s not doing and blame the county for what the state’s not doing because I really feel like our county has put significant investments behind the students — I really think that they do,” Barnes said. “The state, however, doesn’t view our allotment formulas as appropriate.”
Transportation
The most prescient issue for both cohorts was transportation, a common issue at the beginning of the year as families and staff get settled into new routines.
This year transport times to Laney High School, Trask Middle and Murrayville Elementary were extended due to a cut-through being out of service. A portion of Dove Field Drive collapsed due to last week’s heavy flooding, causing buses to redirect onto busy N. College Road to reach the campuses.
Though, as with past years, the district is struggling to find bus drivers. At the forum, Assistant Superintendent of Operations Rob Morgan said his bus driver staff was operating at 85% capacity without accounting for people who call out of work the day of.
Morgan explained it leaves the district scrambling to find drivers at the last minute, often pulling teachers, coaches, teachers assistants and other staff from their positions to drive a bus. The constant switcheroo contributes to confusion over bus numbers, different drivers each trip and, sometimes, late or early arrivals prompting parent complaints.
After the meeting, the district confirmed it has 99 of 116 of its driver positions filled, though it is running 24 double runs in the morning and 30 in the afternoon.
Morgan revealed a large hurdle in the hiring process is not necessarily pay — NHCS offers $18.87 an hour — but rather the time it takes the DMV to administer road tests.
“We’ll have 10 candidates in line in November and on December 1, we’re down to three,” Morgan said. “And it’s because they’re getting dragged out so long that they take other jobs, or they don’t make the background check, or there’s any number of reasons.”
Barnes added he tried to pay for the district to have its own, dedicated instructor, but the DMV would not allow this.
Morgan said the district has raised the issue as high as the governor’s office twice, but never received a response.
A district spokesperson clarified the topic came up among others on two occasions with Gov. Josh Stein — around a year ago and in March this year.
“During both conversations, we expressed concerns about the challenges associated with relying on DMV testing capacity to move candidates through the licensing process in a timely manner,” district spokesperson Anita Baggie wrote in an email to Port City Daily. “The response from the Governor’s Office was supportive, although no immediate solutions were identified.”
Cindy Bliss, principal at Rachel Freeman School of Engineering, said she is still experiencing bus troubles unrelated to the start of the traditional year. Rachel Freeman’s first day of school was Aug. 6.
Bliss explained some of her students are continuing to miss school — contributing to the high absenteeism the district is trying to curb — because they don’t have bus passes, which are needed to board a district bus.
The district has set deadlines for requesting the passes with reminders throughout the summer; however, it receives an influx of new requests at the beginning of the school year.
Aside from the time needed to verify student information, sometimes new requests require the incorporation of additional routes, creating a backlog in issuing the passes.
Still, Bliss said she didn’t understand why it would take 10 days to issue a pass when Rachel Freeman is one of the only schools in session at the beginning of August. She noted communication is already a challenge for the families at her school, who also have to get their bus passes in two weeks before a majority of the district; they also tend to rely on their phones, rather than computers, for completing district paperwork.
Bliss said she thought the district was putting things in place that systemically work against her students
After the meeting, Baggie said Bliss’ concern is understandable.
“We recognize the importance of minimizing delays and continue to refine our procedures each year to improve service,” Baggie said. “When a stop is already established and eligibility can be verified, we make every effort to assign students as quickly as possible to help avoid interruptions to school attendance.”
Funding and facilities
Both the parent and staff cohort brought up issues related to the district budget.
Superintendent Barnes has been clear the district is operating at a subsistence level, even with millions more from the county commissioners this year despite the district’s declining enrollment. Still, some staff members came to the town hall to express their pay levels were preventing the hiring of experienced staff.
Though no teachers raised the issue, HVAC and cafeteria workers, plus occupational and physical therapists, said they are having a hard time hiring and retaining staff.
Barnes thought it might be time to undergo another salary study to ensure district staff’s pay was on par with surrounding districts and districts of the same size.
However, just because the study shows staff should be paid a certain amount doesn’t mean the district has the funding to pay it. The superintendent pointed out the district is limited by the state’s funding formula, which doles out money based on enrollment without, like other states have, weighted amounts for populations who need more support.
“I have 100 grand. Is it OT/PT? Is it HVAC? Is it cafeteria?” Barnes said. “That’s the problem … we have to do and make choices that are really difficult.”
He and school board member Pat Bradford said district leaders have been discussing changes to the state’s funding model with legislators, particularly eliminating the cap on special education funding.
The state currently limits this funding at 13% of the student enrollment, regardless if a district’s special education population exceeds 13% or whether a small group of students take up a large majority of resources, as is the case at NHCS. Barnes said the district spends more than a million dollars in support for 14 students. Even when the state money runs out, public schools are still obligated to accommodate the needs of special education students.
According to Bradford, the legislators they’ve spoken with are amenable to changing the special education funding model.
The state is also exploring a full transition to a weighted funding model; Barnes said the district was invited to a presentation on the matter. Barnes thought the state needed to put $4 billion more into education to “move the needle.”
Another example of the state funding model falling short comes with arts education. Art and music teachers are part of elective teacher allotments, which are doled out based on a certain number of students.
For example, if there was one art teacher per 500 students, schools with less than 500 students would not qualify for their own state-funded teacher. In this scenario, the district could fund the position at a small school using county dollars or share the teacher amongst multiple schools.
Austin Hinson, the band teacher at Williston Middle and New Hanover High schools, questioned the district’s long-term plan for the arts.
“In particular, I’m concerned about the orchestra programs in New Hanover County,” Hinson said. “There is a lot of noise around programs going away — and obviously I’m someone who splits a position right now, so I have those concerns myself for my band programs. But I want to know that we are in a county that can help support the arts.”
Barnes noted the orchestra positions are not funded by the state with “any stretch of the imagination” and thus, he had to trade in a supervisory position to pay for them in this year’s budget.
“I will tell you that I have no interest in closing out those positions,” Barnesa said. “I will also tell you right now, I don’t know how I’m going to fund them next year.”
Port City Daily asked the district about the orchestra program and arts funding in general but did not receive answers by press.
However, the district is conducting a review of its building footprint to potentially reduce the amount of overhead it has. This would likely reduce costs for maintaining the buildings and people needed to staff them.
Adjacent to the funding conversation, some parents and staff also expressed concerns over the district’s facilities. One parent brought up asbestos testing for old facilities, while others noted HVAC failures at schools, remedied by loud portable air units which are disruptive to class.
Barnes said the concerns demonstrated the importance of the bond. The district is proposing $320.5 million-worth of capital needs across the district in a bond referendum on this November’s ballot.
Screen time and tech questions
Coming off the state’s involvement in a landmark settlement with Meta over children’s use of its platforms, many parents worried about the amount of time their students spend using screens.
One parent questioned whether her child uses physical textbooks in class or computers. She wasn’t provided a finite answer. Superintendent Barnes informed the group the district is currently seeking funding for a study to find out how much time students spend with screens in the classroom.
“Just because the computer is being used as a part of a lesson doesn’t mean it’s the only thing that’s happening, but we wanted to drill down and find out exactly what that screen time looks like,” Barnes said.
According to the district, the study is still in its preliminary phase, though the district has already found a partner in The Friday Institute for Educational Innovation, a research arm of North Carolina State University’s College of Education.
In line with the state’s new guidance on purposeful screen use, the district’s goal is to establish a clear baseline of current technology use across schools in order to “assess alignment with guidance, identify gaps, and develop a practical framework for educators.”
At the meeting, Barnes said the district is seeking a grant for the effort; after the meeting, the district confirmed it will ask The Endowment to chip in. There is no cost estimate at this point.
In the meantime, Chief Academic Officer Robin Hamilton assured the town hall cohort that students still use physical texts, particularly novels. She also noted the curriculum has largely shifted to workbooks, where students can complete math problems, for example, in their book rather than copying problems onto a separate sheet of paper.
Hamilton explained reading material, whether online or in textbook form, are only part of classroom instruction.
“Say we’re looking at the Bill of Rights, the first 10 articles of the Constitution,” Barnes explained. “You may read them online, but then you’re spending time in class debating them, discussing them, writing your own Bill of Rights to add to it.”
Additionally, Barnes noted the district’s technology sustainability plan no longer calls for middle schoolers to be provided computers for assignments and to take home. While 1:1 devices are still deemed necessary for high schoolers, which particularly need them for AP and college courses, the removal from middle-school curriculum reduces the district’s technology costs and screen time for pre-teens.
Barnes was clear the district’s goal was not to go back to textbook-only learning, as it would be too expensive for the district to bear with their high replacement rates due to the wear-and-tear and updates.
However, one parent said they would like to have the ability to purchase books for their student, noting physical text was more conducive to comprehension.
A 2024 meta-analysis of 49 studies found students who read on paper consistently scored higher on comprehension tests than those who read the same material on screen. Additionally, an eye-tracking study found those reading print texts frequently re-read important details, while screen readers tend to skim.
There was also a question from one parent about the district’s use of AI, to which Assistant Superintendent of Technology and Digital Learning Dawn Brinson pointed to the district’s website for more information on its use. The district prohibits using the technology for cheating, along with meeting assistants and agentic AI. Brinson did note that the state requires AI literacy, though, so the district cannot rid itself of the technology completely.
Brinson also noted the district is considering making technology and AI use a topic in its Parent and Caregiver Academy.
At Port City Daily, we aim to keep locals informed on top-of-mind news facing the tri-county region. To support our work and help us reach more people in 2026, please, consider helping one of two ways: Subscribe here or make a one-time contribution here.
We appreciate your ongoing support.

According to the district, the study is still in its preliminary phase, though the district has already found a partner in The Friday Institute for Educational Innovation, a research arm of North Carolina State University’s College of Education.

In line with the state’s new guidance on purposeful screen use, the district’s goal is to establish a clear baseline of current technology use across schools in order to “assess alignment with guidance, identify gaps, and develop a practical framework for educators.”

At the meeting, Barnes said the district is seeking a grant for the effort; after the meeting, the district confirmed it will ask The Endowment to chip in. There is no cost estimate at this point.

In the meantime, Chief Academic Officer Robin Hamilton assured the town hall cohort that students still use physical texts, particularly novels. She also noted the curriculum has largely shifted to workbooks, where students can complete math problems, for example, in their book rather than copying problems onto a separate sheet of paper.

Hamilton explained reading material, whether online or in textbook form, are only part of classroom instruction.

“Say we’re looking at the Bill of Rights, the first 10 articles of the Constitution,” Barnes explained. “You may read them online, but then you’re spending time in class debating them, discussing them, writing your own Bill of Rights to add to it.”

Additionally, Barnes noted the district’s technology sustainability plan no longer calls for middle schoolers to be provided computers for assignments and to take home. While 1:1 devices are still deemed necessary for high schoolers, which particularly need them for AP and college courses, the removal from middle-school curriculum reduces the district’s technology costs and screen time for pre-teens.

Barnes was clear the district’s goal was not to go back to textbook-only learning, as it would be too expensive for the district to bear with their high replacement rates due to the wear-and-tear and updates.

However, one parent said they would like to have the ability to purchase books for their student, noting physical text was more conducive to comprehension.

A 2024 meta-analysis of 49 studies found students who read on paper consistently scored higher on comprehension tests than those who read the same material on screen. Additionally, an eye-tracking study found those reading print texts frequently re-read important details, while screen readers tend to skim.

There was also a question from one parent about the district’s use of AI, to which Assistant Superintendent of Technology and Digital Learning Dawn Brinson pointed to the district’s website for more information on its use. The district prohibits using the technology for cheating, along with meeting assistants and agentic AI. Brinson did note that the state requires AI literacy, though, so the district cannot rid itself of the technology completely.

Brinson also noted the district is considering making technology and AI use a topic in its Parent and Caregiver Academy.

articles.article_title: How the NFL uses customer journey technology
articles.heading: Don't miss tomorrow's customer service industry news
articles.summary: The league’s transition to a “fan engagement engine” exemplifies a broader shift in customer journey mapping as brands move from static visualization to real-time orchestration.
articles.content:
When the National Football League released its schedule five years ago, fans received several nearly identical text messages, including “three from your favorite club, and one from the league,” said Amit Khare, director of marketing technology at the NFL.
Fans were opting out.
The problem was particularly acute because about 60% of the NFL’s fans follow more than one team, Khare said.
The league now runs a “fan engagement engine” built on Adobe’s real-time customer data platform, journey optimizer and customer journey analytics, according to Adobe. It integrates with the existing tech stacks for each of the NFL’s 32 teams through more than 80 external systems, unifying fan activity across NFL.com, the NFL App, ticketing and live events. When a schedule drops, an orchestration layer decides which team sends what to whom — and, increasingly, when.
The NFL’s project is one example of a broader shift in customer journey mapping: moving from static visualization to real-time orchestration, and eventually to predicting what a customer will want before they know it.
“That is absolutely the next frontier for enterprises,” said Katie Costanzo, president of customer experience at CSG.
Journey mapping tech
Journey mapping technology exists on a spectrum. According to Daniel O’Sullivan, senior director analyst within Gartner’s global customer service and support research group, that spectrum from least to most sophisticated is as follows:
- A whiteboard and sticky notes.
- Slide decks, such as PowerPoint.
- Digital collaboration tools like Mural and Miro.
- Dedicated journey mapping platforms like Journey Track, TheyDo and CX Omni.
- Real-time journey analytics and orchestration platforms such as those from Adobe, CSG, Medallia and Qualtrics.
For organizations lacking the infrastructure necessary to carry out real-time journey analytics and orchestration, digital collaboration tools and other middle-tier solutions can deliver value by allowing brands to connect data from other business systems to the journey map.
But the analysis is “still fundamentally reactive,” O’Sullivan said.
Real-time journey analytics and orchestration platforms, on the other hand, plug into live event streams and generate journey visuals directly from customer behavior — then act on them.
“There’s no longer the concept of people building out a journey map. Here you’re just piping in a huge stream of data, and it’s creating a Sankey diagram that looks like spaghetti,” O’Sullivan said.
Sankey diagrams visualize the flow and direction of the stages in a journey.
Inside the NFL’s rollout
The NFL’s fan engagement engine sits in the top tier of journey mapping technology. While the clubs already had their own sophisticated data platforms, they weren’t connected or coordinated.
“The missing part was the orchestration layer,” Khare said.
Rather than migrate all 32 teams to a single platform, Khare’s team designed one integration framework, piloted it with four clubs, then rolled it out in phases — updating earlier deployments with learnings from later ones.
During games, the system uses in-stadium signals to time communications around the action. A fan watching the third quarter won’t get a marketing text mid-play, but they may during halftime.
“Real-time orchestration is about finding out the right moment to send out the communication,” Khare said.
Fan opt-outs declined once the messaging overlap disappeared. Draft registrations rose 91%, while ticket conversions jumped 215%, according to Adobe.
The readiness gap
Most organizations don’t have the data foundations that real-time journey mapping and orchestration platforms require, and large organizations tend to overestimate their state of readiness. The hardest piece is identity resolution, such as figuring out that someone browsing a website is the same person who was on the mobile app five minutes earlier.
“There’s a tendency to think that these big companies have got it all figured out, but they often don’t,” O’Sullivan said.
Experts recommend picking a single business problem, such as cart abandonment or subscription churn, and tailoring the data to that use case rather than building a comprehensive foundation first.
“Start small. You do not need to boil the ocean,” Costanzo said.
But even when organizations get the data right, the path to real-time journey mapping and orchestration can stall because of internal politics. That’s because it cuts across customer service, product, digital and marketing, leading to gridlock when it comes to purchasing and implementation.
“These are really horizontal activities that cut across multiple different teams,” O’Sullivan said.
But for organizations that clear both hurdles, the payoff can be substantial when brands move from understanding the customer experience to dictating it.
“The question that we need to start asking is: How do we influence the next best experience for each customer in real time?” Costanzo said.

articles.article_title: AAR appoints new SVP and Chief Digital & Technology Officer
articles.heading: AAR appoints new SVP and Chief Digital & Technology Officer
articles.summary: AAR has announced the appointment of Sanjay Sood as Senior Vice-President and Chief Digital and Technology Officer, effective immediately
articles.content:
AAR has announced the appointment of Sanjay Sood as Senior Vice-President and Chief Digital and Technology Officer, effective immediately.
Sood will lead AAR’s technology organisation, overseeing enterprise systems, infrastructure, cybersecurity, data and analytics, as well as the company’s wider adoption of artificial intelligence and other technologies across its operations. He will report to John M. Holmes, Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer.
Before joining AAR, Sood was Senior Vice-President and Chief Technology Officer at CDW, a leading multi-brand provider of information technology solutions. In this role, he modernised the company’s platforms, data architecture and AI programmes, while managing the technical integration of several acquisitions. He previously held senior technology and product leadership roles at HERE Technologies, where he led global engineering teams and developed emerging products. Earlier in his career, Sood held leadership positions at YP, formerly AT&T Interactive, AllVoices and BuzzLabs.
“Sanjay brings a unique combination of significant experience in large-scale information technology leadership, infrastructure modernization, and AI technology implementation,” said Holmes. “We are pleased to welcome Sanjay to the AAR team. His leadership will be critical as we continue executing our long-term strategy and strengthening the systems and data management that help our business operate effectively.”
“I look forward to helping connect information across the organization, build on the strong foundation already in place, and reinforce the operational discipline that has long defined AAR,” said Sood. “Advancing AAR’s vast data resources is key to driving further value and efficiency for customers.”

articles.heading: How to introduce new technology without replacing human connection | Viewpoint
articles.summary: Ryan Gilmartin of St. John’s explains how technology can improve senior care by supporting employees and preserving human connection in healthcare.
articles.content:
Artificial intelligence has become one of the most talked-about topics in healthcare for good reason. New technologies are transforming everything from clinical documentation to admissions, reimbursement, workforce management, and communication. Every week seems to bring forward another platform that promises to revolutionize the industry.
However, in senior living the question should not be, “What technology should we adopt?” It should be, “How can technology help us better deliver our mission?”
At St. John’s, we do not pursue innovation because it is trendy. We pursue it because every decision we make should ultimately improve the experience of our residents, support our employees, and enhance the quality of care we provide.
Healthcare is, and always will be, a people business. No technology can replace the compassion of a caregiver, the reassurance of a conversation with a family member, or the trust that develops between residents and the people who serve them every day. Those moments define our profession. The best technology does not replace those interactions, but instead it creates more opportunities for them.
One of the greatest opportunities I see over the next five years is technology’s ability to create greater consistency and efficiency across everyday workflows. Healthcare organizations rely on thousands of repetitive processes every day. Many of them are manual, time-consuming, and vulnerable to inconsistency simply because they are completed by busy people juggling countless priorities. Even the best employees can only do so much when every day is filled with competing demands.
When technology removes unnecessary administrative burden, employees spend less time navigating systems and more time doing what only humans can do: caring for people.
Adopting technology should not be about replacing jobs, it should be about empowering employees with tools that help them work more efficiently, more confidently, and with less frustration. When administrative work becomes easier, caregivers gain the most valuable thing and that is time. Time to connect with residents. Time to collaborate with colleagues. Time to focus on the moments that truly matter.
The evaluation of every potential use of technology in healthcare should start with the same question. Does this help us further our mission? If the answer is yes, then we evaluate everything else: implementation requirements, operational impact, financial return, regulatory considerations, and long-term sustainability.
That is why we often work backward. Instead of asking, “What’s the newest technology available?” we ask, “What challenges are preventing our employees from delivering their very best work?” Then we identify solutions designed to remove those barriers.
Innovation is most successful when it is purpose-driven rather than technology-driven. Some of the most impactful technology investments are invisible to residents and families. For example, St. John’s recently implemented an AI driven centralized admissions platform called Profility that consolidates referrals from multiple hospital systems into one dashboard instead of requiring staff to navigate numerous portals and logins. What once involved multiple disconnected systems is now streamlined into one workflow.
When employees spend less time managing fragmented systems, they have more capacity to welcome new residents, answer family questions, and provide the personalized attention that defines exceptional senior care.
The same philosophy applies to reimbursement technology and other operational improvements. When technology increases confidence, accuracy, and efficiency behind the scenes, our employees can focus more energy where it belongs: on the people we serve.
Choosing which new technology to go with is not always the hardest part. Often helping the people who will be working with it every day to navigate the change is what proves to be the more difficult task. Healthcare professionals have developed workflows over many years, often under extraordinary pressure. Asking them to change those routines requires more than installing new software.
It requires communication, education, and persistence. Employees deserve to understand where the organization is going, why the change matters, and how it will improve both their work and the resident experience. Leaders must not assume that enthusiasm will appear on launch day. Adoption happens through ongoing support, training, and reinforcement, which continues long after implementation begins. Technology projects succeed because people succeed and not the other way around.
The pace of innovation will only continue to accelerate and no single leader can keep up alone. That is why I encourage healthcare executives to remain engaged with industry conferences, peer networks, professional organizations, and trusted publications. Many of the most valuable ideas emerge through collaboration with colleagues facing the same challenges.
Perhaps the most important quality that leaders can bring into this next chapter of healthcare is curiosity. Leaders need to be willing to explore new ideas, think beyond today’s challenges, and ask difficult questions. And most importantly, never lose sight of why you are innovating in the first place.
Technology will continue to evolve but our mission to serve people will not. When we use innovation to strengthen rather than replace the human connections at the heart of healthcare, everyone benefits: our employees, our residents, their families, and the communities we serve.
Ryan Gilmartin is chief operating officer at St. John’s.

articles.article_title: The lighting technology advances that have improved Broadway design
articles.heading: The lighting technology advances that have improved Broadway design
articles.summary: In Part 2 of this tech evolution series, designers Ken Billington, Jen Schriever and Anna Watson share innovations that have transformed what and how they create.
articles.content:
In Part 2 of this tech evolution series, designers Ken Billington, Jen Schriever and Anna Watson share innovations that have transformed what and how they create.

“Lighting designers are artists — we paint with light,” said lighting designer Ken Billington, who has been working on Broadway since the 1970s.

If only the job were that simple. “We’re also trying to keep our shows reasonable regarding cost,” he continued. “How do we get our concept onstage — make everything look good, tell the story as necessary — and not be so expensive that we bury the production? If I use some old equipment, is that rental price less than if I use all the brand new stuff? If the show is economical to run, then it runs a long time; if it’s expensive to run, it goes away. It’s a real numbers game.”

As technology evolves, designers are able to do more with light on stages than ever before. Yet, with such a vast expansion of possibilities, come additional decisions to make and considerations to prioritize. In the second of a four-part series , Broadway News spoke with three active Main Stem lighting designers — Tony winner Billington, Tony winner Jen Schriever and Main Stem newcomer Anna Watson — about some notable technological advancements that have made parts of their jobs easier, less time-consuming, more fun and, ultimately, better for audiences.

articles.title: Bees view the world in surprisingly different ways – understanding this could inspire new technology
articles.description: Bees view the world in surprisingly different ways – understanding this could inspire new technology The Conversation

articles.article_title: Bees view the world in surprisingly different ways – understanding this could inspire new technology
articles.heading: Bees view the world in surprisingly different ways – understanding this could inspire new technology
articles.summary: Some of the most impressive visual performances measured in a new study came from rarely studied, solitary species.
articles.content:
One bee has long been regarded as a benchmark for visual performance: the honeybee drone.
These male honeybees (Apis mellifera) have evolved highly specialised eyes for detecting queens during mating flights. They are extraordinarily sensitive to tiny moving objects less than half a degree across. In human terms, that’s like spotting a person more than 250 metres away.
Honeybees have dominated research on bee vision for more than a century. But some of the most impressive visual performances measured in our new study came from rarely studied, solitary species.
While the honeybee lives in massive colonies, most bee species are solitary so must do everything themselves: find food, locate mates, provision their nests. In terms of vision, several of the solitary species we researched outperformed honeybee workers in a number of ways, including the sharpness of images formed by their eyes.
Understanding how these different evolutionary solutions work is important for more than just understanding bee biology. It could provide ideas for nature-inspired technologies, from compact visual sensors to autonomous robots.
How bees’ eyes have adapted
With more than 20,000 species worldwide, bees show extraordinary diversity in lifestyle, body size and ecological role. Some live in open environments; others forage in dense vegetation or in dim light at dawn, dusk and even at night.
Such remarkable diversity prompted us to ask the question: how have bees’ eyes adapted to such different lifestyles and visual demands?
Bees see the world through compound eyes made up of thousands of tiny lenses. These odd-looking structures are their main tools to navigate, locate flowers and identify important landmarks.
Our new study of some daytime-active bee species shows that even bees with similar-looking eyes can achieve impressive visual performance in surprisingly different ways.
Male wool carder bees (Anthidium manicatum), for example, spend much of their day patrolling territories and chasing rivals or potential mates through the air. This bee pushes visual sharpness to the limit with its exceptionally small photoreceptors that minimise optical blur. In contrast, honeybee drones have evolved large lenses that maximise sensitivity.
The Australian blue-banded bee (Amegilla) manages to detect small objects and see sharp images just as well without either of these extreme strategies. Instead, it achieves similar visual performance using a different combination of optical design and sampling.
From the outside, the eyes of these bees all look very similar. But when we looked more closely, we found the size of their visual sensors (photoreceptors) differed greatly.
These light-sensitive structures are a bit like the pixels in a smartphone camera. They sit behind the bees’ tiny eye lenses, converting light into electrical signals. Larger pixels capture more light, improving sensitivity, while smaller ones can help preserve image sharpness.
The challenge – for smartphone designers and evolution alike – is balancing these competing demands.
Something unexpected
Looking at anatomy tells us how the eye is built, but not how well it performs. To answer this question, we recorded directly from individual photoreceptors in living bees.
We used glass microelectrodes with tips just a few tens of nanometers wide – thousands of times thinner than a human hair. That allowed us, for the first time in these species, to measure the tiny electrical signals that single cells produce when the bees were shown tiny objects on a computer display.
Our results revealed something unexpected. The diminutive Australian blue-banded bee lacks the enormous eyes of a honeybee drone, yet achieved a similar level of sensitivity in its photoreceptors.
At first glance, this seems paradoxical. How can bee eyes built so differently perform so similarly?
The answer is that evolution is not working towards a single ideal design. Different species have arrived at similar visual performance through different combinations of optical design, photoreceptor structure and visual sampling.
Our findings show why it is important to look beyond a handful of familiar species. By studying a wider range of bees, we can better understand how different senses have evolved, leading to a variety of adaptive solutions.
This is true not only for vision but for other traits, including how bees respond to environmental stresses such as heat and pesticide exposure.
Unique evolutionary innovations
Through our research, we are just beginning to appreciate the remarkably different ways of seeing the world that bees have evolved.
Different bee species have evolved different solutions to the challenges of seeing their world. For example, the Australian blue-banded bee is a buzz pollinator, able to vibrate flowers to release pollen in a way that honeybees cannot. This makes it a potentially valuable pollinator of crops such as tomatoes in Australia, where bumblebees are not naturally present.
Such diverse evolutionary solutions may also prove useful to engineers. Designers of cameras, robots and autonomous vehicles face many of the same challenges as bees: how to gather enough visual information while keeping sensors small, efficient and affordable.
Bees and other insects have been a fruitful source of inspiration for artificial vision systems. In our previous work, we developed computational models based on insect target motion processing that turned out to be as robust as alternative engineered solutions, with large benefits in processing efficiency.
We have now translated these models on to an autonomous robot that can pursue moving targets within natural scenes and even into autonomous flying drones.
Unfortunately, as bee diversity declines worldwide, there is a risk that we lose not only species, but the unique evolutionary innovations that have taken millions of years to develop.

articles.title: Flock cameras vandalized across north Georgia as backlash to technology grows

articles.article_title: Flock cameras vandalized across north Georgia as backlash to technology grows
articles.heading: Flock cameras vandalized across north Georgia as backlash to technology grows
articles.summary: Police say cameras being spray-painted, turned away from roadways and stolen from their mounting locations.
articles.content:
DECATUR, Ga. — Opposition to Flock Safety cameras is no longer limited to public meetings and social media posts.
In the past few months, more than half a dozen of these cameras have been vandalized.
[DOWNLOAD: Free WSB-TV News app for alerts as news breaks]
In Decatur, Police Chief Scott Richards recently told city leaders the department has dealt with multiple incidents involving Flock cameras.
“We had a pole cut down, had a Flock Safety camera on it,” Richards said.
The department has also reported cameras being spray-painted, turned away from roadways and stolen from their mounting locations.
Those incidents add to other reported cases around Georgia, including damaged cameras in Barrow County and a destroyed camera in Lumpkin County.
“That’s a fight against the system at this point,” said Cobb County resident Nigel McElroy. “I wouldn’t say I’m for it. I’m not for anybody destroying property.”
McElroy said he feels like the technology is an invasion of personal privacy.
“I am infuriated because I don’t want to be tracked at all times, at all moments,” he said.
TRENDING STORIES:
- Judge: Councilwoman can’t serve on panel weighing charges against Stockbridge mayor
- Atlanta rapper sold ‘how-to’ fraud tutorials, ran $6.5 million stolen check scheme
- Teen girl found alone along I-20; man now headed to prison
In the past few months, more than 40 officers have been fired, resigned, arrested or otherwise disciplined following allegations they misused Flock’s license plate reader database for personal reasons.
Georgia State University professor and former police officer Thaddeus Johnson said destroying the cameras is not the answer.
“So while you’re trying to combat injustices, you are breaking the law yourself,” Johnson said. “Two wrongs really don’t make a right.”
However, Johnson said the long-term solution is rebuilding the public’s faith through stronger oversight, clearer policies and safeguards governing how the technology is used.
“If you don’t have the guardrails, policy, personnel and infrastructure in place, things can go awry,” he said.
“Because the technology will not work if the people don’t feel it’s legitimate.”
Authorities have already begun bringing criminal cases in some incidents. In Barrow County, sheriff’s officials announced the arrest of Andrew Lyle Morrison in connection with vandalism of a camera.

articles.article_title: Turning to Technology, USDA Leaders Want Fewer Surprises in Acreage, Yield Estimates
articles.heading: USDA Moves to Overhaul Crop Reports
articles.summary: USDA officials on Tuesday used the opening of the Farm Progress Show to talk about how they are changing USDA's data collection for crop reports that farmers rely on for market decisions. That includes making surveys easier for farmers to fill out, along with using more satellite information and potentially precision-agriculture data.
articles.content:
USDA Moves to Overhaul Crop Reports
Turning to Technology, USDA Leaders Want Fewer Surprises in Acreage, Yield Estimates
BOONE, Iowa (DTN) -- USDA is planning multiple changes to how statistical agencies collect and use data for crop reports, including greater use of satellite imagery and precision-agriculture data.
USDA's monthly crop reports always draw significant scrutiny because of market moves and how heavily farmers rely on those reports to plan and market their crops.
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins on Tuesday brought her roadshow to the Farm Progress Show, laying out new details about USDA's plans to improve the accuracy of crop reports. She also pressed the case that farmers are better off now than they were when the Trump administration began.
"We know we still have a long way to go, but the needle is moving in the right direction," Rollins told participants at the farm show.
Speaking to the crowd, Rollins spotlighted where she sees improvements in the farm economy and pointed to positive moves the Trump administration has made to boost domestic production of fertilizer, increase exports of some commodities such as ethanol, and the administration's decision Monday to require refiners to pick up the full reallocation of 1.7 billion gallons tied to small-refinery exemptions from the Renewable Fuel Standard.
Rollins' main talking point, though, was to announce changes in data reporting and statistics collection at agencies such as the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) and its crop reports. Rollins spent a month holding talks with farmers around the country over the issue. She said there is a need to "fix" both NASS and reports such as the monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE).
"Hearing directly from the farmers, our farmers, some of you here today -- who actually fill out these surveys and rely on the data that comes from them -- has been everything as we have rebuilt this program," Rollins said.
FOUR GOALS TO DATA COLLECTION CHANGES
USDA officials highlighted four goals for the modernization plan, which include reducing burdens on farmers while pulling data from more satellite sources and potentially incorporating data from precision-agriculture tools. Those four goals, as outlined by agency officials, are:
-- Modernize the data reporting experience.
Surveys have become longer and more redundant over time, which is one reason the response level has fallen from more than 60% a decade ago to under 40% in this year's June Acreage report.
"If you want to break this down to a simpler statement, it is to reduce the burden on farmers with regard to surveys and other ways to provide their data into the system," said Scott Hutchins, USDA's undersecretary for Research, Education and Economics.
When it comes to surveys, that would include using information from farmers already in the system, so they don't have to fill out the same redundant information over and over. USDA is also looking at creating applications for farmers to do surveys over their phones.

"So, we're going to move aggressively to identify the ones that make the most sense and the ones that we can implement and reduce to practice. We also are looking to review and redesign surveys to reduce the burden on farmers, so we can have pre-filled-in data," Hutchins said.
-- Enhance acreage and yield estimation.
That was the rub last year when USDA increased corn acreage by more than 4 million acres after the June Acreage report. The department is looking at using more data from NASA satellites, as well as other companies, to make predictions and estimates. "NASA has a whole slate of new tools they have that they're just ready to put to work for us, and so we are developing a continued understanding with them and working with them daily now to move in that direction," Hutchins said. "And these tools will help us with acreage estimation, crop monitoring, yield analysis, disaster assessments, and all of the kinds of things that allow us to be rapid response to understand and to have a much more continuous understanding of how the crops are developing."
He noted how conditions of the corn crop have changed just this past month, particularly due to widespread flooding in Indiana.
-- Integrate data and technology platforms.
Hutchins discussed incorporating precision agricultural data and artificial intelligence (AI) to improve efficiency for USDA agencies -- beyond the statistical reports. That also includes reorganizing to reduce some cross-agency redundancy.
Later this week, NASS will roll out a new tool, "Ag Insights," that will allow people to more easily search for specific agricultural statistics, Hutchins said.
Richard Fordyce, USDA's undersecretary for Farm Production and Conservation, also highlighted precision agricultural tools to improve USDA acreage reporting "to be more farmer-facing." Fordyce noted USDA has been working with manufacturers to look at integrating precision agricultural data to help with acreage reporting.
"That's a huge thing. Farmers are investing in this technology. They're utilizing this technology to make decisions to manage their farms. Why wouldn't we be able to use that data to do an acreage report? It seems simple, but it's actually pretty complex to get to that point, but we're going to get there," Fordyce said.
-- Expand trust and transparency with producers.
Going back to last year's acreage revisions, Hutchins said a major goal is to "minimize and eliminate surprises" in crop reports.
"When we make revisions because we have new data or different data that's significant, it creates a situation where we have to wonder which one of these is accurate," Hutchins said. "Do we have trust in this process? And we know we have to earn that trust. We have to do it continuously. We have to do it with good science and good analytics, and we also need to be much more transparent and talk about not just what we think the answer is in a particular statistic, but how we got there and why we think it's the right answer."
FARMER PERSPECTIVE
Indiana farmer Kip Tom, who served as an ambassador to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization in the first Trump term, was brought on as a USDA adviser on data modernization. Tom said it's important that USDA has the latest science, so farmers have the best information to make market decisions.
"We're going to find out where the gaps are at and see what we can do to fill this, because if we don't do this right, we're going to be subject to hedge funds, big trading companies or others who will have an advantage on this," Tom said. "We can't allow that to happen."
Ben Riensche, an Iowa farmer who has also been advising USDA on data, said another issue that should be considered is when to release WASDE reports. Riensche said the reports should be released during a morning break in the grain trade so that farmers and their market advisers are able to analyze the numbers before major moves in price.
"We've got to be able to provide data equity with the people who have enormous computing power," Riensche said. "I've got to wait until my broker sees it, analyzes it and helps me with the numbers. But when the report comes out, there are people that have the ability to do that in fractions of seconds."
HOW DO YOU DETERMINE ACCURACY?
Farmers often say USDA reports are wrong when they disagree with USDA's numbers. Responding to a question from DTN, Rollins and Hutchins said determining whether a new system is going to be more accurate is one of the challenges.
"It's not an easy question to answer because there's a couple ways to look at it," Hutchins said. "One is over time, how have we varied from what we predicted at a particular point throughout the year to what actually has happened? Because we do all, at the end of the day, know what the destination is and what the actual is -- just way after kind of the market need and so forth. So, we have an opportunity to measure how we've done that."
Hutchins said USDA is looking to implement an "annual scorecard" that would detail where USDA began and how the forecasts compared with the information that the department had at the time.
BEEF ON BEEF
On a separate issue, President Donald Trump will be making more announcements on beef and the cattle herd "at the end of the week," Rollins also told reporters.
Trump has drawn fire from ranching groups over his plan to allow 300,000 metric tons of beef trim into the country at lower tariff levels. Rollins defended Trump's move, saying no president is more "pro-rancher and pro-farmer" while USDA on Monday announced efforts to try to promote heifer retention with an insurance plan and opening more Conservation Reserve Program grassland acres for grazing. But Trump also has to address affordability challenges, Rollins said.
"(Trump) believes it will significantly help the American consumer, especially the American consumer who buys ground beef, which is what most of this will be. We all eat ground beef, but those at the lower end of the socioeconomic ladder, that is usually the primary source of their protein, so he made that decision," Rollins said.
Rollins added she did not know where the beef trim would come from. That was being negotiated by the U.S. Trade Representative's Office. Still, Rollins said there will be more details about beef issues coming directly from Trump later this week.

Ben Riensche, an Iowa farmer who has also been advising USDA on data, said another issue that should be considered is when to release WASDE reports. Riensche said the reports should be released during a morning break in the grain trade so that farmers and their market advisers are able to analyze the numbers before major moves in price.

"We've got to be able to provide data equity with the people who have enormous computing power," Riensche said. "I've got to wait until my broker sees it, analyzes it and helps me with the numbers. But when the report comes out, there are people that have the ability to do that in fractions of seconds."

HOW DO YOU DETERMINE ACCURACY?

Farmers often say USDA reports are wrong when they disagree with USDA's numbers. Responding to a question from DTN, Rollins and Hutchins said determining whether a new system is going to be more accurate is one of the challenges.

"It's not an easy question to answer because there's a couple ways to look at it," Hutchins said. "One is over time, how have we varied from what we predicted at a particular point throughout the year to what actually has happened? Because we do all, at the end of the day, know what the destination is and what the actual is -- just way after kind of the market need and so forth. So, we have an opportunity to measure how we've done that."

Hutchins said USDA is looking to implement an "annual scorecard" that would detail where USDA began and how the forecasts compared with the information that the department had at the time.

BEEF ON BEEF

On a separate issue, President Donald Trump will be making more announcements on beef and the cattle herd "at the end of the week," Rollins also told reporters.

Trump has drawn fire from ranching groups over his plan to allow 300,000 metric tons of beef trim into the country at lower tariff levels. Rollins defended Trump's move, saying no president is more "pro-rancher and pro-farmer" while USDA on Monday announced efforts to try to promote heifer retention with an insurance plan and opening more Conservation Reserve Program grassland acres for grazing. But Trump also has to address affordability challenges, Rollins said.

"(Trump) believes it will significantly help the American consumer, especially the American consumer who buys ground beef, which is what most of this will be. We all eat ground beef, but those at the lower end of the socioeconomic ladder, that is usually the primary source of their protein, so he made that decision," Rollins said.

Rollins added she did not know where the beef trim would come from. That was being negotiated by the U.S. Trade Representative's Office. Still, Rollins said there will be more details about beef issues coming directly from Trump later this week.

articles.title: Dorchester Sheriff’s Citizens Academy aims to build trust as technology evolves
articles.description: Dorchester Sheriff’s Citizens Academy aims to build trust as technology evolves Live 5 News
articles.description_html: Dorchester Sheriff’s Citizens Academy aims to build trust as technology evolves  Live 5 News
articles.article_title: Dorchester Sheriff’s Citizens Academy aims to build trust as technology evolves
articles.heading: Dorchester Sheriff’s Citizens Academy aims to build trust as technology evolves
articles.summary: The Dorchester County Sheriff’s Office is accepting applications for its Citizens Academy, a program that is becoming increasingly important, according to officials, as law enforcement adopts new technology and works to maintain trust with the community.
articles.content:
Dorchester Sheriff’s Citizens Academy aims to build trust as technology evolves
DORCHESTER COUNTY, S.C. (WCSC) — The Dorchester County Sheriff’s Office is accepting applications for its Citizens Academy, a program that is becoming increasingly important, according to officials, as law enforcement adopts new technology and works to maintain trust with the community.
The academy has been offered for about 10 years, but Sheriff Sam Richardson said the program has evolved alongside policing.
This year, participants will get a closer look at tools like Flock cameras and drones to learn how deputies use those technologies to gather information and support investigations.
“It’s one thing to hear about new technology being used by police,” Richardson said. “I want residents to see how it actually fits into the job.”
The eight-week academy will include weekly classes lasting about two hours. Participants will also have opportunities to ride along with deputies and tour the county’s jail.
Richardson said the academy has to continue evolving as the agency finds new ways to serve the community.
“I’m honestly going to think outside the box as often as I can,” Richardson said. “I study other law enforcement offices. I study what other people are doing inside the state that are success stories and throughout the country.”
As sheriff, Richardson said he believes it is important to keep looking for ways to do better.
“I think as a sheriff, you have to be on the cutting edge of doing things,” he said. “I think you can’t be stagnant. I’m constantly trying to improve.”
That mindset is also shaping what residents will learn during the academy.
Richardson said participants will get a better understanding of how deputies gather information, make decisions and use new technology while still maintaining traditional community policing.
“That’s an opportunity for our citizens to get involved in the academy and understand the why behind how we use it, the guardrails that we have in place,” Richardson said. “They get to understand from a practical application standpoint, this is why we utilize equipment like that. This is why we utilize the drones that we have. This is how we take intelligence and use it, but we use it responsibly.”
Richardson said the department also wants residents to understand that the technology is not intended to infringe on their privacy.
“We’re not trying to play Big Brother. We’re trying to respect everybody’s rights,” he said.
The academy also gives residents a firsthand look at the challenges deputies face in the field, from responding to back-to-back calls to navigating traffic and infrastructure throughout the county.
Richardson said that perspective has led to deeper understanding from past participants.
“I’ll have them come out of a situation and say, ‘Sheriff, I didn’t realize what you guys go through. I didn’t realize how often you go from call to call in certain situations,’” Richardson said.
Richardson said that firsthand experience can make participants advocates for the department in their own communities.
“They gain that experience. They now are really good ambassadors for us,” he said.
But Richardson said the relationship benefits the sheriff’s office, too.
“It’s actually not just that it helps citizens,” Richardson said. “I’ve been influenced, and I really like what we gain out of it. That relationship, that bond, works both ways.”
The Citizens Academy typically accepts about 20 to 30 community members. Officials may adjust the location of classes based on where participants live throughout Dorchester County.
The next academy runs from Oct. 5 through Nov. 17. Applications are due this Friday.
Residents who live outside Dorchester County can check with their local law enforcement agencies about similar Citizens Academy programs offered throughout the Lowcountry.

articles.title: Boston’s CIO Has a Simple Rule for Technology: Solve Problems.
articles.description: Boston’s CIO Has a Simple Rule for Technology: Solve Problems. governing.com
articles.description_html: Boston’s CIO Has a Simple Rule for Technology: Solve Problems.  governing.com
articles.article_title: Boston’s CIO Has a Simple Rule for Technology: Solve Problems.
articles.heading: Boston’s CIO Has a Simple Rule for Technology: Solve Problems.
articles.summary: From AI-powered permitting to better online services, Santiago Garces is putting technology to work on the everyday challenges that shape how residents experience government.
articles.content:
This article appears in Governing's Q3 2026 Magazine. You can subscribe here.
Since he arrived in Boston in 2022, CIO Santiago Garces has been heralded for his human-centered approach to the office.
The 39-year-old was a key partner in expanding high-quality Wi-Fi in public housing, granting more residents access to remote work, telehealth and online meetings. It’s the first time the public housing authority has had a partnership of this kind with the CIO. Garces also helped Boston become the first city to remove gender boxes on marriage forms, resolving a concern for trans Bostonians but also reducing the city’s administrative burdens.
Garces has also been an AI leader. Under his tenure, Boston became one of the first cities to issue guidelines around employee use of the technology. He’s since deployed AI in practical, targeted ways to improve services and accessibility. That includes using it to analyze 25 years of permitting applications from residents and businesses, then redesigning the online permitting process according to their needs.
This is “the kind of unglamorous but genuinely impactful work that government technology should be doing more of,” says Beth Noveck, director of Northeastern University’s Burnes Center for Social Change and former White House deputy chief technology officer, who collaborated on the project.
Garces also used AI to deliver better search results for boston.gov, a high-traffic site and primary source of city information for many residents. The change worked — residents are now four times more likely to say they’re able to find what they’re looking for on the site. Another AI project creates a more accurate map of where residents can park.
It wasn’t a linear path to public service for Garces, who’s now been CIO for three different cities. He attended the University of Notre Dame for engineering and entrepreneurship, and didn’t initially consider government work. But eventually he joined with some classmates — excited by South Bend’s new mayor, Pete Buttigieg — to launch enFocus, a nonprofit focused on fostering innovation in government and elsewhere. They began working with the city of South Bend and once he started solving problems for the municipality, he was hooked.
“There’s a tendency of people thinking that, if you’re a technical person, government is frustrating and kind of silly and simple, and actually I found it to be the opposite,” Garces says. “There’s complicated technical problems, but there’s also complicated people problems and systems problems. I think that’s what makes it so addictive.”
Garces was named a 2025 Government Technology* Top 25 Doer, Dreamer and Driver, and, under his tenure, the city won a 2023 What Works Cities Gold Certification.
“Government’s the best enterprise there is,” Garces says. “We are there to make life better. … It’s the one company that everybody has a share in.”

articles.title: Utah’s Blueprint for Governing Emerging Technology
articles.description: Utah’s Blueprint for Governing Emerging Technology Governing
articles.description_html: Utah’s Blueprint for Governing Emerging Technology  Governing
articles.article_title: Utah’s Blueprint for Governing Emerging Technology
articles.heading: Utah’s Blueprint for Governing Emerging Technology
articles.summary: State Sen. Kirk Cullimore has helped put the state at the forefront of AI, data privacy and digital identity policy, crafting approaches designed to be replicated beyond Utah.
articles.content:
This article appears in Governing's Q3 2026 Magazine. You can subscribe here.
Utah has been a powerhouse of emerging technology legislation over the past several years, drawing national and international attention. Driving much of this progress is Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore, 48, who’s gained a reputation for spearheading policies that protect consumers but also spur innovation.
A former music teacher turned lawyer and lawmaker, Cullimore didn’t start out in tech. But as constituents approached him with technology concerns, he dove headfirst into learning about the space. One technology bill led to another, and he became the go-to legislator on tech.
“Senator Cullimore is one of the more technologically savvy legislators that I’ve engaged with,” says Utah’s Chief Privacy Officer Christopher Bramwell. “He’s been on the cutting edge of AI policy.”
In 2024, Cullimore clinched a big win with a first-of-its-kind AI law, SB 149, imposing light regulations on AI use and creating the nation’s first Office of AI Policy. The office works with companies to find ways they can safely pilot new AI uses in Utah. One company is currently testing the use of AI to quickly and easily refill patients’ medication prescriptions.
The conservative American Legislative Exchange Council based its model state AI legislation on SB 149.
“We’re trying to pave a way in this new digital era where government responds properly and where we are looking to protect people from technology overreach while still allowing technology to develop and potentially better our lives,” Cullimore says of his approach to tech legislation.
Pragmatism and consensus building are also strong considerations, he says. To make a meaningful difference, Utah needs to create policies that other states will want to adopt, too. That way, the state avoids the risks of a company simply bypassing Utah or suing to overturn a law.
The senator has also focused on less headline-grabbing tech policies. Cullimore helped Utah become the fourth state in the U.S. to enact a far-reaching consumer data privacy policy. It’s also the only state with what Bramwell deems a “comprehensive” and “modernized” government data privacy policy, thanks in part to Cullimore. The state now has the nation’s first data privacy ombudsperson to handle complaints about government privacy practices.
Building on this success, Cullimore recently introduced legislation that would protect individual privacy as digital IDs come into development. Under the legislation, Utah would spearhead a concept called the State Endorsed Digital Identity, or SEDI, which would focus on maintaining citizens’ digital privacy and creating clear rules for the use of a digital ID. A key priority is making sure the entity accepting the credential can only access the information they need and nothing more. The ACLU praised the legislation, saying Utah is the “only … state asking the right questions” about digital identity.
Cullimore didn’t initially set out to enter politics. For several years, he was the Rental Housing Association of Utah’s government affairs chair. And with his kids in elementary school, he joined the school community council and parent oversight boards. All of which, he says, eventually coalesced into a run for office.
From there, he’s made a name for himself tackling tricky emerging tech policy.
“He [Sen. Cullimore] knows how to get stuff passed in the body, and he is really passionate about these issues,” says Utah Department of Commerce Commissioner Margaret Busse. “He’s really been amazing for Utah.”

articles.title: The intelligent workplace (part 3): Technology’s next transformation of work
articles.description: The intelligent workplace (part 3): Technology’s next transformation of work IT Pro
articles.description_html: The intelligent workplace (part 3): Technology’s next transformation of work  IT Pro
articles.article_title: The intelligent workplace (part 3): Technology’s next transformation of work
articles.heading: The intelligent workplace (part 3): Technology’s next transformation of work
articles.summary: Emerging technologies, evolving skills, and agile workforce strategies will determine which organizations remain competitive in the workplace of 2030
articles.content:
The intelligent workplace (part 3): Technology’s next transformation of work
Emerging technologies, evolving skills, and agile workforce strategies will determine which organizations remain competitive in the workplace of 2030
Part 3: Preparing for the Workplace of 2030
The workplace of 2030 will emerge from the convergence of AI, autonomous agents, robotics, automation, skills intelligence and connected physical and digital environments. Together, they will change how organizations define jobs and create value for their businesses, customers and commercial partners.
Parts 1 and 2 of this series consider how intelligent technologies are transforming the employee experience and changing the way organisations manage performance and workforce development. These shifts are also early signals of a much larger transformation that will reshape the structure of work over the remainder of the decade.
Part 3 looks toward the workplace of 2030. It explores the technologies likely to influence how work is organized and the workforce strategies required to remain competitive. The challenge for organizations is no longer simply adopting AI, but building the adaptability to redesign roles and develop new capabilities as technology continues to evolve.
The scale of the transition will be substantial. The World Economic Forum expects structural change to affect 22% of today’s jobs by 2030. It forecasts that 170 million roles will be created and 92 million displaced, producing a net gain of 78 million jobs. This is not a simple story of technology eliminating employment. It is a redistribution of tasks and opportunities on a scale that will test every organization’s ability to adapt.
The question is not whether the workplace will change, but whether companies can change with it. Preparing for 2030 means building an organization capable of redesigning work and moving skills to where they generate the greatest value.
Emerging technologies will reorganize work
AI will become foundational workplace infrastructure. Adoption is already accelerating. Stanford’s AI Index reports that 88% of surveyed organizations were using AI in 2025, with 70% using generative AI in at least one business function. Generative AI reached approximately 53% of the general population within three years—faster than either the personal computer or the internet. Agent deployment, however, remained in single digits across almost all business functions, showing how early the next stage remains.
Wendy Harris, VP of EMEA at Rippling, says the real shift will come from “the convergence of AI, automation, skills intelligence and autonomous agents.” Instead of organizing work around fixed jobs and rigid processes, companies will increasingly match people and machines to tasks and outcomes in real time.
Sign up today and you will receive a free copy of our Future Focus 2026 report - the leading resource for IT decision-maker insight on priorities and investment areas in AI, security and more.
“The real transformation happens when organizations move away from assigning work based solely on headcount and job titles, and instead allocate tasks to the capabilities best suited to deliver an outcome, whether those capabilities are human, machine or a combination of both,” Ciara Harrington, chief people officer at Skillsoft, tells ITPro.
The transition extends beyond office-based generative AI. Robots will work beside people in factories, hospitals, construction, and logistics. Immersive systems will support training and remote maintenance. The opportunity lies in connecting these technologies to redesigned workflows rather than accelerating yesterday’s processes.
As Part 1 of this series considered, successful workplace transformation depends on more than introducing advanced tools. These technologies must form part of an intelligent employee experience that reduces digital friction and gives people greater capacity for judgment, creativity and collaboration.
Jobs will change faster than they disappear
Predictions of mass technological unemployment obscure a more complex reality. The International Labour Organization estimates that one in four jobs worldwide has some exposure to generative AI, yet only 3.3% of global employment falls within the highest exposure category. Transformation is more likely than wholesale replacement.
Even highly exposed occupations may prove difficult to automate completely. Managers, engineers, and other professionals often depend on social interaction and contextual judgment. AI may take over parts of these roles while increasing the value of the human capabilities surrounding them.
“Every role is made up of hundreds of tasks,” Harris explained. “AI doesn’t eliminate most roles—it changes the balance of those tasks.” Repetitive, administrative, and analytical work can move to technology, creating more space for judgment, creativity, communication, and problem-solving.
That requires organizations to design work at the task and capability level rather than making workforce decisions solely through job titles. Oliver Shaw, CEO of Orgvue, warns that many companies have invested in AI without considering its effect on work or the workforce. His company’s research found that 57% of business leaders deployed AI primarily because competitors had done so, while 78% of organizations had seen AI projects fail or remain stuck in pilots.
“A clear example of this is the PR and marketing industries,” says Shaw. “Both [are] fields that have been at the centre of the conversation on the disproportionate impact of AI adoption on entry-level roles, and what this’ll mean for the future of the industry when entry points are few and far between, and the foundational skills are missing. What these industries are forgetting is to train staff on the critical thinking required to use AI, and the cognitive offloading that occurs when there is too much reliance.”
Leaders risk automating fragments of work without considering which decisions remain human, or how entry-level workers develop expertise when foundational tasks disappear. Organizations should identify where AI can execute and where collaboration produces greater value.
This division of responsibilities also has direct implications for the performance and leadership questions explored in Part 2 of this series. Organizations will need to assess how effectively employees delegate to AI and apply human judgment, while ensuring accountability for consequential decisions remains clearly defined.
Continuous learning becomes core infrastructure
Skills will be the pressure point of the 2030 workplace. Employers expect 39% of workers’ core skills to change by the end of the decade. AI and big data are forecast to be the fastest-growing skills area, followed by networks and cybersecurity and then technological literacy. However, creative thinking, resilience, agility, curiosity, and lifelong learning will also increase in importance.
Technical and human capabilities are not competing categories. According to the OECD, 72% of vacancies in occupations highly exposed to AI already require at least one management skill, while 67% require a business-process skill. The employee who can operate an AI system but cannot question its output will offer limited value.
Jen Paterno, senior behavioral scientist at CoachHub, emphasised that judgment, adaptability, critical thinking, collaboration, and self-awareness develop through experience, reflection, and feedback—not conventional training alone.
“These capabilities are difficult to build through conventional training alone because they develop through experience, reflection, and feedback,” Paterno explained to ITPro.
“Organizations will need more continuous, personalized development models that help employees practice new behaviors in the flow of work. Coaching will also be critical in ensuring people have objective, brave spaces to experiment and ideate with skills that feel more foreign to them.”
The scale of the challenge is considerable. The World Economic Forum predicts that around 59% of the global workforce will require training by 2030. For every 100 workers, 11 may not receive the upskilling or reskilling they need, leaving more than 120 million people at medium-term risk of redundancy. Although 85% of employers intend to prioritize workforce upskilling, the intention must be converted into accessible learning and credible pathways into new work.
Annual courses and static competency frameworks are too slow. Harrington says organizations need systems that identify emerging skills and adapt as requirements evolve. Skillsoft found that although 86% of employees use AI at work, fewer than one-quarter feel equipped to use it effectively. Access without capability risks creating two workforces.
Skills-based models can help companies see capability beyond formal qualifications or job titles. They can also support internal mobility. Half of employers plan to move people from declining roles into growing areas, while 29% of workers requiring training could be upskilled in their current positions and 19% retrained and redeployed elsewhere, according to the World Economic Forum.
Adaptability will define competitive advantage
Workforce strategy must become more dynamic. Leaders need shorter review cycles, real-time skills visibility, plus the ability to test new roles and workflows before scaling them.
