articles.title: ‘We’re in the age of The Jetsons’: How advanced aviation technology will change lives
articles.description: ‘We’re in the age of The Jetsons’: How advanced aviation technology will change lives Fort Worth Report
articles.description_html: ‘We’re in the age of The Jetsons’: How advanced aviation technology will change lives  Fort Worth Report
articles.article_title: ‘We’re in the age of The Jetsons’: How advanced aviation technology will change lives
articles.heading: ‘We’re in the age of The Jetsons’: How advanced aviation technology will change lives
articles.summary: The future of powered flight was the focus of a Texas A&M-Fort Worth panel at the Kimbell Art Museum.
articles.content:
Matt Byrd wants aviation companies to fulfill the promise of “The Jetsons” — the 1960s space-age, animated TV show that brought the concept of flying cars into American living rooms.
As advanced technology grows rapidly, the futuristic transformation of transportation modes is bringing science fiction closer to science fact, participants at a Texas A&M-Fort Worth aviation panel said Aug. 25 at the Kimbell Art Museum.
“This is an incredibly exciting time to be alive,” said Byrd, president and CEO of Hillwood Aviation. “I think we’re at an inflection point in aviation.”
Byrd cited American innovation in aviation since Orville and Wilbur Wright had their first controlled flight in December 1903 at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. By the 1950s, he said, jet-powered flight enabled transatlantic flights from the United States to Europe.
“Now we’re entering automated, electric or hybrid-electric aviation with drone deliveries and people being able to fly,” Byrd said. “It’s incredibly exciting. And it’s just been a mere 123 years to get to this point. What is the future going to hold?”
Excellence in innovation is propelling technology forward, prompting governments worldwide to adopt new transportation modes, including autonomous and piloted vertical-lift aircraft.
Panelists said Fort Worth will benefit from the emerging technology. Educational institutions such as Texas A&M-Fort Worth and Tarrant County College have launched aviation-related workforce programs to keep up with the demand for jobs to service and maintain next-generation aircraft.
Cowtown’s flight path
North Texas became an aviation hub after Fort Worth newspaper publisher Amon G. Carter Sr. offered flight demonstrations eight years after the Wright brothers’ achievement.
French aviator Roland G. Garros, flying a Bleriot XI monoplane, is recorded as the first person to perform a powered flight from Fort Worth on Jan. 11, 1911. Thousands saw the flight at a racetrack known as Fort Worth Driving Park — now the site of Montgomery Plaza off West 7th and Carroll streets. First Flight Park, at 2700 Mercedes Ave. commemorates the historic event and features a replica of Garros’ plane.
Over the decades, Fort Worth hosted three training fields for World War I pilots, operated as a port for dirigibles or airships in the 1920s, and was the site of a B-24 and B-32 airplane bomber factory during World War II.
That facility, known as Air Force Plant 4, now assembles F-35 aircraft produced by Fort Worth-based Lockheed Martin Aeronautics Co.
In 2024, North Texas became the first area approved by the Federal Aviation Administration for commercial drone deliveries with Wing Aviation and Zipline as the companies authorized with carrying out the task.
“North Texas has really been involved in the aviation world for quite some time,” said Dave Martin, a project manager for the Texas A&M system’s Center of Advanced Aviation Technologies.
Ivett Leyva, associate dean for research at Texas A&M-Fort Worth, said North Texas is now known for aviation innovation and leadership.
“Matt talked about the spirit and leadership our country is known for,” she said. “I think that you can breathe, smell, hear (that) in North Texas. North Texas has that going, plus it has industry.”
Air taxis
Although flying cars aren’t yet on the horizon, electric and hybrid-electric vertical-lift aircraft — often called air taxis — are coming to North Texas, possibly as soon as 2027, Byrd said.
Public acceptance of such aircraft is crucial to their success, panelists said.
“Air taxis are a lot closer than we believe,” said moderator Albert Bejarano, associate director for the Center for Advanced Aviation Technologies.
The initial plan is to have the aircraft fly above highways, Byrd said, with safety being of paramount concern.
“Vehicles won’t be certified until they are safe,” Byrd said.
The noise generated by electric and hybrid aircraft is relatively low — about 45 decibels, which Byrd likened to “a soothing sound like wind blowing through the trees.”
Costs for air taxis will be based on a $3 per mile rate. North Texas passengers will soon be able to use the vertical-lift technology to reach Dallas Fort Worth International Airport at a cost of about $100 to “avoid all the traffic,” he said.
Byrd said he expects younger generations to use the aircraft without hesitation.
“The future is here,” he said. “It’s very, very exciting.”
The need for aviation-related mechanics, air traffic controllers and other skilled workers will help North Texas develop its workforce. Leyva referenced a significant shortage of air traffic controllers.
Developing a workforce of skilled workers will help North Texas “secure our place in the history of this inflection point,” Byrd said.
To maintain electric aircraft, the country will need to mine for rare earth minerals in new areas, he added.
Leyva added that work is ongoing to develop biodegradable batteries.
Meanwhile, Byrd said public acceptance of vertical-lift aircraft will take time.
“If they don’t perform, no one’s going to fly them,” he said.
Eric E. Garcia is senior business reporter at the Fort Worth Report. Contact him at eric.garcia@fortworthreport.org.

articles.heading: Fedorov offers drone technology to US in exchange for Patriots, seeks funding for defense tech fund
articles.summary: Mykhailo Fedorov said he is seeking backing from venture capitalists, private investors, and U.S. technology companies for a fund that would invest in Ukrainian defense startups and create new companies focused on battlefield technologies.
articles.content:
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov is seeking U.S. investment for a new defense technology fund and offering to help Washington develop drone capabilities in exchange for Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine, he told the Financial Times in an interview published Aug. 30.

The proposal comes as Fedorov has begun an international trip that has included Italy and the United States after being dismissed by President Volodymyr Zelensky as defense minister.

Fedorov told the FT in Washington that he is seeking backing from venture capitalists, private investors, and U.S. technology companies for a fund that would invest in Ukrainian defense startups and create new companies focused on battlefield technologies.

"This is not exactly a classic venture fund," Fedorov said in an interview. "We're writing a new history of the war."

Fedorov said the fund would initially focus on battlefield robotics, high-speed interceptor drones capable of countering Russia's newer jet-powered attack drones , and low-cost missiles equipped with artificial intelligence.

He also proposed a direct exchange with the United States , saying he would be willing to help Washington "build an army of drones" in return for Patriot interceptors to help Ukraine withstand Russian attacks this winter.

"I'm ready to make that trade," Fedorov told the FT.

Ukraine has faced a critical shortage of Patriot interceptors as Russia has intensified missile and drone attacks against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. The U.S.-made systems are among the few weapons capable of intercepting Russia's ballistic missiles.

Fedorov said Ukraine had already tested high-speed drones designed to bring down Russia's jet-powered attack drones and argued that they could be produced at scale with additional investment.

"We need more jet drones, we need cheap missiles, we need missiles with artificial intelligence," he said. "You can't conduct any kind of dialogue with Putin any other way. He understands only force."

Fedorov served as defense minister from January to July before Zelensky dismissed him in a Cabinet reshuffle. His firing triggered weeks of protests across Ukraine and elevated Fedorov's profile as a potential political rival to Zelensky.

After Zelensky declined to reinstate him as defense minister earlier this month, Fedorov called for wartime elections , a move that divided public opinion.

In an interview with the FT, Fedorov defended his call for elections, saying it was not aimed at replacing Zelensky but at updating the country's governing system.

"This is not against Zelensky, it's not against some specific person," Fedorov said. "It's about the fact that we need to … update the state's operating system."

Fedorov's trip to the U.S. follows a visit to Italy, where he agreed to serve as an unpaid adviser to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto on modern warfare technologies, his press service told the Kyiv Independent on Aug. 28.

Fedorov's press service said his primary focus would remain on projects in Ukraine and efforts to attract international resources for the country's defense technology sector. During his meeting with Crosetto, the two discussed drones, autonomous systems, air defense, and the development of Ukraine's defense technology ecosystem.

The FT reported that Fedorov was also considering similar advisory roles with other partner countries, potentially including France and the United States . He declined to say whether he planned to meet with officials from the Trump administration during his Washington visit.

Fedorov also said he remained in close contact with U.S. billionaire and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , but declined to comment on whether he planned to meet him in the U.S. Ukraine has relied heavily on Musk's Starlink satellite communications system throughout the war.

Previously, Zelensky awarded Musk Ukraine's Order of Liberty on Aug. 26, as Kyiv seeks his approval to use Starlink on drones operating inside Russia.

KALZERO Expands Unified Technology Ecosystem with ZeroTrade and NetPay247
Press Release Date 08-30-2026
KALZERO brings together ZeroTrade and NetPay247 to deliver unified brokerage, card issuing, payments, CRM and business technology infrastructure.
DUBAI, DUBAI, UNITED ARAB EMIRATES, August 30, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- KALZERO has announced the expansion of its technology ecosystem, bringing together brokerage infrastructure, branded card solutions, payments, CRM, automation and operational technology within one connected business environment.
At the center of the ecosystem are specialist technology platforms including **ZeroTrade**, focused on brokerage infrastructure and trading technology, and **NetPay247.com**, providing payment and card technology solutions.
Together, the platforms are designed to help businesses launch financial products under their own brand without having to build or connect every part of the technology stack independently.
## One Ecosystem, Multiple Specialist Platforms
Launching a modern financial business can require trading technology, CRM, customer onboarding, payment infrastructure, card management, reporting, automation and back-office systems.
KALZERO’s approach is to connect these capabilities through an ecosystem of specialized technology brands.
Instead of relying on multiple unrelated providers, businesses can access different parts of their infrastructure through solutions designed to work together.
This gives companies greater flexibility while helping them create a more consistent experience for both customers and internal teams.
## ZeroTrade for Brokerage Infrastructure
**ZeroTrade** provides white-label brokerage infrastructure for businesses looking to launch a new brokerage or modernize an existing operation.
Its technology can support:
* Branded trading platforms
* Broker CRM and back-office systems
* Client portals
* Risk management
* IB and affiliate management
* PAMM and copy trading
* Prop trading infrastructure
* Payment integrations
* Account management
* Reporting and analytics
The objective is to give brokerage businesses greater control over their technology and customer-facing brand.
ZeroTrade can also work alongside existing trading infrastructure, allowing established brokers to introduce a modern client experience while retaining parts of their existing technology environment.
## NetPay247.com for Payments and Card Programs
**NetPay247.com** forms another important part of the KALZERO ecosystem, providing technology for businesses looking to build modern payment and card experiences.
The platform can support branded physical and virtual card programs, payment workflows, customer management and related financial technology infrastructure.
Depending on the applicable program structure and issuing arrangements, businesses can build experiences around:
* Physical and virtual cards
* Customer onboarding
* Card activation and controls
* Digital wallet integration
* Account funding
* Transaction visibility
* Spend management
* Card administration
* Payment workflows
* Reporting and operational controls
The goal is to help businesses create financial products under their own brand while using established technology infrastructure behind the customer experience.
Businesses can learn more about the platform at **NetPay247.com**.
## CRM, Automation and Customer Operations
KALZERO also connects CRM and operational technology across the wider ecosystem.
Businesses can manage leads, customer profiles, onboarding, sales activity, documents, communication, support interactions and internal workflows from connected systems.
Automation can be used across customer onboarding, follow-ups, lead distribution, account activity, reporting and internal operations.
Rather than treating CRM, payments and customer activity as separate systems, KALZERO’s strategy is to make these technologies part of a more connected customer journey.
## White-Label by Design
A major part of the KALZERO model is giving businesses control over their own brand.
Technology across ZeroTrade, NetPay247.com and the wider KALZERO ecosystem can be configured around the client’s customer-facing experience.
This can include branded trading platforms, client portals, dashboards, card programs, CRM systems, payment journeys and operational tools.
KALZERO and its specialist platforms operate behind the infrastructure while the business remains at the center of the customer relationship.
## Built for Businesses That Want to Launch Faster
Developing financial technology internally can require significant engineering resources, integrations and ongoing maintenance.
KALZERO aims to reduce this complexity by providing businesses with configurable infrastructure that can be adapted to different products and operating models.
A company may begin with CRM technology, for example, and later introduce ZeroTrade brokerage infrastructure, NetPay247 payment or card capabilities, additional automation or other connected services.
This modular approach allows businesses to expand their technology as they grow.
## Building the Infrastructure Behind Modern Financial Brands
KALZERO’s wider vision is to create an ecosystem where businesses can launch and operate multiple financial products without managing an increasingly fragmented technology stack.
With **ZeroTrade** supporting brokerage infrastructure and **NetPay247.com** supporting payments and card technology, KALZERO is building a broader foundation for businesses that want to launch, operate and scale under their own brand.
**KALZERO — Build the brand. We power what’s behind it.**
## About KALZERO
KALZERO is a technology and business infrastructure ecosystem providing solutions for companies building modern financial and digital products.
Its ecosystem includes brokerage technology through **ZeroTrade**, payment and card technology through **NetPay247.com**, alongside CRM, back-office systems, client onboarding, automation, analytics and operational management technology.
KALZERO is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and works with businesses looking to build scalable, white-label technology under their own brand.

articles.title: War shows that technology changes military arithmetic but does not abolish it — expert
articles.description: War shows that technology changes military arithmetic but does not abolish it — expert Ukrinform
articles.description_html: War shows that technology changes military arithmetic but does not abolish it — expert  Ukrinform
articles.article_title: War shows that technology changes military arithmetic but does not abolish it — expert
articles.heading: Ukrinform - Ukrainian National News Agency
articles.summary: The war in Ukraine has demonstrated that modern technologies can significantly alter the balance of forces on the battlefield, but they do not eliminate basic military calculations or the need for resources. — Ukrinform.
articles.content:
War shows that technology changes military arithmetic but does not abolish it — expert
Can Kasapoğlu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, stated this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Technology compresses military arithmetic; it does not abolish it. The war in Ukraine has resurrected First World War trenches—and humans must still man and hold them," Kasapoğlu said.
The expert emphasized that even amid rapid technological development, the outcome of a war largely depends on the ability of the sides to provide their forces with the necessary resources and maintain their capacity to conduct military operations.
"Drones do the killing for over 80 percent of the battlefield targets, while Kyiv is shifting frontline logistics to ground robots. Yet this is an adaptation contest, not a Ukrainian monopoly: Russia has learned and institutionalized drone warfare through formations such as Rubicon," Kasapoğlu said.
At the same time, he called the maritime dimension of the Russian-Ukrainian war the most convincing evidence that technology can compensate for a numerical disadvantage.
"Without a navy, Ukraine has damaged or eliminated a share of Russia's Black Sea Fleet and denied it freedom of action. Unmanned surface vessels, USVs, and anti-ship missiles helped prevent an amphibious threat to Odesa," he said.
As Ukrinform reported, Can Kasapoğlu believes that Ukraine is providing NATO countries with invaluable lessons — from the effective use of low-cost technologies on the battlefield to building national resilience and preparing for prolonged wars.
Photo provided by Can Kasapoğlu

articles.title: Adult Learner Finds His Future Through Central Tech’s Diesel Technology Program
articles.description: Adult Learner Finds His Future Through Central Tech’s Diesel Technology Program Sapulpa Times
articles.description_html: Adult Learner Finds His Future Through Central Tech’s Diesel Technology Program  Sapulpa Times
articles.article_title: Adult Learner Finds His Future Through Central Tech's Diesel Technology Program
articles.heading: Adult Learner Finds His Future Through Central Tech’s Diesel Technology Program
articles.summary: When Kyle Adair graduated from high school, he knew exactly what he wanted to do. Growing up with a father who worked as a mechanic, he had always enjoyed t ...
articles.content:
Drumright, Okla. – When Kyle Adair graduated from high school, he knew exactly what he wanted to do. Growing up with a father who worked as a mechanic, he had always enjoyed turning wrenches and working with equipment. What he didn’t know was how to turn that passion into a career.
“I’ve known what I wanted to do. I just didn’t know how to get there,” Adair said.
That path led him to Central Tech’s Diesel Technology program, but not in the way many people might expect. While many students attend Central Tech during their junior and senior years of high school, Adair took a different route. He enrolled as an adult learner after graduation, proving it’s never too late to take the next step toward a career.
Through the CHOICES Tuition Waiver, Adair was able to attend tuition-free and begin building a future in the diesel industry. The waiver gave him the opportunity to take that next step without the financial burden that can often stand in the way of additional training.
To balance school with work, Adair started the program as a half-day student. The flexible schedule allowed him to continue earning a paycheck while building new skills and industry knowledge. After completing his first year, he decided to fully commit to his education and transitioned to full-time training. The additional time in the shop each day allowed him to build confidence, sharpen his skills, and take a more active role in projects.
“You’re able to complete a task more efficiently because you might work with two different groups, but you know what the morning group did versus the afternoon,” Adair said. “You can kind of help guide everybody else along. It allows you more time to dig into stuff.” That extra time also helped him discover something unexpected about himself.
Under the guidance of Diesel Technology Instructor Liam Shaklee, students work on a wide variety of equipment. For Adair, that exposure opened doors he didn’t know existed. “Mr. Shaklee’s done a very good job of having you work on anything from light-duty pickups to tractors to semis,” Adair said. “You get to know what you like to work on and what you don’t like to work on. That’s kind of a fun thing about it.”
That variety helped Adair discover a career path he never expected. “I didn’t know I liked working on tractors until I came here and started going through the coursework,” he said. Like many adult learners, Adair entered the program with an interest in the field but without a clear understanding of where his interests would fit within the industry. The exposure to multiple types of equipment helped him find his niche and ultimately shaped his career direction.
Today, Adair works for P&K Equipment in Stillwater, where he puts those skills to work every day. His journey from adult learner to diesel technician shows how career training can help adults gain skills, earn certifications, and get to work faster.
Since beginning his career at P&K, Adair has continued to make an impact beyond the workplace. His strong work ethic and performance helped strengthen the relationship between Central Tech and the company, creating additional opportunities for future students.
According to Shaklee, Adair’s transition from student to industry professional has come full circle. “Kyle has been a huge resource for Central Tech,” Shaklee said. “He made a great impression at P&K and helped open the door for us to work more closely together.” In just two years, Adair has gone from student to serving on the program’s advisory committee, helping provide industry insight that supports the next generation of diesel technicians. “He’s a great young man with a bright future ahead of him,” Shaklee said. “I’m glad Central Tech was here to help him get the career he wanted started.”
For Adair, the combination of hands-on training, industry-relevant experience, and certifications helped prepare him for the workforce. “It does make it easier to get hired if you have certificates,” Adair said.
His advice is especially relevant for adults who may be considering a career change, pursuing additional training, or looking for a way to turn an interest into a profession. Sometimes the next step is simply finding the right path forward.
To learn more about the CHOICES Tuition Waiver or about adult learner opportunities visit centraltech.edu.
About Central Technology Center: Everyone achieves success.
Central Tech provides hands-on learning and technical education, dedicated to empowering students with practical skills and technical knowledge for immediate application. Powered by the Oklahoma CareerTech system, Central Tech serves 26 diverse communities, offering a wide range of programs that cater to high school students, adults, and industry professionals. With over 400 business partnerships, the tech center provides customized training solutions contributing to economic growth. The Truck Driver Training Program, offered in partnership with other technology centers, spans several locations across Oklahoma. Central Tech fosters a culture of success and lifelong learning.

articles.title: How Modern Technology Is Changing County Fairs in Ohio
articles.description: How Modern Technology Is Changing County Fairs in Ohio My County Link
articles.description_html: How Modern Technology Is Changing County Fairs in Ohio  My County Link
articles.article_title: How Modern Technology Is Changing County Fairs in Ohio | My County Link
articles.heading: How Modern Technology Is Changing County Fairs in Ohio
articles.summary: County fairs have long been an Ohio tradition, bringing together agriculture, entertainment, food, competitions and community. While many fair traditions
articles.content:
County fairs have long been an Ohio tradition, bringing together agriculture, entertainment, food, competitions and community. While many fair traditions remain the same, modern technology is changing how visitors experience these annual events.
One of the biggest changes is the use of smartphones. Fairgoers can use their phones to check schedules, find event information, take photos and share their experiences on social media. Fair organizations can also use websites and social media to quickly announce schedule changes, weather updates and other important information.
Digital ticketing and cashless payments are also becoming more common. Visitors may be able to purchase admission or event tickets online before arriving, while vendors can use mobile payment systems to accept credit cards and digital wallets.
Technology is also playing a growing role in agriculture. Today’s farmers use GPS-guided equipment, drones, sensors, automated feeding systems and other advanced tools. County fairs provide an opportunity for young people and adults to showcase agriculture while introducing visitors to some of the technology being used on modern farms.
Photography and video have changed the fair experience as well. Smartphones, digital cameras and drones can capture everything from livestock competitions to rides and concerts, allowing fair memories to be shared with thousands of people online almost instantly.
Technology can even improve fair safety. Digital communication, security cameras, weather monitoring and emergency notification systems can help organizers respond more quickly when problems arise.
Despite all these changes, technology hasn’t replaced what makes an Ohio county fair special. The livestock barns, midway rides, food stands, competitions and conversations with friends and neighbors remain at the heart of the experience.
Modern technology simply gives county fairs new ways to communicate, operate and connect with the community—helping an old Ohio tradition continue to thrive in a digital world.

articles.title: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | Letters
articles.description: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | Letters The Guardian
articles.description_html: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | Letters  The Guardian
articles.article_title: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | Letters
articles.heading: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced
articles.summary: Letters: Dr Simon Nieder on the global efforts needed to curb the threats posed by AI. Plus letters from Dr Anthony Harris and David Kyler
articles.content:
Timothy Garton Ash is right that serious artificial intelligence risks demand international action, but “AI Hiroshima” may be the wrong picture (Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not, 22 August). Hiroshima was not technology going rogue. Human beings designed the bomb, authorised its use and dropped it. The technology worked much as intended.
AI may one day behave in ways we cannot control, but many of the gravest harms could happen without any dramatic moment when “the AI takes over”. AI might help design a pathogen, find a vulnerability in critical infrastructure or improve a weapons system while people still decide what happens next. Other harms may build almost invisibly through thousands of ordinary decisions – more autonomy here, one safeguard removed there, another consequential task handed over because the system has worked well so far. By the time the danger is obvious, the important decisions may already have been made.
That is also where international agreement could begin. We do not need countries to agree about superintelligence or the probability of human extinction before agreeing that there are some doors AI should never be allowed to open by itself. Weapons systems, critical infrastructure and biological synthesis are obvious places to start. Governments could agree minimum safeguards, require clear human authority for the most consequential actions, keep records of who authorised what and share serious failures and near-misses internationally.
The greatest AI dangers may not arrive with a mushroom cloud. They may arrive quietly, one apparently reasonable step at a time. If we want effective AI governance, we need to fight the right battle, not the most cinematic one.
Dr Simon Nieder
Chesterfield, Derbyshire
Prof Jonathan Michie (Letters, 26 August) reminds us that the Serbelloni group, led by the author’s father, Donald Michie (when he was at Edinburgh University), was weighing the social dangers of artificial intelligence as long ago as 1972. Nor is AI technology itself new, since its roots run back through to Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron of 1957, to the Dartmouth workshop of 1956, and to Alan Turing before that. What is new is that we now have the hardware and software infrastructures to drive it forward at what can sometimes seem to be a terrifying speed.
The Lighthill report of 1973 duly delivered an AI winter in the UK, and the field’s centre of gravity crossed the Atlantic, with the consequences that we all now live with. articles.title: Smart glasses should automatically blur people’s faces while filming, Australia’s online safety regulator says
articles.description: Smart glasses should automatically blur people’s faces while filming, Australia’s online safety regulator says The Guardian
articles.description_html: Smart glasses should automatically blur people’s faces while filming, Australia’s online safety regulator says  The Guardian
articles.article_title: Smart glasses should automatically blur people’s faces while filming, Australia’s online safety regulator says
articles.heading: Smart glasses should automatically blur people’s faces while filming, Australia’s online safety regulator says
articles.summary: Smart glasses with cameras can benefit the vision impaired but companies might pit ‘accessibility benefits against safety and privacy’, says eSafety
articles.content:
Australia’s online safety regulator has urged smart glasses companies to automatically blur people’s faces filmed on the devices, and make it clearer when someone is filming, as the federal government faces pressure to ban the technology.
In advice to industry published on Monday, the office of eSafety commissioner warned that while smart glasses with cameras, such as Meta’s Ray-Ban, can offer accessibility benefits to low vision or blind people, companies might pit “accessibility benefits against safety and privacy considerations,” and noted there was already a backlash to the technology.
Dubbed “pervert glasses” by some, there are reports of women being filmed without their consent and their interactions with a glasses-wearing influencer posted on social media.
The eSafety commission said many companies were placing responsibility on consumers to use the glasses safely, but said “asking people to use a product responsibly is not an adequate safety policy”.
“It also overlooks how smart glasses are actually used.
“The harms linked to covert recording are not hypothetical. They are real and already occurring.”
It warned that so-called “pickup artist” content filmed using the glasses often led to misogynistic comments, and the prevalence of this content could normalise watching, recording and controlling women in public without their knowledge.
The regulator said developers “have a critical opportunity” to embed safer design practices while the technology is evolving.
The design features should include clear visual indicators when recording audio or video that cannot be disabled or obscured, eSafety said.
The glasses should also not be able to identify members of the public, and should automatically blur people’s faces where they have not provided informed consent.
“If we do not act now to prevent design elements from being weaponised to cause harm, we risk unsafe features becoming entrenched,” eSafety said.
The eSafety commissioner currently has no powers to force the companies to make the changes, and the federal government is facing pressure to step in as the market for smart glasses grows.
The attorney-general will separately release an exposure draft for the government’s second round of privacy reforms that will seek to address rules around smart glasses. Guardian Australia understands this will not include a ban on the technology.
After Brisbane city council announced plans last week to ban recording devices, including smart glasses, from public pools, the federal assistant minister for technology, Andrew Charlton, told Seven’s Sunrise program the smart glasses were “a really scary thing” as they became cheaper and more accessible.
“That raises a lot of understandable fears,” he said.
The Australian privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, was asked by the attorney general to assess the privacy implications of the glasses earlier this month, and Charlton said the commissioner could take a number of steps “including banning them”.
It is understood the privacy commissioner also does not have powers to ban the devices but there are moves to change this.
The ABC reported last week that the Greens, with the support of several cross-benchers, plan to introduce a private member’s bill to ban the glasses for 12 months until privacy law catches up.
John Pane, chair of the digital rights group, Electronic Frontiers Australia, said the federal Privacy Act was not designed to cover smart glasses, but said state surveillance device laws could be updated.
“This could be achieved in 12 months,” he said. “We are supportive of an immediate temporary ban on these covert wearable surveillance devices subject to a specific carve out on them remaining available to people who are significantly sight impaired.”
The push to ban smart glasses began with a petition after Guardian Australia’s report earlier this month that Kmart Anko $89 smart glasses had sold out across the country.
Bars, courts, hospitals and other semi-public locations contacted by Guardian Australia this month indicated they did not yet have specific policies regarding smart glasses, with most pointing to existing rules restricting recording.
A number of schools have already begun adding wearable devices to mobile phone bans already in place.
Device bans in individual institutions won’t solve the issue, and the obligations should sit with the companies making the technology and the retailers selling it, said Victoria University’s associate professor in AI governance in education, Janine Arantes.
Arantes said the underlying harms, such as filming without consent, bullying, harassment and privacy violations, must be the policy focus.
“The technology changes – discretion, accessibility, speed and eventually the scale of what can be done – but recording isn’t new, cyberbullying isn’t new, harassment isn’t new, smartphones aren’t new,” she said.
“Just the capability of the technology through which those behaviours can occur is new – [so] why not address the behaviours?”

articles.title: Caterpillar is bringing to AI deployment what it learned from automating mining
articles.description: Caterpillar is bringing to AI deployment what it learned from automating mining TechCrunch
articles.description_html: Caterpillar is bringing to AI deployment what it learned from automating mining  TechCrunch
articles.article_title: Caterpillar is bringing to AI deployment what it learned from automating mining | TechCrunch
articles.heading: Caterpillar is bringing to AI deployment what it learned from automating mining
articles.summary: Caterpillar has spent decades putting autonomous machines to work at remote mining sites. It's now bringing that experience to AI deployment.
articles.content:
Nearly every company that’s trying to deploy artificial intelligence runs into the same problem: it’s hard to integrate the tech into everyday operations. Industrial heavyweight Caterpillar has spent decades dealing with a version of that problem in the physical world, and now it’s using its experience to deploy AI.
Caterpillar’s push into the autonomous space started with mining, where labor shortages and hazardous conditions can make automation particularly useful. Today, it sells automated haul trucks, drilling, underground loaders, dozers, remote-controlled construction equipment, and more. It also offers a software command center, fleet management, and even remote terrain intelligence as part of its autonomous toolkit.
“Now we’re in this super exciting time where we can take all of that learning from mining and bring it into much more dynamic environments, jobsites, quarries, and construction sites,” the company’s CTO, Jaime Mineart, told TechCrunch on the sidelines of the Ai4 conference in Las Vegas earlier this month.
The industrial giant is now applying AI more broadly, including in tools used by technicians and its own employees. One example is the Cat AI Assistant, which lets field technicians standing next to a machine use voice commands to pull up repair procedures, troubleshoot potential problems, and identify parts that may be needed before beginning a repair. Mineart said the tool is now being used by customers, operators and technicians.
The assistant draws on Caterpillar’s proprietary data, which spans information generated by its connected machines. Mineart said Caterpillar has about 1.6 million connected assets globally and more than 16 petabytes of structured data.
The company is also using AI to power software for scanning sites and generating digital twins in manufacturing to analyze operations, she said. And like nearly every other company, Caterpillar is using AI across its enterprise operations, as well as for software development. “We use AI agents to modernize legacy code, generate and test new software, and identify defects earlier,” Mineart said.
But Mineart is quick to point out that building the technology is only part of the challenge, as deploying an autonomous machine is not the same as transforming a site to use AI. Companies also have to rethink how people work alongside the technology and how existing processes need to change.
“The hard part about autonomy and about physical AI is incorporating that technology into the customer jobsite and into the workflows,” she said.
Mineart said the company leans on experienced operators to help train AI systems, leveraging institutional knowledge built over decades. And as machines become more autonomous, some operators may shift from controlling a single machine to overseeing multiple machines from a remote command center.
That transition, however, is creating a new challenge for Caterpillar: training its 118,000 employees. Mineart said the company plans to spend $100 million over the next five years to train its workforce in AI, autonomy and robotics.
That investment is likely being put towards helping the company make the most of the broader boom in AI infrastructure, which is already helping its top-line. Caterpillar’s quarterly revenue reached an all-time high of $20.5 billion in the second quarter, helped by strong demand for power-generation equipment used in data centers. Its power-generation division saw sales spike 72% to $3.10 billion, and CEO Joe Creed said that “no one is slowing down” when it comes to demand for cloud computing and generative AI infrastructure.

articles.title: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI | Gene Marks
articles.description: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI | Gene Marks The Guardian
articles.description_html: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI | Gene Marks  The Guardian
articles.article_title: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI | Gene Marks
articles.heading: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI
articles.summary: Small business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what works
articles.content:
One thing I’ve learned about corporate America is that what it succeeds at ultimately trickles down to benefit small businesses. Bleeding-edge technologies such as the internet, mobile transactions and the cloud were first perfected by large organizations – government and corporations – and now they’re available to the masses at a much lower cost and with better reliability.
The good news is that it’s also the same for what they fail at.
This is the lesson so far with artificial intelligence. Thanks to the billions invested – and in many cases squandered – by big brands, SMBs (small and mid-sized businesses) have learned what works, what doesn’t, where to spend and where to abstain. Small businesses should be grateful. We’re getting the answers without paying for all the mistakes.
What works: AI for software development, customer service, security and voice. Big technology companies are already using AI to write, review and test code, allowing smaller development teams to accomplish more. Other firms have leaned in to AI to help with a variety of customer service processes with some success. IT departments are relying heavily on AI-enabled security platforms to detect and remedy unusual behavior, phishing attacks, and other vulnerabilities. Big brands are rolling out more AI-powered voice systems that answer incoming calls and perform rudimentary actions.
Small businesses are watching. And now doing.
A countless number of the developers laid off by big tech are using AI tools to replicate themselves and provide services for smaller companies on a larger scale, and we’re hiring them.
Big companies have also begun to discover the astronomical computing costs that can result when employees and AI agents consume enormous numbers of tokens. Oh yes, we’ve seen that too. Small businesses like mine have watched large companies throw away billons on large-scale projects with little to show for it. We can’t afford to do the same.
But we’re not scared away. Instead, we’re picking low-hanging fruit.
Big companies have taught smaller businesses how not to advertise their AI investments.
For months, on earnings calls and investor meetings, big company CEOs have gushed over the cost savings and headcount reductions they expect to realize with AI, and this resulted mostly in a backlash from their employees and the general public. SMBs – short of talent and long on needs – have watched and learned to do the opposite, using AI to increase productivity without lowering payroll. As a result, we have become more appealing to workers who are disgusted by the absence of loyalty and terrified over the lack of job protection at their corporate employers.
We have watched corporations implement mass layoffs while using AI as their cover for their mismanagement and over-hiring, only to hire those same employees back. AI is an easy scapegoat. At my company, we’re using AI to increase productivity, not to announce payroll reductions.
Thanks to larger corporations, which have struggled with the reliability and accuracy of agentic AI, SMBs have learned not to trust those agents that are supposed to be doing everything for them … yet. We’re not replacing our accounting, marketing and customer service departments anytime soon. However, we’re using AI more to help analyze our businesses, make recommendations and suggest strategies. We’ll let the big companies beta-test all those agents. We’re patient. And we don’t trust anyone, particularly bots.
Most important, big corporations have taught small business owners like me to trust our guts and have faith in our common sense. All of the predictions made since ChatGPT was first introduced – mass layoffs, universal income, AGI, robots doing laundry, new worlds in the metaverse, self-driving cars – haven’t happened yet. Even OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, recently admitted that their timelines for AI adoption were “too ambitious”. He’s right.
Of course there will be many changes to the way we do business in the future thanks to the progress of artificial intelligence. I’m sure there will be all sorts of tools to increase our productivity and profitability. But you know what? I’ll let the big corporations figure all that out on their dime.

articles.heading: SayRose Introduces a New Era of Aesthetic Technology Gifts at IFA 2026
articles.summary: SHENZHEN, China, Aug.  30, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- SayRose, a lifestyle consumer electronics brand dedicated to aesthetic technology gifts, toda...
articles.content:
Aug. 30, 2026, 08:45 AM




SHENZHEN, China, Aug. 30, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- SayRose, a lifestyle consumer electronics brand dedicated to aesthetic technology gifts, today announced its participation in IFA 2026, where it will introduce its latest product portfolio and present its vision for the future of design-driven consumer technology.
https://www.tiktok.com/@sayrose.de1/video/7669753651769920790?lang=de-DE
During the exhibition, SayRose will showcase a wide range of new products that combine elegant design, practical functionality and everyday usability, reflecting the growing demand for consumer electronics that are not only intelligent, but also expressive and giftable.
Visitors can experience the latest SayRose innovations at Hall 2.2, Booth 110 at Messe Berlin.
https://www.tiktok.com/@sayrose.de1/video/7672686919410634006?lang=de-DE
Introducing Aesthetic Technology Gifts
As consumer expectations continue to evolve, electronics are becoming more than functional devices. They are increasingly viewed as lifestyle products that reflect personal taste, emotional connection and thoughtful design.
Built around this belief, SayRose introduces the concept of Aesthetic Technology Gifts —consumer electronics designed to combine technology, aesthetics and meaningful everyday experiences
Rather than focusing solely on specifications, SayRose creates products that seamlessly integrate into modern lifestyles while offering lasting emotional connection through design.

Products Designed for Everyday Life
At IFA 2026, SayRose will present its newest collection across multiple product categories, including:
- Premium headphones and audio products
- Portable speakers
- Magnetic charging solutions
- Mobile accessories
- Lifestyle digital products
- Gift-oriented consumer electronics
Every SayRose product is created around the philosophy of Design · Emotion · Gift.
Designed for commuting, working, traveling and gifting, each product combines refined aesthetics with practical innovation, making technology feel more personal and meaningful.
A distinctive feature of the SayRose experience is Vikky , the brand's signature IP character.
Rather than serving as a standalone mascot, Vikky is thoughtfully integrated into product design, packaging and interactive details, adding warmth and personality to every interaction.
Whether appearing as collectible design elements or delightful product companions, Vikky transforms everyday electronics into products that people enjoy using, collecting and gifting.
Through the integration of Design, Emotion and Gift , SayRose creates technology that is not only functional, but also memorable.
https://www.tiktok.com/@sayrose.de1/video/7677777397613219094
Designed for Global Partnerships
As demand grows for differentiated lifestyle electronics, SayRose continues expanding its global presence through products built on Design · Emotion · Gift.
The company is actively seeking partnerships with retailers, distributors, e-commerce platforms and gift channels worldwide.
By combining original design, reliable manufacturing and market-oriented innovation, SayRose aims to help global partners deliver products that consumers not only need—but genuinely love.
https://www.tiktok.com/@sayrose.de1/video/7673793889878166806?lang=de-DE
Experience SayRose at IFA 2026
Visitors attending IFA 2026 are invited to explore SayRose's newest innovations and discover how aesthetic design can reshape everyday technology.
IFA 2026
Venue: Messe Berlin
Booth: Hall 2.2, Booth 110
Date: September 4–8, 2026
Industry partners, distributors, retailers and media representatives are welcome to visit the SayRose booth for product demonstrations and business discussions.
About SayRose


SayRose is a lifestyle consumer electronics brand dedicated to creating Aesthetic Technology Gifts for consumers around the world.
Guided by its brand philosophy—Design · Emotion · Gift —SayRose combines thoughtful design, practical innovation and emotional experiences to create products that inspire modern lifestyles.
From everyday essentials to meaningful gifts, SayRose believes technology should not only perform beautifully, but also create emotional connections that last.
As the brand continues expanding internationally, SayRose remains committed to delivering innovative consumer electronics that inspire modern lifestyles and create lasting connections between technology and people.

articles.title: Integration of Biomechanical Analysis and Motion Capture Technology in Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation: A Systematic Review
articles.description: Integration of Biomechanical Analysis and Motion Capture Technology in Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation: A Systematic Review Cureus
articles.description_html: Integration of Biomechanical Analysis and Motion Capture Technology in Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation: A Systematic Review  Cureus
articles.article_title: Integration of Biomechanical Analysis and Motion Capture Technology in Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation: A Systematic Review
articles.heading: Integration of Biomechanical Analysis and Motion Capture Technology in Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation: A Systematic Review
articles.summary: Biomechanical analysis and motion-capture technology have emerged as valuable tools for the objective assessment of human movement in physical therapy and rehabilitation. These technologies provide quantitative information on gait, balance, posture, joint kinematics, and functional performance, thereby supporting clinical decision-making and individualized rehabilitation. Despite increasing clinical adoption, evidence regarding their effectiveness across different rehabilitation populations remains heterogeneous. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the integration of biomechanical analysis and motion-capture technology in physical therapy and rehabilitation. A systematic literature search was conducted across major electronic databases to identify randomized controlled trials evaluating the integration of biomechanical analysis and motion-capture technologies within physical therapy and rehabilitation. Studies that investigated biomechanical analysis, motion-capture systems, wearable sensors, virtual reality, and markerless motion-capture technologies in physical therapy interventions were considered. Methodological quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and a narrative synthesis was performed because of clinical and methodological heterogeneity. The evidence encompassed neurological, musculoskeletal, pediatric, geriatric, and oncological rehabilitation populations. Interventions incorporated Kinect-based rehabilitation, markerless motion capture, wearable sensor systems, virtual reality, robot-assisted gait training, movement biofeedback, and sensor-augmented telerehabilitation. Overall, the evidence indicated improvements in gait, balance, postural control, movement quality, functional mobility, limb-loading symmetry, upper limb function, and quality of life across various rehabilitation settings. Risk of bias assessment indicated generally low risk of bias or some concerns, although concerns related to deviations from intended interventions and reporting practices were observed across the evidence base. The integration of biomechanical analysis and motion-capture technology may enhance objective movement assessment and support functional recovery across diverse rehabilitation populations. These technologies may facilitate individualized rehabilitation and evidence-based clinical decision-making through quantitative movement analysis and feedback. However, methodological heterogeneity highlights the need for standardized assessment protocols and high-quality trials to establish their long-term clinical effectiveness and support broader implementation in rehabilitation practice.

articles.title: Oakland Schools builds AI strategy as educators navigate promise, pitfalls of new technology
articles.description: Oakland Schools builds AI strategy as educators navigate promise, pitfalls of new technology The Oakland Press
articles.description_html: Oakland Schools builds AI strategy as educators navigate promise, pitfalls of new technology  The Oakland Press
articles.article_title: Oakland Schools builds AI strategy as educators navigate promise, pitfalls of new technology
articles.heading: Oakland Schools builds AI strategy as educators navigate promise, pitfalls of new technology
articles.summary: Only 30% of teens in the survey said they had discussed AI safety with a teacher, and just 27% said they had discussed AI literacy.
articles.content:
As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly woven into students’ schoolwork and teachers’ daily routines, Oakland Schools is taking a more deliberate approach: Teach educators how to use the technology, help districts develop policies and keep humans at the center of education.
That effort is being led by Justin Bruno, director of AI Strategy and Innovation at Oakland Schools, who was hired in September 2025 to help develop an all-encompassing strategy for artificial intelligence.
“I think that was evidence of Oakland Schools making this a priority,” Bruno said. “Trying to figure out what sorts of strategies we need to be setting internally around AI, and how that’s going to fit into our operations, and how we do things.”
Bruno recently added Shana Ramin from Royal Oak as an AI consultant to his team, who will work directly with local school districts to help them plan, implement and strategize around emerging challenges and opportunities.
The work comes as schools across Oakland County and the country grapple with a technology that students are already using.
Common Sense Media, an independent non-profit education research group, released a study in August that asked more than 1,000 U.S. students between 13 and 17 years old about how they use AI. Seventy percent said they use AI for schoolwork, and nearly two-thirds of those students said they use it in ways that can shift critical thinking from the students to the technology.
Among teens who use AI for schoolwork, 63% said they get an answer from AI in at least one way: 35% said they get an answer and then fix or improve it based on what they know; 31% said they get an answer and rewrite it to sound like themselves, and 25% said they use an AI-generated answer as-is.
The findings underscore the challenge facing educators. AI is a powerful tool, but it makes it easier for students to bypass the very thinking and practice that assignments are designed to develop.
At the same time, students appear to recognize the trade-offs.
Thirty-eight percent of AI-using teens said the technology leads them to generate fewer of their own ideas, while 39% said they feel they are missing out on learning when they use AI to complete assignments. Yet 66% said AI helps them understand schoolwork, suggesting that students’ experiences with the technology are more complicated than a simple cheating-versus-no-cheating debate.
Common Sense Media cautioned against assuming that students themselves are the primary problem.
“As educators and policymakers weigh risks, we should be cautious about narratives that instinctively blame teens for using AI in schoolwork,” the report said, arguing that schools also need to consider the broader culture and incentives surrounding AI use.
For Oakland Schools, that means focusing on literacy and responsible use rather than relying exclusively on bans.
Training educators to use AI
Oakland Schools has adopted ChatGPT EDU, an education-focused version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, giving staff access to the tool. Because the organization uses Google Workspace, staff also have access to Gemini, another AI platform.
It is rolling out a monthly webinar series designed to help employees understand what the tools can do and how they might fit into everyday workflows.
Districts have designated professional development days throughout the year, and Oakland Schools is increasingly being asked to provide AI training during those sessions. The agency also plans countywide conferences, sessions and webinars for educators who can attend voluntarily.
Educators might learn how to use AI tools in their daily work, but the sessions also will address instructional questions, such as how a social studies teacher might rethink assessments in an era when students can turn to AI or how educators might use emerging tools to better understand student progress.
“There might be a new AI tool that’s just debuted in the last couple years that might be really helpful,” Bruno said. “We’re trying to build those training initiatives.”
Rather than attempting to deliver every message directly to every educator, Oakland Schools is also working with district-level leaders who can help spread AI guidance.
The approach recognizes that each district is at a different point in its AI journey.
Bruno points to Royal Oak as one of the leaders in the county. Avondale Schools also has taken a proactive approach under the leadership of Michelle Gierman, he said. The district has created a Student AI Advisory Council and regularly has students update district leaders on how they are using AI.
He said Oxford Schools is developing guidance for staff and students while considering questions surrounding AI tools and assessment redesign.
Holly Schools is earlier in the process, but has made AI a priority for the school year. The district recently released guidance for staff and is emphasizing professional development, along with expectations that schools and teachers address digital citizenship and AI literacy with students throughout the year.
“There’s some great stuff happening in the county,” Bruno said.
Moving beyond the chatbot debate
The rapid growth of AI has also created a new education technology market.
Companies such as MagicSchool, SchoolAI and Brisk have emerged as prominent AI-focused tools for K-12 education. Unlike general-purpose AI systems, some of these platforms offer additional guardrails and features designed specifically for schools.
That distinction matters as districts decide how students should access AI.
A district might be comfortable giving older students access to a general-purpose tool such as ChatGPT or Gemini while deciding that younger students need a more controlled environment.
But Bruno said schools ultimately need to think beyond simply deciding which tools students can or cannot use.
“We still want to encourage a systemic change,” he said. “Because when kids go home and do that work, they’re going to have access to tools that everyone has access to that can be used for good or for ill.”
The Common Sense report findings reinforce that concern. Among teens who use AI for schoolwork, 44% said an AI tool had been blocked on a school network or device. Of those students, 59% said they simply switched to a personal device to get around the ban.
The report also found a significant gap in AI literacy education. Only 27% of teens said a teacher had ever talked with them about how to use AI safely, while 73% said they had not.
The report also said blanket bans and one-size-fits-all restrictions can prevent some students from benefiting from technology and urged schools to leave room for accommodations based on individual student needs.
For Bruno, the answer lies in teaching students how to navigate AI rather than assuming they can be shielded from it.
Keeping people at the center
Bruno’s approach is rooted in a broader question: What should AI actually be doing in a school?
Education, he said, is fundamentally human and he sees AI as a way to strengthen work educators are already doing.
“Education is such a human-focused thing, and we don’t want to be automating things that would still benefit from the human being the primary deliverer of or facilitator of that service,” he said. “ So by no means am I thinking we’re going to automate or speed up things. It’s more of how can we use AI to do what we’ve always done better for more people.”
That distinction becomes important when considering AI tools that can grade papers or provide feedback on student writing.
Those tools can help a teacher who is overwhelmed by an ever growing workload and class sizes. But Bruno said schools should be careful not to confuse efficiency with educational effectiveness.
“The expertise of that human and the motivation that that human can provide to improve their writing, or to improve their work over time” remain essential, he said.
An AI system may be able to identify weaknesses in a student’s writing, but a teacher can understand the student behind the writing and provide encouragement, context and motivation that a machine cannot replicate in the same way.
That human relationship is something Bruno said should remain central even as schools adopt increasingly sophisticated technology.
A critical year for AI literacy
The Common Sense study suggests schools have little time to waste in developing AI literacy.
Only 30% of teens in the survey said they had discussed AI safety with a teacher, and just 27% said they had discussed AI literacy. Forty-four percent said they had talked with a teacher about rules governing when they should and should not use AI.
The report characterized the current school year as an important opportunity for teachers to begin those conversations.
Students themselves also identified skills they believe will remain important in the future. Among AI-using teens, 55% identified working well with others as an important future skill, 50% cited fact-checking and critical thinking, and 48% cited reading and understanding complex information.
Those are the kinds of skills educators are trying to protect as AI becomes more capable.
For Oakland Schools, the goal is not simply to keep pace with a rapidly changing technology. It is to help districts make thoughtful decisions about where AI belongs — and where it does not.
As a new department, Bruno said, his team is building on work that was already underway at Oakland Schools before he arrived.
“There was great AI work happening before I came on board,” he said. “Oakland Schools were leading lots of great learning, and so now we’re just kind of accelerating that and trying to be a leader in the state.”
He believes the agency is moving in that direction.
The challenge now is to make sure the technology advances without leaving the people at the heart of education behind.

A district might be comfortable giving older students access to a general-purpose tool such as ChatGPT or Gemini while deciding that younger students need a more controlled environment.

But Bruno said schools ultimately need to think beyond simply deciding which tools students can or cannot use.

“We still want to encourage a systemic change,” he said. “Because when kids go home and do that work, they’re going to have access to tools that everyone has access to that can be used for good or for ill.”

The Common Sense report findings reinforce that concern. Among teens who use AI for schoolwork, 44% said an AI tool had been blocked on a school network or device. Of those students, 59% said they simply switched to a personal device to get around the ban.

The report also found a significant gap in AI literacy education. Only 27% of teens said a teacher had ever talked with them about how to use AI safely, while 73% said they had not.

The report also said blanket bans and one-size-fits-all restrictions can prevent some students from benefiting from technology and urged schools to leave room for accommodations based on individual student needs.

For Bruno, the answer lies in teaching students how to navigate AI rather than assuming they can be shielded from it.

Keeping people at the center

Bruno’s approach is rooted in a broader question: What should AI actually be doing in a school?

Education, he said, is fundamentally human and he sees AI as a way to strengthen work educators are already doing.

“Education is such a human-focused thing, and we don’t want to be automating things that would still benefit from the human being the primary deliverer of or facilitator of that service,” he said. “ So by no means am I thinking we’re going to automate or speed up things. It’s more of how can we use AI to do what we’ve always done better for more people.”

That distinction becomes important when considering AI tools that can grade papers or provide feedback on student writing.

Those tools can help a teacher who is overwhelmed by an ever growing workload and class sizes. But Bruno said schools should be careful not to confuse efficiency with educational effectiveness.

“The expertise of that human and the motivation that that human can provide to improve their writing, or to improve their work over time” remain essential, he said.

An AI system may be able to identify weaknesses in a student’s writing, but a teacher can understand the student behind the writing and provide encouragement, context and motivation that a machine cannot replicate in the same way.

That human relationship is something Bruno said should remain central even as schools adopt increasingly sophisticated technology.

A critical year for AI literacy

The Common Sense study suggests schools have little time to waste in developing AI literacy.

Only 30% of teens in the survey said they had discussed AI safety with a teacher, and just 27% said they had discussed AI literacy. Forty-four percent said they had talked with a teacher about rules governing when they should and should not use AI.

The report characterized the current school year as an important opportunity for teachers to begin those conversations.

Students themselves also identified skills they believe will remain important in the future. Among AI-using teens, 55% identified working well with others as an important future skill, 50% cited fact-checking and critical thinking, and 48% cited reading and understanding complex information.

Those are the kinds of skills educators are trying to protect as AI becomes more capable.

For Oakland Schools, the goal is not simply to keep pace with a rapidly changing technology. It is to help districts make thoughtful decisions about where AI belongs — and where it does not.

As a new department, Bruno said, his team is building on work that was already underway at Oakland Schools before he arrived.

“There was great AI work happening before I came on board,” he said. “Oakland Schools were leading lots of great learning, and so now we’re just kind of accelerating that and trying to be a leader in the state.”

He believes the agency is moving in that direction.

The challenge now is to make sure the technology advances without leaving the people at the heart of education behind.

articles.content:
OCEANS
Can Cape Cod scientists save the world's coral reefs? They have a few ideas.
Heather McCarron
Cape Cod Times
Aug. 30, 2026, 6:03 a.m. ET
For people who have never slipped on a snorkeling mask and peered down at a coral reef, it can be easy to view reef loss as a faraway problem confined to tropical waters and coastlines far from Cape Cod.
But Amy Apprill, a Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution scientist who will lead a newly launched coral reef center in Woods Hole, says the stakes are far broader.

articles.article_title: Tech giants warn of AI-powered attacks: the cybersecurity status quo will not be enough | CTech
articles.heading: Tech giants warn of AI-powered attacks: the cybersecurity status quo will not be enough
articles.summary: 150 leading technology and cybersecurity companies are warning that the window to protect critical infrastructure from AI-powered cyberattacks is closing. In a joint open letter, they urge governments and organizations to prioritize cybersecurity, boost investment and provide advanced defenses to essential services.
articles.content:
Tech giants warn of AI-powered attacks: the cybersecurity status quo will not be enough
150 leading technology and cybersecurity companies are warning that the window to protect critical infrastructure from AI-powered cyberattacks is closing. In a joint open letter, they urge governments and organizations to prioritize cybersecurity, boost investment and provide advanced defenses to essential services.
Over 150 leading technology and cybersecurity companies are warning in a joint open letter that the window of opportunity to harden critical infrastructure against AI-powered cyberattacks is limited. The letter calls on governments and organizations to make cybersecurity a top priority, invest resources, and make advanced defensive tools available to essential services such as hospitals and water facilities. The technology giants stress that the offensive capabilities of AI models are advancing rapidly, making global cooperation and the adoption of active, AI-powered defense strategies essential.
“The world has a limited window of opportunity to strengthen its cyber defenses against powerful models capable of carrying out devastating attacks on critical infrastructure,” the companies warned in a letter published over the weekend. The letter bears the signatures of an extraordinary cross-section of the global technology ecosystem. Alongside major technology and AI companies, it has also been signed by major technology firms, including Adobe, Oracle, IBM and Cisco; chipmakers, including AMD, Micron and Arm; cybersecurity companies, including Check Point and Palo Alto Networks; banks and financial institutions, including Visa, Mastercard and Citi; telecommunications companies, including Deutsche Telekom and AT&T; and consulting firms, including BCG and KPMG.
“In the coming months, AI-powered cyberattacks will become far more common and sophisticated as models around the world gain more powerful capabilities,” the letter states. It is signed, among others, by Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Amazon. “The companies and public services our communities depend on - from hospitals and water treatment facilities to the infrastructure that powers the internet - are at risk. But if we act decisively, we can use this window of opportunity to make our digital world far more secure.”
Recent weeks have underscored the threat posed by advanced AI models to cybersecurity defenses, following a series of incidents in which advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta managed to break out of their closed testing environments and attack targets on the open internet, in some cases with alarming success. Earlier this year, Anthropic disclosed that it had developed an AI model with such advanced capabilities for identifying security vulnerabilities that it was forced to restrict access to selected organizations.
In the letter, the companies warn that in light of the new reality, the security status quo will not be enough. They said that legacy bugs, broad access permissions, misconfigurations, insecure software, weak authentication mechanisms and outdated technologies have left systems exposed. Security teams, particularly those protecting critical infrastructure, have suffered from a historic lack of resources and urgently need tools and resources. Defenders must be empowered with AI-powered cybersecurity capabilities, and a collective response must be mobilized. A global response is needed, with new partnerships to find solutions to evolving cyber threats.
Among other measures, the letter urges organizations to make cybersecurity defenses a top priority, and cybersecurity companies to make AI-powered tools available for protecting critical infrastructure. The signatories are calling on governments to coordinate cybersecurity defenses at the local, national and international levels by strengthening cooperation with industry and increasing investment in the field. “Give hospitals, water companies and local governments AI-powered defensive capabilities,” the letter states. Companies developing advanced AI models are urged to ensure responsible access to their models and build transparency and security tools.
We can make the digital infrastructure we all depend on more secure, the letter states. “We call on industry leaders and governments to bring the full weight of their technology, resources and expertise to this effort. Together, we can turn today’s advances in AI into sustained security improvements that benefit us all.”

articles.title: Wolverhampton and Walsall trusts to use speech-to-text technology
articles.description: Wolverhampton and Walsall trusts to use speech-to-text technology BBC
articles.description_html: Wolverhampton and Walsall trusts to use speech-to-text technology  BBC
articles.article_title: Wolverhampton and Walsall trusts to use speech-to-text technology
articles.heading: Two NHS trusts to use speech-to-notes technology
articles.summary: The technology was trialled in an eight-month pilot at the Walsall Trust, which was successful.
articles.content:
Two NHS trusts to use speech-to-notes technology
Technology that listens to patient consultations and generates notes will be rolled out at two NHS trusts, after a successful pilot scheme.
The project at Walsall Healthcare "on average reduced clinicians' documentation time to less than four minutes per patient", The Royal Wolverhampton said.
Equipment listened "securely" and automatically generated "structured clinical notes, which are reviewed, edited where necessary and approved before being added to the patient's record", it explained.
The Royal Wolverhampton, which has a strategic partnership with Walsall Healthcare, said the technology would "initially be introduced in Emergency Departments and outpatient specialties across both Trusts, and across all areas by 2028".
According to The Royal Wolverhampton, new digital ambient voice technology [AVT] "helps clinicians better focus on their consultations".
It added that the decision to introduce it followed a eight-month pilot at the Walsall Trust, which proved to be a success.
'Bring benefits'
The technology was tested by clinicians in the emergency department, medical same-day emergency care, dermatology, ENT [ear, nose and throat] and audiology, as well as obstetrics and gynaecology.
Group deputy chief executive and chief strategy officer at both trusts, Simon Evans, said they were "committed to adopting innovative digital solutions across all our care services to bring benefits".
Implementing the technology would "support our clinicians to deliver patient care by reducing the administrative burden, giving them back more time during a consultation", he added.
Walsall Healthcare lead for quality improvement and AVT, Dr Jamil Aslam, said its initial pilot had released "tens of thousands of hours back to frontline teams across multiple specialties, including the emergency department".
Following the pilot, Heidi Health was chosen as the trusts' preferred supplier.
Its Europe director, Raghav Sharma, said: "This partnership marks a step forward for the Trusts, giving their clinicians the time and capacity to focus on patient care, rather than paperwork.
"We're committed to easing the administration pressure on NHS staff across the Midlands region", he added.
